ca0-san-ysidro-port-of-entry.q: Why is the San Ysidro Port of Entry so famous?
alts: Why do people say this border is such a big deal?
ca0-san-ysidro-port-of-entry.a: Federal officials call it the busiest land port in the Western Hemisphere. Interstate 5 begins right here at the Mexican border.
ca0-san-ysidro-port-of-entry.quote: Interstate 5 begins at the Mexican border, at the San Ysidro Port of Entry, which federal officials call the busiest land port in the Western Hemisphere.

ca0-san-ysidro-port-of-entry.q: How old is the San Ysidro Port of Entry?
alts: Has there been a border here for a long time?
ca0-san-ysidro-port-of-entry.a: There has been a border inspection station in San Ysidro since the early 1900s. The main port was built in 1973 and a big rebuild was finished in 2019.
ca0-san-ysidro-port-of-entry.quote: There has been a border inspection station in San Ysidro since the early 1900s

ca0-san-ysidro-port-of-entry.q: Is any of the old San Ysidro Port of Entry still standing?
alts: Is any of it still the old part?
Is there an old building here, like really old?
ca0-san-ysidro-port-of-entry.a: Yes. A Mission Revival customs house from the early 1930s still stands, and it holds offices today.
ca0-san-ysidro-port-of-entry.quote: a Mission Revival customs house from the early 1930s still stands and holds offices

ca0-san-ysidro-port-of-entry.q: How big is the San Ysidro Port of Entry?
alts: How many lanes does it have?
ca0-san-ysidro-port-of-entry.a: Cars line up across 34 lanes to enter the United States here.
ca0-san-ysidro-port-of-entry.quote: with cars lining up across 34 lanes

ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.a: This is the homeland of the Kumeyaay Nation. Kumeyaay people live on both sides of the border today, with 13 bands in San Diego County and more communities in Baja California.
ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.quote: Kumeyaay people live on both sides today, with 13 bands in San Diego County and more communities in Baja California.

ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.q: How big is the Kumeyaay homeland?
alts: How far does their land go?
ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.a: Kumeyaay country runs from the Pacific to the Colorado River. Along the coast it stretches from about Oceanside to south of Ensenada.
ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.quote: Kumeyaay country runs from the Pacific to the Colorado River, and along the coast from about Oceanside to south of Ensenada

ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.q: How long have the Kumeyaay lived around San Diego?
alts: How long have they been here?
How many years ago did they start living here?
ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.a: Kumeyaay tradition holds that the people have lived around San Diego since 10,000 BC.
ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.quote: Kumeyaay tradition holds that the people have lived around San Diego since 10,000 BC.

ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.q: Why did the Spanish call them Diegueños?
alts: Why did they get another name, mom?
ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.a: The Spanish named them Diegueños after Mission San Diego. In Mexico, the Kumeyaay are known as Kumiai.
ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.quote: The Spanish called them Diegueños, after Mission San Diego, and in Mexico they are known as Kumiai.

ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.q: How does the border affect the Kumeyaay?
alts: What does the border do to them?
Did a wall cut through their land?
ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.a: Since 1848 the international border has run right through Kumeyaay country. Families and ceremonies still cross the line, and about 1,900 Kumiai came to hold special visas to attend events on the US side.
ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.quote: Families and ceremonies still cross the line, and about 1,900 Kumiai came to hold special visas to attend events on the US side.

ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.q: What happened here with the border wall in 2020?
alts: Did anyone fight the wall, dad?
ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.a: In 2020, as border wall construction sped up, Kumeyaay women led protests. The La Posta Band sued to stop building through a sacred burial ground.
ca1-kumeyaay-homeland.quote: In 2020, as border wall construction sped up, Kumeyaay women led protests, and the La Posta Band sued to stop building through a sacred burial ground.

ca3-tijuana-river.q: Where does the Tijuana River start and where does it end?
alts: Where does it start and end?
Where does the river come from, and where does it go?
ca3-tijuana-river.a: It rises in the mountains of Baja California, runs through Tijuana in a concrete channel, then crosses into the United States for its last few miles to the sea.
ca3-tijuana-river.quote: The Tijuana River rises in the mountains of Baja California, runs through Tijuana in a concrete channel, and crosses into the United States near here

ca3-tijuana-river.q: What was the Little Landers colony near the Tijuana River?
alts: Who used to farm here a long time ago?
Was there a town here once?
ca3-tijuana-river.a: William Smythe started it in 1908. Each member farmed about 2 acres and all the buying and selling was shared. It lasted until a great flood wiped out the farms in 1916.
ca3-tijuana-river.quote: In 1908, William Smythe started the Little Landers colony nearby, where each member farmed about 2 acres and all the buying and selling was shared.

ca3-tijuana-river.q: What is there to do in the Tijuana River Valley today?
alts: Can we walk or hike there?
ca3-tijuana-river.a: A regional park of more than 1,800 acres fills much of the valley, with trails for walking and horseback riding. Surfers have also chased big winter waves off the river mouth since at least 1937.
ca3-tijuana-river.quote: Today a regional park of more than 1,800 acres fills much of the valley, with trails for walking and horseback riding

alts: Why were the beaches closed because of it?
ca3-tijuana-river.a: Yes. The river carries Tijuana's sewage overflows, and in 2013 beaches near its mouth were closed for 204 days. In 2020, a trade agreement set aside $300 million to fight the pollution.
ca3-tijuana-river.quote: The river also carries Tijuana's sewage overflows, and in 2013 beaches near its mouth were closed for 204 days.

alts: What is that giant silver thing?
Why is there a huge airplane wing standing up?
ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.a: It's a 93-foot stainless steel test wing for a World War II bomber, standing on end. Locals sometimes call it the Silver Wing.
ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.quote: a 93-foot stainless steel test wing for a World War II bomber stands on end. Locals sometimes call it the Silver Wing.

ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.q: Who was John J. Montgomery and why does the Silver Wing honor him?
alts: Who was the guy the wing is for?
ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.a: In the spring of 1884 he made glider flights of up to 600 feet from the rim of Otay Mesa. Some historians count them as the first controlled flights of a heavier-than-air craft in America.
ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.quote: in the spring of 1884 made glider flights of up to 600 feet from the rim of Otay Mesa.

ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.q: How did Montgomery design his glider wings?
alts: How did he make it work?
How did the old glider fly, kid question?
Where did he get his ideas?
ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.a: He shaped his first glider's wing on the curve of a seagull's. Then he studied turkey vultures and gave his next glider hinged wing flaps, an early form of today's ailerons.
ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.quote: Montgomery shaped his first glider's wing on the curve of a seagull's.

ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.q: When was the Montgomery memorial built?
alts: When did they put it up?
ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.a: The memorial was dedicated in 1950. It honors flights Montgomery made back in 1884.

ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.q: What happened to John Montgomery later in life?
alts: Did the glider guy get hurt, kid question?
ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.a: He later taught at Santa Clara College. He died in a glider crash in San Jose in 1911.
ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.quote: He later taught at Santa Clara College and died in a glider crash in San Jose in 1911.

ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.q: Is there a freeway named after Montgomery?
alts: Is the road named for him?
Did they name this highway after him?
ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.a: Yes. In 1949 the road from the border to downtown San Diego was named the John J. Montgomery Freeway. His family's Fruitland Ranch once stood where the freeway now runs.
ca4-montgomery-s-silver-wing.quote: in 1949 the road from the border to downtown San Diego was named the John J. Montgomery Freeway.

ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.q: Who was Charles Hatfield, the rainmaker?
alts: Was he a real rainmaker, like with magic?
ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.a: Charles Hatfield was a self-styled rainmaker who called himself a moisture accelerator. In 1915 San Diego's city council voted to pay him $10,000 to fill a reservoir.
ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.quote: In 1915, San Diego's city council voted to pay Charles Hatfield, a self-styled rainmaker, $10,000 to fill a reservoir.

ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.q: What happened in the rainmaker's flood?
alts: Did the rain really just keep coming?
ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.a: In January 1916 the rain came and kept coming. On January 27 the Lower Otay Dam burst and sent a wall of water 40 feet high down the Otay River valley.
ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.quote: On January 27 the Lower Otay Dam burst and sent a wall of water 40 feet high down the Otay River valley

ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.q: Did anyone die in the rainmaker's flood?
alts: Did people get hurt in it?
ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.a: Yes. The flood reportedly killed about 20 people, though accounts vary, among them 11 Japanese American farmers.
ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.quote: The flood reportedly killed about 20 people, though accounts vary, among them 11 Japanese American farmers.

ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.q: What else did the storms damage besides the Otay Dam?
alts: Did the storm wreck other stuff?
ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.a: The storms overflowed the Sweetwater Dam too, washed away bridges, stranded trains and cut phone lines.
ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.quote: The storms overflowed the Sweetwater Dam too, washed away bridges, stranded trains and cut phone lines.

ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.q: Did San Diego ever pay Hatfield?
alts: Did he get paid for it?
Did the rainmaker get his money?
ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.a: No. The council refused to pay unless he accepted the blame for damages. He sued, and in 1938 the courts ruled the rain an act of God, so he was cleared but never paid.
ca5-the-rainmaker-s-flood.quote: He sued, and in 1938 the courts ruled the rain an act of God, so he was cleared but never paid.

ca6-south-bay-salt-works.q: How old is the South Bay Salt Works?
alts: How long have they been making salt here, Dad?
ca6-south-bay-salt-works.a: People have harvested salt here since at least 1871. That makes it the second-longest-running business in San Diego, after the San Diego Union-Tribune newspaper.
ca6-south-bay-salt-works.quote: People have harvested salt here since at least 1871, which makes the South Bay Salt Works the second-longest-running business in San Diego

ca6-south-bay-salt-works.q: How big are the South Bay Salt Works ponds?
alts: Are those ponds really big, Dad?
How much salt do they make?
ca6-south-bay-salt-works.a: The ponds cover more than a thousand acres. They yield about 75,000 tons of salt a year.
ca6-south-bay-salt-works.quote: Its ponds cover more than a thousand acres and yield about 75,000 tons of salt a year.

ca6-south-bay-salt-works.q: What birds can you see at the South Bay Salt Works?
alts: Are there animals at that place?
Are there lots of birds there, Mom?
ca6-south-bay-salt-works.a: Ninety-four kinds of birds use the area, including endangered California least terns. The salty ponds breed brine shrimp and brine flies, which are a feast for birds.
ca6-south-bay-salt-works.quote: Ninety-four kinds of birds use the area, and a 2010 count found more than 20,000 birds, including endangered California least terns.

ca6-south-bay-salt-works.q: What happened to the South Bay Salt Works in 1916?
alts: What happened to it in the flood?
Did the salt ponds get wrecked, Dad?
ca6-south-bay-salt-works.a: The 1916 flood wiped out the ponds. Rebuilding took until the 1950s.
ca6-south-bay-salt-works.quote: The 1916 flood wiped out the ponds, and rebuilding took until the 1950s.

ca6-south-bay-salt-works.q: Why is the South Bay Salt Works special on the West Coast?
alts: Why can they make salt here, Mom?
ca6-south-bay-salt-works.a: On the West Coast, only San Francisco Bay and San Diego Bay have the natural conditions for making sea salt.
ca6-south-bay-salt-works.quote: On the West Coast, only San Francisco Bay and San Diego Bay have the natural conditions for making sea salt.

alts: What does the name of that town mean?
ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.a: Chula Vista is Spanish for beautiful view. The name was suggested by the designer of the Sweetwater Dam.
ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.quote: Chula Vista is Spanish for beautiful view, a name suggested by the designer of the Sweetwater Dam.

ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.q: Why was Chula Vista called the Lemon Capital?
alts: Why did they grow so many lemons here, Dad?
ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.a: Water from the Sweetwater Dam irrigated the farmland, and for a time Chula Vista was the largest lemon-growing center in the world. By 1911 about 4,000 acres were lemon groves.
ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.quote: for a time Chula Vista was the largest lemon-growing center in the world. By 1911 about 4,000 acres were lemon groves

ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.q: Who brought lemons to Chula Vista?
alts: Who planted the first lemons here?
ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.a: Lemons were introduced by a retired professor from the University of Wisconsin.
ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.quote: Lemons were introduced by a retired professor from the University of Wisconsin.

ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.q: What happened to the lemon groves in Chula Vista?
alts: Where did all the lemon trees go?
ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.a: In 1941 Rohr Aircraft moved to town, and with workers off at war or at the factory, the farmland was sold. The groves never came back.
ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.quote: in 1941, Rohr Aircraft moved to town, and its 11,000 workers built power units for B-24 Liberator bombers.

ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.q: What else did farmers grow in Chula Vista besides lemons?
ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.a: Japanese American farmers made celery a big crop too. In 1931 lemons brought in $1 million and celery $600,000.
ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.quote: Japanese American farmers made celery a big crop too, and in 1931 lemons brought in $1 million and celery $600,000.

ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.q: Does Chula Vista still celebrate its lemon history?
alts: Is there a lemon party there?
ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.a: Yes, the city's Lemon Festival still pays tribute to the old groves.
ca7-chula-vista-the-old-lemon-capital.quote: The city's Lemon Festival still pays tribute to them.

ca8-sweetwater-marsh.q: Why does Sweetwater Marsh matter so much?
alts: Why is it such a big deal?
Why do they protect this swampy place?
ca8-sweetwater-marsh.a: More than 90 percent of San Diego Bay's old wetlands have been filled, drained or diked, which is why this surviving piece matters. It's part of a national wildlife refuge.
ca8-sweetwater-marsh.quote: More than 90 percent of the bay's old wetlands have been filled, drained or diked, which is why this piece matters.

ca8-sweetwater-marsh.q: What kind of animals and plants live at Sweetwater Marsh?
alts: What animals can I see there, Mom?
ca8-sweetwater-marsh.a: The refuge breeds endangered light-footed Ridgway's rails, and over 200 kinds of birds have been recorded there. It's also the only place in the U.S. where yerba reuma grows wild.
ca8-sweetwater-marsh.quote: The refuge breeds endangered light-footed Ridgway's rails, and it is the only place in the United States where a plant called yerba reuma grows wild.

ca8-sweetwater-marsh.q: What happened at Gunpowder Point near Sweetwater Marsh?
alts: Why is it called Gunpowder, was there really gunpowder?
ca8-sweetwater-marsh.a: From 1916 to 1920, the Hercules Powder Company ran a 30-acre plant there, turning kelp into acetone and potash, a key ingredient in smokeless gunpowder during World War I.
ca8-sweetwater-marsh.quote: From 1916 to 1920, the Hercules Powder Company ran a 30-acre plant on this shore, turning kelp into acetone and potash

ca8-sweetwater-marsh.q: What can we do at Sweetwater Marsh?
alts: What is there to do at that place?
Can we see cool animals there?
ca8-sweetwater-marsh.a: You can walk trails 1.5 miles out to the bay, or visit the Living Coast Discovery Center, a zoo and aquarium with green sea turtles, sharks, rays and eagles.
ca8-sweetwater-marsh.quote: Trails lead 1.5 miles out to the bay

ca8-sweetwater-marsh.q: Who used the Sweetwater Marsh area before it became a refuge?
alts: Did anyone live there long ago?
Who was there first, like way back?
ca8-sweetwater-marsh.a: The Kumeyaay fished, hunted and gathered here. Later, from 1916 to 1920, a powder company ran a plant on the shore.
ca8-sweetwater-marsh.quote: The Kumeyaay fished, hunted and gathered here.

ca8-sweetwater-marsh.q: What is the Living Coast Discovery Center at Sweetwater Marsh?
alts: What's that zoo and aquarium thing there?
Is there a zoo with sharks there?
ca8-sweetwater-marsh.a: It's a zoo and aquarium inside the refuge. It opened in 1987 as the Chula Vista Nature Interpretive Center and has green sea turtles, sharks, rays and bald and golden eagles.
ca8-sweetwater-marsh.quote: a zoo and aquarium that opened in 1987 as the Chula Vista Nature Interpretive Center, with green sea turtles, sharks, rays and bald and golden eagles.

ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.q: Why is it called National City?
alts: Why did they name it that?
How did National City get its name, mom?
ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.a: It's named after a ranch. Spanish soldiers grazed horses on El Rancho del Rey, which became Rancho de la Nación after Mexico won independence, and the Kimball brothers kept the name National.
ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.quote: After Mexico won independence it became Rancho de la Nación, the Ranch of the Nation.

ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.q: How big was the ranch National City started on?
alts: Was that ranch really huge, dad?
ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.a: It was huge: 26,000 acres. Spanish soldiers grazed their horses there, on land called El Rancho del Rey, the Ranch of the King.
ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.quote: Spanish soldiers grazed their horses on 26,000 acres here called El Rancho del Rey, the Ranch of the King.

ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.a: Three Kimball brothers from San Francisco. In 1868 they bought the whole rancho and founded the town, keeping the name National.
ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.quote: In 1868 three Kimball brothers from San Francisco bought the whole rancho and kept the name National for the town they founded.

ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.q: What did the Kimball brothers build in National City?
alts: Did the brothers make anything cool?
What's in it from back then?
ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.a: They built the area's first roads and railroad, a post office and a wharf. Frank Kimball's house even had a bathtub and hot running water.
ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.quote: The brothers built the area's first roads and railroad, a post office and a wharf.

ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.q: What happened when the trains came to National City?
alts: Why were trains such a big deal there?
Did the trains do something big, mom?
ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.a: When transcontinental trains arrived in November 1885, one of the biggest land booms in California history began.
ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.quote: When transcontinental trains arrived in November 1885, one of the biggest land booms in California history began.

ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.q: Why was National Avenue called the Mile of Bars?
alts: What is the Mile of Bars?
Why was that street nicknamed that, dad?
ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.a: Sailors' bars there earned National Avenue the nickname Mile of Bars. The city later remade it as the Mile of Cars, one of the first auto malls in the world.
ca11-national-city-s-royal-ranch.quote: Later, sailors' bars earned National Avenue the nickname Mile of Bars, and the city remade it as the Mile of Cars

ca13-naval-base-san-diego.q: What is Naval Base San Diego?
alts: What is that base with all the ships?
ca13-naval-base-san-diego.a: It's the main home port of the US Pacific Fleet. More than 50 ships tie up at its 13 piers along the bay.
ca13-naval-base-san-diego.quote: belong to Naval Base San Diego, the main home port of the US Pacific Fleet. More than 50 ships tie up at its 13 piers

ca13-naval-base-san-diego.q: How many people work at Naval Base San Diego?
alts: Do a lot of people work on that base?
ca13-naval-base-san-diego.a: Over 24,000 military personnel and 10,000 civilians work on the base.
ca13-naval-base-san-diego.quote: over 24,000 military personnel and 10,000 civilians work on the base

ca13-naval-base-san-diego.q: How big is Naval Base San Diego compared to other bases?
alts: Is that the biggest Navy base ever?
ca13-naval-base-san-diego.a: It's the second-largest surface ship base in the world, after Naval Station Norfolk.
ca13-naval-base-san-diego.quote: It is the second-largest surface ship base in the world, after Naval Station Norfolk.

ca13-naval-base-san-diego.q: How did Naval Base San Diego get started?
alts: Who made that base and when?
ca13-naval-base-san-diego.a: A company building concrete ships for World War I used the shore in 1918. The Navy took over, and in February 1922 it opened as the Destroyer Base, San Diego.
ca13-naval-base-san-diego.quote: In 1918, a company building concrete ships for World War I used this shore.

ca13-naval-base-san-diego.q: What did Naval Base San Diego do in World War II?
alts: What did it do in the war?
Did that base fix ships in World War II?
What happened there in the war?
ca13-naval-base-san-diego.a: It was renamed the Repair Base. From 1943 to 1945, its crews repaired, overhauled or converted more than 5,000 ships.
ca13-naval-base-san-diego.quote: During World War II it was renamed the Repair Base, and from 1943 to 1945 its crews repaired, overhauled or converted more than 5,000 ships.

ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.q: When did the Coronado Bridge open?
alts: When did they build that big bridge, anyone know?
ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.a: The San Diego-Coronado Bridge opened in 1969. It's the long, curving bridge you can see arching over the bay.
ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.quote: The long, curving bridge over the bay is the San Diego-Coronado Bridge, opened in 1969.

ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.q: Why does the Coronado Bridge curve so much?
alts: Why does it curve like that?
Why isn't the bridge just straight?
ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.a: The Navy wanted 200 feet of clearance for its ships. The bridge curves 80 degrees to gain enough length to climb that high at a reasonable grade.
ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.quote: The Navy wanted 200 feet of clearance for its ships, so the bridge curves 80 degrees to gain enough length to climb that high at a reasonable grade.

ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.q: What is Chicano Park famous for?
alts: Why do people go to that park under the bridge?
ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.a: Chicano Park sits under the bridge ramps and has the largest collection of outdoor murals in the United States.
ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.quote: Under its ramps, beside this freeway, lies Chicano Park, home to the largest collection of outdoor murals in the United States.

ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.q: How did Chicano Park get started?
alts: Why did people fight for the park?
ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.a: The city promised a park but started preparing a parking lot instead. Neighbors and students occupied the land for twelve days, planting trees, flowers and cactus, until the city agreed to build the park.
ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.quote: Neighbors and students occupied the land for twelve days, planting trees, flowers and cactus, until the city agreed to build the park.

ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.q: What happened to the Barrio Logan neighborhood?
alts: What happened to the neighborhood there?
ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.a: The freeway split the mostly Mexican American neighborhood in 1963, and the bridge ramps divided it again in 1969. More than 5,000 homes and businesses were removed.
ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.quote: More than 5,000 homes and businesses were removed.

ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.q: Why are the pillars at Chicano Park painted?
alts: Why are the concrete pillars covered in paintings?
ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.a: Artist Salvador Torres proposed turning the gray concrete pillars into a giant canvas, and painting began in 1973.
ca14-coronado-bridge-and-chicano-park.quote: Artist Salvador Torres proposed turning the gray concrete pillars into a giant canvas, and painting began in 1973.

alts: How long has it been around?
Is El Indio really old, Dad?
ca18-el-indio.a: It began in 1940 as a family tortilla shop. Since 1947 it has served food from its spot on India Street.
ca18-el-indio.quote: El Indio began in 1940 as a family tortilla shop, and since 1947 it has served food from a spot on India Street

ca18-el-indio.a: Ralph Pesqueira Sr. is the founder. He adapted his Sonoran grandmother's recipe for flautas when aircraft factory workers asked him for a portable lunch.
ca18-el-indio.quote: workers from the aircraft factory across the street asked founder Ralph Pesqueira Sr. for a portable lunch.

ca18-el-indio.q: How did El Indio get its taquitos?
alts: How did it start making them?
Where did the taquito come from, Mom?
ca18-el-indio.a: During World War II, nearby aircraft factory workers wanted a portable lunch. Ralph Pesqueira Sr. adapted his Sonoran grandmother's flauta recipe for them.
ca18-el-indio.quote: He adapted his Sonoran grandmother's recipe for flautas, and he claimed credit for naming the little rolled tacos taquitos.

ca18-el-indio.q: Did El Indio really invent the taquito?
alts: Did they make the first taquito, Dad?
ca18-el-indio.a: Not for sure. Los Angeles has a rival claim: Cielito Lindo, opened on Olvera Street in 1934.
ca18-el-indio.quote: Los Angeles has a rival claim to the taquito's early days: Cielito Lindo, opened on Olvera Street in 1934.

ca18-el-indio.q: Is El Indio still run by the same family?
alts: Is the family still there, Mom?
ca18-el-indio.a: Yes, the Pesqueira family still runs El Indio. It started as a family tortilla shop in 1940.
ca18-el-indio.quote: The Pesqueira family still runs El Indio.

ca18-lindbergh-field.q: Why is it called Lindbergh Field?
alts: Who is Lindbergh, and why is the airport named after him?
ca18-lindbergh-field.a: It's named for Charles Lindbergh. His plane, the Spirit of St. Louis, was built near here in 1927, and San Diego was so proud that Lindbergh lent the airport his name.
ca18-lindbergh-field.quote: In 1927 the Ryan company built the Spirit of St. Louis near here for Charles Lindbergh's flight across the Atlantic.

alts: How old is the airport, anyone know?
ca18-lindbergh-field.a: San Diego voted bonds for an airport in 1928, and it was dedicated that August as Lindbergh Field. 140 Navy and 82 Army planes flew over for the celebration.
ca18-lindbergh-field.quote: It was dedicated that August as Lindbergh Field, while 140 Navy and 82 Army planes flew over.

ca18-lindbergh-field.q: Why does the San Diego skyline look so even?
alts: Why are all the downtown buildings the same height?
Why are there no really tall skyscrapers?
ca18-lindbergh-field.a: Because the airport is so close, federal rules since the 1970s have kept downtown buildings to 500 feet or less. That's why the skyline looks so even.
ca18-lindbergh-field.quote: Because the airport is so close, federal rules since the 1970s have kept downtown buildings to 500 feet or less, which is why the skyline looks so even.

ca18-lindbergh-field.q: What's Liberator Way named after at Lindbergh Field?
alts: Why is there a street called Liberator Way?
What did they build here in the war?
ca18-lindbergh-field.a: During World War II, Consolidated Aircraft built warplanes next door. The street is still named Liberator Way, after its B-24 Liberator.
ca18-lindbergh-field.quote: During World War II, Consolidated Aircraft built warplanes next door, and a street here is still named Liberator Way, after its B-24 Liberator.

ca18-lindbergh-field.q: Is Lindbergh Field still called that today?
ca18-lindbergh-field.a: Not officially. The name changed to San Diego International Airport in 2003, and it's still the airport where jets land today.
ca18-lindbergh-field.quote: The name changed to San Diego International Airport in 2003.

alts: What went on up on that hill, mom?
ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.a: Spain founded its first fort and mission in California there in 1769. It sat above Kosa'aay, a Kumeyaay village of 30 to 40 families.
ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.quote: Presidio Hill, where Spain founded its first fort and mission in California in 1769, above Kosa'aay, a Kumeyaay village of 30 to 40 families.

alts: Why's the village called a funny name?
ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.a: Kosa'aay means drying out place. It was the name of the Kumeyaay village below Presidio Hill.
ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.quote: the people of Kosa'aay, whose name means drying out place, gave them food and water.

ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.q: What can we see at Old Town San Diego State Historic Park?
alts: What's there to see in it?
Are there old houses to look at in that park?
ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.a: The preserved town has five original adobes, plus museums. Up on Presidio Hill there's the Spanish Revival Serra Museum, but nothing of the old fort survives above ground.
ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.quote: That town is preserved as Old Town San Diego State Historic Park, with five original adobes, and the park and its museums

ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.q: Why did people leave Old Town?
alts: Why did it stop being the main town?
Where did everybody go from there?
ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.a: Old Town was the heart of San Diego until the 1860s. Then Alonzo Horton's New Town by the harbor, today's downtown, drew people away.
ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.quote: Old Town was the heart of San Diego until the 1860s, when Alonzo Horton's New Town by the harbor, today's downtown, drew people away.

ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.q: Is Mission San Diego de Alcalá still around?
alts: Did the mission always stay on the hill?
ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.a: Yes. In 1774 the mission moved a few miles up the valley from Presidio Hill, and Mission San Diego de Alcalá still stands there today.
ca19-old-town-and-presidio-hill.quote: In 1774 the mission moved a few miles up the valley, where Mission San Diego de Alcalá still stands.

ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.q: Is Mission San Diego de Alcalá still used today?
alts: Do people still go to church there like for real?
ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.a: Yes, it's still a working parish.
ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.quote: Founded in 1769, it was the first of California's 21 missions and is still a working parish.

ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.q: Did the mission always stand where it is now?
alts: Was it always in that spot?
Did they move the mission or something?
Was it built somewhere else first?
ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.a: No. It began on a hill near the harbor and moved to its current site in 1774.
ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.quote: The mission began on a hill near the harbor and moved here in 1774.

ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.q: What happened at Mission San Diego de Alcalá in 1775?
alts: Did something bad happen at that mission?
ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.a: People from several Kumeyaay villages burned the mission in 1775. Father Luis Jayme was killed in the revolt, and thirteen alleged leaders were jailed afterward.
ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.quote: in 1775 people from several Kumeyaay villages burned the mission.

ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.q: Who is buried at Mission San Diego de Alcalá?
alts: Is there a grave at that mission?
ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.a: Father Luis Jayme, who was killed in the 1775 revolt, is buried by the altar.
ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.quote: Father Luis Jayme was killed in the 1775 revolt, and he is buried by the altar.

ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.q: Is the church at Mission San Diego de Alcalá the original building?
alts: Is the church there really old, or new?
ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.a: Not quite. The church you see today is a 1931 rebuild of the church that was dedicated in 1813.
ca20-mission-san-diego-de-alcal.quote: The church you see today is a 1931 rebuild of the church dedicated in 1813.

ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.q: Was Mission Bay always a park?
alts: Did people make this whole bay?
Is the bay real or built?
ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.a: No. It started as a shifting maze of lagoons and tidal marsh. From the late 1940s, dredges moved 25 million cubic yards of sand and silt to build the islands and coves of Mission Bay Park.
ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.quote: Starting in the late 1940s, dredges moved 25 million cubic yards of sand and silt to build the islands and coves of Mission Bay Park

ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.q: Why is it called Mission Bay?
alts: Where did that name come from?
ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.a: The name comes from an 1888 poem by Rose Hartwick Thorpe. Before that, the explorer Cabrillo named it False Bay in 1542.
ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.quote: The name Mission Bay comes from an 1888 poem by Rose Hartwick Thorpe.

ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.q: What did Mission Bay used to be called?
ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.a: The explorer Cabrillo named this water False Bay in 1542, when it was a shifting maze of lagoons and tidal marsh.
ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.quote: The explorer Cabrillo named this water False Bay in 1542, when it was a shifting maze of lagoons and tidal marsh.

ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.q: Did the San Diego River really change its path?
alts: Where did the river used to go?
ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.a: Yes. Before 1821 the river usually emptied into San Diego Bay, until a flood that fall swung it into False Bay in a single night, though no rain fell on the coast.
ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.quote: Before 1821 it usually emptied into San Diego Bay, until a flood that fall swung it into False Bay in a single night

ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.q: What happened at Mission Bay in 1974?
alts: What was the first race there?
ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.a: On September 25, 1974, Mission Bay hosted the first modern race to be called a triathlon, with 46 athletes.
ca21-mission-bay-and-san-diego-river.quote: On September 25, 1974, Mission Bay hosted the first modern race to be called a triathlon, with 46 athletes.

alts: How high is that hill, is it a big mountain?
ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.a: Mount Soledad is 823 feet high. On top there's a 29-foot cross and some TV towers.
ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.quote: The big hill west of the freeway is Mount Soledad, 823 feet high, with a 29-foot cross and TV towers on top.

ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.q: What is the big cross on Mount Soledad?
alts: What's that cross on top of it?
Why is there a giant cross on the hill?
ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.a: It's a 29-foot cross on the summit, dedicated in 1954. It was fought over in court for about 25 years as a religious symbol on public land, until a private memorial association bought the ground in 2015.
ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.quote: The cross on the summit, dedicated in 1954, was fought over in court for about 25 years as a religious symbol on public land

ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.q: Is there an earthquake fault under the I-5 here?
alts: Can the ground really shake here, like a big earthquake?
ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.a: Yes, the Rose Canyon Fault runs north from downtown San Diego beneath this freeway. Scientists estimate it produces a magnitude 6.9 quake about every 700 years on average.
ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.quote: scientists estimate it produces a magnitude 6.9 quake about every 700 years on average.

ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.q: Who was Rose Canyon named after?
alts: Who was Rose, the guy it's named for?
ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.a: Rose Canyon honors Louis Rose, a German Jewish immigrant who arrived in 1850 and was San Diego's first known Jewish resident. In 1853 he bought 650 acres there for a ranch and a tannery.
ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.quote: honors Louis Rose, a German Jewish immigrant who arrived in 1850 and was San Diego's first known Jewish resident.

ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.q: Who lived in Rose Canyon before the Spanish came?
alts: Did anyone live there before that?
Did Native Americans live in the canyon?
ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.a: The Kumeyaay village of Jamo stood on Rose Creek at the mouth of the canyon before the Spanish came.
ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.quote: Before the Spanish came, the Kumeyaay village of Jamo stood on Rose Creek at the mouth of the canyon.

ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.q: Did anyone famous live on Mount Soledad?
alts: Did a famous person live up there?
Did somebody famous live on that hill?
ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.a: Yes, Dr. Seuss spent his last years in a house on the mountain.
ca26-mount-soledad-and-rose-canyon.quote: Dr. Seuss spent his last years in a house on the mountain.

ca28-san-diego-california-temple.q: How old is the San Diego California Temple?
alts: Mom, when did that big white building get built?
ca28-san-diego-california-temple.a: It was dedicated in 1993. It was the church's third temple in California.
ca28-san-diego-california-temple.quote: Dedicated in 1993, it was the church's third temple in California.

ca28-san-diego-california-temple.q: How tall are the spires on the San Diego California Temple?
ca28-san-diego-california-temple.a: The spires rise about 200 feet. A gold-leaf statue of the angel Moroni stands on top of the eastern one.
ca28-san-diego-california-temple.quote: Its spires rise about 200 feet, and a gold-leaf statue of the angel Moroni stands on top of the eastern one.

ca28-san-diego-california-temple.q: Who designed the San Diego California Temple?
ca28-san-diego-california-temple.a: Architect William S. Lewis designed it with Dennis and Shelly Hyndman, a Roman Catholic couple who had never been inside a Latter-day Saint temple.
ca28-san-diego-california-temple.quote: Architect William S. Lewis designed it with Dennis and Shelly Hyndman, a Roman Catholic couple who had never been inside a Latter-day Saint temple

ca28-san-diego-california-temple.q: How many spires does the San Diego California Temple have?
alts: How many spires does it have?
Why does that building have so many pointy towers?
ca28-san-diego-california-temple.a: Ten in all, counting the four small spires at the base of each tower, plus the two tall ones.
ca28-san-diego-california-temple.quote: Counting four small spires at the base of each tower, there are ten spires in all.

ca28-san-diego-california-temple.q: What is the San Diego California Temple made of?
alts: Why is that building so white?
ca28-san-diego-california-temple.a: The white exterior is plaster mixed with marble chips. The designers avoided Southern California staples like stucco, tile and arches.
ca28-san-diego-california-temple.quote: The white exterior is plaster mixed with marble chips.

ca28-san-diego-california-temple.q: What happened at the San Diego California Temple in 1993?
alts: Did lots of people visit it?
ca28-san-diego-california-temple.a: About 720,000 people toured it during its open house, well over the 600,000 expected.
ca28-san-diego-california-temple.quote: About 720,000 people toured it during its open house in 1993, well over the 600,000 expected.

ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.q: What is special about the Torrey pines?
alts: Why are those trees such a big deal?
ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.a: Torrey pines are the rarest pine in North America. They grow wild only here and on a small strip just north in Del Mar.
ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.quote: Torrey pines grow, the rarest pine in North America. This kind grows wild only here and on a small strip just north in Del Mar.

ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.q: What does Peñasquitos Lagoon mean in Spanish?
alts: What does the name mean, Mom?
ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.a: Peñasquitos is Spanish for the little cliffs. The lagoon spreads about 500 acres of marsh beside the bluffs where the Torrey pines grow.
ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.quote: Los Peñasquitos Lagoon, Spanish for the little cliffs, spreads about 500 acres of marsh beside bluffs

ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.q: Why do the Torrey pines look so twisted?
alts: Why do they look like that?
Why are the trees all bent and funny?
ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.a: Sea winds twist the exposed trees into shapes like giant bonsai.
ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.quote: Sea winds twist the exposed trees into shapes like giant bonsai.

ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.q: How did Torrey Pines become a protected reserve?
ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.a: It began in 1899, when George Marston persuaded the city to set aside 364 acres. Later, newspaperwoman Ellen Browning Scripps bought more land and gave it to the city.
ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.quote: It began in 1899, when George Marston persuaded the city to set aside 364 acres, and newspaperwoman Ellen Browning Scripps later bought more land and gave it to the city.

ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.q: Can you see whales at Torrey Pines?
alts: Can we see whales from it?
ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.a: Yes, from the cliffs you can see gray and humpback whales during their migrations.
ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.quote: From the cliffs, gray and humpback whales can be seen during their migrations.

ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.q: How big is Torrey Pines State Natural Reserve?
ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.a: The reserve covers 2,000 acres of cliffs and trails, and a mature tree's roots can spread 246 feet.
ca33-torrey-pines-and-pe-asquitos-lagoon.quote: Torrey Pines State Natural Reserve, 2,000 acres of cliffs and trails.

ca36-del-mar-racetrack.q: Who started the Del Mar racetrack?
ca36-del-mar-racetrack.a: Singer Bing Crosby and businessman William Quigley founded the track. Crosby even stood at the main gate on opening day to welcome the crowd.
ca36-del-mar-racetrack.quote: Singer Bing Crosby and businessman William Quigley founded the track, and on opening day, July 3, 1937, Crosby himself stood at the main gate welcoming 15,000 fans.

ca36-del-mar-racetrack.q: When did the Del Mar racetrack open?
alts: How long has this place been around?
ca36-del-mar-racetrack.a: It opened on July 3, 1937. About 15,000 fans came that first day, and Bing Crosby greeted them at the main gate.
ca36-del-mar-racetrack.quote: on opening day, July 3, 1937, Crosby himself stood at the main gate welcoming 15,000 fans.

ca36-del-mar-racetrack.q: What is the Del Mar racetrack famous for?
alts: What happened there that was famous?
Did anything cool happen at the horse place?
ca36-del-mar-racetrack.a: It hosted the 1938 match race between Seabiscuit and Ligaroti. It was the first thoroughbred race NBC radio broadcast nationwide, and Seabiscuit won by a nose.
ca36-del-mar-racetrack.quote: the track held a $25,000 winner-take-all match race between Seabiscuit and Ligaroti, the first thoroughbred race NBC radio broadcast nationwide, and Seabiscuit won by a nose.

ca36-del-mar-racetrack.q: Are there still horse races at the Del Mar racetrack?
alts: Can we watch horses run there?
ca36-del-mar-racetrack.a: Yes. Live racing runs from July into early September, with a second meet in November. The grounds also host the San Diego County Fair.
ca36-del-mar-racetrack.quote: Live racing runs from July into early September, with a second meet in November.

ca36-del-mar-racetrack.q: How big is the Del Mar racetrack?
ca36-del-mar-racetrack.a: The grounds cover 370 acres, and they also hold the San Diego County Fair.
ca36-del-mar-racetrack.quote: The 370-acre grounds are also home to the San Diego County Fair.

ca36-del-mar-racetrack.q: What was here before this part of the freeway?
alts: Was there something else here, Dad?
ca36-del-mar-racetrack.a: A Navy airfield was built here in the 1920s, and during World War II Navy blimps flew patrols from it. The state closed the airport in 1959 and used its land for Interstate 5.
ca36-del-mar-racetrack.quote: The state closed the airport in 1959, and its land went into building Interstate 5.

ca39-san-elijo-lagoon.q: How big is San Elijo Lagoon?
alts: Is that lagoon really huge, like a giant lake?
ca39-san-elijo-lagoon.a: San Elijo Lagoon is a 915-acre reserve, which is where Escondido Creek meets the sea.
ca39-san-elijo-lagoon.quote: The freeway crosses San Elijo Lagoon, a 915-acre reserve where Escondido Creek meets the sea.

ca39-san-elijo-lagoon.q: Who lived at San Elijo Lagoon long ago?
alts: Did Native people live there way back?
ca39-san-elijo-lagoon.a: It is Kumeyaay land, and people gathered food along this shore for at least 8,500 years. Their shell heaps hold scallops, clams, shark and abalone.
ca39-san-elijo-lagoon.quote: People gathered food along this shore for at least 8,500 years, and their shell heaps hold scallops, clams, shark and abalone.

ca39-san-elijo-lagoon.q: What lives at San Elijo Lagoon?
alts: What animals and plants are in it?
Are there lots of birds there?
What can you see there, nature-wise?
ca39-san-elijo-lagoon.a: The reserve counts about 300 kinds of birds and more than 300 kinds of plants.
ca39-san-elijo-lagoon.quote: Today the reserve counts about 300 kinds of birds and more than 300 kinds of plants.

ca41-encinitas-the-little-oaks.q: Who lived in Encinitas before it was a city?
alts: Were there people here before the oaks got a name?
ca41-encinitas-the-little-oaks.a: People from the Kumeyaay village of Jeyal, near San Elijo Lagoon. They met the Portolá expedition in 1769, which then named this valley Los Encinos.
ca41-encinitas-the-little-oaks.quote: In 1769 the Portolá expedition met people from the Kumeyaay village of Jeyal near San Elijo Lagoon and named this valley Los Encinos, for its oak forest.

ca41-encinitas-the-little-oaks.q: When did Encinitas become a city?
alts: How long has this been a city, mom?
ca41-encinitas-the-little-oaks.a: Today's city formed in 1986 from five communities, including Cardiff-by-the-Sea, Leucadia and Olivenhain. A Mexican land grant, Rancho Las Encinitas, came way earlier, in 1842.
ca41-encinitas-the-little-oaks.quote: A Mexican land grant called Rancho Las Encinitas followed in 1842, and today's city formed in 1986 from five communities, including Cardiff-by-the-Sea, Leucadia and Olivenhain.

alts: Is there anything cool here for surfers?
ca41-encinitas-the-little-oaks.a: Its surf break, Swami's, named for Paramahansa Yogananda, whose temple has been a landmark since the 1930s. The break even gets a mention in the Beach Boys song Surfin' U.S.A.
ca41-encinitas-the-little-oaks.quote: Its famous surf break, Swami's, is named for Paramahansa Yogananda, whose Self-Realization Fellowship temple has been a local landmark since the 1930s

ca41-encinitas-the-little-oaks.q: What's the Cardiff Kook in Encinitas?
alts: What is that statue, the surfer one?
Is there a funny statue here?
ca41-encinitas-the-little-oaks.a: A 16-foot bronze surfer statue in Cardiff. Local surfers decided it had terrible form, so they named it the Cardiff Kook, surfer slang for a wannabe. Pranksters keep dressing it up.
ca41-encinitas-the-little-oaks.quote: In Cardiff, local surfers decided that a 16-foot bronze surfer statue called Magic Carpet Ride had terrible form, so they named it the Cardiff Kook, surfer slang for a wannabe.

ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.q: How did the Ecke family start growing poinsettias?
alts: How did they start growing it?
Who started the poinsettia thing, mom?
ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.a: Albert Ecke, a German immigrant, began growing poinsettias in Los Angeles in 1909 and sold them from street stands. The family moved the business to Encinitas in 1923.
ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.quote: Albert Ecke, a German immigrant, began growing poinsettias in Los Angeles in 1909 and sold them from street stands.

ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.q: What made the Ecke poinsettias so bushy and full?
alts: How did they make it so bushy?
How come the flowers looked so big, dad?
ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.a: Grafting two varieties together gave fuller, bushier plants. Albert's son Paul worked out the grafting technique.
ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.quote: By grafting two varieties together they grew fuller, bushier plants

ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.q: How did poinsettias become a Christmas flower?
alts: How did it get tied to Christmas?
Why do we see poinsettias at Christmas, mom?
Who made it a Christmas thing?
ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.a: Paul Ecke Jr. sent poinsettias to TV stations to display from Thanksgiving to Christmas. He also promoted them on The Tonight Show and Bob Hope's Christmas specials.
ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.quote: his grandson Paul Jr. tied the plant to Christmas by sending free poinsettias to TV stations to display from Thanksgiving to Christmas

ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.q: How big was the Ecke poinsettia business?
alts: How much of the market did it have?
Was it a really big deal, dad?
How many poinsettias did they sell?
ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.a: Until the 1990s the Eckes had a virtual monopoly on the Christmas flower. As late as 2008 the family business still served about half the world market and 70 percent of the American one.
ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.quote: As late as 2008, the family business still served about half the world market and 70 percent of the American one.

ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.q: Where do poinsettias grow in the wild?
alts: Where do poinsettias come from, mom?
What did the Aztecs call it?
ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.a: Wild poinsettias grow from Mexico to Guatemala. The Aztecs called the plant cuetlaxochitl.
ca43-ecke-poinsettia-ranch.quote: Wild poinsettias grow from Mexico to Guatemala, and the Aztecs called the plant cuetlaxochitl.

ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.a: Batiquitos Lagoon covers 610 acres of tidal wetland, right where San Marcos Creek meets the sea.
ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.quote: Batiquitos Lagoon, 610 acres of tidal wetland where San Marcos Creek meets the sea.

ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.q: Why is it called Batiquitos Lagoon?
ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.a: The name comes from batequi, a northwestern Mexican word for a watering hole dug in a streambed. It was borrowed from the Yaqui language.
ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.quote: Its name comes from batequi, a northwestern Mexican word for a watering hole dug in a streambed, borrowed from the Yaqui language.

ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.q: How long have people lived around Batiquitos Lagoon?
alts: How long have people lived there?
Did people live here a really long time ago?
ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.a: People have lived around this lagoon for more than 9,000 years.
ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.quote: People have lived around this lagoon for more than 9,000 years.

ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.q: What happened to Batiquitos Lagoon over the years?
alts: Why did the lagoon get sick?
ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.a: A century of roads and building blocked the tides, and the lagoon silted up with only five kinds of fish left. A restoration that began in 1997 reopened it to the sea.
ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.quote: After homesteaders arrived in the 1870s, a century of roads and building projects blocked the tides.

ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.q: Can we walk at Batiquitos Lagoon?
alts: Is there a trail we can do with the stroller?
ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.a: Yes, a 1.75-mile nature trail follows the north shore. It is friendly to strollers and wheelchairs.
ca44-batiquitos-lagoon.quote: A 1.75-mile nature trail follows the north shore, and it is friendly to strollers and wheelchairs.

alts: What is it with all those flowers on the hill?
Why is the whole hill covered in flowers?
ca47-the-flower-fields.a: They are 55 acres of Giant Tecolote ranunculus on a hillside. The flowers bloom for six to eight weeks, from early March into early May.
ca47-the-flower-fields.quote: These are The Flower Fields, 55 acres of Giant Tecolote ranunculus, which bloom for six to eight weeks from early March into early May.

ca47-the-flower-fields.q: Who owns The Flower Fields and who grows the flowers?
alts: Who plants all the flowers, mom?
ca47-the-flower-fields.a: The Ecke family of poinsettia fame owns the land, and Mellano and Company grows the flowers. The main crop is ranunculus bulbs.
ca47-the-flower-fields.quote: Today the Ecke family of poinsettia fame owns the land, Mellano and Company grows the flowers, and the main crop is ranunculus bulbs.

ca47-the-flower-fields.q: How did ranunculus start growing at The Flower Fields?
ca47-the-flower-fields.a: Horticulturist Luther Gage brought ranunculus to the area in the 1920s. Decades later, grower Edwin Frazee moved his ranunculus business to these coastal hillsides.
ca47-the-flower-fields.quote: Horticulturist Luther Gage brought ranunculus to the area in the 1920s, and decades later grower Edwin Frazee moved his ranunculus business to these coastal hillsides.

ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.q: Who runs the Carlsbad Strawberry Company?
alts: Who owns the strawberry farm, Mom?
ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.a: It's run by third-generation farmer Jimmy Ukegawa. It's a pick-your-own farm, so visitors can pick their own berries.
ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.quote: belong to the Carlsbad Strawberry Company, a pick-your-own farm run by third-generation farmer Jimmy Ukegawa.

ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.q: When is strawberry picking season at the Carlsbad Strawberry Company?
alts: When can we pick strawberries, Dad?
ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.a: Picking season usually runs from March through July. Seedlings go in each October, and the first berries come around the start of the year.
ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.quote: Seedlings go in each October, the first berries come around the start of the year, and picking season usually runs from March through July.

ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.q: How did the Carlsbad Strawberry Company get started with pick-your-own?
alts: How did it start letting people pick?
Why did the farm let people pick berries?
ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.a: In the late 1990s the family's farm was struggling with rising costs. In the early 2000s Jimmy began opening the fields for pick-your-own days.
ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.quote: In the late 1990s the Ukegawa family's farm was struggling with rising costs, and in the early 2000s Jimmy began opening the fields for pick-your-own days.

ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.q: What kind of strawberries grow at the Carlsbad Strawberry Company?
alts: What kind of berries are they?
What berries do they grow, Mom?
ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.a: The farm grows a single variety, the Albion strawberry. It's one of San Diego's most popular pick-your-own farms.
ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.quote: It grows a single variety, the Albion strawberry, and in fall its pumpkin patch can draw up to 1,500 people a night.

ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.q: Does the Carlsbad Strawberry Company have anything besides strawberries?
alts: Is there more than berries there?
ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.a: Yes, in fall it has a pumpkin patch that can draw up to 1,500 people a night.
ca48-carlsbad-strawberry-company.quote: in fall its pumpkin patch can draw up to 1,500 people a night.

ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.q: What does the Carlsbad desalination plant do?
alts: How do they make drinking water from the ocean?
ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.a: It draws in about 100 million gallons of seawater a day and pushes it through reverse osmosis filters, turning half into drinking water.
ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.quote: It draws in about 100 million gallons of seawater a day and pushes it through reverse osmosis filters, turning half into drinking water

ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.q: How much of San Diego's water comes from the desal plant?
alts: How much of our water comes from it?
Is that plant a big deal for drinking water?
ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.a: About 7 percent of what the San Diego region uses. It opened in 2015 as the largest desalination plant in the Western Hemisphere.
ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.quote: opened in 2015 as the largest in the Western Hemisphere

ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.q: How long did it take to build the Carlsbad desal plant?
alts: How long did it take to build it?
Was it hard to build, Mom?
ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.a: Nearly 14 years to permit, design and build. It cost about $1 billion with its pipelines and survived five lawsuits.
ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.quote: The desalination plant took nearly 14 years to permit, design and build, cost about $1 billion with its pipelines, and survived five lawsuits

ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.q: Who is the Carlsbad desalination plant named after?
ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.a: It's named for Bud Lewis, Carlsbad's mayor for almost 25 years.
ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.quote: It is named for Bud Lewis, Carlsbad's mayor for almost 25 years.

ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.q: What happened to the big smokestack at Agua Hedionda?
alts: Where did the giant chimney go?
Is the power plant still there?
ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.a: The Encina Power Station, with its 400-foot smokestack, shut down in 2018 and was torn down between 2020 and 2022.
ca49-agua-hedionda-and-the-desal-plant.quote: The power plant, with its 400-foot smokestack, shut down in 2018 and was torn down between 2020 and 2022.

alts: Why's this town named Carlsbad, anyway?
ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.a: It's named for a spa town in Bohemia. Tests on a well here found the water chemically similar to that of some of the world's most famous spas, so the town took the name of the Bohemian spa of Karlsbad.
ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.quote: so the town was named for the Bohemian spa of Karlsbad, now Karlovy Vary in the Czech Republic

ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.q: Who dug the first well in Carlsbad?
alts: Who found the water, a pirate?
ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.a: A former sailor named John Frazier dug a well here in the 1880s. He offered its water at the train stop, which became known as Frazier's Station.
ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.quote: In the 1880s a former sailor, John Frazier, dug a well here and offered its water at the train stop

ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.q: What happened to Carlsbad when land prices fell?
ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.a: Land prices fell across the county in 1887. Farms of citrus, avocados and olives kept the town going.
ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.quote: When land prices fell across the county in 1887, farms of citrus, avocados and olives kept the town going.

ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.q: Can you still see Carlsbad's first well?
alts: Can we see the old well?
Is the first well still there?
ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.a: You can still see the site of Frazier's first well at Alt Karlsbad, a copy of a German Hanseatic house on Carlsbad Boulevard.
ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.quote: The site of Frazier's first well can still be seen at Alt Karlsbad, a copy of a German Hanseatic house on Carlsbad Boulevard.

ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.q: When did Carlsbad become a city?
alts: How old is it as a city?
ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.a: Carlsbad became a city in 1952, to avoid being annexed by Oceanside.
ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.quote: Carlsbad became a city in 1952, to avoid being annexed by Oceanside.

ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.q: Is there a volcano near Carlsbad?
alts: Is there a real volcano nearby?
ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.a: Yes, inland there's a 513-foot extinct volcano called Mount Calavera. It stands in a nature preserve.
ca50-carlsbad-s-mineral-water.quote: Inland, a 513-foot extinct volcano called Mount Calavera stands in a nature preserve.

ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.q: How big is Buena Vista Lagoon?
ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.a: Buena Vista Lagoon covers 223 acres. It sits on the border between Carlsbad and Oceanside.
ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.quote: Buena Vista Lagoon, the 223-acre border between Carlsbad and Oceanside and California's first ecological reserve.

ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.q: What is Buena Vista Lagoon famous for?
alts: Why is that lagoon special, like, what's the big deal?
ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.a: It's California's first ecological reserve. It's also a freshwater lagoon, unlike its neighbors, because a weir holds back the sea.
ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.quote: A weir about 100 yards from the beach holds it back from the sea, so unlike its neighbors it is a freshwater lagoon.

ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.q: Did pink flamingos really show up at Buena Vista Lagoon?
alts: Were there really flamingos at that lagoon?
ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.a: Yes, in the 1970s a flock of pink flamingos turned up. Locals thought they escaped from the San Diego Zoo, but the zoo insisted it was missing none.
ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.quote: In the 1970s a flock of pink flamingos turned up on the lagoon.

ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.q: Besides birds, what animals live at Buena Vista Lagoon?
alts: Are there other animals there, not just birds?
ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.a: The lagoon is home to 18 kinds of mammals and 14 kinds of reptiles and amphibians, besides all the birds.
ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.quote: Besides birds, the lagoon is home to 18 kinds of mammals and 14 kinds of reptiles and amphibians.

ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.q: Is there a nature center at Buena Vista Lagoon?
alts: Can we visit a nature center at it?
Is there something to see at the lagoon besides water?
ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.a: Yes, the Buena Vista Audubon Society runs a nature center on the lagoon's shore.
ca51-buena-vista-lagoon.quote: The Buena Vista Audubon Society runs a nature center on its shore.

ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.q: How long is the Oceanside Pier?
alts: How big is that pier, like how many football fields?
ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.a: The Oceanside pier is 1,942 feet long. That makes it the second-longest wooden pier on the West Coast.
ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.quote: Oceanside's wooden pier, 1,942 feet long, is the second-longest wooden pier on the West Coast.

ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.q: How old is the Oceanside Pier?
alts: Has that pier been there forever?
ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.a: The first pier went up in 1888, the year the city incorporated. Today's pier is the sixth one, and it opened in 1987.
ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.quote: The first one went up in 1888, the year the city incorporated, and storms have wrecked it again and again.

ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.q: Why has the Oceanside Pier been rebuilt so many times?
alts: Why did it keep getting rebuilt?
Why does the pier keep breaking?
ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.a: Storms have wrecked the pier again and again. The one standing today is the sixth, and it opened in 1987.
ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.quote: storms have wrecked it again and again. Today's pier, the sixth, opened in 1987.

ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.q: What happened to the diner at the end of the Oceanside Pier?
alts: Where did the diner go? I'm hungry!
ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.a: A fire destroyed the old diner at the far end of the pier in April 2024. Rebuilding was expected to begin in 2027.
ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.quote: In April 2024 a fire destroyed the old diner at its far end, and rebuilding was expected to begin in 2027.

ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.q: Who lived in the Oceanside area before the town was founded?
alts: Were there people there before the town?
ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.a: The city stands on Payómkawichum land, where the village of Wiyóoya stood at the mouth of the San Luis Rey River. Andrew Jackson Myers settled the original townsite in 1882.
ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.quote: The city stands on Payómkawichum land, where the village of Wiyóoya stood at the mouth of the San Luis Rey River.

ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.q: What is Cafe 101 in Oceanside famous for?
alts: Is there an old diner we can see?
ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.a: Cafe 101 has been a fixture since 1928 and is often called the oldest cafe on the historic Highway 101 route. Greyhound buses once stopped out front.
ca54-oceanside-and-its-pier.quote: Cafe 101 has been a fixture since 1928, and it is often called the oldest cafe on the historic route.

ca53-mission-san-luis-rey.q: When was Mission San Luis Rey founded?
alts: How long ago did they start this place, like way back?
ca53-mission-san-luis-rey.a: Mission San Luis Rey was founded in 1798. It is California mission number 18 in founding order.
ca53-mission-san-luis-rey.quote: Founded in 1798, it grew to be the largest of California's missions and is nicknamed the King of the Missions.

ca53-mission-san-luis-rey.q: What is special about the church at Mission San Luis Rey?
alts: Is the church shaped like something cool?
ca53-mission-san-luis-rey.a: The church from 1815 is the only surviving mission church built in the shape of a cross.
ca53-mission-san-luis-rey.quote: The church from 1815 is the only surviving mission church built in the shape of a cross.

ca53-mission-san-luis-rey.q: Who was Pablo Tac from Mission San Luis Rey?
alts: Who was he, the guy born at the mission?
Who's Pablo Tac, did he do something cool?
ca53-mission-san-luis-rey.a: Pablo Tac was born at the mission around 1822. A priest took him to Rome as a boy, and he wrote down the Luiseño language and the story of his people.
ca53-mission-san-luis-rey.quote: Pablo Tac was born at the mission around 1822. A priest took him to Rome as a boy, and he wrote down the Luiseño language

ca53-mission-san-luis-rey.q: Whose homeland is Mission San Luis Rey in?
alts: Who lived here before the mission?
Who were the first people here?
ca53-mission-san-luis-rey.a: It lies in the homeland of the Payómkawichum, the people the Spanish named Luiseño. Six federally recognized Luiseño tribes have reservations in Southern California today.
ca53-mission-san-luis-rey.quote: It lies in the homeland of the Payómkawichum, the people the Spanish named Luiseño.

ca55-camp-pendleton.a: It covers more than 125,000 acres and has 17 miles of coastline.
ca55-camp-pendleton.quote: more than 125,000 acres with 17 miles of coastline

ca55-camp-pendleton.q: Who was Camp Pendleton named after?
ca55-camp-pendleton.a: It is named for Major General Joseph Pendleton, who long pushed for a West Coast Marine base.
ca55-camp-pendleton.quote: The base is named for Major General Joseph Pendleton, who long pushed for a West Coast Marine base.

ca55-camp-pendleton.q: What was Camp Pendleton before it was a Marine base?
alts: Was it always a base, Mom?
ca55-camp-pendleton.a: It was Rancho Santa Margarita y Las Flores until 1942, when the Marines turned it into a World War II training base. Before that it was a cattle ranch.
ca55-camp-pendleton.quote: It was Rancho Santa Margarita y Las Flores until 1942, when the Marines turned it into a training base for World War II.

ca55-camp-pendleton.q: What wildlife lives on Camp Pendleton?
alts: Are there any rare animals on it?
ca55-camp-pendleton.a: Its wild lands still shelter rare species, among them western snowy plovers and the Pacific pocket mouse.
ca55-camp-pendleton.quote: Its wild lands still shelter rare species, among them western snowy plovers and the Pacific pocket mouse.

ca55-camp-pendleton.q: What happened at Camp Pendleton in 1975?
alts: What did it do for refugees?
ca55-camp-pendleton.a: In 1975 it became the first US military base to take in Vietnamese evacuees, more than 50,000 of them.
ca55-camp-pendleton.quote: In 1975 it became the first US military base to take in Vietnamese evacuees, more than 50,000 of them.

ca57-santa-margarita-river.q: Why is it called the Santa Margarita River?
alts: Why did they name it that?
Why's the river got a girl's name?
ca57-santa-margarita-river.a: The Portolá expedition camped beside it on July 20, 1769, and named it for Saint Margaret of Antioch.
ca57-santa-margarita-river.quote: The Portolá expedition camped beside it on July 20, 1769, and named it for Saint Margaret of Antioch.

ca57-santa-margarita-river.q: How long is the Santa Margarita River?
alts: How far does this river go?
Where does the river start and end?
ca57-santa-margarita-river.a: It runs about 31 miles from near Temecula to the sea. Its lower 10 miles spread out into a wide floodplain across Camp Pendleton.
ca57-santa-margarita-river.quote: It runs about 31 miles from near Temecula to the sea, and its lower 10 miles spread into a wide floodplain across Camp Pendleton.

ca57-santa-margarita-river.q: Was there ever a plan to dam the Santa Margarita River?
alts: Did they ever try to dam it?
Why isn't there a dam on it?
Did people fight over the water?
ca57-santa-margarita-river.a: Yes. The Navy and the Fallbrook water district fought over its water for decades. In 2018 the district sold its riverside land, ending a dam plan more than 60 years old.
ca57-santa-margarita-river.quote: in 2018 the district sold its riverside land, ending a plan more than 60 years old to dam it.

ca57-santa-margarita-river.q: What animals live along the Santa Margarita River?
alts: What kind of animals does it have?
Are there any fish or birds in it?
ca57-santa-margarita-river.a: Endangered least Bell's vireos and southwestern willow flycatchers breed in its streamside habitat. In 2019, Pacific lampreys returned for the first time since 1940.
ca57-santa-margarita-river.quote: Endangered least Bell's vireos and southwestern willow flycatchers depend on its streamside habitat to breed.

ca57-santa-margarita-river.q: What did the railroad have to do with the Santa Margarita River?
alts: Was there a train here once?
Who built things along the river?
ca57-santa-margarita-river.a: In 1881 the California Southern Railroad followed the river up Temecula Canyon, crossing it on 241 bridges. Chinese Americans worked on the line.
ca57-santa-margarita-river.quote: In 1881 the California Southern Railroad followed the river up Temecula Canyon, crossing it on 241 bridges, and Chinese Americans worked on the line.

ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.q: Why is it called the Surf Line railroad?
alts: Why do they call it that?
How come it's named the Surf Line, is it by the ocean?
ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.a: It's named the Surf Line because in places the tracks run within 100 feet of the Pacific Ocean.
ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.quote: named because in places it runs within 100 feet of the Pacific

ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.q: When was the Surf Line railroad finished?
alts: How old is that train track, like super old?
ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.a: The Surf Line was finished from Oceanside to Santa Ana in 1888.
ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.quote: Finished from Oceanside to Santa Ana in 1888

ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.q: What happened to the first railroad route into San Diego?
alts: What happened to the first one, did it break?
Did the old train track get wrecked by water?
What went wrong with the first track?
ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.a: Floods wrecked the first route inland. In February 1884, more than 40 inches of rain fell in four weeks and washed out two-thirds of the canyon line.
ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.quote: In February 1884, more than 40 inches of rain fell in four weeks, washing out two-thirds of the canyon line

ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.q: What trains run on the Surf Line railroad today?
alts: Are there real trains on it now?
ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.a: Amtrak's Pacific Surfliner and the Coaster commuter trains share the tracks, and freight trains use them too, often at night.
ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.quote: Today Amtrak's Pacific Surfliner and the Coaster commuter trains share the tracks, and freight trains, often at night

ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.q: What is the Surf Line railroad famous for?
alts: Why is that train line important?
ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.a: Today it is the second-busiest passenger rail corridor in the United States. It also became the only line into San Diego from the north.
ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.quote: Today it is the second-busiest passenger rail corridor in the United States.

ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.q: What kind of freight does the Surf Line railroad carry?
alts: What do the freight trains haul on it?
What's on the cargo trains, anything cool?
ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.a: Freight trains, often running at night, haul loads that include military vehicles for Camp Pendleton.
ca59-the-surf-line-railroad.quote: freight trains, often at night, haul loads that include military vehicles for Camp Pendleton

ca62-las-flores-and-las-pulgas.q: Why is it called Las Pulgas?
alts: Why is that called the fleas?
Why do they call it fleas, Mom?
ca62-las-flores-and-las-pulgas.a: Las Pulgas means the fleas. A mission survey party camped in the canyon and got badly bitten, and the name stuck.
ca62-las-flores-and-las-pulgas.quote: Las Pulgas means the fleas, after a mission survey party that camped in the canyon and got badly bitten.

ca62-las-flores-and-las-pulgas.q: How old is the Las Flores Adobe?
alts: How long ago was it built?
ca62-las-flores-and-las-pulgas.a: The big U-shaped ranch house was built in 1867 and 1868 by Marco Forster. It's now a National Historic Landmark.
ca62-las-flores-and-las-pulgas.quote: a big U-shaped ranch house built in 1867 and 1868 by Marco Forster and now a National Historic Landmark

ca62-las-flores-and-las-pulgas.q: What happened at Las Flores in 1838?
alts: What happened there in the old days?
ca62-las-flores-and-las-pulgas.a: In April 1838, rival Californio forces fought here over who would govern Alta California.
ca62-las-flores-and-las-pulgas.quote: In April 1838, rival Californio forces fought here over who would govern Alta California.

ca62-las-flores-and-las-pulgas.q: Who built the original Las Flores station?
ca62-las-flores-and-las-pulgas.a: Luiseño and Acjachemen people, moved here by the mission, built the station's tile-roofed chapel and hostel around three sides of a square.
ca62-las-flores-and-las-pulgas.quote: Luiseño and Acjachemen people, moved here by the mission, built the station's tile-roofed chapel and hostel around three sides of a square

ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.q: What is the San Clemente Border Patrol checkpoint?
alts: Why is there a police stop on the freeway?
ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.a: It's a permanent Border Patrol checkpoint, one of 33 fixed checkpoints near the Mexican border. Agents here may briefly stop and question drivers.
ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.quote: stands a permanent Border Patrol checkpoint, one of 33 fixed checkpoints near the Mexican border.

ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.q: Why is there a checkpoint so far from the border?
alts: Why is it so far from Mexico?
Why are they checking us way up here?
ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.a: These checkpoints sit 25 to 75 miles from the border on major highways. They're a third layer of enforcement, after agents at the line and roving patrols.
ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.quote: The checkpoints stand 25 to 75 miles from the border on major highways, a third layer of enforcement after agents at the line and roving patrols.

ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.q: What famous court case started at the San Clemente checkpoint?
alts: Did something important happen at that checkpoint?
Did a court case start there, Mom?
ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.a: United States v. Martinez-Fuerte, decided in 1976. The Supreme Court upheld the power to briefly stop and question drivers here, and the case began with a stop at this checkpoint.
ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.quote: The Supreme Court upheld that power in 1976 in United States v. Martinez-Fuerte, a case that began with a stop at this checkpoint.

ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.q: Who was Martinez-Fuerte and what happened to him here?
alts: Who was the guy in the court case?
ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.a: Amado Martinez-Fuerte was stopped here and charged with illegally transporting two passengers who had come in through San Ysidro. His case went to the Supreme Court.
ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.quote: The 1976 case began when Amado Martinez-Fuerte was stopped here and charged with illegally transporting two passengers who had come in through San Ysidro.

ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.q: Do US citizens need papers at the San Clemente checkpoint?
alts: Do we need papers to go through it?
Do we have to show ID there?
ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.a: US citizens need no papers here. But drivers aren't allowed to go on until agents are satisfied.
ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.quote: US citizens need no papers here, but drivers are not allowed to go on until agents are satisfied.

ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.q: How did the Supreme Court rule on the checkpoint stops?
alts: Is it legal for them to stop us at that checkpoint?
Did the judges say the stops were okay?
ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.a: The court ruled 7 to 2 that such stops do not violate the Fourth Amendment. Critics still argue that the checkpoints are unconstitutional.
ca67-san-clemente-border-patrol-checkpoi.quote: The court ruled 7 to 2 that such stops do not violate the Fourth Amendment

ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.q: Why did the San Onofre nuclear plant shut down?
alts: Why'd they turn the power plant off, Dad?
ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.a: Its last two reactors were shut down in January 2012, after early wear turned up on more than 3,000 tubes in new steam generators. Southern California Edison retired the plant for good in 2013.
ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.quote: after early wear turned up on more than 3,000 tubes in new steam generators, and in 2013 Southern California Edison retired the plant for good

ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.q: What were the two giant domes at San Onofre?
alts: What are those big round things, Mom?
ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.a: They were the containment buildings around the plant's reactors. The plant was long known for its two giant round domes by the beach.
ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.quote: was long known for its two giant round domes, the containment buildings around its reactors

ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.q: Are the San Onofre domes still standing?
