alts: Can we still see the big domes?
ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.a: Crews are taking the plant apart, and removal of the domes was set to begin in 2027. So they may be partly or entirely gone.
ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.quote: Crews are taking it apart, and removal of the domes was set to begin in 2027, so they may be partly or entirely gone.

ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.q: How much power did San Onofre supply?
alts: How much electricity did it make?
Did it power a lot of houses?
How big a deal was it?
ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.a: Until 2012 the plant supplied about a fifth of the power for large parts of Southern California.
ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.quote: Until 2012 the plant supplied about a fifth of the power for large parts of Southern California.

ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.q: What happens to the used nuclear fuel at San Onofre?
alts: Where did the nuclear fuel go?
Is the fuel still there, Dad?
ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.a: It stays on site, sealed in 123 steel canisters inside concrete, until the federal government takes it away. Edison calls that duty decades overdue.
ca71-san-onofre-nuclear-plant.quote: The used nuclear fuel stays here, sealed in 123 steel canisters inside concrete, until the federal government takes it away

ca71-san-onofre-and-trestles.q: Why is San Onofre called San Onofre?
ca71-san-onofre-and-trestles.a: San Onofre is Spanish for Saint Onuphrius, a hermit from fourth-century Egypt.
ca71-san-onofre-and-trestles.quote: San Onofre, Spanish for Saint Onuphrius, a hermit from fourth-century Egypt, is a 3,000-acre state beach

ca71-san-onofre-and-trestles.q: Why are the surf breaks called Trestles?
alts: What's a trestle, is that a bridge?
ca71-san-onofre-and-trestles.a: They're named for a wooden railroad trestle that surfers walked under to reach the beach. A concrete bridge replaced the wooden one in 2012.
ca71-san-onofre-and-trestles.quote: named for a wooden railroad trestle that surfers walked under to reach the beach

ca71-san-onofre-and-trestles.a: Lower Trestles hosted the pro surfing world tour for many years, and Trestles is set to host the 2028 Olympic surfing contests.
ca71-san-onofre-and-trestles.quote: Lower Trestles hosted the pro surfing world tour for many years, and Trestles is set to host the 2028 Olympic surfing contests.

ca71-san-onofre-and-trestles.q: How big is San Onofre State Beach?
ca71-san-onofre-and-trestles.a: It's a 3,000-acre state beach with more than 2.5 million visitors a year, on Marine Corps land leased to California.
ca71-san-onofre-and-trestles.quote: is a 3,000-acre state beach on Marine Corps land leased to California, with more than 2.5 million visitors a year

ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.q: Why is it called Nixon's Western White House?
alts: Why is that called the Western White House?
Why did people call it the Western White House?
ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.a: The press nicknamed it the Western White House after President Richard Nixon bought the house in 1969. Its real name is La Casa Pacifica, the house of peace.
ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.quote: The press nicknamed it the Western White House.

ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.q: Who built Nixon's Western White House?
alts: Who made this big house, and when?
ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.a: It was built in 1926 for Hamilton Cotton, one of San Clemente's founding financiers. It's a Spanish-style mansion, and Nixon bought it in 1969.
ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.quote: The Spanish-style mansion was built in 1926 for Hamilton Cotton, one of San Clemente's founding financiers

ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.q: Who visited Nixon's Western White House?
alts: Did any famous people come to the house?
ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.a: Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev and the president of Mexico visited. Earlier, Hamilton Cotton entertained President Franklin Roosevelt there.
ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.quote: Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev and the president of Mexico visited

ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.q: What did Nixon change at the Western White House?
alts: What did he change about it?
Did Nixon build anything at the house?
ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.a: Some changes were made for the Secret Service, including a 1,500-foot wall around much of the nearly six-acre estate. Pat Nixon also brought a magnolia seedling from Andrew Jackson's tree at the White House.
ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.quote: Nixon's changes, some made for the Secret Service, included a 1,500-foot wall wrapped around much of the nearly six-acre estate

ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.q: What happened to Nixon's Western White House after he resigned?
alts: What happened to it after he quit?
Where did Nixon go after he resigned?
ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.a: After Nixon resigned, he retired here to write his memoirs. The Nixons sold the estate in 1980.
ca72-nixon-s-western-white-house.quote: after Nixon resigned he retired here to write his memoirs

alts: Why is it called Panhe, Mom?
ca72-panhe-and-los-cristianitos.a: Panhe means "the place at the water." It's the name of one of the largest Acjachemen villages, inland of the freeway in the San Mateo campground area of San Onofre State Beach.
ca72-panhe-and-los-cristianitos.quote: is Panhe, the place at the water. It was one of the largest Acjachemen villages

alts: Is that place really that old, Dad?
ca72-panhe-and-los-cristianitos.a: Panhe is more than 8,000 years old. When the Spanish arrived, perhaps 300 people lived there.
ca72-panhe-and-los-cristianitos.quote: more than 8,000 years old, with perhaps 300 people when the Spanish arrived

ca72-panhe-and-los-cristianitos.q: Why is Panhe still important today?
alts: Do people still go there, Dad?
ca72-panhe-and-los-cristianitos.a: It remains a sacred, ceremonial and burial site for the Acjachemen people. They hold a festival there each year to honor their ancestors.
ca72-panhe-and-los-cristianitos.quote: It remains a sacred, ceremonial and burial site for the Acjachemen people, who hold a festival there each year to honor their ancestors.

ca72-panhe-and-los-cristianitos.q: What happened at Los Cristianitos in 1769?
alts: What did the explorers do there, Mom?
ca72-panhe-and-los-cristianitos.a: The Portolá expedition camped near San Mateo Creek on July 22, 1769. Missionaries were allowed to baptize two dying girls, and a state plaque marks the first Christian baptism in Alta California.
ca72-panhe-and-los-cristianitos.quote: On July 22, 1769, the Portolá expedition camped near San Mateo Creek.

ca72-panhe-and-los-cristianitos.a: Padre Crespí called the place Los Cristianos, and the name later became Cristianitos, which means "the little Christians." It's now the name of the creek, the canyon and the Cristianitos Road exit.
ca72-panhe-and-los-cristianitos.quote: Crespí called the place Los Cristianos, and the name later became Cristianitos, the little Christians

ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.q: Who founded Spanish Village by the Sea?
ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.a: Ole Hanson, a former mayor of Seattle, laid out the town in 1925 on old rancho land by the ocean.
ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.quote: In 1925 Ole Hanson, a former mayor of Seattle, laid out a 2,000-acre town on old rancho land by the ocean

ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.q: What happened to Spanish Village by the Sea in the Great Depression?
alts: What happened to it back then?
Did the town get in trouble, like, a long time ago?
ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.a: Hanson lost his house and all his other holdings, and the town's population fell 70 percent, to about 250 people.
ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.quote: When the Great Depression hit, he lost the house and all his other holdings, and the town's population fell 70 percent, to about 250 people.

ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.q: How big was Spanish Village by the Sea supposed to be?
alts: How large is the town, like, really big?
ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.a: Hanson laid out a 2,000-acre town. He pictured it as a clean canvas five miles long and a mile and a half wide.
ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.quote: Hanson pictured his town as a clean canvas five miles long and a mile and a half wide.

ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.q: What is Casa Romantica in Spanish Village by the Sea?
alts: What's that mansion on the bluff?
Who lives in the big house on the cliff?
ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.a: It was Hanson's mansion on the bluff. Today it's a city-owned cultural center above the pier.
ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.quote: Casa Romantica is now a city-owned cultural center above the pier.

ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.q: What is special about Clarence Lobo Elementary School?
ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.a: Opened in 1994, it was the first school in California named for an Indigenous leader. Clarence Lobo was chief of the Acjachemen people from 1946 to 1985.
ca76-spanish-village-by-the-sea.quote: It was the first school in California named for an Indigenous leader.

ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.q: Why is it called Dana Point?
alts: Who is Dana, and why does the point have his name?
ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.a: It's named for Richard Henry Dana Jr., who sailed here in 1835 on the brig Pilgrim and wrote about it in Two Years Before the Mast.
ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.quote: Dana Point is named for Richard Henry Dana Jr., who sailed here in 1835 on the brig Pilgrim and wrote about it in Two Years Before the Mast.

ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.q: What were the hides at Dana Point?
alts: What was that hide thing about?
Why were they throwing cow skins off a cliff?
ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.a: Cowhides from Mission San Juan Capistrano were brought to the cliffs, and sailors flung them out to the beach below. Dana compared the job to flying a kite without a string.
ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.quote: Cowhides from Mission San Juan Capistrano were brought to the cliffs, and sailors flung them out to the beach below, a job Dana compared to flying a kite without a string.

ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.q: What did Richard Henry Dana think of Dana Point?
alts: What did he say about it?
Did the guy it's named after like it here?
ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.a: Dana called this stretch the only romantic spot on the coast.
ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.quote: Dana called this stretch the only romantic spot on the coast.

ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.q: What is Dana Point famous for?
ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.a: Hobie Alter opened what is called the world's first retail surf shop there in 1954. It also holds the trademarked title Dolphin and Whale Watching Capital of the World.
ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.quote: Hobie Alter opened what is called the world's first retail surf shop in Dana Point in 1954.

ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.q: What is the Festival of Whales in Dana Point?
alts: Is there a whale thing there?
Do they have a whale party?
ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.a: Dana Point has held a Festival of Whales since the early 1970s, over two weekends each March.
ca79-dana-point-and-the-hides.quote: The town has held a Festival of Whales since the early 1970s, over two weekends each March

ca82-mission-san-juan-capistrano.q: How old is Mission San Juan Capistrano?
alts: How long ago did they build this mission, like, a really long time?
ca82-mission-san-juan-capistrano.a: It was founded in 1776. It is California mission number 7 in founding order.
ca82-mission-san-juan-capistrano.quote: Founded in 1776, it is famous for its swallows and for the ruins of the Great Stone Church

ca82-mission-san-juan-capistrano.q: What is Mission San Juan Capistrano famous for?
alts: Why do people come to this place, is it the birds?
ca82-mission-san-juan-capistrano.a: It is famous for its swallows and for the ruins of the Great Stone Church, which fell in an earthquake in 1812.
ca82-mission-san-juan-capistrano.quote: it is famous for its swallows and for the ruins of the Great Stone Church, which fell in an earthquake in 1812

ca82-mission-san-juan-capistrano.q: What happened to the Great Stone Church at the mission?
alts: Why is the big church broken, did it fall down?
ca82-mission-san-juan-capistrano.a: It collapsed on December 8, 1812, during Mass, and about 40 people died. It needed the labor of the whole Native community to build.
ca82-mission-san-juan-capistrano.quote: It collapsed on December 8, 1812, during Mass, and about 40 people died.

ca82-mission-san-juan-capistrano.q: Whose land is Mission San Juan Capistrano on?
alts: Who were the first people at this place?
ca82-mission-san-juan-capistrano.a: It stands on Acjachemen homeland. Acjachemen families still live in this region and keep their language and traditions alive.
ca82-mission-san-juan-capistrano.quote: Acjachemen families still live in this region and keep their language and traditions alive.

ca83-putuidem-village.a: Putuidem was a mother village of the Acjachemen people, one that gave rise to other villages. It stood just off the freeway, about a mile north of the mission.
ca83-putuidem-village.quote: Putuidem, a mother village of the Acjachemen people that gave rise to other villages.

ca83-putuidem-village.q: How did the Acjachemen people get their name?
ca83-putuidem-village.a: A village story says the chief's daughter Coronne died suddenly and her body became a mound of earth. The grieving people slept in a pyramid shape called acjachema, which gave the Acjachemen their name.
ca83-putuidem-village.quote: the grieving people slept in a pyramid shape called acjachema, which gave the Acjachemen their name.

ca83-putuidem-village.q: What happened to Putuidem village when the mission was built?
ca83-putuidem-village.a: The mission was built right beside it in 1776, and the village was drained of people to serve the mission.
ca83-putuidem-village.quote: When the mission was built beside it in 1776, the village was drained of people to serve the mission.

ca83-putuidem-village.q: What is at the Putuidem village site today?
ca83-putuidem-village.a: Much of the site lies under the sports fields and performing arts center of JSerra Catholic High School. In late 2021 a park north of the school opened to commemorate the village.
ca83-putuidem-village.quote: Much of the site now lies under the sports fields and performing arts center of JSerra Catholic High School.

ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.q: Why is it called Trabuco Creek?
alts: Why is that creek named that?
Why's the creek called Trabuco, what's it mean?
ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.a: Trabuco is Spanish for blunderbuss, a kind of old shotgun. The story goes a soldier lost his blunderbuss here, and the creek was named for it.
ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.quote: Trabuco is Spanish for blunderbuss, a kind of old shotgun.

ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.q: What's the story of the lost gun at Trabuco Creek?
alts: What happened to the gun there?
Did someone really lose a gun by the creek?
ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.a: In July 1769 a soldier with the Portolá expedition, camped on a bluff above the creek, found his blunderbuss missing. It was never found, and the creek was named for it.
ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.quote: in July 1769 a soldier with the Portolá expedition, camped on a bluff above the creek, found his blunderbuss missing.

ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.q: How long is Trabuco Creek and where does it go?
alts: How big is the creek, where does it start?
ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.a: Arroyo Trabuco is a 22-mile creek. It runs out of the Santa Ana Mountains to meet San Juan Creek beside the mission.
ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.quote: a 22-mile creek that runs out of the Santa Ana Mountains to meet San Juan Creek beside the mission.

ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.q: Who lived along Trabuco Creek before the Spanish?
alts: Who lived by it long ago?
Were there Native Americans at the creek?
ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.a: Acjachemen and Payómkawichum people lived along the creek for some 8,000 years before the Spanish came.
ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.quote: Acjachemen and Payómkawichum people lived along the creek for some 8,000 years before the Spanish came.

ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.q: What wildlife lived in Trabuco Creek?
alts: Any animals in the creek, like bears?
ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.a: In its natural state it had one of the most significant steelhead trout runs in Orange County, and steelhead were sighted again in 2003 and 2005. The last California grizzly in the Santa Ana Mountains was shot near Trabuco Canyon.
ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.quote: it had one of the most significant steelhead trout runs in Orange County, and steelhead were sighted in it again in 2003 and 2005.

ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.q: What does Trabuco Creek look like under the freeway?
alts: What happens to it under the road?
Does the creek go under the freeway?
Where does the water go here?
ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.a: Under the freeway the creek squeezes through twin culverts, then drops into a small canyon toward San Juan Capistrano.
ca83-trabuco-creek-s-lost-gun.quote: Under the freeway the creek squeezes through twin culverts, then drops into a small canyon toward San Juan Capistrano.

ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.q: Who owned Rancho Mission Viejo originally?
alts: Who first put that ranch together?
ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.a: Don Juan Forster put the ranch together in the 1840s. He was the brother-in-law of Governor Pío Pico, and at one point he held about 200,000 acres.
ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.quote: Don Juan Forster, brother-in-law of Governor Pío Pico, put the ranch together in the 1840s and at one point held about 200,000 acres

ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.q: Who was here before the ranch at Rancho Mission Viejo?
alts: Did anyone live on that land before the ranch?
ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.a: Before the ranch, the land held the Acjachemen village of Piwiva.
ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.quote: Before the ranch, this land held the Acjachemen village of Piwiva.

ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.q: How big is Rancho Mission Viejo?
ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.a: It is still about 23,000 acres. It was once much bigger: Don Juan Forster held about 200,000 acres at one point.
ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.quote: lies Rancho Mission Viejo, the old mission ranch, still about 23,000 acres.

ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.q: Is Rancho Mission Viejo still a working ranch today?
ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.a: Yes. The O'Neill family descendants still run it as a working ranch, with cattle, orchards and a nature reserve.
ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.quote: His descendants still run it as a working ranch, with cattle, orchards and a nature reserve.

ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.q: What grows at Rancho Mission Viejo?
alts: What fruit comes from that ranch?
ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.a: The old orange groves gave way to lemons and avocados. More than 9,000 avocado trees and 63,000 lemon trees are harvested year-round.
ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.quote: The ranch's orange groves have given way to lemons and avocados, and more than 9,000 avocado trees and 63,000 lemon trees are harvested year-round.

ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.q: What happened to the ranch land over time at Rancho Mission Viejo?
alts: Did that land get sold off?
Where did all the ranch land go?
Is the town of Mission Viejo from it?
ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.a: In the early 1940s the San Diego County part went to the military to expand Camp Pendleton. In 1963 the family and its partners built the planned community of Mission Viejo on ranch land.
ca86-rancho-mission-viejo.quote: In 1963 the family and its partners started the Mission Viejo Company and built the 11,000-acre planned community of Mission Viejo on ranch land.

ca89-saddleback.q: How tall is Saddleback's highest peak?
alts: How big is the mountain, is it huge?
ca89-saddleback.a: Its higher summit, Santiago Peak, rises 5,689 feet. That makes it the highest point in Orange County.
ca89-saddleback.quote: Its higher summit, Santiago Peak, rises 5,689 feet, the highest point in Orange County

ca89-saddleback.q: Who is Modjeska Peak named after?
ca89-saddleback.a: Helena Modjeska, a Polish stage star who lived in a canyon at its foot in her later years. She is regarded as the greatest actress in the history of Polish theater.
ca89-saddleback.quote: named for Helena Modjeska, a Polish stage star who lived in a canyon at its foot in her later years.

ca89-saddleback.q: What are all those antennas on Saddleback?
alts: Why does the mountain have antennas on top?
ca89-saddleback.a: The crown of antennas on Santiago Peak sends radio signals across much of five counties.
ca89-saddleback.quote: its crown of antennas sends radio signals across much of five counties.

ca89-saddleback.q: Does it ever snow on Saddleback?
alts: Can you see snow on the mountain?
ca89-saddleback.a: Yes. During most winters, snow falls on Santiago Peak at least once.
ca89-saddleback.quote: During most winters, snow falls on it at least once.

ca89-saddleback.q: What happened to Saddleback in the 2024 fire?
alts: Did the mountain catch on fire?
ca89-saddleback.a: In September 2024 the Airport Fire burned about 24,000 acres and crossed the ridge of Santiago Peak, damaging some of its radio equipment.
ca89-saddleback.quote: In September 2024 the Airport Fire, named for a model airplane club near where it started in Trabuco Canyon, burned about 24,000 acres

ca94-el-toro-y.q: Why is it called the El Toro Y?
alts: Why's it called El Toro, kid-style, like what does the name mean?
ca94-el-toro-y.a: It's named for the old town of El Toro, which is Spanish for the bull, and for the Marine air station next door. The town later renamed itself Lake Forest in 1991.
ca94-el-toro-y.quote: It is named for the old town of El Toro, Spanish for the bull, which renamed itself Lake Forest in 1991, and for the Marine air station next door.

ca94-el-toro-y.q: What is the El Toro Y?
alts: What's that big junction, kids want to know?
ca94-el-toro-y.a: It's where Interstate 5 and Interstate 405 meet. The interchange is at exit 94.
ca94-el-toro-y.quote: This is the El Toro Y, where Interstate 5 and Interstate 405 meet.

ca94-el-toro-y.q: How busy did the El Toro Y get?
alts: How much traffic does it get?
How many cars go through there, a kid might ask?
ca94-el-toro-y.a: From 1975 to 2002, traffic here more than tripled, to 356,000 vehicles a day. By the early 1990s it was one of the most congested interchanges in the world.
ca94-el-toro-y.quote: From 1975 to 2002, traffic here more than tripled, to 356,000 vehicles a day

ca94-el-toro-y.q: How wide is the El Toro Y?
alts: How big is that road, a kid would ask?
ca94-el-toro-y.a: After a widening finished in 1997, the road here was 26 lanes wide.
ca94-el-toro-y.quote: after a widening finished in 1997 the road here was 26 lanes wide.

ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.q: How long did the Marines fly from El Toro?
alts: How long was that base open?
How many years did the Marines use it?
ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.a: The Marines flew from El Toro air station from 1942 until it closed in 1999.
ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.quote: the Marines flew from El Toro air station from 1942 until it closed in 1999.

ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.q: What was El Toro before it was a Marine base?
alts: What was on that land before the base?
What did they grow there, before the planes?
What was the land used for?
ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.a: It was part of James Irvine's ranch, and the land held the largest lima bean field in North America. The Marine Corps paid $100,000 for 4,000 acres of it.
ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.quote: The Marine Corps paid James Irvine $100,000 for 4,000 acres of his ranch, land that then held the largest lima bean field in North America.

ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.q: Who designed the El Toro Marine base patch?
alts: Who made the flying bull patch?
ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.a: The base's patch, a flying bull, was designed by Walt Disney Studios in 1944.
ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.quote: The base's patch, a flying bull, was designed by Walt Disney Studios in 1944.

ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.q: What happened at El Toro when Nixon resigned?
alts: What did Nixon do at that base?
Why did Nixon fly to El Toro?
ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.a: On the day he resigned in 1974, Richard Nixon flew from Andrews Air Force Base to El Toro.
ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.quote: On the day he resigned in 1974, Richard Nixon flew from Andrews Air Force Base to El Toro.

ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.q: What is El Toro Marine air base today?
alts: What happened to it after it closed?
Is there anything to see there now?
Did they turn it into an airport?
ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.a: Airport opponents won in 2002. About 1,300 acres became the Orange County Great Park, where the Great Park Balloon rises 400 feet above the surrounding land.
ca95-el-toro-marine-air-base.quote: About 1,300 acres became the Orange County Great Park, where the Great Park Balloon rises 400 feet above the surrounding land.

ca97-the-irvine-ranch.q: How big was the Irvine Ranch?
alts: Was that ranch really huge, like how many miles?
How wide was the Irvine Ranch?
ca97-the-irvine-ranch.a: It was huge. The Irvine Ranch once stretched 23 miles from the ocean to the Santa Ana River, and by 1918 it grew 60,000 acres of lima beans.
ca97-the-irvine-ranch.quote: which once stretched 23 miles from the ocean to the Santa Ana River

ca97-the-irvine-ranch.q: How did the Irvine Ranch get started?
alts: Who started the farm, and when?
ca97-the-irvine-ranch.a: James Irvine and his partners began it in 1864 from old Mexican land grants. It happened after a drought killed a rancher's livestock and forced him to sell.
ca97-the-irvine-ranch.quote: James Irvine and his partners began it in 1864 from old Mexican land grants, after a drought killed a rancher's livestock and forced him to sell.

ca97-the-irvine-ranch.q: Why did Irvine's men meet the railroad crews with shotguns?
alts: Why did they use shotguns on the railroad workers?
Did cowboys really point guns at train builders?
What happened with the railroad and the ranch?
ca97-the-irvine-ranch.a: Southern Pacific crews laid track across the ranch without permission, so Irvine's ranch hands met them with shotguns. He let the rival Santa Fe railway build through instead.
ca97-the-irvine-ranch.quote: When Southern Pacific crews laid track across the ranch without permission, Irvine's ranch hands met them with shotguns, and he let the rival Santa Fe railway build through instead.

ca97-the-irvine-ranch.q: How did the Irvine Ranch become the city of Irvine?
alts: How did it turn into a city?
Where did the farm fields go?
Why is the city called Irvine?
ca97-the-irvine-ranch.a: In 1961 the Irvine Company sold 990 acres to the University of California for one dollar, and architect William Pereira planned a city around the campus. The new city took the family's name.
ca97-the-irvine-ranch.quote: In 1961 the Irvine Company sold 990 acres to the University of California for one dollar, and architect William Pereira planned a city of 50,000 around the new campus

ca97-the-irvine-ranch.q: How many people live in Irvine today?
alts: Is it a big city now?
When did Irvine become a city?
ca97-the-irvine-ranch.a: More than 300,000 people live there now. Irvine became a city in 1971.
ca97-the-irvine-ranch.quote: Irvine became a city in 1971 and now has more than 300,000 people.

ca100-jamboree-road.q: Why is it called Jamboree Road?
alts: How did Jamboree Road get its name, mom?
ca100-jamboree-road.a: It's named for a Boy Scout campout. In 1953 the National Scout Jamboree was held on ranch land nearby, and the muddy trail to it was later paved and renamed Jamboree Road.
ca100-jamboree-road.quote: Jamboree Road is named for a Boy Scout campout. In 1953 the Irvine Company let the National Scout Jamboree use ranch land

alts: Were there really a lot of kids camping here?
ca100-jamboree-road.a: Thousands of tents went up on ranch land, and between 45,000 and 50,000 Scouts came, by different counts. It was the first national jamboree held west of the Mississippi.
ca100-jamboree-road.quote: Between 45,000 and 50,000 Scouts came, by different counts

ca100-jamboree-road.q: Where was the Jamboree held, exactly?
alts: Where did all those tents go?
ca100-jamboree-road.a: On Irvine Company ranch land where Newport Beach's Fashion Island now stands. Back then it was reached only by a muddy two-lane trail.
ca100-jamboree-road.quote: the Irvine Company let the National Scout Jamboree use ranch land where Newport Beach's Fashion Island now stands

ca100-jamboree-road.q: Did anyone famous come to the Jamboree?
ca100-jamboree-road.a: Yes, Bob Hope was the master of ceremonies. He joked that with Scouts from so many other countries, they were like the United Nations in short pants.
ca100-jamboree-road.quote: the master of ceremonies, Bob Hope, joked that with boys from so many other countries they were like the United Nations in short pants

ca100-jamboree-road.q: How did the Scouts get to the Jamboree?
alts: How did they get there back then?
ca100-jamboree-road.a: Some came by rail. The Irvine Company helped build a road from a stop on the Santa Fe's San Diegan train, so Scouts could ride in.
ca100-jamboree-road.quote: The Irvine Company also helped build a road from a stop on the Santa Fe's Los Angeles to San Diego train, the San Diegan, so Scouts could come by rail.

ca100-jamboree-road.q: How long is Jamboree Road today?
alts: Is it a really long road?
ca100-jamboree-road.a: Jamboree Road runs 15.8 miles, from the edge of Balboa Island to the hills of Orange.
ca100-jamboree-road.quote: Today Jamboree Road runs 15.8 miles, from the edge of Balboa Island to the hills of Orange.

ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.q: Why did the Navy build the Tustin blimp hangar?
alts: Why are there giant barns for blimps, Dad?
ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.a: The Navy built two giant wooden hangars during World War II for blimps that patrolled the coast. The south hangar is the one still standing today.
ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.quote: South of the freeway stands one of two giant wooden hangars the Navy built during World War II for blimps that patrolled the coast.

ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.q: How big is the Tustin blimp hangar?
alts: Is it really as tall as 17 floors?
ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.a: The surviving south hangar is more than 1,000 feet long and 17 stories tall. It's one of the largest wooden structures ever built.
ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.quote: The surviving south hangar is more than 1,000 feet long and 17 stories tall, one of the largest wooden structures ever built.

ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.q: What is the Tustin blimp hangar made of?
alts: What is it made out of?
Is it really made of wood?
What kind of wood is it?
ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.a: It's built of Douglas fir from Oregon. In 1993 the American Society of Civil Engineers named the hangars a historic civil engineering landmark.
ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.quote: The hangars were built of Douglas fir from Oregon, and in 1993 the American Society of Civil Engineers named them a historic civil engineering landmark.

ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.q: What happened to the other Tustin blimp hangar?
alts: Did one of the hangars burn down?
Where did the other one go?
ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.a: The north hangar burned in a fire on November 7, 2023. Firefighters let it burn because its roof could collapse, and crews began tearing down what was left that December.
ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.quote: Firefighters let the north hangar burn because its roof could collapse, and crews began tearing down what was left that December.

ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.q: Is the Tustin blimp hangar still used today?
alts: Are there real blimps in there now?
ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.a: Yes. The south hangar is still used to store and service Goodyear blimps, which come back every year for maintenance and inspections.
ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.quote: The south hangar is still used to store and service Goodyear blimps, which come back every year for maintenance and inspections.

ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.q: Has the Tustin blimp hangar been in any movies?
alts: Have I seen it in a show?
ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.a: Yes. The hangars appeared in movies and shows including The Hindenburg, The X-Files, Pearl Harbor and Star Trek.
ca101-tustin-s-giant-blimp-hangar.quote: The hangars appeared in movies and shows including The Hindenburg, The X-Files, Pearl Harbor and Star Trek.

ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.q: How many orange trees did Orange County's groves once have?
alts: How many trees were in those groves?
Were there like a million orange trees here?
How many oranges trees were there?
ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.a: By 1948 Orange County had 67,263 acres of Valencia oranges, with more than five million trees.
ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.quote: by 1948 it had 67,263 acres of them, more than five million trees

ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.q: Why did Orange County's orange groves disappear?
alts: Where did all the orange trees go, mom?
ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.a: After the war, a housing boom took over. In 1949 alone, nearly 7,000 acres of orange trees disappeared, and more fell each year as housing tracts spread.
ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.quote: In 1949 alone, nearly 7,000 acres of orange trees disappeared, and each year more fell as housing tracts spread.

ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.q: Who planted the first commercial Valencia orange grove in Orange County?
alts: Who planted the very first orange trees?
ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.a: R. H. Gilman planted the first commercial grove of spring-ripening Valencias in 1875, on land that is now the Cal State Fullerton campus.
ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.quote: The first commercial grove of spring-ripening Valencias was planted in 1875 by R. H. Gilman, on land that is now the Cal State Fullerton campus.

ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.q: How important were oranges to Orange County's economy?
alts: Did lots of people work with oranges?
Was citrus a big deal back then?
ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.a: Very important. By 1936 citrus brought in two-thirds of the county's farm income, and in 1919 perhaps a third of the workers in the city of Orange had citrus-related jobs.
ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.quote: By 1936 citrus brought in two-thirds of the county's farm income

ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.q: What happened to the packing houses at Orange County's orange groves?
alts: Where did the oranges get packed?
ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.a: At their peak in the early 1940s, 45 packing houses were running. The last one, Villa Park Orchards, moved to Ventura County in 2006.
ca103-orange-county-s-orange-groves.quote: At their peak in the early 1940s, 45 packing houses were running

ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.q: Why does the Santa Ana Zoo have 50 monkeys?
alts: Why does it have to keep that many monkeys?
Why are there so many monkeys there?
ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.a: Joseph Prentice gave the city the land in 1949 on the condition that the zoo keep at least 50 monkeys at all times.
ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.quote: Joseph Prentice gave the city the land in 1949 on the condition that the zoo keep at least 50 monkeys at all times.

ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.q: When did the Santa Ana Zoo open?
alts: How long has the zoo been there, mom?
ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.a: The Santa Ana Zoo opened on March 8, 1952, in Prentice Park, right beside the freeway.
ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.quote: Right beside the freeway, in Prentice Park, is the Santa Ana Zoo, which opened on March 8, 1952.

ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.q: What animals can we see at the Santa Ana Zoo?
alts: Are there cool animals at the zoo?
ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.a: It keeps more than a dozen kinds of primates and focuses on Central and South American animals and plants. Giant anteaters, rheas and guanacos live in Tierra de las Pampas.
ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.quote: Giant anteaters, rheas and guanacos live in Tierra de las Pampas, the Land of the Grasses.

ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.q: What's the story behind the Santa Ana Zoo's train?
alts: Where did that train come from?
ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.a: Its first engine, built in 1954, ran 44 years at Santa's Village in Sky Forest. When that park closed in 1998, the zoo's friends group bought the train and volunteers restored it.
ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.quote: when that park closed in 1998, the zoo's friends group bought the train and volunteers restored it.

ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.q: What's new at the Santa Ana Zoo for monkeys?
alts: Did it get new monkey homes?
Is there a new monkey exhibit?
ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.a: River's Edge opened in 2025 as a reworked home for howler monkeys, spider monkeys and tamarins.
ca104-santa-ana-zoo-s-50-monkeys.quote: the same year River's Edge opened, a reworked home for howler monkeys, spider monkeys and tamarins.

alts: How long has this town been around, Dad?
ca105-santa-ana-the-county-seat.a: The modern town of Santa Ana was founded in 1869. The land itself was granted way back in 1810 as a rancho to José Antonio Yorba.
ca105-santa-ana-the-county-seat.quote: The modern town was founded in 1869 and became the seat of the new Orange County in 1889.

alts: Who got the land that became it?
Who was that guy who owned all the land?
ca105-santa-ana-the-county-seat.a: He was a sergeant in the Spanish army who was granted Rancho Santiago de Santa Ana in 1810. His rancho covered today's Santa Ana, Orange, Tustin, Irvine and Costa Mesa.
ca105-santa-ana-the-county-seat.quote: West of the freeway, Santa Ana grew on Rancho Santiago de Santa Ana, granted in 1810 to José Antonio Yorba, a sergeant in the Spanish army.

ca105-santa-ana-the-county-seat.q: What's the story behind the Santa Ana winds?
alts: Is that where the Santa Ana winds got their name?
Why are the hot winds called that, Mom?
ca105-santa-ana-the-county-seat.a: The hot, dry autumn winds are named for Santa Ana Canyon, which they seem to blow out of. City boosters disliked the name and spread a false story that it came from a phrase for devil wind.
ca105-santa-ana-the-county-seat.quote: The hot, dry autumn winds called Santa Anas are named for Santa Ana Canyon, which they seem to blow out of.

ca107-santa-ana-river.q: How long is the Santa Ana River?
alts: How far does that river run, like how many miles?
ca107-santa-ana-river.a: It runs 96 miles from the San Bernardino Mountains to the sea. It's the largest river entirely within Southern California.
ca107-santa-ana-river.quote: the largest river entirely within Southern California, running 96 miles from the San Bernardino Mountains to the sea

ca107-santa-ana-river.q: Why is it called the Santa Ana River?
alts: Why do they call it that?
Who gave the river its name, and why Santa Ana?
ca107-santa-ana-river.a: Soldiers with the Portolá expedition named it Río de Santa Ana in July 1769, probably because they had just celebrated Saint Anne's Day.
ca107-santa-ana-river.quote: Soldiers with the Portolá expedition named it Río de Santa Ana in July 1769, probably because they had just celebrated Saint Anne's Day.

ca107-santa-ana-river.q: What did Native people call the Santa Ana River?
alts: Did it have another name before that?
What's the old name for the river, before the soldiers came?
ca107-santa-ana-river.a: The Tongva and Acjachemen name for the river is Wanaawna.
ca107-santa-ana-river.quote: The Tongva and Acjachemen name for the river is Wanaawna.

ca107-santa-ana-river.q: Did the Santa Ana River ever flood?
alts: Did the river ever get really wild and flood stuff?
ca107-santa-ana-river.a: Yes. In 1862 it burst its banks and killed 20 to 40 people. In 1938 it flooded Anaheim and Orange under up to 4 feet of water, killing almost 60 people.
ca107-santa-ana-river.quote: In the Great Flood of 1862 it burst its banks and killed 20 to 40 people, and in 1938 it flooded Anaheim and Orange under up to 4 feet of water

ca107-santa-ana-river.q: What does the Santa Ana River do for people today?
alts: Do people get drinking water from the river?
ca107-santa-ana-river.a: Its water soaks down through sand and gravel in the spreading grounds to refill the aquifer that supplies about half of the county's tap water.
ca107-santa-ana-river.quote: where it soaks down through sand and gravel to refill the aquifer that supplies about half of the county's tap water

ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.q: When was the Crystal Cathedral built?
alts: When did they finish that giant glass church, Mom?
ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.a: It was finished in 1980. It was built as the Crystal Cathedral, and today it is called Christ Cathedral.
ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.quote: built as the Crystal Cathedral and finished in 1980

ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.q: Is the Crystal Cathedral really made of crystal?
alts: Is it actually made of crystal?
Is that glass building real crystal, Dad?
ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.a: No. Despite the name, no crystal glass was used. It has 10,000 rectangular panes that are mirrored outside and see-through inside.
ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.quote: Despite the name, no crystal glass was used.

ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.q: What is the Crystal Cathedral famous for?
alts: Why is that glass church so special, Dad?
ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.a: When it opened, it was described as the largest glass building in the world. It's also known for the Hour of Power broadcasts, which reached about 20 million viewers.
ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.quote: when it opened it was described as the largest glass building in the world

ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.q: Who started the Crystal Cathedral church?
ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.a: Robert and Arvella Schuller started the congregation in 1955 at the Orange Drive-In Theatre. Robert preached from the roof of the concession stand while people listened in their cars.
ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.quote: Robert and Arvella Schuller started the congregation in 1955 at the Orange Drive-In Theatre

ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.q: How does the Crystal Cathedral survive earthquakes?
alts: Won't that glass building break, Dad?
ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.a: The glass is held on with silicone glue to ride out earthquakes. The building was designed to withstand a magnitude 8.0 quake.
ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.quote: The glass is held on with silicone glue to ride out earthquakes

ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.q: Who owns the Crystal Cathedral today?
alts: Does anyone use that glass church now, Mom?
ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.a: Since 2019 it has been the cathedral of the Catholic Diocese of Orange. The diocese bought the campus in 2012 and renamed the church Christ Cathedral.
ca107-the-crystal-cathedral.quote: Since 2019 it has been the cathedral of the Catholic Diocese of Orange.

alts: Did the Angels always play here, Mom?
How long has the stadium been there?
ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.a: The Los Angeles Angels have played at Angel Stadium since 1966. Only Fenway Park, Wrigley Field and Dodger Stadium are older among major league ballparks still in use.
ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.quote: Among major league ballparks still in use, only Fenway Park, Wrigley Field and Dodger Stadium are older.

ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.q: Why did they move the Big A?
alts: Why isn't it in left field anymore?
Why did they move that sign?
ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.a: When the stands were enlarged and enclosed for the Rams, the Big A was moved 1,300 feet to the parking lot.
ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.quote: When the stands were enlarged and enclosed for the Rams, it was moved 1,300 feet to the parking lot.

ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.q: Did football teams play at Angel Stadium too?
alts: Did the Rams play in that stadium?
ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.a: Yes, the Los Angeles Rams played football at the stadium from 1980 to 1994.
ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.quote: From 1980 to 1994 the Los Angeles Rams played football here too.

ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.q: What happened to the Angels before they came to Anaheim?
alts: Where did the Angels play first?
Where did they play before Anaheim?
Were the Angels always in Anaheim?
ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.a: Founded in 1961, the Angels spent four seasons at Dodger Stadium before coming to Anaheim. They were the first major league team to start out in California rather than move there.
ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.quote: they spent four seasons at Dodger Stadium before coming to Anaheim.

ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.q: Does the Big A's halo light up?
alts: Does it light up at night?
Does it glow when they win?
ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.a: Yes. For years it blinked after dark when the Angels won. Since at least 2023 it stays lit, shining brighter after a win.
ca109-angel-stadium-and-the-big-a.quote: since at least 2023 it stays lit, shining brighter after a win.

ca110-disneyland.q: What happened on Disneyland's opening day?
alts: What went wrong on opening day for it?
Was opening day a disaster, Dad?
ca110-disneyland.a: About 28,000 people came, many with counterfeit tickets or by climbing the fence. It hit 100 degrees, Main Street's fresh asphalt went soft, and it became known as Black Sunday.
ca110-disneyland.quote: about 28,000 people came, roughly half with counterfeit tickets or by climbing the fence.

ca110-disneyland.q: How many people watched Disneyland open on TV?
alts: Did people see it open on television?
Did lots of people watch it on TV, Dad?
ca110-disneyland.a: An estimated 70 million people watched the opening on live television, in a country of 165 million.
ca110-disneyland.quote: An estimated 70 million people watched the opening on live television, in a country of 165 million.

ca111-anaheim-s-german-vineyards.a: Anaheim was founded in 1857 by 50 German families from San Francisco. Most of them were carpenters and craftsmen who had never made wine.
ca111-anaheim-s-german-vineyards.quote: Anaheim was founded in 1857 by 50 German families from San Francisco, who bought some 1,160 acres near the Santa Ana River for 2 dollars an acre to grow grapes.

alts: Where did that name come from?
Why does the name sound so weird?
ca111-anaheim-s-german-vineyards.a: The German settlers named it Annaheim, which means home by the Santa Ana River.
ca111-anaheim-s-german-vineyards.quote: They named it Annaheim, home by the Santa Ana River.

ca111-anaheim-s-german-vineyards.q: What happened to the Anaheim vineyards?
alts: Why aren't there vineyards there anymore?
Where did all the grapes go?
ca111-anaheim-s-german-vineyards.a: In 1884 a disease struck the vines, and within a year the wine industry was gone. It is now called Pierce's disease, and walnuts, lemons and oranges replaced the vineyards.
ca111-anaheim-s-german-vineyards.quote: In 1884 a disease struck the vines, and within a year the wine industry was gone.

ca111-anaheim-s-german-vineyards.q: Who planted the vines in Anaheim's German vineyards?
ca111-anaheim-s-german-vineyards.a: Chinese workers planted hundreds of thousands of vines and dug a 16-mile canal. The colonists had recruited 30 Chinese laborers in San Francisco.
ca111-anaheim-s-german-vineyards.quote: The colonists recruited 30 Chinese laborers in San Francisco, and Chinese workers planted hundreds of thousands of vines and dug a 16-mile canal.

alts: Did anyone call it something else?
What did the Spanish speakers call it?
ca111-anaheim-s-german-vineyards.a: Yes. Spanish-speaking neighbors called the settlement Campo Alemán, which means the German Field.
ca111-anaheim-s-german-vineyards.quote: Spanish-speaking neighbors called the settlement Campo Alemán, the German Field.

ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.q: How did Knott's Berry Farm get started?
alts: How did Knott's start, like, way back?
ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.a: Knott's Berry Farm began in 1923 as a roadside berry stand. It grew from there, and today the park draws more than 4 million visitors a year.
ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.quote: Knott's Berry Farm began in 1923 as a roadside berry stand.

alts: Why do they call them boysenberries, is that a person?
ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.a: Walter Knott named them after Rudolph Boysen, who originally grew the big berry. Knott found a few frail vines on Boysen's old farm, nursed them back to health, and sold the berries from 1932.
ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.quote: Knott nursed them back to health, sold the big berries at his stand from 1932, and called them boysenberries after their originator.

ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.a: Rudolph Boysen grew the big berry that became the boysenberry. He was also Anaheim's first park superintendent.
ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.quote: Rudolph Boysen was Anaheim's first park superintendent.

ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.q: How popular is the Knott's chicken today?
alts: Do lots of people eat the chicken, or what?
ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.a: Very popular. The restaurant serves more than 1.5 million chicken dinners each year.
ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.quote: Today the park draws more than 4 million visitors a year, and the restaurant serves more than 1.5 million chicken dinners each year.

ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.q: What is the Ghost Town at Knott's?
alts: Is there a real ghost town there?
ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.a: In 1940 Walter Knott began a replica Ghost Town honoring pioneers like his own grandparents, who came to California by covered wagon in 1868.
ca116-knott-s-chicken-and-boysenberries.quote: in 1940 Walter began a replica Ghost Town honoring pioneers like his own grandparents, who came to California by covered wagon in 1868.

ca118-la-mirada-s-olive-ranch.q: What did they grow on the La Mirada ranch?
alts: What kind of trees did they have, Buddy?
ca118-la-mirada-s-olive-ranch.a: McNally surrounded his home, Windermere Ranch, with olive, orange and lemon groves. Later guides also mention walnut groves around town.
ca118-la-mirada-s-olive-ranch.quote: surrounded his home, Windermere Ranch, with olive, orange and lemon groves.

ca118-la-mirada-s-olive-ranch.q: What did McNally make at the La Mirada ranch?
alts: What did they do with the olives?
Did they make something there, Buddy?
ca118-la-mirada-s-olive-ranch.a: He built a plant to press fine olive oil. He also built a railroad station to ship his oil and fruit across the country.
ca118-la-mirada-s-olive-ranch.quote: He built a plant to press fine olive oil and a railroad station to ship his oil and fruit across the country.

ca118-la-mirada-s-olive-ranch.q: How did La Mirada grow from a ranch into a city?
alts: What happened to the ranch land?
Where did all the houses come from, Buddy?
ca118-la-mirada-s-olive-ranch.a: The land went to developers, and in the early 1950s La Mirada was promoted as a completely planned city. By 1960 it went from about 100 homes to more than 8,000.
ca118-la-mirada-s-olive-ranch.quote: Houses went up so fast that by 1960 the town had grown from about 100 homes to more than 8,000.

ca118-la-mirada-s-olive-ranch.q: What is at McNally's old home site in La Mirada today?
alts: Is anything left of the ranch, Buddy?
ca118-la-mirada-s-olive-ranch.a: McNally's home site is now Neff Park.
ca118-la-mirada-s-olive-ranch.quote: McNally's home site is now Neff Park.

alts: What's the big old ranch thing here?
ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.a: It was a huge Spanish land grant given in 1784 to Manuel Nieto, a former soldier. It covered the land between the Santa Ana and Los Angeles rivers, from Mission San Gabriel down to the sea.
ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.quote: In 1784 the Spanish governor gave a former soldier, Manuel Nieto, the use of all the land between the Santa Ana and Los Angeles rivers, from Mission San Gabriel down to the sea.

ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.q: How big was Rancho Los Nietos?
ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.a: It started at about 300,000 acres, one of the first and largest Spanish land concessions in California. After the mission padres protested, Nieto still kept about 167,000 acres.
ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.quote: Rancho Los Nietos started at about 300,000 acres, one of the first and largest Spanish land concessions in California.

ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.q: What cities are on Rancho Los Nietos today?
alts: Which towns are on that old ranch?
ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.a: Norwalk, Downey, Buena Park, Anaheim, Whittier and Long Beach all sit on parts of it today.
ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.quote: Norwalk, Downey, Buena Park, Anaheim, Whittier and Long Beach all sit on parts of it today.

ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.q: How did Norwalk get its name?
ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.a: The railroad crossed a spot first called the North-walk. Gilbert Sproul surveyed a town site there, and in 1874 the name was recorded as Norwalk.
ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.quote: Three days after the Anaheim Branch Railroad first crossed what was called the North-walk, Gilbert Sproul surveyed a town site, and in 1874 the name was recorded as Norwalk.

ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.q: How did the railroad help start Norwalk?
alts: What did the railroad do here?
ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.a: The Sproul brothers from Oregon bought 463 acres here in 1869. When the railroad came in 1873, they deeded it 23 acres on the condition that it build a passenger stop.
ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.quote: In 1869 the Sproul brothers from Oregon bought 463 acres here, and when the railroad came in 1873 they deeded it 23 acres on the condition that it build a passenger stop.

ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.q: What was Norwalk known for in 1900?
alts: What did people do here back then?
Was it all cows and farms?
ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.a: By 1900 Norwalk was a dairy center with some of Southern California's largest sugar beet farms. Many of the dairy farmers who came in the early 1900s were Dutch.
ca121-norwalk-and-rancho-los-nietos.quote: By 1900 it was a dairy center with some of Southern California's largest sugar beet farms, and many of the dairy farmers who came in the early 1900s were Dutch.

ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.q: How did Santa Fe Springs get its name?
alts: Why is it called Santa Fe Springs?
Why's the town called springs, mom?
ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.a: It's named for mineral springs. Dr. James Fulton turned them into a sulfur spa in the 1870s, and the Santa Fe Railway bought them in 1886.
ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.quote: Santa Fe Springs takes its name from mineral springs that Dr. James Fulton turned into a sulfur spa in the 1870s, and that the Santa Fe Railway bought in 1886.

ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.q: What happened at the Santa Fe Springs gusher in 1921?
alts: Did oil really shoot out of the ground, dad?
ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.a: A well called Union-Bell blew in as a 2,500-barrel gusher in 1921. It set off an oil rush.
ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.quote: In 1921 a well called Union-Bell blew in as a 2,500-barrel gusher and set off an oil rush.

ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.q: How rich was the Santa Fe Springs oil field?
alts: Was it a big oil field?
Was there lots of oil, mom?
ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.a: Within a year it was considered one of the richest fields in petroleum history. In the 1920s it produced as much as 345,000 barrels a day.
ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.quote: Within a year the field was considered one of the richest in petroleum history, and in the 1920s it produced as much as 345,000 barrels a day.

ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.q: How did promoters sell people on Santa Fe Springs oil?
alts: How did they get investors there?
ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.a: They bused would-be investors to the field, served lunch in circus tents, and told stories of fortunes made in oil. In 1923 the state limited how much stock could be sold in a well.
ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.quote: Promoters bused would-be investors to the oil field, served them a free lunch in circus tents, and told stories of fortunes made in oil.

ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.q: What famous car was born in Santa Fe Springs?
alts: Did a famous car start there?
Was something cool built there, mom?
ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.a: The Shelby Cobra. In 1962 Carroll Shelby set up shop in Dean Moon's speed shop here and fitted lightweight roadsters with a 260-cubic-inch V8.
ca123-santa-fe-springs-gusher.quote: In 1962 Carroll Shelby set up shop in Dean Moon's speed shop here.

ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.q: How did the Rio Hondo get started?
alts: How did it come to be a separate river?
Did the river just split in two, kid style?
ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.a: The two rivers were once one restless system. After a flood in the late 1860s the San Gabriel cut a new course, and its old bed became the Rio Hondo.
ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.quote: after a flood in the late 1860s it cut a new course, leaving its old bed to become the Rio Hondo

ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.q: What is the San Gabriel River named after?
alts: Why is it called San Gabriel?
ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.a: It's named for Mission San Gabriel, which was founded beside the river in 1771.
ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.quote: The river is named for Mission San Gabriel, founded beside it in 1771

ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.q: What happened here in the Mexican-American War?
alts: Was there a battle near it?
Did soldiers fight here, like for real?
ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.a: On January 8, 1847, American troops won the Battle of Río San Gabriel on the west bank of what is now the Rio Hondo, near Washington Boulevard.
ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.quote: On January 8, 1847, during the Mexican-American War, American troops won the Battle of Río San Gabriel

ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.q: Who lived along the San Gabriel River long ago?
alts: Did people live along it back then?
Were there Native Americans here, kid asking?
ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.a: At least 26 Tongva villages stood along the river.
ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.quote: at least 26 Tongva villages stood along it

ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.q: Is the San Gabriel River still used today?
alts: Is it a real river or just a ditch, kid asking?
ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.a: Yes. Spreading grounds now soak storm water into the ground, and about a third of the water used in southeast Los Angeles County comes from the San Gabriel.
ca124-san-gabriel-river-and-rio-hondo.quote: About a third of the water used in southeast Los Angeles County comes from the San Gabriel.

ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.a: Downey is named for John Gately Downey, the youngest governor California ever had.
ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.quote: Downey, southwest of the freeway, is named for John Gately Downey, the youngest governor California ever had.

ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.q: What did Downey build for the Apollo moon missions?
alts: What did they make there for Apollo?
Did they build stuff for the Moon there?
ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.a: Its big aircraft plant, run by North American Aviation, built all of the Apollo command and service modules. Nine of them carried astronauts to the Moon.
ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.quote: built all of the Apollo command and service modules, nine of which carried astronauts to the Moon.

ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.q: How old is the Downey McDonald's?
alts: Is that the oldest McDonald's ever?
ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.a: It's the oldest McDonald's, a walk-up stand from 1953. It still has its original golden arches, two tall arches of sheet metal.
ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.quote: stands the oldest McDonald's, a walk-up stand from 1953 that still has its original golden arches, two tall arches of sheet metal.

ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.q: Who was Speedee at the Downey McDonald's?
alts: Who's that guy on the sign?
ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.a: Speedee was a hamburger-headed chef who was McDonald's mascot before Ronald McDonald. The Downey stand got a custom sign of him in 1959.
ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.quote: In 1959 it got a custom sign of Speedee, a hamburger-headed chef who was McDonald's mascot before Ronald McDonald.

ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.q: What can we see at the old Downey aircraft plant site?
alts: Is there anything to see there now?
Is there a real space capsule?
ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.a: Part of the site is now the Columbia Memorial Space Center. Out front is BP-12, the first Apollo capsule to fly.
ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.quote: Part of the site is now the Columbia Memorial Space Center, with BP-12, the first Apollo capsule to fly, out front.

ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.q: Did the Downey McDonald's almost get torn down?
alts: Did they almost lose the old McDonald's?
ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.a: Yes. After the 1994 Northridge earthquake the company closed it and planned to tear it down, but the Downey City Council stopped the demolition. It reopened in 1996.
ca125-downey-apollo-and-mcdonald-s.quote: After the 1994 Northridge earthquake the company closed it and planned to tear it down, but the Downey City Council stopped the demolition

alts: Is that wall really ancient, like a real palace?
ca129-the-citadel.a: It was built in 1929, so it's not ancient at all. It only looks like an ancient palace. It started out as a tire factory.
ca129-the-citadel.quote: That long wall decorated like an ancient palace was built in 1929 as the Samson Tire and Rubber Company factory.

ca129-the-citadel.q: Why does The Citadel look like an ancient palace?
alts: Why does it look like that?
Why is there a giant castle wall by the freeway?
ca129-the-citadel.a: Its architects modeled it on the castle of the Assyrian king Sargon II, in a style called Exotic Revival.
ca129-the-citadel.quote: Its architects modeled it on the castle of the Assyrian king Sargon II, in a style called Exotic Revival

ca129-the-citadel.q: What was The Citadel before it was an outlet center?
alts: What was it used for before?
Did they make something in that castle?
ca129-the-citadel.a: It was the Samson Tire and Rubber Company factory. Tires were made here until 1978.
ca129-the-citadel.quote: Tires were made here until 1978, and the old factory front is now the face of the Citadel Outlets.

ca129-the-citadel.q: What is The Citadel used for today?
alts: Can we go shopping in the castle?
ca129-the-citadel.a: The old factory front is now the face of the Citadel Outlets, an outlet center, with a hotel beside it.
ca129-the-citadel.quote: the city of Commerce bought the site in 1983 and had it redeveloped into an outlet center with a hotel beside it.

ca129-the-citadel.q: What was the land around The Citadel before the factory?
alts: What was the area like way back?
ca129-the-citadel.a: It was ranch land. Its turn toward industry began in 1887, when the Santa Fe Railway built its main line through.
ca129-the-citadel.quote: This was ranch land, and its turn toward industry began in 1887, when the Santa Fe Railway built its main line through.

ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.q: Which building has the thin spire on the Downtown LA skyline?
alts: What's that tower with the spike on top?
Which one is the pointy building?
ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.a: That's the Wilshire Grand Center, finished in 2017. Look for the tall downtown tower topped by a thin spire.
ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.quote: The one with a thin spire on top is the Wilshire Grand Center, finished in 2017.

ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.q: How tall is the Wilshire Grand Center?
alts: How tall is it, counting the spire?
Is that the biggest building ever?
ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.a: Counting the spire it stands 1,100 feet. That makes it the tallest building in the United States west of Chicago.
ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.quote: Counting the spire it stands 1,100 feet, the tallest building in the United States west of Chicago

ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.q: Why do so many Los Angeles towers have flat tops?
alts: Why are they flat on top?
Why don't the buildings have pointy tops?
ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.a: A 1974 city fire rule required rooftop helipads on tall buildings, so many towers around the Wilshire Grand have flat tops.
ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.quote: Many towers around it have flat tops because a 1974 city fire rule required rooftop helipads on tall buildings.

ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.q: What is El Pueblo near downtown Los Angeles?
alts: What happened at that old part of the city?
What's the oldest place in LA?
ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.a: It's near where the city was founded in 1781. Its Avila Adobe, built in 1818, is the oldest house still standing in the city.
ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.quote: Its Avila Adobe, built in 1818 with a roof sealed by tar from the La Brea Tar Pits, is the oldest house still standing in the city.

ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.q: What is Olvera Street and how did it start?
ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.a: A campaign to save the Avila Adobe led to Olvera Street. It opened on Easter Sunday 1930 as a Mexican marketplace.
ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.quote: A campaign to save it led to Olvera Street, which opened on Easter Sunday 1930 as a Mexican marketplace.

ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.q: What is the old County General Hospital building?
alts: Why is it called the Great Stone Mother?
ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.a: It's an Art Deco giant from 1933 nicknamed the Great Stone Mother. It once held 3,000 beds, and its replacement nearby was renamed LA General in 2023.
ca133-downtown-los-angeles-skyline.quote: the old County General Hospital, an Art Deco giant of 1933 nicknamed the Great Stone Mother, which once held 3,000 beds.

ca134-the-sears-tower.q: How big is the Sears tower building?
alts: How much space does it have?
ca134-the-sears-tower.a: The building has nine stories holding about 11 acres of floor space, and the tower on top rises 226 feet.
ca134-the-sears-tower.quote: Its nine stories held about 11 acres of floor space

ca134-the-sears-tower.q: What was the Sears building used for?
alts: What did they do in that building?
What was in there, kid-style: what did people do inside?
ca134-the-sears-tower.a: It was a mail-order building that shipped catalog orders to the Rocky Mountain and Pacific Coast states.
ca134-the-sears-tower.quote: shipping catalog orders to the Rocky Mountain and Pacific Coast states

ca134-the-sears-tower.q: Did workers really roller skate at the Sears building?
alts: Did they really skate in it?
Wait, did people skate inside there?
ca134-the-sears-tower.a: Yes! Workers filled orders on roller skates, gliding through the aisles and dropping items onto corkscrew slides that carried them down to waiting trucks and trains.
ca134-the-sears-tower.quote: workers filled orders on roller skates, gliding through the aisles and dropping items onto corkscrew slides

ca134-the-sears-tower.q: Is the Sears tower still in use today?
alts: Does it still work as a Sears?
ca134-the-sears-tower.a: The mail-order center closed in 1992 and the ground-floor store closed in 2021 after nearly 94 years. Plans for its future have come and gone since the 1990s.
ca134-the-sears-tower.quote: The mail-order center closed in 1992, ending jobs for 585 full-time and 775 part-time workers

ca134-the-sears-tower.q: Who tried to buy the Sears building?
alts: Did someone try to save it?
Was there a famous person who wanted it?
ca134-the-sears-tower.a: Boxer Oscar De La Hoya, a Boyle Heights native who shopped there as a child with his mother, tried twice to buy and revive the building.
ca134-the-sears-tower.quote: Boxer Oscar De La Hoya, a Boyle Heights native who shopped there as a child with his mother, tried twice to buy and revive the building.

ca134-east-los-angeles-interchange.q: Which freeways meet at the East Los Angeles Interchange?
alts: Which roads come together at it?
What highways are all tangled up here?
ca134-east-los-angeles-interchange.a: Interstate 5, Interstate 10, U.S. 101 and State Route 60 all meet here, on 135 acres of Boyle Heights.
ca134-east-los-angeles-interchange.quote: where Interstate 5, Interstate 10, U.S. 101 and State Route 60 meet on 135 acres of Boyle Heights

ca134-east-los-angeles-interchange.q: Is the East Los Angeles Interchange really the busiest in the world?
alts: Are there a ton of cars here?
ca134-east-los-angeles-interchange.a: It's often called the busiest freeway interchange in the world. A 2008 count put more than 550,000 vehicles a day through its southern part.
ca134-east-los-angeles-interchange.quote: A 2008 count put more than 550,000 vehicles a day through its southern part, and it is often called the busiest freeway interchange in the world.

ca134-east-los-angeles-interchange.q: What is the East Los Angeles Interchange's official name?
ca134-east-los-angeles-interchange.a: It's officially the Eugene A. Obregon Memorial Interchange, honoring a Marine who received the Medal of Honor.
ca134-east-los-angeles-interchange.quote: It is officially the Eugene A. Obregon Memorial Interchange, honoring a Marine who received the Medal of Honor.

ca134-east-los-angeles-interchange.q: Did people in Boyle Heights fight the freeway that led to this interchange?
alts: Did anyone try to stop it?
ca134-east-los-angeles-interchange.a: Yes. Eastside residents fought the freeway because it would wipe out large parts of Boyle Heights. Councilman Edward Roybal chaired a committee to block or reroute it, but it was built anyway.
ca134-east-los-angeles-interchange.quote: Eastside residents fought it because it would cut through and wipe out large parts of Boyle Heights.

ca135-mission-san-gabriel.q: How old is Mission San Gabriel?
alts: Is that place really old, like ancient?
ca135-mission-san-gabriel.a: It was founded in 1771. It's California mission number 4 in founding order.
ca135-mission-san-gabriel.quote: Founded in 1771, it stands in Tongva homeland, and about 6,000 Native people are buried on its grounds.

ca135-mission-san-gabriel.q: Who is Toypurina and what did she do at Mission San Gabriel?
alts: Who was the lady who fought the mission?
ca135-mission-san-gabriel.a: Toypurina was a medicine woman who helped organize a revolt against the mission in 1785. It failed, and she was baptized under pressure and sent to a mission far to the north.
ca135-mission-san-gabriel.quote: In 1785 a medicine woman named Toypurina helped organize a revolt against the mission.

ca135-mission-san-gabriel.q: Why did Toypurina's revolt at Mission San Gabriel start?
alts: Why were they fighting the mission?
ca135-mission-san-gabriel.a: It began after the governor banned baptized Tongva people from holding their dances. At her trial she said she was angry that the missionaries had settled on her people's land.
ca135-mission-san-gabriel.quote: Toypurina's revolt began after the governor banned baptized Tongva people from holding their dances.

ca135-mission-san-gabriel.q: Whose land is Mission San Gabriel on?
ca135-mission-san-gabriel.a: It stands in Tongva homeland. About 6,000 Native people are buried on its grounds.
ca135-mission-san-gabriel.quote: Founded in 1771, it stands in Tongva homeland, and about 6,000 Native people are buried on its grounds.

ca135-mission-san-gabriel.q: What happened to Mission San Gabriel in 2020?
ca135-mission-san-gabriel.a: A fire destroyed the church roof in 2020. The grounds reopened in 2023 with an exhibit on Native history.
ca135-mission-san-gabriel.quote: A fire destroyed the church roof in 2020, and the grounds reopened in 2023 with an exhibit on Native history.

ca135-mission-san-gabriel.q: How many Native people were baptized at Mission San Gabriel?
alts: How many people did they baptize?
What does the museum say about it?
ca135-mission-san-gabriel.a: The mission museum names 7,054 Native people baptized there from 1771 to 1848.
ca135-mission-san-gabriel.quote: The mission museum names 7,054 Native people baptized here from 1771 to 1848.

alts: Mom, what was Yaanga, like a town?
ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.a: Yaanga was the largest and most influential Tongva village in the region. It stood where downtown Los Angeles is today, across the river from here.
ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.quote: where downtown Los Angeles now stands, was Yaanga, recorded as the largest and most influential Tongva village in the region

ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.q: What was El Aliso at Yaanga?
alts: Was there a giant tree in the village?
ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.a: El Aliso was a great sycamore growing at the center of Yaanga. It became a landmark known to traders from as far away as present-day Yuma.
ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.quote: At its center grew a great sycamore later called El Aliso, a landmark known to traders from as far away as present-day Yuma.

ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.q: When did the Spanish arrive at Yaanga?
alts: When did they show up there?
When did the Spanish people come, Dad?
ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.a: The Portolá expedition reached Yaanga in 1769. Then in 1781, Spanish settlers founded the pueblo of Los Angeles right next to it.
ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.quote: The Portolá expedition reached Yaanga in 1769, and in 1781 Spanish settlers founded the pueblo of Los Angeles next to it.

ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.q: How big was the Tongva homeland?
alts: How much land did the Tongva have?
ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.a: The Tongva homeland, called Tovaangar, covers about 4,000 square miles. It spans the Los Angeles Basin and the southern Channel Islands.
ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.quote: The Tongva homeland, Tovaangar, covers about 4,000 square miles of the Los Angeles Basin and the southern Channel Islands.

ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.q: Is anything left of Yaanga today?
alts: Is any of it still there?
Can we find the village now?
ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.a: Traces of Yaanga have turned up around Union Station and the old Plaza. In 1994 California recognized the Tongva as the aboriginal tribe of the Los Angeles Basin.
ca135-yaanga-and-the-tongva.quote: Traces of Yaanga have turned up around Union Station and the old Plaza.

ca137-arroyo-seco-parkway.q: How old is the Arroyo Seco Parkway?
alts: When did that road open, mom?
ca137-arroyo-seco-parkway.a: It was dedicated on December 30, 1940, and opened the next day. That makes it one of the oldest freeways in the United States.
ca137-arroyo-seco-parkway.quote: one of the oldest freeways in the United States. It was dedicated on December 30, 1940, and opened the next day

ca137-arroyo-seco-parkway.q: What's special about driving the Arroyo Seco Parkway?
alts: Why's that road so curvy, mom?
ca137-arroyo-seco-parkway.a: It has tight curves and short ramps with no room to speed up, and they've barely changed. One side runs through four Art Deco tunnels in Elysian Park.
ca137-arroyo-seco-parkway.quote: Its tight curves and short ramps, with no room to speed up, have barely changed

alts: How long has it been around?
How old is this park, like really old?
ca138-elysian-park-and-chavez-ravine.a: Elysian Park was created in 1886. At 600 acres, it's one of the largest parks in Los Angeles.
ca138-elysian-park-and-chavez-ravine.quote: Elysian Park, created in 1886 and, at 600 acres, one of the largest parks in Los Angeles.

alts: What's that ravine tucked in the hills?
What is that place, is it a stadium?
ca138-elysian-park-and-chavez-ravine.a: Chavez Ravine is tucked into the Elysian Park hills, and it is the home of Dodger Stadium.
ca138-elysian-park-and-chavez-ravine.quote: Tucked into them is Chavez Ravine, home of Dodger Stadium.

ca138-elysian-park-and-chavez-ravine.q: Who used to live in Chavez Ravine?
alts: Did people live in it before the stadium?
Were there houses where the stadium is, mister?
ca138-elysian-park-and-chavez-ravine.a: By the 1940s it held three close-knit, mostly Mexican American neighborhoods: La Loma, Palo Verde and Bishop. Many families lived there because of housing discrimination elsewhere in the city.
ca138-elysian-park-and-chavez-ravine.quote: three close-knit, mostly Mexican American neighborhoods, La Loma, Palo Verde and Bishop, where many families lived because of housing discrimination elsewhere in the city.

ca138-elysian-park-and-chavez-ravine.q: What was the Battle of Chavez Ravine?
alts: What happened to the homes in it?
Why did the families have to leave, and who fought?
ca138-elysian-park-and-chavez-ravine.a: The city bought or condemned the homes for public housing that was later dropped. In 1958 voters approved trading 352 acres to the Dodgers, and the last holdouts lost a ten-year struggle.
ca138-elysian-park-and-chavez-ravine.quote: In 1958 voters approved a deal trading 352 acres of the ravine to the Dodgers, and the last holdouts lost a ten-year struggle known as the Battle of Chavez Ravine.

alts: How old is it, the stadium?
Is the baseball stadium really old?
What was that old water ditch?
What's the Mother Trench, kids ask?
ca138-elysian-park-and-chavez-ravine.a: It's an earthen ditch, the first water system of Los Angeles, dug by the city's founders in 1781. A brick piece survives beside the light-rail tracks at Los Angeles State Historic Park.
ca138-elysian-park-and-chavez-ravine.quote: the founders of Los Angeles dug their first water system in 1781, an earthen ditch called the Zanja Madre, or Mother Trench.

ca141-los-angeles-river.q: Why is the Los Angeles River lined with concrete?
alts: Why did they pave the river, Buddy?
ca141-los-angeles-river.a: Most of it was lined with concrete after the deadly flood of 1938.
ca141-los-angeles-river.quote: Most of it was lined with concrete after the deadly flood of 1938

ca141-los-angeles-river.q: Why are there plants growing in the Los Angeles River?
alts: Why does it have plants and sandbars?
Why isn't the bottom all concrete like the rest?
ca141-los-angeles-river.a: In this 11-mile stretch, called the Glendale Narrows, the groundwater sits so high that the bottom was left unpaved. That's why willows, reeds and sandbars grow right in the river.
ca141-los-angeles-river.quote: in this 11-mile stretch, the Glendale Narrows, the groundwater sits so high that the bottom was left unpaved

ca141-los-angeles-river.q: What birds can we see at the Los Angeles River?
alts: Are there any birds in the river, Buddy?
ca141-los-angeles-river.a: Birdwatchers here count great blue herons, snowy and great egrets, black-crowned night herons, cormorants and even American white pelicans. Look for white egrets or gray herons standing in the shallow water.
ca141-los-angeles-river.quote: Birdwatchers here count great blue herons, snowy and great egrets, black-crowned night herons, cormorants and even American white pelicans.

ca141-los-angeles-river.q: Can people walk or bike along the Los Angeles River?
alts: Is there a path along it?
Can we ride bikes by the river, Buddy?
ca141-los-angeles-river.a: Yes, a 7.4-mile bike and walking path follows the river, much of it right beside the freeway.
