ca141-los-angeles-river.quote: A 7.4-mile bike and walking path follows the river, much of it right beside the freeway.

ca141-los-angeles-river.q: Can you kayak or fish in the Los Angeles River?
alts: Can you really fish in that river, Buddy?
ca141-los-angeles-river.a: Fishing is still legal all year, and by 2019 kayaking on the river had become common. Steelhead trout swam here before the concrete came.
ca141-los-angeles-river.quote: Steelhead trout swam here before the concrete came, and fishing is still legal all year.

ca141-griffith-park.q: Who gave Griffith Park to Los Angeles?
alts: Who gave it to the city?
Who was the guy that gave the park away?
ca141-griffith-park.a: Griffith J. Griffith gave the first 3,015 acres to the people of Los Angeles as a Christmas gift on December 16, 1896. He asked that the park be open to all.
ca141-griffith-park.quote: On December 16, 1896, Griffith J. Griffith gave the first 3,015 acres to the people of Los Angeles as a Christmas gift.

ca141-griffith-park.a: It's more than 4,000 acres of chaparral and parkland. The city calls it the largest urban-wilderness municipal park in the United States.
ca141-griffith-park.quote: more than 4,000 acres of chaparral and parkland that the city calls the largest urban-wilderness municipal park in the United States

ca141-griffith-park.q: What can we see and do at Griffith Park?
alts: What's there to do in it?
What's in the park, anything cool?
ca141-griffith-park.a: The observatory, the Greek Theatre and trails to the Hollywood Sign are all inside the park.
ca141-griffith-park.quote: The observatory, the Greek Theatre and trails to the Hollywood Sign are all inside the park.

ca141-griffith-park.q: Was there really an ostrich farm at Griffith Park?
alts: Was it once an ostrich farm?
ca141-griffith-park.a: Yes. Griffith leased part of his land for an ostrich farm, since ostrich feathers decorated women's hats. The city's zoo later opened on the old farm in 1912.
ca141-griffith-park.quote: Griffith had bought Rancho Los Feliz in 1882 and leased part of it for an ostrich farm, since ostrich feathers decorated women's hats.

ca141-griffith-park.q: Why do people picnic in old cages at Griffith Park?
alts: Why are there picnic tables in cages?
Can we eat lunch in a zoo cage?
Is there a old zoo there?
ca141-griffith-park.a: The old zoo closed in 1966, and some empty enclosures were left standing with picnic tables inside. So people now picnic in the old cages.
ca141-griffith-park.quote: when it closed in 1966 some empty enclosures were left standing with picnic tables inside, so people now picnic in the old cages

ca141-griffith-park.q: Did a mountain lion really live in Griffith Park?
alts: Did it have a mountain lion?
Are there real mountain lions in there?
ca141-griffith-park.a: Yes. A mountain lion known as P-22 made these hills his home from 2012 to 2022.
ca141-griffith-park.quote: From 2012 to 2022, a mountain lion known as P-22 made these hills his home.

ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.q: What was the 1933 Griffith Park fire?
alts: What happened at Griffith Park, like, a long time ago?
ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.a: It was a brush fire on October 3, 1933, that killed at least 29 men who had volunteered or been ordered to fight it.
ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.quote: On October 3, 1933, a brush fire in Griffith Park killed at least 29 men who volunteered or were ordered to fight it.

ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.q: How big was the 1933 Griffith Park fire?
alts: Was it a huge fire, or a little one?
ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.a: It burned only about 47 acres, yet for 85 years it was the deadliest wildfire in California history.
ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.quote: The fire burned only about 47 acres, yet for 85 years it was the deadliest wildfire in California history.

ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.q: How did the 1933 Griffith Park fire start?
alts: What made the fire begin, anyway?
ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.a: It started a little after 2 in the afternoon in a pile of debris in Mineral Wells Canyon, in the hills west of the freeway.
ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.quote: It started a little after 2 in the afternoon in a pile of debris in Mineral Wells Canyon, in the hills west of the freeway.

ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.q: Why did so many people die in the Griffith Park fire?
alts: Why did it turn so deadly?
Why couldn't they just put it out?
ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.a: With no piped water nearby, men beat at flames with shovels. Untrained foremen set ill-judged backfires, and around 3 o'clock the wind shifted and the fire overtook the workers.
ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.quote: At about 3 o'clock the wind shifted, and the fire rushed up Dam Canyon, jumped a hastily dug firebreak and overtook the workers, injuring more than 100.

ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.q: Was there a memorial for the 1933 Griffith Park fire victims?
alts: Is there a memorial for it?
Did anyone get a monument, or what?
ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.a: A memorial plaque was placed at the park entrance, but it can no longer be found. The courts also ruled the victims could not be compensated, because they had been hired informally.
ca144-the-1933-griffith-park-fire.quote: the memorial plaque placed at the park entrance can no longer be found.

ca144-zoo-autry-and-travel-town.q: What is at the Zoo, Autry and Travel Town stop?
alts: What's there to do at that stop?
What are the three places there?
ca144-zoo-autry-and-travel-town.a: It's three family stops on the north side of Griffith Park: the Los Angeles Zoo, the Autry Museum of the American West, and Travel Town, a railroad museum.
ca144-zoo-autry-and-travel-town.quote: Three family stops sit along the north side of Griffith Park: the Los Angeles Zoo, the Autry Museum of the American West, and Travel Town, a railroad museum

ca144-zoo-autry-and-travel-town.q: Who started the Autry Museum of the American West?
ca144-zoo-autry-and-travel-town.a: Actor Gene Autry founded his museum of the West here in 1988.
ca144-zoo-autry-and-travel-town.quote: Actor Gene Autry founded his museum of the West here in 1988.

ca144-zoo-autry-and-travel-town.q: What was the land under the zoo parking lot used for before?
alts: What was it before the zoo?
What was here a long time ago?
ca144-zoo-autry-and-travel-town.a: It was the old Griffith Park Aerodrome, an airfield used from 1912 until 1939 by aviation pioneers such as Glenn Martin, Bill Boeing and Donald Douglas.
ca144-zoo-autry-and-travel-town.quote: all sit on the old Griffith Park Aerodrome, an airfield used from 1912 until 1939 by aviation pioneers such as Glenn Martin, Bill Boeing and Donald Douglas.

ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.q: How old is the Grand Central Air Terminal?
alts: Is that building really old, like way back?
ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.a: The terminal building dates to 1928. It opened with fanfare on February 22, 1929.
ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.quote: The terminal opened with fanfare on February 22, 1929, designed like a classic railroad station in Spanish and Art Deco styles.

ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.q: What was the Lindbergh Line at Grand Central Air Terminal?
alts: What was that Lindbergh Line thing?
Did people fly planes and ride trains at the same time?
ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.a: It was a 48-hour coast-to-coast trip with planes by day and trains by night. Grand Central became its western end in July 1929.
ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.quote: In July 1929 it became the western end of the Lindbergh Line, a 48-hour coast-to-coast trip with planes by day and trains by night.

ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.q: Who flew into the Grand Central Air Terminal in 1933?
alts: Did somebody famous land at that airport?
Who made the first round trip flight?
ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.a: Albert Forsythe and Charles Anderson landed here in 1933. It was the first round-trip flight across the country by Black pilots.
ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.quote: In 1933, Albert Forsythe and Charles Anderson landed here on the first round-trip flight across the country by Black pilots.

ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.q: What did Howard Hughes build near Grand Central Air Terminal?
alts: What did he build at that airport?
Did Howard Hughes make a plane there?
ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.a: Howard Hughes built his record-setting H-1 racer in a small building on Air Way in 1935.
ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.quote: Howard Hughes built his record-setting H-1 racer in a small building on Air Way in 1935.

ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.q: What happened at Grand Central Air Terminal during World War II?
alts: What did it do in the war?
Did they hide the airport in the war?
ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.a: The government camouflaged the field and trained pilots on it during World War II.
ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.quote: During World War II the government camouflaged the field and trained pilots on it.

ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.q: Where did the old Grand Central runway go?
alts: What happened to the runway there?
Where did the planes used to take off from?
ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.a: The old runway is now a city street, Grand Central Avenue.
ca145-grand-central-air-terminal.quote: The old runway is now a city street, Grand Central Avenue.

ca146-verdugo-mountains.q: How tall are the Verdugo Mountains?
alts: How big are those mountains, Dad?
ca146-verdugo-mountains.a: The Verdugo Mountains top out at 3,126 feet, a rocky range rising east of the freeway.
ca146-verdugo-mountains.quote: The rocky range rising east of the freeway is the Verdugo Mountains, topping out at 3,126 feet.

ca146-verdugo-mountains.q: Why are they called the Verdugo Mountains?
alts: Who is Verdugo, and why are the mountains named after him?
ca146-verdugo-mountains.a: They are named for José María Verdugo, a Spanish soldier who came north with the 1769 expedition and in 1784 received Rancho San Rafael.
ca146-verdugo-mountains.quote: They are named for José María Verdugo, a Spanish soldier who came north with the 1769 expedition and in 1784 received Rancho San Rafael

alts: What did that guy do here?
Was Verdugo a real person, like a soldier?
ca146-verdugo-mountains.a: He was a Spanish soldier who retired from the army in 1798 to ranch full time. He soon had nearly 2,000 head of cattle.
ca146-verdugo-mountains.quote: Verdugo retired from the army in 1798 to ranch full time, and he soon had nearly 2,000 head of cattle.

ca146-verdugo-mountains.q: How much land did Verdugo's rancho cover?
ca146-verdugo-mountains.a: Rancho San Rafael was about 36,000 acres. That land now holds Glendale and Burbank.
ca146-verdugo-mountains.quote: Rancho San Rafael, about 36,000 acres that now hold Glendale and Burbank.

ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.q: Why is Burbank called the Media Capital of the World?
alts: Why do they call it that?
Why is this town so famous, Buddy?
ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.a: Burbank is commonly known as the Media Capital of the World. Warner Bros. and the Walt Disney Company both have their headquarters here, in the Media District.
ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.quote: Warner Bros. and the Walt Disney Company both have their headquarters here, in the Media District, a couple of miles west of the freeway.

ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.q: When did Warner Bros. and Disney come to Burbank?
alts: When did the cartoon people move in?
ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.a: Warner Bros. took over the First National studio lot in 1928. Disney finished its Burbank studio on Buena Vista Street in 1939, after the success of Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs.
ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.quote: Warner Bros. took over the First National studio lot in 1928, and Disney, after the success of Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, finished its Burbank studio

ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.q: What famous movie was filmed in Burbank?
alts: What was filmed at that studio?
Were any big movies made there, Buddy?
ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.a: Most of Casablanca's major scenes were shot on Stage 1 at Warner Bros. in 1942. Even its foggy airport scene was made on the stage.
ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.quote: Most of Casablanca's major scenes were shot on Stage 1 at Warner Bros. in 1942.

alts: Why didn't they build it there?
Why is Disneyland somewhere else, Buddy?
ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.a: Walt Disney first hoped to build a Mickey Mouse Park beside his studio, but his aides said the land was too small. A city council member also said they didn't want the carny atmosphere. He built Disneyland in Anaheim instead.
ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.quote: Walt Disney first hoped to build a Mickey Mouse Park beside his studio, but his aides said the land was too small

ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.q: Can you tour a movie studio in Burbank?
alts: Can we go on a studio tour, Buddy?
ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.a: Warner Bros. runs public backlot tours, while Disney is the only major studio that does not. Check before going for what's currently offered.
ca147-burbank-the-media-capital.quote: Warner Bros. runs public backlot tours, while Disney is the only major studio that does not.

ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.q: How did Lockheed hide its factory during World War II?
alts: How did they hide it from the air?
How do you hide a whole factory, Dad?
ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.a: They covered the factory with a huge painted tarp showing a quiet country neighborhood, with rubber cars and hundreds of fake trees made of chicken wire and feathers.
ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.quote: It was covered with a huge painted tarp showing a quiet country neighborhood, with rubber cars and hundreds of fake trees made of chicken wire and feathers.

ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.q: How many planes did Lockheed build in World War II?
alts: How many did they make in the war?
Did they make a lot of airplanes, Mom?
ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.a: Lockheed and its Vega company built 19,278 planes during the war.
ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.quote: Lockheed and its Vega company built 19,278 planes during the war.

ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.q: What is the Skunk Works and where did the name come from?
alts: Where did that name come from?
Why is it called Skunk Works, are there skunks?
ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.a: It was Lockheed's secret design shop, which took its nickname from the Li'l Abner comic strip. Work began there in 1943 on a secret jet fighter.
ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.quote: In 1943 Lockheed secretly began a jet fighter here, and its secret design shop took the nickname Skunk Works from the Li'l Abner comic strip.

ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.q: What famous planes came out of the Skunk Works?
alts: Did they make any cool planes?
ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.a: That team went on to create the U-2 spy plane, the SR-71 Blackbird and the F-117 stealth fighter.
ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.quote: That team went on to create the U-2 spy plane, the SR-71 Blackbird and the F-117 stealth fighter.

ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.q: What is at Lockheed's old Burbank site today?
alts: Can we still see the old factory?
ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.a: Aerospace work in Burbank ended in 1992. A shopping center on Empire Avenue now covers part of the old Skunk Works site.
ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.quote: Aerospace work in Burbank ended in 1992. A shopping center on Empire Avenue now covers part of the old Skunk Works site.

ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.q: What is the airport next to Lockheed's factory called?
alts: Did the airport have a lot of names?
ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.a: Lockheed bought the airport in 1940 and ran it as Lockheed Air Terminal. The field has gone by at least six names, and today it is Hollywood Burbank Airport.
ca149-lockheed-s-hidden-factory.quote: Lockheed bought the airport in 1940 and ran it as Lockheed Air Terminal, and the field has gone by at least six names, today Hollywood Burbank Airport.

ca150-sun-valley-s-thorny-name.q: What was Sun Valley called before it was Sun Valley?
alts: What was it called before that?
What was its old name, Dad?
ca150-sun-valley-s-thorny-name.a: It was first Wixánga, a Fernandeño Tongva village. Later it was called Roscoe, until residents chose Sun Valley in 1950.
ca150-sun-valley-s-thorny-name.quote: Long before it was Sun Valley, this was Wixánga, a Fernandeño Tongva village whose name means something like place of the thorns

ca150-sun-valley-s-thorny-name.a: It means something like place of the thorns, named for the prickly pear cactus that grew here.
ca150-sun-valley-s-thorny-name.quote: whose name means something like place of the thorns, for the prickly pear cactus growing here.

ca150-sun-valley-s-thorny-name.q: Why was Sun Valley once called Roscoe?
alts: Where did the name Roscoe come from?
ca150-sun-valley-s-thorny-name.a: The name Roscoe reportedly came from a railroad crew member. A general store here served as post office and water stop for the Southern Pacific line.
ca150-sun-valley-s-thorny-name.quote: The name Roscoe reportedly came from a railroad crew member.

alts: Does the wash fill with water, Mom?
ca150-sun-valley-s-thorny-name.a: Yes, it sits at the foot of the Verdugo Mountains and is prone to flash floods. Nearby Tujunga Wash is usually dry and carries much water only during and after storms.
ca150-sun-valley-s-thorny-name.quote: Sitting at the foot of the Verdugo Mountains, the neighborhood is prone to flash floods.

ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.q: Who started growing wheat in the San Fernando Valley?
alts: Who were the wheat farmers, Dad?
ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.a: J. B. Lankershim and Isaac Van Nuys began dry-farming wheat across the southern half of the San Fernando Valley in 1874.
ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.quote: In 1874, J. B. Lankershim and Isaac Van Nuys began dry-farming wheat across the southern half of the San Fernando Valley.

ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.q: How big was wheat farming in the valley?
alts: Was it a big deal back then?
Was there really that much wheat, Mom?
ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.a: By 1876 the valley was the biggest wheat-growing area in Los Angeles County.
ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.quote: By 1876 the valley was the biggest wheat-growing area in Los Angeles County

ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.q: Where did the valley's wheat get shipped to?
alts: Did the wheat go far away, Dad?
ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.a: In 1876 they sent the first wheat shipment from San Pedro Harbor to Europe.
ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.quote: that year they sent the first wheat shipment from San Pedro Harbor to Europe.

ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.q: Why did valley farmers stop growing wheat?
ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.a: Droughts showed they needed steady water. After Los Angeles Aqueduct water arrived after 1913, farms switched from wheat to irrigated crops.
ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.quote: When Los Angeles Aqueduct water arrived after 1913, farms switched from wheat to irrigated crops

ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.q: What did the valley grow after the wheat?
alts: What did they plant after that?
ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.a: Farms grew corn, beans, squash and cotton, plus orchards of apricots, persimmons and walnuts, and big groves of oranges and lemons.
ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.quote: corn, beans, squash and cotton, orchards of apricots, persimmons and walnuts, and big groves of oranges and lemons.

ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.q: What happened to the valley's farms?
alts: Where did all the farms go, Mom?
ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.a: After World War II the valley's population grew fivefold in 15 years, and suburbs replaced nearly all the farms, leaving only a few groves.
ca152-when-the-valley-grew-wheat.quote: suburbs replaced nearly all the farms, leaving only a few groves.

alts: Why's this place got such a weird name?
ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.a: The name comes from Pakoinga, a Native village here whose name meant entrance. Spanish ears heard the ng sound as an m, and that's how it became Pacoima.
ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.quote: Pacoima takes its name from Pakoinga, the name of a Native village here meaning entrance; Spanish ears heard its ng sound as an m.

ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.q: Who is Ritchie Valens and why is Pacoima his hometown?
alts: Who was he, and did he really come from here?
Who's the famous guy from here?
ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.a: Ritchie Valens was born Richard Valenzuela right here in Pacoima in 1941. He turned the Mexican folk song La Bamba into a rock and roll hit in 1958.
ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.quote: born Richard Valenzuela here in 1941, who turned the Mexican folk song La Bamba into a rock and roll hit in 1958.

alts: Did something bad happen to that singer?
What happened to the La Bamba guy?
ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.a: He died at just 17 in a February 1959 plane crash in Iowa. Buddy Holly died in the same crash.
ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.quote: He died at 17 in a February 1959 plane crash in Iowa along with Buddy Holly.

ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.q: Did Ritchie Valens go to school in Pacoima?
alts: Did he go to school around here?
Did he sing at his school when he was a kid?
ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.a: Yes, he went to Pacoima Junior High. He brought his guitar to school and sang for friends on the bleachers.
ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.quote: As a student at Pacoima Junior High, Valens brought his guitar to school and sang for friends on the bleachers.

ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.q: Is anything named after Ritchie Valens near Pacoima?
alts: Is there something named after him?
Is there a road for that singer?
ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.a: Yes, the stretch of I-5 between the 170 and 118 freeways is named the Ritchie Valens Memorial Highway.
ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.quote: the stretch of I-5 between the 170 and 118 freeways is named the Ritchie Valens Memorial Highway.

ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.q: What is Pacoima's history in the San Fernando Valley?
alts: Why did people move there way back?
ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.a: After World War II, Pacoima became the center of African American life in the San Fernando Valley, because racial covenants kept Black families out of many other neighborhoods.
ca155-pacoima-ritchie-valens-hometown.quote: After World War II, Pacoima became the center of African American life in the San Fernando Valley

ca157-mission-san-fernando.q: When was Mission San Fernando founded?
alts: How long ago did they start this place, like in olden times?
ca157-mission-san-fernando.a: Mission San Fernando was founded in 1797. It is California mission number 17 in founding order.
ca157-mission-san-fernando.quote: Founded in 1797, the mission gave its name to the San Fernando Valley.

ca157-mission-san-fernando.q: Who lived and worked at Mission San Fernando?
alts: Who stayed at that place back then?
ca157-mission-san-fernando.a: Tataviam, Tongva and Chumash families lived and worked at the mission. It was built on a farming settlement called Achooykomenga.
ca157-mission-san-fernando.quote: The people who lived and worked here included Tataviam, Tongva and Chumash families.

ca157-mission-san-fernando.q: What is the old long building at Mission San Fernando?
alts: What can we see at it that is still original?
Is any of it really old, like for real?
ca157-mission-san-fernando.a: It's the convento, finished in 1822, and it is original. It was a guesthouse for travelers on El Camino Real.
ca157-mission-san-fernando.quote: The long convento, finished in 1822, is original. It was a guesthouse for travelers on El Camino Real.

ca157-mission-san-fernando.q: Did anything bad happen to Mission San Fernando's church?
alts: Is the church still the old one?
Did the church fall down or something?
ca157-mission-san-fernando.a: Yes, the 1971 earthquake destroyed the church. It was rebuilt by 1974.
ca157-mission-san-fernando.quote: The church was destroyed by the 1971 earthquake and rebuilt by 1974.

ca158-the-dam-that-almost-failed.q: What happened at the dam that almost failed?
alts: Why did the dam almost fail, Mom?
ca158-the-dam-that-almost-failed.a: During the San Fernando earthquake on February 9, 1971, part of the Lower Van Norman Dam slid into its reservoir. Only about 5 feet of dam was left above the water.
ca158-the-dam-that-almost-failed.quote: part of the Lower Van Norman Dam slid into its reservoir, leaving only about 5 feet of dam above the water

ca158-the-dam-that-almost-failed.q: How many people had to leave when the dam almost failed?
alts: How many people did it affect?
Did people have to run away from the dam?
ca158-the-dam-that-almost-failed.a: Eighty thousand people living below the dam were evacuated, and they stayed away for days.
ca158-the-dam-that-almost-failed.quote: Eighty thousand people living below it were evacuated for days.

ca158-the-dam-that-almost-failed.q: How did they keep the dam from failing completely?
alts: How did they stop it from collapsing?
What did the workers do about the water?
ca158-the-dam-that-almost-failed.a: The reservoir was only about half full, which was lucky. Crews drained it as fast as the damaged outlets allowed, lowering it 13.5 feet in three and a half days.
ca158-the-dam-that-almost-failed.quote: Crews drained it as fast as the damaged outlets allowed, lowering it 13.5 feet in three and a half days.

ca158-the-dam-that-almost-failed.q: What happened to the old dams afterward?
alts: Did they build a new dam, Mom?
ca158-the-dam-that-almost-failed.a: The old dams were retired, and a new Los Angeles Dam was built between them in a more stable spot. The near miss also changed how engineers judge earthquake safety at dams.
ca158-the-dam-that-almost-failed.quote: The old dams were retired, a new Los Angeles Dam was built between them in a more stable spot

alts: Why's this town called Sylmar, Mom?
ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.a: Sylmar joins Latin words for forest and sea. It was named for the sea of olive trees that once covered these slopes. The name was adopted in 1893.
ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.quote: Sylmar's name, adopted in 1893, joins Latin words for forest and sea, for the sea of olive trees that covered these slopes.

ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.q: How big were Sylmar's olive groves?
alts: Were there really a ton of olive trees?
ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.a: In 1894 up to 1,700 acres were planted. By 1906 the groves were said to be the largest olive grove in the world.
ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.quote: In 1894 up to 1,700 acres were planted, and by 1906 the groves were said to be the largest olive grove in the world.

ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.q: Where did Sylmar's olives come from?
alts: Who planted all those olive trees?
ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.a: They trace back to Mission San Fernando, which tended about 70 acres of olive trees and crushed the fruit for oil. In the 1890s the Los Angeles Olive Growers Association planted the foothills.
ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.quote: Sylmar's olives trace back to Mission San Fernando, which tended about 70 acres of olive trees and crushed the fruit for oil.

ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.q: Who picked the olives in Sylmar?
alts: Who did all the picking, Dad?
ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.a: In the early 1900s, about 300 Japanese workers picked the olives each season. They lived in a village of tents.
ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.quote: In the early 1900s, about 300 Japanese workers picked the olives each season and lived in a village of tents.

ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.q: What happened to the olive company's land?
alts: Did they sell the farm, Mom?
ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.a: In 1938 the company put its land up for sale. It was still planted in olives, lemons, oranges and figs.
ca159-sylmar-s-sea-of-olives.quote: In 1938 the company put its land up for sale, still planted in olives, lemons, oranges and figs.

ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.q: What is the Sylmar Converter Station?
alts: What's that big power place for?
ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.a: It's the south end of the Pacific DC Intertie, a power line running 846 miles from the Columbia River near The Dalles, Oregon. The station turns direct current into the alternating current Los Angeles uses.
ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.quote: the Sylmar Converter Station, the south end of the Pacific DC Intertie, a power line that runs 846 miles from the Columbia River near The Dalles, Oregon

ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.q: How long is the Pacific DC Intertie power line?
alts: How long is that power line?
How far does the electricity travel to get here?
ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.a: The line runs 846 miles, all the way from the Columbia River near The Dalles, Oregon, down to this station near Los Angeles.
ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.quote: a power line that runs 846 miles from the Columbia River near The Dalles, Oregon

ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.q: When was the Pacific DC Intertie built?
alts: When did they finish that thing?
ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.a: The intertie was completed in 1970. It was built to bring cheaper hydroelectric power from dams on the Columbia River.
ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.quote: The intertie was completed in 1970 to bring cheaper hydroelectric power from dams on the Columbia River

ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.q: Why does Los Angeles get power from the Columbia River?
alts: Why does it come from so far away?
Why bring electricity all the way from Oregon?
ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.a: It brings cheaper hydroelectric power from dams on the Columbia River. At the time, it was estimated to save Los Angeles customers about 600,000 dollars a day.
ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.quote: at the time it was estimated to save Los Angeles customers about 600,000 dollars a day

ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.q: How much power does the Sylmar Converter Station handle?
alts: How many homes does it power?
Is it a lot of power?
ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.a: It converts up to 3,100 megawatts. That's enough power for two to three million Los Angeles households.
ca159-power-from-the-columbia-river.quote: That is enough power for two to three million Los Angeles households.

ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.q: What are the Los Angeles Aqueduct Cascades?
alts: What is that water staircase on the hill?
Why is there a waterfall by the freeway?
ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.a: It's the end of the Los Angeles Aqueduct, where water from the eastern Sierra Nevada tumbles down a long concrete water staircase on the hillside.
ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.quote: water from the eastern Sierra Nevada tumbles down the Cascades, the end of the Los Angeles Aqueduct

ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.q: When did the first water reach the Cascades?
alts: When did the water first come down, like, how long ago?
ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.a: The first water arrived on November 5, 1913. Chief engineer William Mulholland said, "There it is. Take it."
ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.quote: When the first water arrived on November 5, 1913, chief engineer William Mulholland said, "There it is. Take it."

ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.q: How does the water get to the Los Angeles Aqueduct Cascades?
alts: How does it get here without pumps?
How does the water get all the way down here, Dad?
ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.a: It moves by gravity alone. The original aqueduct runs 233 miles from the eastern Sierra Nevada.
ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.quote: The original aqueduct runs 233 miles and moves its water by gravity alone.

ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.q: How hard was it to build the Los Angeles Aqueduct?
alts: Who built it and how long did it take?
Did lots of people have to build it?
ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.a: It took thousands of workers and 164 tunnels, a job compared to the Panama Canal.
ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.quote: Building it took thousands of workers and 164 tunnels, a job compared to the Panama Canal.

ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.q: Where does the Cascades water come from?
alts: Where does it come from originally?
Where's all this water from, anyway?
ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.a: It comes from the Owens Valley, homeland of the Paiute people. The diversions ended most farming there and devastated Owens Lake.
ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.quote: The water comes from the Owens Valley, homeland of the Paiute people, where the diversions ended most farming and devastated Owens Lake.

ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.q: How far can the water travel to reach the Cascades?
alts: How far does it go, like, total?
How long is the whole thing?
ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.a: After an extension finished in 1940, water can travel 338 miles from near Tioga Pass to reach the Cascades.
ca161-los-angeles-aqueduct-cascades.quote: An extension finished in 1940 moved the system's northernmost intake to near Tioga Pass, so water can travel 338 miles to reach the Cascades.

ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.q: Why is it called the Clarence Wayne Dean Memorial Interchange?
alts: Who was that guy it's named for?
ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.a: It is named for Clarence Wayne Dean, a Los Angeles police motorcycle officer killed in the 1994 collapse. He was riding to work when he could not stop in time and fell from a broken ramp.
ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.quote: On January 17, 1994, Los Angeles police motorcycle officer Clarence Wayne Dean was riding to work when he could not stop in time and fell from a broken ramp.

ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.q: How wide is I-5 at the Newhall Pass Interchange?
alts: How many lanes does it have?
How many lanes are here, like a lot?
ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.a: Parts of I-5 here are up to 21 lanes wide. It's a tangle of ramps where I-5 meets the Antelope Valley Freeway.
ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.quote: This tangle of ramps, where I-5 meets the Antelope Valley Freeway, is the Newhall Pass interchange, and parts of I-5 here are up to 21 lanes wide.

ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.q: What are the separate truck lanes at the Newhall Pass Interchange?
alts: What are those lanes that loop around it?
Why are there extra lanes looping around?
What are the side lanes for?
ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.a: The separate truck lanes that loop around the main lanes are the original four-lane freeway, built as US 99.
ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.quote: The separate truck lanes that loop around the main lanes are the original four-lane freeway, built as US 99.

ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.q: Where do the main lanes of I-5 go at Newhall Pass?
alts: How does the main road get through here?
Why does the freeway go around Newhall Pass?
ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.a: The main lanes follow a bypass through Weldon and Gavin canyons, built by 1930 to avoid Newhall Pass itself.
ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.quote: The main lanes follow a bypass through Weldon and Gavin canyons, built by 1930 to avoid Newhall Pass itself.

ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.q: What exit is the Newhall Pass Interchange?
alts: What exit are we looking for?
ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.a: It's Exit 162. Look for flyover ramps curving high above the lanes on tall columns.
ca162-newhall-pass-interchange.quote: Look for flyover ramps curving high above the lanes on tall columns.

ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.q: What happened at the Oak of the Golden Dream?
alts: What happened here at that tree?
Why is there a gold tree thing here?
ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.a: Francisco López found gold flakes clinging to wild onion roots near an oak tree on March 9, 1842. The state's landmark plaque calls it California's first authenticated gold discovery.
ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.quote: Francisco López made what the state's landmark plaque calls California's first authenticated gold discovery, on March 9, 1842.

ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.q: How does the Oak of the Golden Dream compare to the Sutter's Mill gold strike?
alts: Was it before the famous gold rush find?
Did they find gold here before Sutter's Mill?
ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.a: It came first. López's find happened six years before the famous strike at Sutter's Mill.
ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.quote: That was six years before the famous strike at Sutter's Mill, and the tree is now called the Oak of the Golden Dream.

ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.q: Did Francisco López just stumble onto the gold by accident?
alts: Was it really luck that he found it?
Did he know what he was looking for?
ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.a: Not really. The dream story is just legend. López had studied mineralogy at the University of Mexico and was actually searching for gold.
ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.quote: In fact he had studied mineralogy at the University of Mexico and was searching for gold.

ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.q: How many people came to mine gold near the Oak of the Golden Dream?
alts: Did lots of people come after that?
Did a bunch of miners show up?
ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.a: About 2,000 people came, mostly from the Mexican state of Sonora. They mined by panning, sluicing and dry washing.
ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.quote: About 2,000 people, mostly from the Mexican state of Sonora, came to mine the area by panning, sluicing and dry washing.

ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.q: What happened to the mine at the Oak of the Golden Dream?
alts: What happened to the gold mine there?
ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.a: During the Mexican-American War, the rancho's owner destroyed the mine to keep it from the United States.
ca162-oak-of-the-golden-dream.quote: During the Mexican-American War, the rancho's owner destroyed the mine to keep it from the United States.

alts: What's this cut in the mountain, Mom?
ca163-beale-s-cut.a: It's a slot dug through the mountain with picks and shovels, so stagecoaches could cross the pass. It was eventually deepened to 90 feet.
ca163-beale-s-cut.quote: stagecoaches crossed this pass through Beale's Cut, a slot dug through the mountain with picks and shovels and eventually deepened to 90 feet

alts: Who made this giant hole, Dad?
ca163-beale-s-cut.a: Edward Beale won the right to collect tolls here in 1863. He used Chinese immigrant workers to do most of the digging.
ca163-beale-s-cut.quote: Edward Beale, who won the right to collect tolls here in 1863, used Chinese immigrant workers to do most of the digging.

ca163-beale-s-cut.q: What is Beale's Cut famous for in movies?
alts: Was it ever in a movie?
Did a cowboy really jump over it?
ca163-beale-s-cut.a: In a 1923 John Ford film, cowboy star Tom Mix is filmed leaping across it. Historians still debate whether it was Mix, a stuntman or a camera trick.
ca163-beale-s-cut.quote: In a 1923 film by director John Ford, cowboy star Tom Mix is filmed leaping across it

ca163-beale-s-cut.q: Did stagecoaches really go through Beale's Cut?
alts: Did they use it back then?
Did real cowboy wagons go through there?
ca163-beale-s-cut.a: Yes. Butterfield Overland Mail coaches running to San Francisco used the cut, back before tunnels and freeways.
ca163-beale-s-cut.quote: Butterfield Overland Mail coaches running to San Francisco used the cut.

ca163-beale-s-cut.q: What happened to Beale's Cut in the earthquake?
alts: Did the mountain fall down, Dad?
ca163-beale-s-cut.a: The 1994 earthquake collapsed part of the cut. That left it about 30 feet deep.
ca163-beale-s-cut.quote: the 1994 earthquake collapsed part of the cut, leaving it about 30 feet deep.

alts: Who was he, the guy this park is named after?
ca167-william-s-hart-park.a: William S. Hart was a silent film cowboy and one of the most popular movie stars of the late 1910s. He was known for gritty westerns and a pinto horse named Fritz.
ca167-william-s-hart-park.quote: Hart was one of the most popular movie stars of the late 1910s, known for gritty westerns and a pinto horse named Fritz.

ca167-william-s-hart-park.q: What can we see at William S. Hart Park?
alts: What is there to do at it?
Are there animals there, or just old stuff?
ca167-william-s-hart-park.a: You'll find his Spanish-style mansion, trails and a barnyard of farm animals, all on a 265-acre ranch. The mansion holds his collection, including Native American artifacts and works by Charles Russell.
ca167-william-s-hart-park.quote: now a 265-acre park with his Spanish-style mansion, trails and a barnyard of farm animals.

ca167-william-s-hart-park.q: How did William S. Hart's ranch become a park?
alts: Why is that ranch a public park now?
Why can we go to his house?
ca167-william-s-hart-park.a: Hart left the ranch to Los Angeles County when he died in 1946. He said the people gave him their nickels, dimes and quarters, and he wanted them to have his home.
ca167-william-s-hart-park.quote: Hart left it to Los Angeles County when he died in 1946.

ca167-william-s-hart-park.q: What was William S. Hart's ranch called?
alts: Did it have a name before it was a park?
What did he call his house?
ca167-william-s-hart-park.a: Hart called his ranch La Loma de los Vientos. He retired there after his 1925 film Tumbleweeds and made no more feature films.
ca167-william-s-hart-park.quote: he retired to this ranch, called La Loma de los Vientos, and made no more feature films.

ca167-william-s-hart-park.q: Did William S. Hart always act in cowboy movies?
alts: Was he an actor his whole life?
How did he get into the movies?
When did he start acting in films?
ca167-william-s-hart-park.a: No. He came to the movies from the Shakespearean stage in 1914, when he was nearly 50.
ca167-william-s-hart-park.quote: He came to the movies from the Shakespearean stage in 1914, when he was nearly 50.

ca167-william-s-hart-park.q: Who runs William S. Hart Park today?
alts: Is it still run by the county?
Can we tour that house now?
Who's in charge of it now?
ca167-william-s-hart-park.a: The City of Santa Clarita took over the park and museum from the county in 2025. It offers guided house tours.
ca167-william-s-hart-park.quote: The City of Santa Clarita took over the park and museum from the county in 2025 and offers guided house tours.

ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.q: What is special about the Pico Number 4 oil well?
alts: Why do people say that well matters?
What's the deal with the old oil well?
ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.a: It became the first commercially successful oil well in the western United States after striking oil on September 26, 1876. It is often called the longest continuously operating oil well in the world.
ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.quote: Well Number 4 struck oil on September 26, 1876, and became the first commercially successful oil well in the western United States.

ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.q: Who built the Pico Number 4 oil well?
alts: Who was the guy that made that thing?
ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.a: Driller Charles Mentry built the drill stem from old railroad car axles. In 1877, oil spurted to the top of the 65-foot derrick.
ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.quote: Driller Charles Mentry built his drill stem from old railroad car axles, and in 1877 oil spurted to the top of the 65-foot derrick.

ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.q: What happened to the oil from Pico Number 4?
alts: Where did the oil go after it came out?
ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.a: Mentry laid California's first oil pipeline to a refinery in Newhall. That refinery is called the oldest existing refinery in the world.
ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.quote: He then laid California's first oil pipeline, to a refinery in Newhall that is called the oldest existing refinery in the world.

ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.q: What was Mentryville near the Pico Number 4 oil well?
alts: What was the town near it?
Was there a town by the oil well?
Was there a bar in that old oil town?
ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.a: Mentryville was a boom town down the canyon, with a schoolhouse and a gas-lit tennis court. It had no bar, because Mentry reportedly banned drinking and swearing.
ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.quote: The boom town of Mentryville grew up just down the canyon, with a schoolhouse and a gas-lit tennis court but no bar

ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.q: Did people use oil here before the Pico Number 4 well?
alts: Did anyone know about oil there before it?
Did Native people use the oil?
ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.a: Yes. Long before the well, the Tataviam and Tongva people used oil from seeps here as medicine.
ca167-pico-number-4-oil-well.quote: Long before, the Tataviam and Tongva people used oil from seeps here as medicine.

alts: Why are they called the Tataviam?
ca169-tataviam-homeland.a: Tataviam means people on the south slope. The name comes from the neighboring Kitanemuk language.
ca169-tataviam-homeland.quote: a name that means people on the south slope in the neighboring Kitanemuk language

alts: Who were they and where did they live?
ca169-tataviam-homeland.a: The Tataviam are the native people whose homeland centers on the Santa Clarita Valley. They lived in about 20 villages in and around the valley.
ca169-tataviam-homeland.quote: They lived in about 20 villages in and around the valley, with summer and winter settlements

ca169-tataviam-homeland.q: What did the Portolá expedition see at the Tataviam village?
alts: What happened when they arrived here in 1769?
What did the explorers find here?
ca169-tataviam-homeland.a: When the Portolá expedition camped by the river in August 1769, they found a large village. They even watched a wedding celebration.
ca169-tataviam-homeland.quote: found a large village and watched a wedding celebration

ca169-tataviam-homeland.q: Are the Tataviam still around today?
ca169-tataviam-homeland.a: Yes, their tribe today is the Fernandeño Tataviam Band of Mission Indians, governed from San Fernando. Their land conservancy, founded in 2018, has had more than 550 acres returned.
ca169-tataviam-homeland.quote: Its land conservancy, founded in 2018, has had more than 550 acres of ancestral land returned.

ca170-santa-clara-river.q: How long is the Santa Clara River?
alts: How far does that river go, like how many miles?
ca170-santa-clara-river.a: The Santa Clara River runs 83 miles to the Pacific Ocean. It's also one of the least altered rivers in Southern California.
ca170-santa-clara-river.quote: runs 83 miles to the Pacific and is one of the least altered rivers in Southern California

ca170-santa-clara-river.q: Why is it called the Santa Clara River?
alts: Who named this river and why, and what's it named after?
ca170-santa-clara-river.a: Spanish explorers named it on August 9, 1769, for Saint Clare of Assisi.
ca170-santa-clara-river.quote: Spanish explorers named it on August 9, 1769, for Saint Clare of Assisi

ca170-santa-clara-river.q: What animals live along the Santa Clara River?
alts: Are there any fish or turtles in that river, kids want to know?
ca170-santa-clara-river.a: The river still shelters threatened wildlife, including the unarmored threespine stickleback, steelhead trout, southwestern pond turtles and least Bell's vireos.
ca170-santa-clara-river.quote: The river still shelters threatened wildlife. Among them are a small fish called the unarmored threespine stickleback, steelhead trout, southwestern pond turtles and least Bell's vireos.

ca170-santa-clara-river.q: Why is the area called Santa Clarita?
alts: Why is it called Santa Clarita?
Why's it a little Santa Clara, what does that mean?
ca170-santa-clara-river.a: The valley became known as little Santa Clara, Santa Clarita, to tell it apart from Santa Clara in Northern California.
ca170-santa-clara-river.quote: the valley later became known as little Santa Clara, Santa Clarita, to tell it apart from Santa Clara in Northern California

ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.q: How old is Six Flags Magic Mountain?
alts: When did that park open, like how long ago?
ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.a: Six Flags Magic Mountain opened on May 29, 1971.
ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.quote: belong to Six Flags Magic Mountain, which opened on May 29, 1971.

ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.q: What is Six Flags Magic Mountain famous for?
alts: Why is that park such a big deal?
ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.a: Roller coasters. In 2022 it became the first amusement park to offer 20 coasters, and it still has one of the biggest collections of coasters anywhere.
ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.quote: In 2022 it became the first amusement park to offer 20 roller coasters.

ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.q: Who built Six Flags Magic Mountain?
alts: Who made that park, like who started it?
ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.a: The Newhall Land and Farming Company built it, in partnership with Sea World's founder. Six Flags bought the park in 1979.
ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.quote: The park was built by the Newhall Land and Farming Company in partnership with Sea World's founder.

ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.q: Why is it called Six Flags Magic Mountain?
alts: Is there a real magic mountain there?
ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.a: It took its name from Magic Mountain, a peak east of the Santa Clarita Valley.
ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.quote: It took its name from Magic Mountain, a peak east of the Santa Clarita Valley.

ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.q: What was special about the Colossus coaster at Magic Mountain?
alts: Was there a really big wooden coaster there?
ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.a: Colossus, from 1978, was then the fastest and largest dual-track wooden coaster in the world.
ca170-six-flags-magic-mountain.quote: Its Colossus coaster of 1978 was then the fastest and largest dual-track wooden coaster in the world.

ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.q: What was the Death Valley rescue?
alts: Who got saved in Death Valley?
ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.a: In January 1850, William Lewis Manly and John Rogers got supplies and animals here to rescue their gold-seeking emigrant party, stranded and starving in Death Valley.
ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.quote: In January 1850, William Lewis Manly and John Rogers reached it and got supplies and animals to rescue their gold-seeking emigrant party, stranded and starving in Death Valley

ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.q: Who went to rescue the stranded party?
alts: Who were the rescuers at that place?
Who saved the people, who were the guys?
ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.a: William Lewis Manly and John Rogers reached the rancho headquarters in January 1850 and got supplies and animals to help their stranded emigrant party.
ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.quote: In January 1850, William Lewis Manly and John Rogers reached it and got supplies and animals to rescue their gold-seeking emigrant party

ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.q: How big was Rancho San Francisco?
ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.a: The rancho covered 48,612 acres, granted in 1839 to Antonio del Valle. Much of today's Santa Clarita lies inside its old boundaries.
ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.quote: The rancho's 48,612 acres were granted in 1839 to Antonio del Valle, and much of today's Santa Clarita lies inside its old boundaries.

ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.q: How did Newhall and Saugus get their names?
alts: Where did the names come from, like Saugus?
ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.a: Henry Newhall gave the railroad a right of way, and it named its new town Newhall. He named the first station Saugus, after his hometown in Massachusetts.
ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.quote: Newhall gave the Southern Pacific a right of way, and the railroad named its new town Newhall. He named the first station on the line Saugus, after his hometown in Massachusetts.

ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.q: What happened to the rancho later?
alts: Who owns that land now, or did it get sold?
ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.a: After floods and droughts, the family sold most of it in 1862, and it eventually passed to Henry Newhall. In 1936 his grandson-in-law, Atholl McBean, found oil on the property.
ca172-the-death-valley-rescue.quote: After floods and droughts, the family sold most of it in 1862, and it eventually passed to Henry Newhall, who paid 2 dollars an acre.

ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.q: What happened at the St. Francis Dam?
alts: Mom, what's the story with that dam?
ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.a: The St. Francis Dam failed just before midnight on March 12, 1928, in San Francisquito Canyon. The flood killed at least 431 people as it raced down to the sea.
ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.quote: Just before midnight on March 12, 1928, the St. Francis Dam failed in San Francisquito Canyon, about 10 miles north of Santa Clarita.

ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.q: How many people died in the St. Francis Dam disaster?
alts: How many people did it kill?
Did a lot of people die there?
ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.a: At least 431 people were killed. It is considered the second-deadliest dam failure in American history.
ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.quote: killing at least 431 people. It is considered the second-deadliest dam failure in American history.

ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.q: Who built the St. Francis Dam?
alts: Who was in charge of building that dam?
ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.a: It was part of the Los Angeles Aqueduct system, designed and built under William Mulholland. Its failure ended his career.
ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.quote: The dam was part of the Los Angeles Aqueduct system, designed and built under William Mulholland, and its failure ended his career.

ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.q: How far did the St. Francis Dam flood travel?
alts: Did the water really reach the ocean?
ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.a: The flood tore down the canyon and along the Santa Clara River to the sea. It reached the ocean south of Ventura around 5:30 in the morning, nearly two miles wide.
ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.quote: The flood reached the ocean south of Ventura around 5:30 in the morning, nearly two miles wide.

ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.q: What did the St. Francis Dam flood destroy?
alts: Did it wipe out a town?
ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.a: It flooded at least four miles of the state's main north-south highway and washed away the settlement of Castaic Junction. Downstream, 84 workers died at a power company construction camp.
ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.quote: It flooded at least four miles of the state's main north-south highway and washed away the settlement of Castaic Junction.

ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.q: Is the St. Francis Dam disaster site a national monument?
ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.a: Yes. In 2019, Congress made the site the Saint Francis Dam Disaster National Monument.
ca172-st-francis-dam-disaster.quote: In 2019, Congress made the site the Saint Francis Dam Disaster National Monument.

ca173-val-verde-the-black-palm-springs.q: Why is Val Verde called the Black Palm Springs?
alts: Why do they call it that?
Why's it called the Black Palm Springs, Mom?
ca173-val-verde-the-black-palm-springs.a: Black investors founded it as a resort community in 1924, when African Americans were often barred from public beaches and pools. Ella Fitzgerald and Lena Horne appeared there.
ca173-val-verde-the-black-palm-springs.quote: Black investors led by Sidney Dones founded a resort community in 1924, when African Americans were often barred from public beaches and pools.

ca173-val-verde-the-black-palm-springs.a: Black investors led by Sidney Dones founded it in 1924. It began as Eureka Villa, on ranch land whose owner, Laura Janes, had opened it to African Americans in the 1910s.
ca173-val-verde-the-black-palm-springs.quote: It began as Eureka Villa, on ranch land whose white owner, Laura Janes, had opened it to African Americans in the 1910s.

alts: What kind of name is Val Verde?
ca173-val-verde-the-black-palm-springs.a: Val Verde is Spanish for green valley. Today it is a community by that name, in the hills west of the freeway.
ca173-val-verde-the-black-palm-springs.quote: Today it is the community of Val Verde, Spanish for green valley.

ca173-val-verde-the-black-palm-springs.q: What happened to Val Verde after the 1960s?
alts: Why did people move away, Mom?
ca173-val-verde-the-black-palm-springs.a: After civil rights reforms in the 1960s opened other neighborhoods, many families moved away.
ca173-val-verde-the-black-palm-springs.quote: After civil rights reforms in the 1960s opened other neighborhoods, many families moved away.

ca176-five-mile-grade-crossover.q: Why are the downhill lanes on a gentler grade at the Five Mile Grade?
alts: Why is it built so the downhill part is gentler?
Why did they make the hill easier for trucks?
What's the deal with the runaway trucks?
ca176-five-mile-grade-crossover.a: The downhill lanes got a gentler grade to cut down on runaway trucks.
ca176-five-mile-grade-crossover.quote: the downhill lanes got a gentler grade to cut down on runaway trucks

ca176-five-mile-grade-crossover.q: What is the old road next to the Five Mile Grade crossover?
alts: What's the older road next to it?
What was here before the freeway, kid?
Is there an old road beside it?
ca176-five-mile-grade-crossover.a: One set of lanes is the old four-lane Ridge Route Alternate, widened between 1948 and 1952. The other was added to the east, next to the original 1915 Ridge Route.
ca176-five-mile-grade-crossover.quote: One set of lanes is the old four-lane Ridge Route Alternate, widened between 1948 and 1952.

ca176-five-mile-grade-crossover.q: How big did the Five Mile Grade freeway end up being?
alts: How many lanes did it end up with?
ca176-five-mile-grade-crossover.a: The plan began as a six-lane freeway and grew to eight lanes before the work was finished in 1970.
ca176-five-mile-grade-crossover.quote: The plan began as a six-lane freeway and grew to eight lanes before the work was finished in 1970.

alts: Where does the name of it come from?
What does Castaic mean, anyone know?
ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.a: Castaic comes from the Chumash word Kaštiq, which means the eye.
ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.quote: Castaic takes its name from the Chumash word Kaštiq, meaning the eye.

ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.q: How old is Castaic Dam and how big is it?
alts: Is the big dam really huge, like how tall?
ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.a: Castaic Dam was finished in 1973. It rises 340 feet and stretches nearly a mile.
ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.quote: Castaic Dam, finished in 1973, rises 340 feet and stretches nearly a mile, holding Castaic Lake

ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.q: What is Castaic Lake used for?
alts: What does it do, is it just a lake?
Why did they make this lake, where does the water go?
ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.a: It sits at the end of the West Branch of the California Aqueduct. Water from Northern California rests here before flowing on to millions of people around Los Angeles.
ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.quote: Water from Northern California rests here before flowing on to millions of people around Los Angeles.

ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.q: How did the town of Castaic begin?
alts: When did it start as a town?
How did this place get started, long ago?
ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.a: Modern Castaic began in 1887 as a Southern Pacific siding called Castaic Junction.
ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.quote: Modern Castaic began in 1887 as a Southern Pacific siding called Castaic Junction.

ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.q: Was anything famous filmed at Castaic Lake?
alts: Was that lake in a movie or TV show?
Was it on TV, like Power Rangers?
ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.a: Yes. Many of the Mighty Morphin Power Rangers show's action scenes were filmed at the lake.
ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.quote: Fans of the Mighty Morphin Power Rangers may know the lake, because many of the show's action scenes were filmed here.

ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.q: What happened here in the Hughes Fire?
alts: Did it burn near that lake?
Was there a big fire by the lake?
ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.a: In January 2025 the Hughes Fire burned 10,425 acres east of the lake. At its height, more than 30,000 people were under evacuation orders.
ca176-castaic-lake-and-its-name.quote: In January 2025 the Hughes Fire burned 10,425 acres east of the lake, and at its height more than 30,000 people were under evacuation orders.

ca183-the-old-ridge-route.q: What was the old Ridge Route?
ca183-the-old-ridge-route.a: It was the first paved highway linking Los Angeles directly with the San Joaquin Valley. The original 1915 road winds along the ridgetops from Castaic toward Gorman.
ca183-the-old-ridge-route.quote: It was the first paved highway linking Los Angeles directly with the San Joaquin Valley

ca183-the-old-ridge-route.q: How twisty was the old Ridge Route?
alts: How many turns did it have?
Why was that road so curvy, mom?
ca183-the-old-ridge-route.a: Very twisty. Between Castaic and Gorman it had 697 turns, which added up to about 97 complete circles in 36 miles.
ca183-the-old-ridge-route.quote: between Castaic and Gorman its 697 turns added up to about 97 complete circles in 36 miles

ca183-the-old-ridge-route.q: How fast could cars go on the old Ridge Route?
alts: What was the speed limit on it?
Could cars go fast on that old road?
ca183-the-old-ridge-route.a: Not fast at all. Between Castaic and Quail Lake the speed limit was 15 miles an hour.
ca183-the-old-ridge-route.quote: Between Castaic and Quail Lake the speed limit was 15 miles an hour.

ca183-the-old-ridge-route.q: Where did travelers stay on the old Ridge Route?
alts: Where did people eat and sleep on that road?
ca183-the-old-ridge-route.a: Roadhouses served travelers along the way, including the National Forest Inn, the Tumble Inn and Sandberg's Summit Hotel, a log lodge from 1914.
ca183-the-old-ridge-route.quote: Roadhouses served travelers along the way, including the National Forest Inn, the Tumble Inn and Sandberg's Summit Hotel, a log lodge from 1914

ca183-the-old-ridge-route.q: Is the old Ridge Route still open today?
alts: Can we drive on that old road?
ca183-the-old-ridge-route.a: Much of it is now closed to cars. About 17.6 miles of it in the Angeles National Forest went on the National Register of Historic Places in 1997.
ca183-the-old-ridge-route.quote: About 17.6 miles of it in the Angeles National Forest went on the National Register of Historic Places in 1997

ca183-the-old-ridge-route.q: Who helped get the old Ridge Route protected?
alts: Who got that road on the historic register?
ca183-the-old-ridge-route.a: Retired engineer Harrison Scott deserves much of the credit. About 17.6 miles of the road went on the National Register of Historic Places in 1997, thanks largely to him.
ca183-the-old-ridge-route.quote: went on the National Register of Historic Places in 1997, thanks largely to retired engineer Harrison Scott.

ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.q: What is Highway 99 under the lake?
alts: What is that road under the water?
Is there really a road under the lake?
ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.a: It's an old highway now covered by Pyramid Lake. It opened in 1933 as the three-lane Ridge Route Alternate, later US 99, through the canyon of Piru Creek.
ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.quote: In 1933 the three-lane Ridge Route Alternate, later US 99, opened through the canyon of Piru Creek

ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.q: How did Highway 99 end up under Pyramid Lake?
alts: How did it end up underwater?
Kid: how does a road get under a lake?
ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.a: After Pyramid Dam was finished, the rising water covered the old road. By 1972 it was fully under the lake.
ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.quote: After Pyramid Dam was finished, rising water covered the old road, and by 1972 it was fully under the lake.

ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.q: What was the suicide lane on old Highway 99?
alts: What was that middle lane for?
Kid: why was the middle lane scary?
ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.a: It was the middle lane of the three-lane road. Drivers in both directions used it for passing, which is how it got its nickname.
ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.quote: with a middle lane that drivers in both directions used for passing, nicknamed the suicide lane

ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.q: Why is it called Pyramid Lake?
alts: Why is that lake named that?
Kid: is there a pyramid in the lake?
Where did the name come from?
ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.a: It's named for Pyramid Rock, a pointed chunk of mountain left behind in 1932 when road builders cut through a ridge for the highway. The rock still stands in front of the dam.
ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.quote: The lake takes its name from Pyramid Rock, a pointed chunk of mountain left behind in 1932

ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.q: Can you still see any of the old Highway 99 today?
alts: Is any of it still above water?
Kid: can we see the old road?
ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.a: Yes. A piece of the old road at the lake's north end now serves as a boat ramp. The dam there stands 386 feet high.
ca191-highway-99-under-the-lake.quote: Today a piece of the old road at the lake's north end serves as a boat ramp, and the dam stands 386 feet high.

ca191-vista-del-lago.q: How much water is in the lake at Vista del Lago?
alts: How much water does it hold?
Is the lake really big, how much water is in it?
ca191-vista-del-lago.a: Pyramid Lake holds about 180,000 acre-feet of State Water Project water, pumped up from the San Joaquin Valley and over the Tehachapi Mountains.
ca191-vista-del-lago.quote: The lake holds about 180,000 acre-feet of State Water Project water, pumped up from the San Joaquin Valley and over the Tehachapi Mountains.

ca191-vista-del-lago.q: Where does the water go after Pyramid Lake?
alts: Where does it go from there?
Does the water just stay in the lake?
ca191-vista-del-lago.a: It drops 1,060 feet through the 7.2-mile Angeles Tunnel, 30 feet across, to the Castaic Power Plant at the upper end of Castaic Lake.
ca191-vista-del-lago.quote: From the lake, water drops 1,060 feet through the 7.2-mile Angeles Tunnel, 30 feet across, to the Castaic Power Plant at the upper end of Castaic Lake.

ca191-vista-del-lago.q: What does the Castaic Power Plant do?
alts: What does it do with the water?
ca191-vista-del-lago.a: It makes electricity at times of peak demand, and it can also pump water back uphill to store energy.
ca191-vista-del-lago.quote: The plant makes electricity at times of peak demand, and it can pump water back uphill to store energy.

ca191-vista-del-lago.q: Can you boat or fish at Pyramid Lake?
alts: Can we do stuff on it?
Can we go on the lake in a boat?
ca191-vista-del-lago.a: Yes, Pyramid Lake offers boating, fishing and picnic sites, including five that can be reached only by boat.
ca191-vista-del-lago.quote: Pyramid Lake offers boating, fishing and picnic sites, including five that can be reached only by boat.

ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.q: What is Quail Lake used for?
alts: Why is there a lake here, is it for swimming?
ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.a: Quail Lake stores water for the West Branch of the California Aqueduct. Water pumped up to the lake flows by gravity through a pipeline to a power plant at Pyramid Lake.
ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.quote: stores water for the West Branch of the California Aqueduct. Water pumped up to the lake flows by gravity through a pipeline to a power plant at Pyramid Lake.

ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.q: Is Quail Lake really on the San Andreas Fault?
alts: Is it actually sitting on the fault?
Wait, is this lake on top of an earthquake crack?
ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.a: Yes. Quail Lake lies in the rift zone of the San Andreas Fault, and the fault itself slices right through nearby Gorman.
ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.quote: lies in the rift zone of the San Andreas Fault and stores water for the West Branch of the California Aqueduct. Water pumped up

ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.q: When did the San Andreas Fault last break here?
alts: When was the last earthquake near it?
When did the ground last shake here, how long ago?
ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.a: This part of the San Andreas last broke on January 9, 1857. It is often called the last Big One in Southern California, and this section has not had a large quake since.
ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.quote: This part of the San Andreas last broke on January 9, 1857, in one of the largest earthquakes recorded in the United States, about magnitude 7.9.

ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.q: How big was the 1857 earthquake near Quail Lake?
alts: Was the quake here a really big one?
ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.a: It was about magnitude 7.9, one of the largest earthquakes recorded in the United States. The rupture ran about 225 miles, from Parkfield to Wrightwood.
ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.quote: The rupture ran about 225 miles, from Parkfield to Wrightwood, and the ground slipped about 15 feet on average.

ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.q: How far did the ground move in the 1857 earthquake?
alts: How much did the ground slip there?
How far did the earth move in that quake?
ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.a: The ground slipped about 15 feet on average along a rupture about 225 miles long, running from Parkfield to Wrightwood.
ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.quote: The rupture ran about 225 miles, from Parkfield to Wrightwood, and the ground slipped about 15 feet on average.

ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.q: Did anyone die in the 1857 earthquake near Quail Lake?
alts: Was anybody hurt in that quake?
Did people die when the ground shook here?
ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.a: Only two deaths were reported. One was a woman in nearby Gorman, killed when an adobe house collapsed.
ca198-quail-lake-on-the-fault.quote: One of only two deaths reported was a woman in nearby Gorman, killed when an adobe house collapsed.

ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.q: Why is the town called Gorman?
ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.a: It's named for James Gorman, who reportedly worked at Fort Tejon as a teamster and herder. In 1867 or 1868 he bought the log roadhouse here, which became known as Gorman's Station.
ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.quote: The town is named for James Gorman, who reportedly worked at Fort Tejon as a teamster and herder and in 1867 or 1868 bought the log roadhouse here

ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.q: How old is Gorman as a place people stop?
alts: How long has it been around?
Did people stop here a long time ago?
ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.a: Very old. People have stopped here for centuries. It was the Tataviam village of Kulshra'jek, a trading crossroads, and a local historian calls it one of California's oldest continuously used roadside rest stops.
ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.quote: People have stopped here for centuries: it was the Tataviam village of Kulshra'jek, a trading crossroads

ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.q: What happened here with the stagecoaches?
alts: What did stagecoaches do at Gorman's Station?
Did cowboys and horses come through here?
ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.a: Stagecoach drivers changed horses here. They used six horses to pull a coach up the pass from Bakersfield.
ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.quote: Stagecoach drivers changed horses here, using six to pull a coach up the pass from Bakersfield.

ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.q: Why are the hills around Gorman covered in flowers?
alts: When does it get all orange and purple?
Why are the hills so colorful?
ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.a: After a wet winter, spring poppies and lupine can blanket the hills around Gorman. Look for the orange California poppies, best in April and May.
ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.quote: California poppies and lupine can blanket the hills around Gorman.

ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.q: What was the yellow umbrella art at Gorman?
alts: Did someone put umbrellas on the mountains here?
Why were there giant yellow umbrellas?
ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.a: In 1991 the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude placed 1,760 large yellow umbrellas along the roadsides and up the mountainsides around Gorman and Tejon Pass. The show closed early after a woman was crushed by a windblown umbrella.
ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.quote: In 1991 the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude placed 1,760 large yellow umbrellas from the roadsides up the mountainsides around Gorman and Tejon Pass

ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.q: Can we do a wildflower tour near Gorman?
alts: Is there a place to see flowers up close?
Can kids see the flowers on a tour?
ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.a: Next door, Hungry Valley State Vehicular Recreation Area offers guided wildflower tours from mid-April through May. Its guide notes poppies close on cloudy, windy days and at night.
ca202-gorman-and-its-wildflowers.quote: offers guided wildflower tours from mid-April through May; its guide notes that poppies close on cloudy, windy days and at night.

ca204-tejon-pass-summit.q: How high is Tejon Pass summit?
alts: How high up is it here?
Are we really high up right now?
ca204-tejon-pass-summit.a: Near the top of Tejon Pass, I-5 reaches 4,144 feet. That's the highest point of the freeway in California.
ca204-tejon-pass-summit.quote: Near the top of Tejon Pass, I-5 reaches 4,144 feet, its highest point in California, close to the line between Los Angeles and Kern counties.

ca204-tejon-pass-summit.q: Why is it called Tejon Pass?
alts: Why's it named after a badger?
ca204-tejon-pass-summit.a: Tejón is Spanish for badger. The dead badger behind the name was actually found in 1806 at a different canyon, about 15 miles northeast.
ca204-tejon-pass-summit.quote: Tejón is Spanish for badger, though the dead badger behind the name was found in 1806 at a different canyon, about 15 miles northeast.

ca204-tejon-pass-summit.q: What was Tejon Pass called before?
alts: Did it always have that name?
Did it used to be called something else?
ca204-tejon-pass-summit.a: Lieutenant Pedro Fages crossed in 1772 and called it Portezuelo de Cortes. Later it was the Castac Pass, then the Fort Tejon Pass, and finally just Tejon Pass.
ca204-tejon-pass-summit.quote: Lieutenant Pedro Fages crossed this pass in 1772 and called it Portezuelo de Cortes. Later it was the Castac Pass, then the Fort Tejon Pass

ca204-tejon-pass-summit.q: What makes Tejon Pass special geologically?
alts: What's special about the ground here?
ca204-tejon-pass-summit.a: The pass sits where California's two largest faults, the San Andreas and the Garlock, meet.
ca204-tejon-pass-summit.quote: The pass sits where California's two largest faults, the San Andreas and the Garlock, meet.

ca204-tejon-pass-summit.q: Does snow close I-5 at Tejon Pass?
alts: Does it get closed by snow there?
ca204-tejon-pass-summit.a: Yes. Snow and ice close I-5 here an average of three to five times a winter, between October and April. The Highway Patrol usually closes it outright because of the steep grade and heavy traffic.
ca204-tejon-pass-summit.quote: Snow and ice close I-5 here an average of three to five times a winter, between October and April.

ca204-tejon-pass-summit.q: What exit is Tejon Pass summit?
alts: Which exit do we take for it?
ca204-tejon-pass-summit.a: Tejon Pass summit is at exit 204.

ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.q: What happened at the Brink's jewelry heist?
alts: What happened there with the jewelry?
Mom, what did the thieves do?
ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.a: Thieves cut the padlock on a Brink's trailer at a truck stop and stole about two dozen of its 73 bags of jewelry. It all took place within 27 minutes.
ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.quote: Within 27 minutes, thieves cut the trailer's padlock and made off with about two dozen of its 73 bags of jewelry.

ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.q: When did the Brink's jewelry heist happen?
alts: Was this a long time ago, Dad?
ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.a: It happened at 2 in the morning on July 11, 2022, when the Brink's truck pulled into a truck stop at the Frazier Mountain Park Road exit.
ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.quote: At 2 in the morning on July 11, 2022, a Brink's tractor-trailer carrying jewelry from a show in San Mateo to one in Pasadena

ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.q: How much was stolen in the Brink's jewelry heist?
alts: How many millions did they get?
ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.a: Brink's put the loss at 8.7 million dollars, but some estimates reach 100 million, since some jewelers admitted listing less than the true value to keep insurance costs down.
ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.quote: Brink's put the loss at 8.7 million dollars, based on the values the jewelers had declared.

ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.q: How did the thieves pull off the Brink's heist so fast?
alts: How did they do it so quickly?
How did they carry all those heavy bags?
ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.a: Each bag weighed 70 to 100 pounds, so moving that many so fast suggests several thieves. Most missing bags came from the front, so they seemed to know which ones they wanted.
ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.quote: Each bag weighed 70 to 100 pounds, so moving that many so fast suggests several thieves

ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.q: Where were the guards during the Brink's jewelry heist?
alts: Where were they when it happened?
Why didn't the guards stop them?
ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.a: One guard went inside the truck stop to eat while the other slept in the cab. The trailer was secured with just a padlock and a plastic seal.
ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.quote: One guard went inside to eat while the other slept in the cab.

ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.q: Did they ever catch the Brink's jewelry thieves?
alts: Did the robbers get caught, Mom?
ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.a: In 2025, federal prosecutors indicted seven Los Angeles area men accused of following delivery trucks and stealing from them at truck stops. Some of the jewelry was recovered.
ca205-the-brink-s-jewelry-heist.quote: In 2025 federal prosecutors indicted seven Los Angeles area men accused of following delivery trucks and stealing from them at truck stops

alts: How big is that mountain, mom?
ca205-frazier-mountain.a: Frazier Mountain is 8,017 feet high. It's a broad, pine-covered peak west of the pass.
ca205-frazier-mountain.quote: The broad, pine-covered peak west of the pass is Frazier Mountain, 8,017 feet high.

ca205-frazier-mountain.q: What did the Chumash call Frazier Mountain?
alts: What was it called before Frazier?
Did Native Americans have a name for the mountain?
ca205-frazier-mountain.a: The Chumash call it Toshololo, the mountain of the east. It's named for its place east of Mount Pinos and tied to the morning star and the spring equinox.
ca205-frazier-mountain.quote: To the Chumash people it is Toshololo, the mountain of the east, named for its place east of Mount Pinos and tied to the morning star and the spring equinox.

ca205-frazier-mountain.q: Why is it called Frazier Mountain?
alts: Who's Frazier, and why's the mountain his?
ca205-frazier-mountain.a: Its English name honors William Frazer, a miner who worked here in the 1850s.
ca205-frazier-mountain.quote: Its English name honors William Frazer, a miner who worked here in the 1850s.

ca205-frazier-mountain.q: What was Frazier Mountain's wood used for?
alts: Did people cut the trees on it?
Did they build something with the trees, dad?
ca205-frazier-mountain.a: In 1854, lumber was cut from its trees for the new Army post at Fort Tejon.
