ca205-frazier-mountain.quote: In 1854, lumber was cut from Frazier Mountain's trees for the new Army post at Fort Tejon.

ca205-frazier-mountain.q: Is there a town named after Frazier Mountain?
alts: Is there a town on it?
Does anybody live on the mountain?
ca205-frazier-mountain.a: Yes, Frazier Park. It was founded in 1925 on the mountain's north side and took the mountain's name in 1926.
ca205-frazier-mountain.quote: The town of Frazier Park, founded in 1925 on the mountain's north side, took the mountain's name in 1926.

alts: Is that ranch really huge, like how many acres?
ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.a: Tejon Ranch is more than 270,000 acres, and it's the largest single piece of private land in California.
ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.quote: more than 270,000 acres and the largest single piece of private land in California

ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.q: How many cattle are on Tejon Ranch?
alts: How many cows are there on it?
How many cows can you see, like a million?
ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.a: Cattle graze about 250,000 acres of the ranch, with up to 12,000 head depending on the season.
ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.quote: Cattle graze about 250,000 acres of it, up to 12,000 head depending on the season.

ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.q: How did Tejon Ranch get started?
alts: Who owned that ranch first, way back?
Where did the ranch come from?
ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.a: It grew from four Mexican land grants of the 1840s, which Edward Fitzgerald Beale bought between 1855 and 1866.
ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.quote: The ranch grew from four Mexican land grants of the 1840s, which Edward Fitzgerald Beale bought between 1855 and 1866.

ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.q: What else grows on Tejon Ranch besides cattle?
alts: Does it grow other stuff too?
Do they grow nuts or fruit there, like for snacks?
ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.a: A little less than 6,000 acres grow pistachios, almonds, wine grapes, alfalfa and now olives.
ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.quote: A little less than 6,000 acres grow pistachios, almonds, wine grapes, alfalfa and now olives.

ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.q: How can you tell winter is over at Tejon Ranch?
alts: How do they know spring is here on it?
What do baby cows do in spring, and what flowers pop up?
ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.a: The ranch says you know winter is over when orange poppies spill across the hills and young calves trail their mothers.
ca207-tejon-ranch-cattle.quote: you know winter is over when orange poppies spill across the hills and young calves trail their mothers

alts: How long ago did that lake get here, Dad?
ca207-castac-lake-the-eye.a: Castac Lake formed about 10,000 years ago. Sediment washed down by Cuddy Creek dammed a valley along the Garlock Fault.
ca207-castac-lake-the-eye.quote: a natural salty lake that formed about 10,000 years ago when the fan of sediment washed down by Cuddy Creek dammed a valley along the Garlock Fault

ca207-castac-lake-the-eye.q: Why is it called Castac Lake, the eye?
alts: Why do they call it that?
Why is the lake called an eye?
ca207-castac-lake-the-eye.a: The Chumash, Kitanemuk and Yokuts peoples all named it for an eye.
ca207-castac-lake-the-eye.quote: The Chumash, Kitanemuk and Yokuts peoples all named it for an eye.

ca207-castac-lake-the-eye.q: Who lived near Castac Lake long ago?
alts: Were there any villages by the lake, Mom?
ca207-castac-lake-the-eye.a: Several villages stood near its shores. One was Sasau, an Emigdiano Chumash village on the north side of the lake.
ca207-castac-lake-the-eye.quote: Several villages stood near its shores, including the Emigdiano Chumash village of Sasau on the north side.

ca207-castac-lake-the-eye.q: What happened at Castac Lake in 1772?
alts: Did anything happen to it in 1772?
ca207-castac-lake-the-eye.a: In 1772 Pedro Fages named it Salinas de Cortes.
ca207-castac-lake-the-eye.quote: In 1772 Pedro Fages named it Salinas de Cortes

ca210-fort-tejon.q: What was Fort Tejon used for?
alts: What did the soldiers do there, mom?
ca210-fort-tejon.a: Fort Tejon was an Army post from 1854 to 1864, sitting on the main route between the Central Valley and Southern California.
ca210-fort-tejon.quote: Fort Tejon, an Army post from 1854 to 1864 on the main route between the Central Valley and Southern California.

ca210-fort-tejon.q: Did Fort Tejon really have camels?
ca210-fort-tejon.a: Yes. From 1858 it was the western end of the Army's experiment with camels as pack animals. The soldiers found them hardy but temperamental, and they spooked the cavalry's horses.
ca210-fort-tejon.quote: From 1858 it was the western end of the Army's experiment with camels as pack animals.

ca210-fort-tejon.q: What happened at Fort Tejon during the 1857 earthquake?
alts: What did the earthquake do to it?
Did the fort fall down in an earthquake?
ca210-fort-tejon.a: The great 1857 earthquake on the San Andreas Fault badly damaged most of the fort's adobe buildings, and the quake became known by the fort's name.
ca210-fort-tejon.quote: The great 1857 earthquake on the San Andreas Fault badly damaged most of its adobe buildings and became known by the fort's name.

ca210-fort-tejon.q: Is Fort Tejon a park you can visit today?
alts: Can we go inside the fort?
ca210-fort-tejon.a: Yes. Since 1940 it has been a state historic park, with restored barracks, 300-year-old valley oaks and living history demonstrations.
ca210-fort-tejon.quote: Since 1940 the fort has been a state historic park, with restored barracks, 300-year-old valley oaks and living history demonstrations.

ca210-fort-tejon.q: Who was stationed at Fort Tejon?
alts: Who lived in the fort, dad?
ca210-fort-tejon.a: The First U.S. Dragoons called it home until the Civil War. It was also a stop on the Butterfield Overland Mail.
ca210-fort-tejon.quote: Fort Tejon was home to the First U.S. Dragoons until the Civil War, and it was also a stop on the Butterfield Overland Mail.

ca210-fort-tejon.q: What hard history happened at Fort Tejon?
alts: Did anything sad happen at the fort?
ca210-fort-tejon.a: In July 1863, after soldiers killed hundreds of Paiute people in the Owens Valley, about 850 survivors were marched to Fort Tejon.
ca210-fort-tejon.quote: in July 1863, after soldiers killed hundreds of Paiute people in the Owens Valley, about 850 survivors were marched to Fort Tejon.

alts: Who's the guy buried under that tree?
ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.a: Almost nothing is known about him. The Catholic symbol on his carving suggests he may have been a French-Canadian trapper.
ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.quote: Almost nothing else is known about him; the Catholic symbol on the carving suggests he may have been a French-Canadian trapper.

alts: Did a bear really get him?
ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.a: He was killed by a grizzly in October 1837 and buried under a valley oak. He is the earliest known victim of a bear attack in California.
ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.quote: he is the earliest known victim of a bear attack in California.

ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.q: What is carved into Peter Lebeck's oak?
alts: What does it say on that tree?
ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.a: Someone carved his epitaph into the tree: Peter Lebeck, killed by a X bear, October 17, 1837. Early settlers called grizzlies X bears.
ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.quote: Someone carved his epitaph into the tree: Peter Lebeck, killed by a X bear, October 17, 1837.

ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.q: Where is the original bark from Peter Lebeck's oak?
alts: Can we see the carved bark?
Where did they put the bark?
ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.a: That piece of bark is now in the museum at Fort Tejon.
ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.quote: That piece of bark is now in the museum at Fort Tejon.

ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.q: Is the town of Lebec named after Peter Lebeck?
alts: Is that why the town is called Lebec?
Why is the town named Lebec?
ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.a: Yes, the nearby town of Lebec is named for him.
ca210-peter-lebeck-s-oak.quote: The nearby town of Lebec is named for him

ca210-the-grapevine-grade.q: Why is it called the Grapevine?
alts: Why's it named after grapes, is that real?
ca210-the-grapevine-grade.a: The name comes from wild California grapevines. In 1772 Pedro Fages called this canyon Cañada de las Uvas, the canyon of the grapes.
ca210-the-grapevine-grade.quote: The name comes from wild California grapevines: in 1772 Pedro Fages called this canyon Cañada de las Uvas, the canyon of the grapes.

ca210-the-grapevine-grade.q: How steep is the Grapevine grade?
alts: Is it a really big hill, how high do we go down?
ca210-the-grapevine-grade.a: It's a 6 percent grade that runs 5 miles and drops about 1,600 feet through Grapevine Canyon.
ca210-the-grapevine-grade.quote: a 6 percent grade that runs 5 miles and drops about 1,600 feet

ca210-the-grapevine-grade.q: What are those escape ramps on the Grapevine?
alts: What are the ramps for big trucks that fall off the road?
ca210-the-grapevine-grade.a: Escape ramps branch off the downhill lanes for big rigs whose brakes fail. You can spot them as steep ramps built just for trucks.
ca210-the-grapevine-grade.quote: Escape ramps branch off the downhill lanes for big rigs whose brakes fail

ca210-the-grapevine-grade.q: Do cars have trouble on the Grapevine?
alts: Do cars have problems on it?
Do car engines get too hot on the big hill?
ca210-the-grapevine-grade.a: In hot weather, car engines often overheat on the long uphill lanes of the Grapevine.
ca210-the-grapevine-grade.quote: in hot weather car engines often overheat on the long uphill lanes

ca210-the-grapevine-grade.q: What happened at Dead Man's Curve on the Grapevine?
alts: Why is it called Dead Man's Curve, what happened?
ca210-the-grapevine-grade.a: On the old road, the bend called Dead Man's Curve saw many wrecks. In July 1932, truck driver Jack Klieby steered his gasoline truck off the road to avoid oncoming cars and died when it burst into flames.
ca210-the-grapevine-grade.quote: In July 1932, truck driver Jack Klieby steered his gasoline truck off the road to avoid hitting oncoming cars and died when it burst into flames.

ca215-california-s-first-reservation.q: When did California's first reservation start?
alts: How old is that reservation, like for real?
ca215-california-s-first-reservation.a: It began in 1853, when these mountains became the site of California's first Indian reservation, the Sebastian, or Tejon, Reservation.
ca215-california-s-first-reservation.quote: In 1853 they became the site of California's first Indian reservation, the Sebastian, or Tejon, Reservation, which reached from Tejon Canyon west to Grapevine Canyon.

ca215-california-s-first-reservation.q: Who set up California's first reservation?
alts: Who made that reservation, and why?
ca215-california-s-first-reservation.a: Edward Beale, the federal superintendent of Indian affairs, set it up on a private Mexican land grant.
ca215-california-s-first-reservation.quote: Edward Beale, the federal superintendent of Indian affairs, set it up on a private Mexican land grant.

ca215-california-s-first-reservation.q: Who lived on California's first reservation?
alts: Which people were on that land?
ca215-california-s-first-reservation.a: These mountains are the ancestral homeland of the Tejon Indian Tribe, made up of Kitanemuk, Yokuts, Paiute and Chumash people. The state marker says 500 to 2,000 people lived there.
ca215-california-s-first-reservation.quote: These mountains are ancestral homeland of the Tejon Indian Tribe, a federally recognized tribe of Kitanemuk, Yokuts, Paiute and Chumash people based in Bakersfield.

ca215-california-s-first-reservation.q: What did people grow on California's first reservation?
alts: What kind of food did they farm?
Did they have crops and stuff?
ca215-california-s-first-reservation.a: Residents planted wheat, barley and corn, and Tejon Creek watered gardens, vineyards and orchards.
ca215-california-s-first-reservation.quote: Residents planted wheat, barley and corn, and Tejon Creek watered gardens, vineyards and orchards.

ca215-california-s-first-reservation.q: Why did California's first reservation close?
ca215-california-s-first-reservation.a: Drought, crop disease and settlers' cattle eating the crops wore it down. It closed in 1864, and many people were forced at gunpoint to the new Tule River Reservation near Porterville.
ca215-california-s-first-reservation.quote: Drought, crop disease and settlers' cattle eating the crops wore it down.

ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.q: How high does the Edmonston Pumping Plant lift the water?
alts: How high does it lift the water?
How far up do they push the water, anyway?
ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.a: It lifts California Aqueduct water 1,926 feet up and over the Tehachapi Mountains, sending it toward Southern California.
ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.quote: the Edmonston Pumping Plant lifts California Aqueduct water 1,926 feet up and over the Tehachapi Mountains toward Southern California.

ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.q: How powerful is the Edmonston Pumping Plant?
alts: Is this thing really strong, like the strongest ever?
ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.a: Apart from pumped-storage power plants, it is the most powerful water-lifting system in the world. At full capacity its pumps can send nearly 2 million gallons a minute uphill.
ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.quote: Apart from pumped-storage power plants, it is the most powerful water-lifting system in the world.

ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.q: How big are the pumps at Edmonston?
alts: Are the pumps taller than a house?
ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.a: There are 14 pumps. Each motor and pump unit stands 65 feet tall and weighs 420 tons, and the pumps reach six floors down.
ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.quote: Each motor and pump unit stands 65 feet tall and weighs 420 tons, and the pumps reach six floors down.

ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.q: How does the water get over the mountain at Edmonston?
alts: How does it get the water over the mountain?
Do the pipes go through the mountain?
Where does the water go when it goes uphill?
ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.a: Two giant pipes, 12.5 to 14 feet across, climb the mountain inside a tunnel 8,400 feet long. Each one always holds 8.5 million gallons of water.
ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.quote: Two pipes 12.5 to 14 feet across climb the mountain inside a tunnel 8,400 feet long, and each always holds 8.5 million gallons of water.

ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.q: How much electricity does the Edmonston Pumping Plant use?
alts: How much power does it use?
Does it need its own power line?
ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.a: Running every pump takes up to 787 megawatts of electricity, and it is delivered on its own power line.
ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.quote: Running every pump takes up to 787 megawatts of electricity, delivered on its own power line.

ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.q: What happens to the water after it goes over the top at Edmonston?
alts: What happens to it after it goes over the top?
Where does the water go next?
ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.a: Over the top, the aqueduct splits into the West and East Branches. Before reaching Edmonston, the water climbs in steps at three earlier plants: Buena Vista, Teerink and Chrisman.
ca215-water-lifted-over-the-mountains.quote: Over the top, the aqueduct splits into West and East Branches.

ca215-where-the-valley-begins.q: How big is the Central Valley that begins here?
alts: Mom, how huge is this valley?
ca215-where-the-valley-begins.a: It runs about 450 miles long and is 40 to 60 miles wide. It covers about 18,000 square miles, roughly 11 percent of California.
ca215-where-the-valley-begins.quote: The whole Central Valley is 40 to 60 miles wide and covers about 18,000 square miles, about 11 percent of California.

ca215-where-the-valley-begins.q: How high up are we where the valley begins?
alts: Are we up in the mountains still, Dad?
ca215-where-the-valley-begins.a: The freeway reaches the southern tip of the San Joaquin Valley at about 1,500 feet above sea level, at the foot of the Grapevine.
ca215-where-the-valley-begins.quote: At the foot of the Grapevine, the freeway reaches the southern tip of the San Joaquin Valley, about 1,500 feet above sea level.

ca215-where-the-valley-begins.q: How much does the road drop coming down from Tejon Pass?
alts: How much does it drop to get here?
Why did my ears pop coming down?
ca215-where-the-valley-begins.a: Between Tejon Pass and here, the road changes elevation by more than 2,600 feet in about 12 miles.
ca215-where-the-valley-begins.quote: Between Tejon Pass and here, the road changes elevation by more than 2,600 feet in about 12 miles.

ca215-where-the-valley-begins.q: What did the southern end of the valley look like before farming?
alts: What was it like before the farms?
Did animals used to live here, Mom?
ca215-where-the-valley-begins.a: It was desert grassland with marshes and big lakes like Tulare, Buena Vista and Kern. Herds of tule elk and pronghorn lived here.
ca215-where-the-valley-begins.quote: Before farming, it was desert grassland, with marshes, big lakes such as Tulare, Buena Vista and Kern, and herds of tule elk and pronghorn.

ca215-where-the-valley-begins.q: How much of the valley's natural grassland is left?
alts: Is any of it still wild?
ca215-where-the-valley-begins.a: Only about 1 percent of the valley's original grassland is intact today, and more than 7 million acres are irrigated.
ca215-where-the-valley-begins.quote: Today only about 1 percent of the valley's original grassland is intact, and more than 7 million acres are irrigated.

ca215-where-the-valley-begins.q: Does the Central Valley have its own earthquake faults?
alts: Can the ground shake here, Dad?
ca215-where-the-valley-begins.a: No. The valley has no earthquake faults of its own, though faults surround it on both sides.
ca215-where-the-valley-begins.quote: it has no earthquake faults of its own, though faults surround it on both sides.

alts: Is it a mountain or a hill, Dad?
ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.a: Wheeler Ridge is a fold in the earth's crust that is still growing. It sits where the mountains meet the valley floor.
ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.quote: is Wheeler Ridge, a fold in the earth's crust that is still growing

ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.q: Is Wheeler Ridge really still growing?
alts: Wait, does the ridge really grow?
ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.a: Yes. It is being pushed up over a thrust fault, and geologists have found that the fold is getting longer at its eastern end, toward the east-southeast.
ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.quote: geologists have found that the fold is getting longer at its eastern end, toward the east-southeast

ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.q: How do scientists know Wheeler Ridge is growing?
alts: How can they tell it's growing?
How do they know it's moving, Mom?
ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.a: The evidence is written in the land. Streams crossing the eastern end bend east-southeast, deflected by the rising rock growing in front of them.
ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.quote: Streams that cross the eastern end of the ridge bend toward the east-southeast, deflected as the rising rock grows in front of them.

ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.q: What is the wind gap on Wheeler Ridge?
alts: What is that gap on top of it?
ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.a: It is an old stream channel left high and dry on the crest. It sits at the same height as the canyon a nearby stream uses today, a sign the stream was pushed aside as the ridge rose.
ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.quote: On the crest sits a wind gap, an old stream channel left high and dry, at the same height as the canyon a nearby stream uses today

ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.q: What fault system is Wheeler Ridge part of?
alts: Is it on an earthquake fault, Mom?
ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.a: It belongs to the Pleito-Wheeler Ridge thrust fault system, which has been active since the late Pleistocene.
ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.quote: It belongs to the Pleito-Wheeler Ridge thrust fault system, which has been active since the late Pleistocene.

ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.q: Is Wheeler Ridge connected to the 1952 earthquake?
alts: Was there ever a big earthquake there, Dad?
ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.a: Possibly. The White Wolf Fault caused the 1952 earthquake, and it may merge with the Pleito thrust fault at its southwestern end.
ca219-wheeler-ridge-a-growing-fold.quote: The White Wolf Fault, which caused the 1952 earthquake, may merge with the Pleito thrust fault at its southwestern end.

alts: How big was that earthquake, Mom?
ca221-the-1952-earthquake.a: It was a magnitude 7.3 quake, the strongest in California since 1906. It broke the White Wolf Fault near Wheeler Ridge at 4:52 in the morning on July 21, 1952.
ca221-the-1952-earthquake.quote: the White Wolf Fault broke near Wheeler Ridge in a magnitude 7.3 earthquake, the strongest in California since 1906

ca221-the-1952-earthquake.q: Did anyone die in the 1952 earthquake?
alts: Did people die in that earthquake?
ca221-the-1952-earthquake.a: Yes, it killed 12 people, and the mountain town of Tehachapi was hit hardest. A month later, a big aftershock killed two more people in Bakersfield.
ca221-the-1952-earthquake.quote: It killed 12 people, and the mountain town of Tehachapi was hit hardest.

ca221-the-1952-earthquake.q: What damage did the 1952 earthquake do?
alts: What happened to the ground and stuff?
ca221-the-1952-earthquake.a: Rows of cotton in the valley fields were shifted sideways, one of them by 3 feet. Railroad tunnels with thick concrete walls also cracked.
ca221-the-1952-earthquake.quote: rows of cotton were found shifted sideways, one of them by 3 feet.

ca221-the-1952-earthquake.q: What happened to the railroad tunnels in the 1952 earthquake?
alts: What happened to the tunnels in it?
Did the train tunnels get squished?
How long till the trains ran again?
ca221-the-1952-earthquake.a: Tunnels southeast of Bealville cracked, and the gap between two entrances shrank by up to 8 feet. A crew of a thousand workers reopened the line in 25 days.
ca221-the-1952-earthquake.quote: the gap between two tunnel entrances shrank by up to 8 feet. A crew of a thousand workers reopened the line in 25 days.

ca221-the-1952-earthquake.q: How long is the White Wolf Fault?
alts: How big is the crack in the ground?
ca221-the-1952-earthquake.a: The White Wolf Fault is about 56 miles long. The shaking in 1952 started at its southwestern end, near here.
ca221-the-1952-earthquake.quote: The White Wolf Fault is about 56 miles long, and the shaking started at its southwestern end, near here.

ca221-the-1952-earthquake.q: Did the White Wolf Fault shake again after 1952?
alts: Did the ground shake again after that?
ca221-the-1952-earthquake.a: Yes. A magnitude 5.8 aftershock hit a month later on August 22, and the same fault shook Wheeler Ridge again in 2005 with a magnitude 5.2 quake.
ca221-the-1952-earthquake.quote: The same fault shook Wheeler Ridge again in 2005, with a magnitude 5.2 quake.

ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.q: Why did they build I-5 here instead of using Highway 99?
alts: Why didn't they just make that the Interstate?
Why didn't they use the other road, Dad?
ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.a: I-5 was chosen because it skips the valley's big cities, like Bakersfield and Fresno, for a faster, more direct trip.
ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.quote: It was chosen as the Interstate route because it skips the valley's big cities, such as Bakersfield and Fresno, for a faster, more direct trip.

ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.q: When did the West Side Freeway open?
alts: How old is this road, Dad?
ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.a: The section from here to Los Banos opened in 1972. Construction began in the early 1960s and the whole freeway was finished in three phases, with the Sacramento link done by 1979.
ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.quote: The section between here and Los Banos opened in 1972.

ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.q: What was the West Side Freeway like when it first opened?
alts: What was it like back then?
Was it scary out here when it was new?
ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.a: It was a long, lonely road with no businesses beside it. The nearest towns were miles away and usually out of sight, and running out of gas was common.
ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.quote: When this section opened, it was a long, lonely road with no businesses beside it

ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.q: Where did all the travel stops along I-5 come from?
alts: How did the stops get here?
Why are there stops at the exits, Mom?
ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.a: Travel stops grew up at the exits over the years. The road started out with no businesses beside it, so they were added gradually.
ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.quote: Travel stops grew up at the exits over the years.

ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.q: Will the West Side Freeway get bigger someday?
alts: Will they add more lanes to it?
Can they make the road wider, Dad?
ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.a: Maybe. The wide median between Wheeler Ridge and Tracy leaves room to widen the freeway to six or eight lanes someday.
ca221-start-of-the-west-side-freeway.quote: The wide median between Wheeler Ridge and Tracy leaves room to widen the freeway to six or eight lanes someday.

ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.q: What happened with James Dean's speeding ticket?
alts: Why did James Dean get pulled over?
ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.a: On September 30, 1955, a Highway Patrol officer pulled Dean over near here and wrote him a speeding ticket. He was driving north on Highway 99, headed to a sports car race in Salinas.
ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.quote: a Highway Patrol officer pulled him over near here and wrote him a speeding ticket

ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.q: Where was James Dean going when he got the ticket?
alts: Where was that guy going in his race car?
ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.a: He was on his way to a sports car race in Salinas. The Salinas Road Race was set for October 2.
ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.quote: entered the Salinas Road Race for October 2

ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.q: What happened to James Dean after his speeding ticket?
alts: What happened to him after that?
Was he okay after the ticket?
ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.a: Later that same day, Dean was killed in a crash farther along his trip. He was only 24 years old.
ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.quote: Later that same day, Dean was killed in a crash farther along his trip.

ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.q: Who was James Dean and what was he famous for?
alts: Who was that guy, was he famous?
ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.a: Dean was an actor who had made only three major films: East of Eden, Rebel Without a Cause, and Giant. Giant came out after his death.
ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.quote: Dean was 24 and had made only three major films: East of Eden, Rebel Without a Cause, and Giant, which came out after his death.

ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.q: Who wrote James Dean's speeding ticket?
ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.a: The officer was O. V. Hunter of the California Highway Patrol. He wrote the ticket at about 3:30 in the afternoon.
ca225-james-dean-s-speeding-ticket.quote: The officer who wrote Dean's ticket, at about 3:30 in the afternoon, was O. V. Hunter of the California Highway Patrol.

ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.q: Why is it called Wind Wolves Preserve?
alts: Why is it named after wolves, are there wolves there?
ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.a: The name describes tall grass bending and parting in gusts of wind, like unseen animals running across the slopes.
ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.quote: The name describes tall grass bending and parting in gusts of wind, like unseen animals running across the slopes.

ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.q: How big is Wind Wolves Preserve?
alts: Is it a really huge park?
ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.a: It covers 93,000 acres of grassland, oak and canyon. Its owner, The Wildlands Conservancy, calls it the largest nonprofit nature preserve on the West Coast.
ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.quote: 93,000 acres of grassland, oak and canyon that its owner, The Wildlands Conservancy, calls the largest nonprofit nature preserve on the West Coast.

ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.q: What animals live at Wind Wolves Preserve?
alts: What animals can you see there?
Are there any cool animals there?
ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.a: Tule elk live there. 19 were released in 1998 and the herd has grown to about 500. California condors also forage over it.
ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.quote: In 1998, 19 tule elk were released here, and the herd has grown to about 500.

ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.q: What kinds of land are in Wind Wolves Preserve?
alts: What is it like inside it?
What does it look like there, is it all grass?
ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.a: The land climbs from about 640 feet to more than 6,000 feet, through grassland, oak savanna, pinyon and juniper, and conifer forest.
ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.quote: The land climbs from about 640 feet to more than 6,000 feet, through grassland, oak savanna, pinyon and juniper, and conifer forest.

ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.q: Who lived on the land of Wind Wolves Preserve before?
ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.a: It is part of the homeland of Chumash, Yokuts and Kitanemuk peoples. Later it was part of an 1842 Mexican land grant, Rancho San Emidio, and a cattle ranch until the 1990s.
ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.quote: It is part of the homeland of Chumash, Yokuts and Kitanemuk peoples.

ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.q: What can you do at Wind Wolves Preserve?
alts: Is there anything to do there?
ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.a: A spring nature festival brings guided hikes and wildflower viewing. Since 1996, more than 157,000 Kern County students have come for outdoor classes.
ca225-wind-wolves-preserve.quote: a spring nature festival brings guided hikes and wildflower viewing.

ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.q: What happened at the Lakeview Gusher?
alts: Mom, what was the oil thing that blew up?
ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.a: In March 1910 an oil well called Lakeview Number One blew out near Maricopa and would not stop. It gushed for 18 months and destroyed the derrick.
ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.quote: Near Maricopa, in March 1910, an oil well called Lakeview Number One blew out and would not stop. For 18 months it gushed

ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.q: How much oil came out of the Lakeview Gusher?
alts: How much oil came out of it?
Was it a lot of oil, like a whole lake?
ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.a: About 9 million barrels in all. It is often called the largest accidental oil spill in history.
ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.quote: about 9 million barrels in all, and it is often called the largest accidental oil spill in history

ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.q: How did they pick the spot for the Lakeview Gusher?
alts: How did they pick that spot?
How did they know where to dig for oil?
ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.a: Legend says the spot was chosen because clumps of red grass were thought to mean oil. Drilling began on New Year's Day 1909.
ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.quote: began drilling on New Year's Day 1909, and legend says the spot was chosen because clumps of red grass were thought to mean oil.

ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.q: Did they stop the Lakeview Gusher or save any oil?
alts: Did they save any of it?
Did anyone try to stop the oil?
ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.a: Workers threw up sandbag dams and dikes and piped some oil to tanks 2.5 miles away, saving about 40 percent. It never caught fire.
ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.quote: Workers threw up sandbag dams and dikes to hold back a river of crude and piped some of it to tanks 2.5 miles away, saving about 40 percent.

ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.q: Is there anything to see at the Lakeview Gusher site?
alts: Is there anything to see there?
Is there a sign or something?
ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.a: A state landmark plaque marks the site off Highway 33.
ca225-the-lakeview-gusher.quote: A state landmark plaque marks the site off Highway 33.

ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.q: Who is the saint the San Emigdio Mountains are named for?
alts: Who is that saint it's named after?
Who was the guy these mountains are named after?
ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.a: They are named for Saint Emygdius, an early Christian martyr. He was a bishop in Ascoli Piceno, Italy.
ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.quote: They are named for Saint Emygdius, an early Christian martyr whom Catholics call on for protection from earthquakes.

ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.q: Why is a saint connected to earthquakes?
alts: Why do people pray to him about earthquakes?
Why is he the earthquake saint, mom?
ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.a: In 1703 a violent earthquake shook the region around Ascoli Piceno but spared the city. People gave Emygdius the credit, and from then on he was invoked against earthquakes.
ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.quote: In 1703 a violent earthquake shook the region but spared the city, people gave him the credit, and from then on he was invoked against earthquakes.

ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.q: How high do the San Emigdio Mountains get?
alts: How big are those mountains, Dad?
ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.a: The range tops out at 7,492 feet. Its highest peaks, including San Emigdio Mountain, Tecuya Mountain and Brush Mountain, are all above 7,000 feet.
ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.quote: the San Emigdio Mountains, which top out at 7,492 feet.

ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.q: What mountain ranges do the San Emigdio Mountains connect?
alts: Do these mountains go on forever?
ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.a: The range links the Tehachapi Mountains with the Temblor Range. Temblor is Spanish for tremor.
ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.quote: The range links the Tehachapi Mountains with the Temblor Range, whose own name is Spanish for tremor.

ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.q: Is there a creek in the San Emigdio Mountains?
alts: Is there a river up there?
ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.a: Yes, San Emigdio Creek runs year-round. It carries the same name down San Emigdio Canyon.
ca228-mountains-named-for-a-saint.quote: San Emigdio Creek, which runs year-round, carries the same name down San Emigdio Canyon.

alts: What was it before it dried up?
Was there really a lake here, like a real one?
What's the deal with Kern Lake?
ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.a: The flat fields here were once Kern Lake, the smallest of three big lakes at the south end of the valley. It was the first lake the Kern River fed.
ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.quote: The flat fields near the freeway here were once Kern Lake, the smallest of three big lakes at the south end of the valley. It was the first lake the Kern River fed.

ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.q: Why is Kern Lake empty now?
alts: Where did all the water go, kid-style?
ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.a: People diverted the Kern River for farms in the 1800s, and that left the lake a dry bed.
ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.quote: Diverting the river for farms in the 1800s left it a dry bed.

ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.q: Did Kern Lake connect to other lakes?
alts: Did it join up with anything else?
Did the lake ever run into another lake?
Was it connected to other water?
ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.a: Yes. Water ran west through a channel called Connecting Slough into Buena Vista Lake, and in wet years the two joined into one large lake.
ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.quote: water ran west through a channel called Connecting Slough into Buena Vista Lake, and in wet years the two joined into one large lake.

ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.q: How big was Kern Lake compared to the other lakes?
alts: Was it the biggest lake in the valley?
ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.a: It was the smallest of three big lakes at the south end of the valley. Tulare Lake, to the north, was the largest of all.
ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.quote: Kern Lake, the smallest of three big lakes at the south end of the valley.

ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.q: Where did the water go when the lakes overflowed?
alts: Did the lakes ever spill over?
Where did all that extra water end up?
Did it ever run out to the ocean?
ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.a: Overflow from Kern and Buena Vista lakes ran north into Tulare Lake. Tulare Lake spilled into the San Joaquin River in 19 of the 29 years from 1850 to 1878, but never again after that.
ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.quote: Tulare Lake in turn spilled north into the San Joaquin River in 19 of the 29 years from 1850 to 1878, but never again after that.

ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.q: How did the Central Valley lakes get started?
alts: Where did these lakes come from?
Was there a giant lake here once?
Was the whole valley underwater, like way back?
ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.a: All three lakes were remnants of a far bigger one, Lake Corcoran, which covered the Central Valley until about 600,000 years ago, when a new outlet broke through at San Francisco Bay and drained it.
ca230-kern-lake-s-empty-bed.quote: All three lakes were remnants of a far bigger one, Lake Corcoran, which covered the Central Valley until about 600,000 years ago

ca239-kern-county-nut-country.q: What kind of trees are in the Kern County nut country?
alts: What are those trees in rows?
ca239-kern-county-nut-country.a: Many of the neat rows of trees here are almonds and pistachios. Look for orchards planted in long, straight rows.
ca239-kern-county-nut-country.quote: Many of the neat rows of trees in Kern County are almonds and pistachios.

ca239-kern-county-nut-country.q: Are nuts Kern County's biggest crop?
alts: Is that the main thing grown there?
ca239-kern-county-nut-country.a: Not quite. In 2022 Kern's most valuable farm product was grapes, mostly table grapes, followed by citrus, almonds and milk.
ca239-kern-county-nut-country.quote: Kern's most valuable farm product in 2022 was grapes, mostly table grapes, followed by citrus, almonds and milk

ca239-kern-county-nut-country.q: How long has California been growing pistachios commercially?
alts: When did they start the pistachio farms?
ca239-kern-county-nut-country.a: Not very long. California's first commercial pistachio harvest came only in 1976.
ca239-kern-county-nut-country.quote: California's first commercial pistachio harvest came only in 1976.

ca244-taft-once-called-moron.q: Why was Taft once called Moron?
alts: Why did they name a town Moron?
ca244-taft-once-called-moron.a: Locals asked the railroad to name the station Moro, but the railroad feared confusion with Morro Bay and named it Moron instead, back when the word did not yet mean anything unkind.
ca244-taft-once-called-moron.quote: the railroad worried it would be confused with Morro Bay and named it Moron instead, back when the word did not yet mean anything unkind

ca244-taft-once-called-moron.q: Who is the town of Taft named after?
alts: Is Taft named after a president?
When did it get its new name?
ca244-taft-once-called-moron.a: Taft is named for President William Howard Taft. The town took the new name in 1909.
ca244-taft-once-called-moron.quote: In 1909 the town took a new name, for President William Howard Taft.

alts: Why is there a town out here?
ca244-taft-once-called-moron.a: It began as Siding Number Two on the Sunset Railroad, built to carry crude oil out and bring drinking water in. It exists only because of nearby oil.
ca244-taft-once-called-moron.quote: Taft began as Siding Number Two on the Sunset Railroad, which was built to carry crude oil out and bring drinking water in.

ca244-taft-once-called-moron.q: What can we see in Taft?
alts: What's there to do in that town?
Is there anything cool to see?
ca244-taft-once-called-moron.a: There's a bronze monument 37 feet tall of oil workers on a derrick in the middle of town. The West Kern Oil Museum keeps a historic wooden derrick.
ca244-taft-once-called-moron.quote: In the middle of town, a bronze monument 37 feet tall shows oil workers on a derrick, and the West Kern Oil Museum keeps a historic wooden derrick.

ca244-taft-once-called-moron.q: Which exit do I take for Taft?
alts: How do we get to Taft?
ca244-taft-once-called-moron.a: Take exit 244 and follow Highway 119 to Taft.
ca244-taft-once-called-moron.quote: Highway 119 leads to Taft, an oil town at the valley's southwest edge.

alts: What was that lake out there?
Was there really a big lake here, Mom?
ca244-buena-vista-lake.a: Much of the farmland here was once Buena Vista Lake. The Kern River fed it, and it was the second largest of the lakes in the Tulare Basin.
ca244-buena-vista-lake.quote: much of the farmland was once Buena Vista Lake, fed by the Kern River and the second largest of the lakes in the Tulare Basin

ca244-buena-vista-lake.q: Who lived at Buena Vista Lake?
alts: Did people live there long ago?
Did kids live by the lake way back?
ca244-buena-vista-lake.a: A Yokuts village called Tulamniu stood on the south shore, lived in for several centuries. Its people spoke Buena Vista Yokuts.
ca244-buena-vista-lake.quote: On its south shore stood Tulamniu, a Yokuts village lived in for several centuries

ca244-buena-vista-lake.q: What happened at Buena Vista Lake in 1933?
alts: What did they do to that old village?
Did scientists dig up the village, Dad?
ca244-buena-vista-lake.a: The Smithsonian Institution excavated the village site in 1933 and 1934. It is now California Historical Landmark 374.
ca244-buena-vista-lake.quote: in 1933 and 1934 the Smithsonian Institution excavated it; it is now California Historical Landmark 374

ca244-buena-vista-lake.q: Is there still water at Buena Vista Lake?
alts: Is it still a lake today?
Is the lake all gone now?
ca244-buena-vista-lake.a: Two small lakes, Lake Webb and Lake Evans, now sit on part of the old bed. They were created in 1973 for recreation.
ca244-buena-vista-lake.quote: Lake Webb and Lake Evans were created in 1973 for recreation

ca244-buena-vista-lake.q: Did Buena Vista Lake ever refill?
alts: Did the lake fill up again, Dad?
ca244-buena-vista-lake.a: Yes, a little. In June 2023, after a snowpack three times normal in the southern Sierra, the Kern River began refilling the top of the old lake, a few feet deep.
ca244-buena-vista-lake.quote: In June 2023, after a snowpack three times normal in the southern Sierra, the Kern River began to refill the top of the old lake

ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.q: Why is it called the Kern River?
alts: Who is the Kern River named after, anyway?
ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.a: John C. Frémont named it in 1845 for Edward Kern, the mapmaker of his expedition. As the story goes, Kern nearly drowned in its rushing water.
ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.quote: John C. Frémont named the river in 1845 for Edward Kern, the mapmaker of his expedition, who, as the story goes, nearly drowned in its rushing water.

ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.q: Did the Kern River have other names before this one?
alts: Did it always have that name?
What did people call the river before Kern?
ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.a: Yes. In 1776 the Spanish missionary Francisco Garcés called it the Río de San Felipe. Before Frémont, people locally called it Po-sun-co-la.
ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.quote: Long before that, in 1776, the Spanish missionary Francisco Garcés had called it the Río de San Felipe.

ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.q: Where does the Kern River start and where does it go?
alts: Where does the river begin, Dad?
ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.a: It starts high in the Sierra Nevada northwest of Mount Whitney and drops through a deep canyon to Bakersfield. In flood years, extra water spills into the California Aqueduct.
ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.quote: The Kern starts high in the Sierra Nevada northwest of Mount Whitney and drops through a deep canyon to Bakersfield.

ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.q: What happened to the Kern River in the 1857 earthquake?
alts: What did the earthquake do to it?
Did the river really flow backward?
ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.a: Accounts say the great earthquake of 1857 briefly made the river flow backward.
ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.quote: Accounts say the great earthquake of 1857 briefly made the river flow backward.

ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.q: Is the Kern River in trouble today?
ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.a: In 2022 American Rivers listed the lower Kern among America's most endangered rivers because its last 25 miles had dried up.
ca246-crossing-the-kern-river.quote: in 2022 the group American Rivers listed the lower Kern among America's most endangered rivers because its last 25 miles had dried up.

ca246-kern-water-bank.q: What is the Kern Water Bank?
ca246-kern-water-bank.a: It's a huge area where water is spread into basins in wet years and soaks into the ground. It's saved underground for dry years.
ca246-kern-water-bank.quote: In wet years, water is spread into more than 80 basins and slowly soaks into the ground, where it is saved for dry years.

ca246-kern-water-bank.q: How big is the Kern Water Bank?
alts: Is it a really big place, like huge?
ca246-kern-water-bank.a: It covers about 32 square miles of the southern San Joaquin Valley. It can store 1.5 million acre-feet underground.
ca246-kern-water-bank.quote: the Kern Water Bank covers about 32 square miles of the southern San Joaquin Valley.

ca246-kern-water-bank.q: How does the Kern Water Bank get the water back out?
alts: How does it get the water out again?
How do they get the water back up?
ca246-kern-water-bank.a: About 8,800 acres are recharge basins, and 91 wells pump the water back up when it is needed.
ca246-kern-water-bank.quote: About 8,800 acres of the bank are recharge basins, and 91 wells pump the water back up when it is needed.

ca246-kern-water-bank.q: What animals live at the Kern Water Bank?
alts: What kind of wildlife is at it?
Are there lots of birds there?
ca246-kern-water-bank.a: When the basins fill in wet years they look like lakes, and wildlife moves in. The general manager has counted 240 kinds of birds and as many as 35,000 water birds.
ca246-kern-water-bank.quote: The bank's general manager has counted 240 kinds of birds there and as many as 35,000 water birds

ca246-kern-water-bank.q: Where does the Kern Water Bank's water come from?
alts: Where does it get its water?
Where does all the water come from?
ca246-kern-water-bank.a: It takes in water from the Kern River and from the state and federal water projects.
ca246-kern-water-bank.quote: It takes in water from the Kern River and from the state and federal water projects.

ca246-kern-water-bank.q: Who owns the Kern Water Bank?
alts: Who's in charge of that place?
ca246-kern-water-bank.a: It's a public-private partnership. The largest share, 57 percent, is controlled by Stewart and Lynda Resnick, owners of brands including Pom Wonderful and Halos.
ca246-kern-water-bank.quote: It is a public-private partnership, and the largest share, 57 percent, is controlled by Stewart and Lynda Resnick

ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.q: How many elk live at Tule Elk State Natural Reserve?
alts: How many elk can we actually see there, mom?
ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.a: The reserve keeps a herd of about 30 to 35 tule elk on nearly 1,000 acres, and you watch them from a viewing platform.
ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.quote: keeps a herd of about 30 to 35 tule elk on nearly 1,000 acres, watched from a viewing platform

alts: Are those elk different from other elk?
ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.a: These elk are found only in California. About half a million once roamed the state, but by the 1870s they were thought to be extinct.
ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.quote: These elk are found only in California. About half a million once roamed the state, but by the 1870s they were thought to be extinct

ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.q: How old is Tule Elk State Natural Reserve?
alts: How long has it been here?
ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.a: The reserve was established in 1932 as the Tupman Zoological Reserve.
ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.quote: The reserve was established in 1932 as the Tupman Zoological Reserve

ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.q: Is it worth stopping at Tule Elk State Natural Reserve?
alts: Will we see real elk there?
ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.a: Yes, if you like wildlife. You can watch the herd from a viewing platform, and the park suggests bringing binoculars. The elk are most active from late summer through early autumn.
ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.quote: The elk are most active from late summer through early autumn.

ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.q: Did elk from the reserve start other herds?
alts: Did they spread to other places?
Are there elk anywhere else because of it?
Do other places have these elk?
ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.a: Yes. Elk from here have helped start other herds, including those in the Owens Valley and near San Luis Obispo.
ca253-tule-elk-state-natural-reserve.quote: elk from here have helped start other herds, including those in the Owens Valley and near San Luis Obispo

ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.q: What is the Teapot Dome scandal about the Elk Hills?
alts: Why is that a scandal, what happened?
ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.a: In 1922 Interior Secretary Albert Fall leased the Elk Hills to oilman Edward Doheny without competitive bidding. Doheny had quietly lent Fall 100,000 dollars, and the deal became part of the Teapot Dome scandal.
ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.quote: In 1922 Interior Secretary Albert Fall leased them, without competitive bidding, to oilman Edward Doheny, who had quietly lent Fall 100,000 dollars with no interest.

ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.q: Who went to prison over the Elk Hills oil deal?
alts: Did anybody go to jail for it?
Did somebody get in trouble, like go to jail?
ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.a: Albert Fall was convicted in 1929 of taking bribes from Doheny. He became the first Cabinet member to go to prison, while Doheny was acquitted of paying them.
ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.quote: Convicted in 1929 of taking bribes from Doheny, Fall became the first Cabinet member to go to prison, while Doheny was acquitted of paying them.

ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.q: Why did the Navy own the Elk Hills?
alts: Why did the Navy have it?
Why does the Navy get hills, what for?
ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.a: In 1912 President Taft made the Elk Hills the nation's first Naval Petroleum Reserve. That meant the oil was saved for the Navy.
ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.quote: In 1912 President Taft made them the nation's first Naval Petroleum Reserve, oil saved for the Navy.

ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.q: How much oil has come out of the Elk Hills?
alts: How much oil did it make?
How many barrels came out of those hills?
Is that a lot of oil?
ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.a: The field has produced close to 1.5 billion barrels of oil. Production peaked in 1981, when one oil pool alone yielded 42 million barrels.
ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.quote: production peaked in 1981, when one oil pool alone yielded 42 million barrels.

ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.q: What do the Elk Hills look like from the freeway?
alts: What are those bare hills out there?
ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.a: Look for long, low, bare hills along the west side of the valley. They sit over one of the most productive oil fields in the country.
ca253-elk-hills-and-teapot-dome.quote: The low hills to the west are the Elk Hills, over one of the most productive oil fields in the country.

ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.q: How did Henry Miller become the Cattle King?
alts: How did he get so rich?
How'd he get all those cows?
ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.a: He came west in 1850 as a butcher and teamed up with Charles Lux in 1858. Their company bought up Spanish and Mexican land grants and became California's largest cattle producer.
ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.quote: Miller came west in 1850 as a butcher and teamed up with another German immigrant, Charles Lux, in 1858.

ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.q: How much land did Henry Miller own?
alts: How much ground did he have?
ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.a: At its height his company owned about 1.4 million acres outright and controlled nearly 22,000 square miles across California, Nevada and Oregon.
ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.quote: At its height the company owned about 1.4 million acres outright and controlled nearly 22,000 square miles of land in California, Nevada and Oregon.

ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.q: Was Henry Miller really his name?
alts: Did he have a fake name?
ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.a: No. He was born Heinrich Kreiser in Germany. He used the name Henry Miller from a ticket he bought in New York and kept it for life.
ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.quote: He was born Heinrich Kreiser in Germany.

ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.q: How rich was Henry Miller when he died?
alts: How much money did he leave?
ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.a: When Miller died in 1916, his estate was appraised at about 40 million dollars.
ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.quote: When Miller died in 1916, his estate was appraised at about 40 million dollars.

ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.q: Do Henry Miller's descendants still live around here?
ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.a: Some of his descendants still farm around Los Banos and in Kern County.
ca257-henry-miller-the-cattle-king.quote: Some of his descendants still farm around Los Banos and in Kern County.

alts: What is that big electrical yard?
What's all that wire stuff for?
ca262-midway-substation.a: It's a big electrical yard near Buttonwillow where Southern California Edison's power lines meet PG&E's grid.
ca262-midway-substation.quote: The big electrical yard about a mile east of Buttonwillow is Midway Substation. Here Southern California Edison's power lines, which cross the mountains to the south, meet PG&E's grid.

ca262-midway-substation.q: Which way does the power flow at Midway Substation?
alts: Which way does it send the power?
Does the electricity go up or down?
ca262-midway-substation.a: It depends on the season. In winter, power often flows north toward the Pacific Northwest, and in summer it flows south for air conditioners.
ca262-midway-substation.quote: In winter, power often flows north toward the Pacific Northwest, where people run heaters; in summer it flows south for air conditioners.

ca262-midway-substation.q: What is Path 15 at Midway Substation?
alts: What is Path 15 for that place?
Why do they call it Path 15?
ca262-midway-substation.a: Midway is the southern end of Path 15, part of the Pacific AC Intertie. Path 26's three 500,000-volt lines also end here, crossing the Tehachapi Mountains toward the Antelope Valley.
ca262-midway-substation.quote: Midway is the southern end of Path 15, part of the Pacific AC Intertie.

ca262-midway-substation.q: When was the Pacific AC Intertie built, and why?
alts: When did they build it, and why?
Why did they build all those lines way back?
ca262-midway-substation.a: It was built in the 1970s and 1980s so California and the Southwest could use extra hydropower from the Northwest without building new power plants.
ca262-midway-substation.quote: The intertie was built in the 1970s and 1980s so California and the Southwest could use extra hydropower from the Northwest without building new power plants.

ca262-midway-substation.q: What is Path 26 at Midway Substation?
alts: What is Path 26 for that place?
Where do those big lines go over the mountains?
ca262-midway-substation.a: Midway is the northern end of Path 26, three Edison lines of 500,000 volts that cross the Tehachapi Mountains toward the Antelope Valley.
ca262-midway-substation.quote: Midway is also the northern end of Path 26, three Edison lines of 500,000 volts that cross the Tehachapi Mountains toward the Antelope Valley.

ca262-midway-substation.q: What lines connect to Midway Substation from the coast?
alts: Where do the power lines from the coast come in at it?
Does the coast plug into that place?
ca262-midway-substation.a: Two big lines from the Diablo Canyon Power Plant on the coast cross the coastal mountains to reach Midway.
ca262-midway-substation.quote: Two big lines from the Diablo Canyon Power Plant on the coast cross the coastal mountains to reach Midway.

alts: Why is that town named that?
How did Buttonwillow get its name, huh?
ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.a: The town is named for a single tree. Oddly, it is not a willow at all. It is a buttonbush.
ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.quote: The town of Buttonwillow is named for a single tree, and it is not a willow at all. It is a buttonbush.

ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.q: What is special about the Buttonwillow tree?
alts: What's so special about that tree?
Why is one tree such a big deal, is it magic?
ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.a: It was a lone landmark on an old trail across the valley. It is now California Historical Landmark 492.
ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.quote: A lone one here stood out as a landmark on an old trail across the valley

ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.q: Who used the Buttonwillow tree as a meeting place?
alts: Who met at that tree long ago?
Did people hang out at the tree way back, like kids or what?
ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.a: The Yokuts used it as a meeting place long before settlers held stock rodeos beside it.
ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.quote: it was a Yokuts meeting place long before settlers held stock rodeos beside it

ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.q: When was the town of Buttonwillow founded?
alts: How old is the town, is it really old?
ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.a: It was founded in 1895. It was first called Buena Vista, but the name quickly became Buttonwillow.
ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.quote: When the town was founded in 1895 it was first called Buena Vista, but the name quickly became Buttonwillow.

ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.q: What do people do in Buttonwillow today?
alts: What is that town known for now?
What do they grow or do there, anything fun?
ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.a: Cotton farming is its main industry, and locals call this cotton country. Nearby, Buttonwillow Raceway Park hosts sports car club races.
ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.quote: Cotton farming is its main industry, and locals call this cotton country.

ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.q: Is Buttonwillow a good stop for drivers?
alts: Can we stop there on the way?
Is there stuff to stop at there, are we taking a break?
ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.a: Yes, it is a major stop for drivers, with gas stations, restaurants and travel centers at the Highway 58 exit.
ca262-the-buttonwillow-tree.quote: for drivers it is a major stop, with gas stations, restaurants and travel centers at the Highway 58 exit.

alts: What's the balance point thing, Mom?
ca262-california-s-balance-point.a: It's the center of population of California. The Census Bureau finds it by imagining a flat, weightless map of the state with every resident given the same weight, then finding where it would balance.
ca262-california-s-balance-point.quote: The Census Bureau finds it by imagining a flat, weightless map of the state with every resident given the same weight, then finding the point where the map would balance.

ca262-california-s-balance-point.q: How does the Census Bureau find California's balance point?
alts: How do they figure it out?
How can they find the middle of everybody?
ca262-california-s-balance-point.a: They imagine a flat, weightless map of the state where every resident weighs the same. Then they find the spot where that map would balance.
ca262-california-s-balance-point.quote: imagining a flat, weightless map of the state with every resident given the same weight, then finding the point where the map would balance

ca262-california-s-balance-point.q: Where is California's balance point today?
ca262-california-s-balance-point.a: In 2020 it landed between Buttonwillow and Shafter. Since 1970 it has stayed within about 10 miles of Buttonwillow.
ca262-california-s-balance-point.quote: Since 1970, that point has stayed within about 10 miles of Buttonwillow.

ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.q: What are the McKittrick Tar Pits?
ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.a: They're places where natural asphalt oozes out of the ground from the oil field below. The pits trapped animals during the ice ages.
ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.quote: natural asphalt oozes out of the ground from the oil field below

ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.q: What animals were found in the McKittrick Tar Pits?
alts: What did they find in it?
What kind of dinosaurs were in there?
ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.a: Fossils found here include saber-toothed cats, short-faced bears, American lions, ground sloths, bison and mammoths.
ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.quote: Fossils found here include saber-toothed cats, short-faced bears, American lions, ground sloths, bison and mammoths.

ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.q: Who used the asphalt at McKittrick Tar Pits?
alts: Did people live here, like Native Americans?
ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.a: Yokuts people mined the asphalt and used it to waterproof things, for decoration and for trade. Settlers began mining it in the 1860s.
ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.quote: Yokuts people mined the asphalt and used it to waterproof things, for decoration and for trade, and settlers began mining it in the 1860s.

ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.q: What makes the McKittrick Tar Pits special?
alts: Is it like the La Brea Tar Pits?
ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.a: They're counted among only five natural asphalt lake areas in the world, and three of those are in California: here, La Brea and Carpinteria.
ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.quote: The pits are counted among only five natural asphalt lake areas in the world, and three of those are in California

alts: Where does the name come from?
ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.a: The town is named for Captain William McKittrick, a local landowner and rancher. About 100 people live there.
ca263-mckittrick-tar-pits.quote: The town is named for Captain William McKittrick, a local landowner and rancher, and about 100 people live there.

ca268-cotton-country.q: Why does cotton grow so well in the San Joaquin Valley?
alts: Why is it good cotton land here?
Why do they grow so much cotton here, Dad?
ca268-cotton-country.a: The valley has sandy loam soils, a long growing season without rain, big irrigation systems, and few pests like the boll weevil. That made it ideal cotton land.
ca268-cotton-country.quote: Sandy loam soils, a long growing season without rain, big irrigation systems and relative freedom from pests like the boll weevil made the San Joaquin Valley ideal cotton land.

alts: What was that special cotton called?
ca268-cotton-country.a: Acala is a strain developed at the cotton research station in nearby Shafter. It became so important that state laws in 1925 made it the only cotton allowed in key areas.
ca268-cotton-country.quote: A strain called Acala, developed at the cotton research station in nearby Shafter, became so important that state laws passed in 1925 made it the only cotton allowed in key areas.

ca268-cotton-country.q: What happened in the 1933 cotton pickers strike?
alts: Why did the cotton pickers strike, Mom?
ca268-cotton-country.a: More than 18,000 cotton pickers, mostly Mexican migrant workers, went on strike, and 3,500 lived in a four-acre camp outside Corcoran. The federal government stepped in to force both sides to negotiate.
ca268-cotton-country.quote: In 1933, more than 18,000 cotton pickers in the southern valley, mostly Mexican migrant workers, went on strike, and 3,500 of them lived in a four-acre camp outside Corcoran.

ca268-cotton-country.q: How did machines change cotton farming?
alts: What did they do about hand picking?
Do robots pick the cotton now, Dad?
ca268-cotton-country.a: After World War II, mechanical pickers sharply cut the need for hand labor.
ca268-cotton-country.quote: After World War II, mechanical pickers sharply cut the need for hand labor.

ca268-cotton-country.q: Is cotton still grown in California today?
alts: Do they still grow it around here?
Is there still cotton here, Mom?
ca268-cotton-country.a: Yes, though it declined after 2000 as new insect pests arrived and other crops paid better. Kings County, to the north, is still California's top cotton county, growing mostly Pima cotton.
ca268-cotton-country.quote: Kings County, to the north, is still California's top cotton county, growing mostly Pima cotton.

ca268-the-temblor-range.q: How tall are the Temblor Range mountains?
alts: Are those mountains really big, Dad?
ca268-the-temblor-range.a: The peaks average about 3,500 feet. The highest, McKittrick Summit, reaches 4,331 feet.
ca268-the-temblor-range.quote: The peaks average about 3,500 feet, and the highest, McKittrick Summit, reaches 4,331 feet.

ca268-the-temblor-range.q: How old is the Temblor Range?
alts: Are those mountains really old, Mom?
ca268-the-temblor-range.a: It's actually young. It rose mostly within the last few million years, pushed up by the San Andreas and other faults.
ca268-the-temblor-range.quote: The range is young: it rose mostly within the last few million years, pushed up by the San Andreas and other faults.

ca268-the-temblor-range.q: Why are there sea fossils in the Temblor Range?
alts: Were there really sea animals in those mountains?
ca268-the-temblor-range.a: Its rocks hold marine fossils because seawater once covered this end of the valley.
ca268-the-temblor-range.quote: Its rocks hold marine fossils, because seawater once covered this end of the valley.

ca268-the-temblor-range.q: What happened to the McKittrick oil field?
alts: Did a mountain fall down, Dad?
ca268-the-temblor-range.a: Sometime in the last 1.8 million years, a huge block of shale slid down the range's northeastern side, traveled about 3 miles and buried the McKittrick oil field.
ca268-the-temblor-range.quote: a block of shale more than 6 miles long, a mile wide and over 2,000 feet thick slid down the range's northeastern side

ca268-the-temblor-range.q: Can you drive across the Temblor Range?
alts: Are there roads through those mountains, Mom?
ca268-the-temblor-range.a: Yes. Highway 58 crosses the range at 3,750 feet, and Highway 46 uses its lowest pass, Polonio Pass, at 1,750 feet.
ca268-the-temblor-range.quote: Highway 58 crosses the range at 3,750 feet, and Highway 46 uses its lowest pass, Polonio Pass, at 1,750 feet.

ca273-san-joaquin-kit-fox.q: What is the San Joaquin kit fox?
alts: What is it, that fox with the big ears?
Is that a real fox, or like a tiny dog?
ca273-san-joaquin-kit-fox.a: It's an endangered fox with huge ears that lives on the dry west side of the valley. Kit foxes are the smallest wild members of the dog family in North America.
ca273-san-joaquin-kit-fox.quote: This dry west side of the valley is home to the San Joaquin kit fox, an endangered fox with huge ears.

ca273-san-joaquin-kit-fox.q: What does the San Joaquin kit fox eat?
alts: What does it eat, and when does it hunt?
Does it come out at night, and what does it catch?
ca273-san-joaquin-kit-fox.a: It hunts mostly at night, and mainly goes after kangaroo rats.
ca273-san-joaquin-kit-fox.quote: It hunts mostly at night, mainly for kangaroo rats.

ca273-san-joaquin-kit-fox.q: Where do San Joaquin kit foxes live today?
alts: Where can it still be found now?
Where do the foxes live, are there any near here?
ca273-san-joaquin-kit-fox.a: Its largest populations live in western Kern County, in and around the Elk Hills and the Buena Vista Valley. Some even live in Bakersfield.
ca273-san-joaquin-kit-fox.quote: Today its largest populations live in western Kern County, in and around the Elk Hills and the Buena Vista Valley.

ca275-downhill-all-the-way.q: How does the California Aqueduct move water without pumps?
alts: How does it move the water without pumps?
How does the water in the canal keep moving, anyway?
ca275-downhill-all-the-way.a: Gravity does the work. The canal is built on a slight grade, so the water flows downhill on its own along this stretch.
ca275-downhill-all-the-way.quote: The canal is built on a slight grade so gravity does the work.

ca275-downhill-all-the-way.q: How much of the aqueduct runs downhill by gravity here?
alts: How far does that downhill stretch go?
How long is the part with no pumps, mom?
ca275-downhill-all-the-way.a: From the Coastal Branch split south of Kettleman City, the water runs about 66 miles to the Buena Vista Pumping Plant, the first of four plants.
ca275-downhill-all-the-way.quote: From the Coastal Branch split south of Kettleman City, its water runs about 66 miles to the Buena Vista Pumping Plant

ca275-downhill-all-the-way.q: What happens to the water after the Buena Vista Pumping Plant?
alts: Where does it go after that plant?
Does the water ever go uphill, dad?
ca275-downhill-all-the-way.a: Buena Vista is the first of four plants that lift the water toward and over the Tehachapi Mountains.
ca275-downhill-all-the-way.quote: the first of four plants that lift it toward and over the Tehachapi Mountains

ca275-downhill-all-the-way.q: Who uses the water in the California Aqueduct?
alts: Who is all that water for?
Who gets the water from the big canal, mom?
ca275-downhill-all-the-way.a: The aqueduct carries water for about 35 million people and 5.7 million acres of farmland.
ca275-downhill-all-the-way.quote: The aqueduct carries water for about 35 million people and 5.7 million acres of farmland

ca275-downhill-all-the-way.q: Why is the land sinking along the California Aqueduct?
alts: Why is the ground sinking near it?
Is the ground really sinking, dad?
ca275-downhill-all-the-way.a: Pumping groundwater has made land along parts of the canal sink. NASA's GRACE satellites measure the Tulare Basin sinking about a foot a year.
ca275-downhill-all-the-way.quote: pumping groundwater has made land along parts of the canal sink. NASA's GRACE satellites measure the Tulare Basin sinking about a foot a year.

ca275-downhill-all-the-way.q: Why is a sinking aqueduct a problem?
alts: Why does it matter if that sags?
What's wrong if the canal sags, mom?
ca275-downhill-all-the-way.a: A sagging canal carries less water and costs more to run.
ca275-downhill-all-the-way.quote: A sagging canal carries less water and costs more to run.

ca278-blackwells-corner.q: Why is it called Blackwells Corner?
alts: Why did they name it that?
Who was Blackwell, and why is the place named after him?
ca278-blackwells-corner.a: It is named for George Blackwell, who started a rest stop there in 1921.
ca278-blackwells-corner.quote: Blackwells Corner is named for George Blackwell, who started a rest stop there in 1921.

ca278-blackwells-corner.q: What is Blackwells Corner famous for?
alts: Why do people talk about this place?
ca278-blackwells-corner.a: James Dean stopped there in 1955, and it is often described as the last place he was seen alive before his fatal crash near Cholame.
ca278-blackwells-corner.quote: James Dean stopped there in 1955, and it is often described as the last place he was seen alive before his fatal crash near Cholame.

alts: How long has it been there?
ca278-blackwells-corner.a: It goes back to 1921, when George Blackwell started a rest stop there.
ca278-blackwells-corner.quote: Blackwells Corner is named for George Blackwell, who started a rest stop there in 1921.

ca278-blackwells-corner.q: What happened to James Dean after Blackwells Corner?
alts: What happened to him after he left there?
Did something bad happen to James Dean?
ca278-blackwells-corner.a: Driving west near Cholame around 5:45 that evening, a driver coming the other way turned across his path, and Dean could not stop in time.
ca278-blackwells-corner.quote: At about 5:45 that evening, near Cholame, a college student driving the other way turned left across his path toward Highway 41, and Dean could not stop in time.

ca278-lost-hills.q: How did Lost Hills get its name?
alts: Why's this town called Lost Hills, Mom?
ca278-lost-hills.a: Lost Hills is named for the low Lost Hills range that sits right beside the town.
ca278-lost-hills.quote: takes its name from the low Lost Hills range beside it

ca278-lost-hills.q: How many people live in Lost Hills?
alts: Is Lost Hills a big town?
ca278-lost-hills.a: Lost Hills is a small town of about 2,400 people.
ca278-lost-hills.quote: Lost Hills, a town of about 2,400 people a couple of miles west of the freeway

ca278-lost-hills.q: What do people in Lost Hills do for work?
alts: What do the people in that town do all day?
ca278-lost-hills.a: Many residents work for the Wonderful Company, which has a pistachio and almond processing plant in town.
ca278-lost-hills.quote: Many residents work for the Wonderful Company, whose pistachio and almond processing plant is here.

ca278-lost-hills.q: What is the lizard bridge in Lost Hills?
alts: Why is the bridge shaped like that?
Why is there a lizard bridge?
ca278-lost-hills.a: It's a green footbridge over Highway 46, shaped like a lizard. The Wonderful Company paid for it after a pedestrian was killed crossing the highway.
ca278-lost-hills.quote: the Wonderful Company paid for a green footbridge over the highway. It is shaped like a lizard

ca278-lost-hills.q: What happens to the pistachios around Lost Hills?
alts: What do they do with the nuts?
How do they pick pistachios, Dad?
ca278-lost-hills.a: Each fall the pistachio trees are shaken and the nuts are hauled to processing plants. At the Lost Hills plant, workers sort them by hand.
ca278-lost-hills.quote: Each fall, pistachio trees are shaken and the nuts hauled to processing plants; at the one in Lost Hills, workers sort them by hand.

ca278-lost-hills.q: Is Lost Hills near the freeway exit?
alts: What exit do we take for that?
ca278-lost-hills.a: Lost Hills is at exit 278, and the town sits about 2 miles off the freeway.

ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.q: How did the Lost Hills oil field get started?
alts: How did they find the oil, anyway?
ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.a: In July 1910, two drillers named Martin and Dudley were digging a water well for livestock. At 530 feet they struck oil instead, and the Lost Hills oil field was born.
ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.quote: At 530 feet they struck oil instead, and the Lost Hills oil field was born.

ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.q: Who discovered the Lost Hills oil field?
alts: Who was the guy that found the oil?
ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.a: Two drillers named Martin and Dudley found it in July 1910. They were drilling a water well for livestock in the low hills when they hit oil.
ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.quote: In July 1910, two drillers named Martin and Dudley were drilling a water well for livestock in the low hills west of here.

ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.q: What was the Bellevue blowout at Lost Hills?
alts: Was there a giant fire here?
ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.a: In November 1998, a wildcat well hit gas under enormous pressure and burst into flame. The pillar of fire was about 340 feet tall and burned for 14 days.
ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.quote: It burst into flame, knocked over the drilling rig and melted nearby equipment, and the pillar of fire, about 340 feet tall

ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.q: Are the Lost Hills really sinking?
alts: Why are the hills getting lower?
ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.a: Yes. The hills rise barely 200 feet above the valley, and so much oil has been pumped out that parts of them have sunk as much as 8 feet.
ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.quote: so much oil has been pumped out that parts of them have sunk as much as 8 feet.

ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.q: What trouble does the sinking ground cause at Lost Hills?
alts: What happened to the well that collapsed?
Did anything fall in a hole there?
What breaks when the ground sinks?
ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.a: In 1976, a Getty Oil well collapsed into a crater more than 15 feet deep. It took its concrete pad and pump down with it.
ca280-lost-hills-oil-field.quote: in 1976 a Getty Oil well collapsed into a crater more than 15 feet deep, taking its concrete pad and pump with it.

ca284-tule-fog-season.q: Why is it called tule fog?
alts: Why do they call it that?
Why's the fog got a weird name?
ca284-tule-fog-season.a: It's named for the tule marshes of the Central Valley. It's a thick ground fog that fills the valley's southern end from November through March.
ca284-tule-fog-season.quote: The thick ground fog, named for the tule marshes of the Central Valley

alts: When can we get the fog, mom?
ca284-tule-fog-season.a: Tule fog can fill this southern end of the valley from November through March.
ca284-tule-fog-season.quote: From November through March, tule fog can fill this southern end of the valley.

ca284-tule-fog-season.q: How thick does tule fog get?
alts: How bad can it get in it?
Can we see anything in the fog?
ca284-tule-fog-season.a: Inside it, visibility is usually less than 600 feet. It can drop to almost nothing within a few feet.
ca284-tule-fog-season.quote: Inside it, visibility is usually less than 600 feet, and it can drop to almost nothing within a few feet.

alts: How does the fog get made?
ca284-tule-fog-season.a: It forms on long, calm nights after a good rain, when the damp ground cools. It's a low cloud trapped by the surrounding mountains and pressed down by warmer air above.
ca284-tule-fog-season.quote: It forms on long, calm nights after a good rain, when the damp ground cools.

ca284-tule-fog-season.q: How big does tule fog get?
alts: Is it just here or everywhere?
ca284-tule-fog-season.a: It can stretch more than 400 miles, from Bakersfield all the way to Red Bluff. It can also linger for days or even weeks.
ca284-tule-fog-season.quote: It can stretch more than 400 miles, from Bakersfield all the way to Red Bluff.

ca284-tule-fog-season.q: Is tule fog good for anything?
ca284-tule-fog-season.a: Yes. Almonds, cherries, pistachios and peaches need a long winter chill, and tule fog helps supply it.
ca284-tule-fog-season.quote: Farmers count on it too: almonds, cherries, pistachios and peaches need a long winter chill, and tule fog helps supply it.

ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.q: How old is Kern National Wildlife Refuge?
alts: How long has this place been around, mom?
ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.a: It was set aside on November 18, 1960.
ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.quote: The refuge was set aside on November 18, 1960.

ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.q: How big is Kern National Wildlife Refuge?
alts: Is it a huge place, dad?
ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.a: It protects 11,249 acres of desert uplands, an old river corridor and marsh.
ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.quote: Kern National Wildlife Refuge protects 11,249 acres of desert uplands, an old river corridor and marsh

ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.q: What can we do at Kern National Wildlife Refuge?
alts: Is there anything fun for kids to do there?
ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.a: You can drive its auto tour routes or walk its nature trails. It also has programs from waterfowl hunting to wildlife watching.
ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.quote: Its auto tour routes and nature trails are free to visit, and about 8,200 people a year come for programs from waterfowl hunting to wildlife watching.
