ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.q: What animals and habitat does Kern National Wildlife Refuge protect?
alts: Are there cool animals there, mom?
ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.a: Besides its marshes, it protects a remnant of the valley's original desert uplands and habitat for several endangered species.
ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.quote: Besides its marshes, it protects a remnant of the valley's original desert uplands and habitat for several endangered species.

ca288-kern-national-wildlife-refuge.q: What exit is Kern National Wildlife Refuge?
alts: Which exit do we take for it?
What exit do we get off at, dad?

ca293-kern-and-kings-county-line.q: How did Kings County get its name?
alts: How did it get that name?
Why is it called Kings, are there kings here?
ca293-kern-and-kings-county-line.a: It's named for the Kings River. Spanish soldiers called that river the River of the Holy Kings, which later became the Kings River.
ca293-kern-and-kings-county-line.quote: Kings County, carved out of Tulare County in 1893, takes its name from the Kings River, which Spanish soldiers called the River of the Holy Kings.

ca293-kern-and-kings-county-line.q: Why is it called the River of the Holy Kings?
alts: Why did they name that river that?
What kings were they talking about, mom?
ca293-kern-and-kings-county-line.a: Moraga's Spanish expedition camped beside it on January 6, 1806, the feast of the Epiphany, when Christians honor the three wise men. So they named it El Río de los Santos Reyes.
ca293-kern-and-kings-county-line.quote: Gabriel Moraga's Spanish expedition camped beside that river on January 6, 1806, the feast of the Epiphany, when Christians honor the three wise men

ca293-kern-and-kings-county-line.q: How did Kern County get its name?
ca293-kern-and-kings-county-line.a: Kern County takes its name from the Kern River. The county was formed in 1866.
ca293-kern-and-kings-county-line.quote: Kern County, formed in 1866, takes its name from the Kern River.

alts: What is it, and how do people catch it?
What's that fungus in the dust, mom?
ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.a: Valley fever is an illness caused by a fungus called Coccidioides that lives in the soil. People catch it by breathing in its spores. It is not contagious.
ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.quote: Coccidioides, a fungus that causes valley fever, also called San Joaquin Valley fever. Its spores rise into the air when dusty ground is stirred up

ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.q: Can I catch valley fever from another person?
alts: Can I get sick from you if you have it?
Does it spread person to person?
ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.a: No. It is not contagious. People catch it by breathing in the fungus spores that rise from dusty ground.
ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.quote: people catch it by breathing them in. It is not contagious, and about 60 percent of people who are infected have few or no symptoms.

ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.q: What does grow and blow mean for valley fever?
alts: What does that grow and blow thing mean?
How does the dirt make people sick?
ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.a: The fungus grows in the soil after rain. Then dry, windy weather lifts its spores into the air, where people can breathe them in.
ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.quote: the fungus grows in the soil after rain, then dry, windy weather lifts its spores.

ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.q: Are valley fever cases getting more common?
alts: Are more people catching it now?
ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.a: Yes. Kern County had about 1,000 cases in 2014 and 3,000 in 2021, and California reported nearly 12,500 cases in 2024, the most the state has documented.
ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.quote: Kern County recorded about 1,000 in 2014 and 3,000 in 2021, and California reported nearly 12,500 cases in 2024, the most the state has documented.

ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.q: How can we avoid valley fever while driving through?
alts: What should we do about it in a dust storm?
How do we keep from getting it?
ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.a: The CDC advises avoiding dusty places. During dust storms, stay inside with the windows closed.
ca296-valley-fever-in-the-dust.quote: The CDC advises avoiding dusty places and, during dust storms, staying inside with the windows closed.

ca300-the-coastal-branch.q: How long is the Coastal Branch?
alts: How far does that water pipe go, Dad?
ca300-the-coastal-branch.a: The Coastal Branch runs 116 miles. It splits off the California Aqueduct and heads for the coast.
ca300-the-coastal-branch.quote: The Coastal Branch runs 116 miles, climbing through five pumping plants to deliver water to San Luis Obispo, Santa Maria and Santa Barbara.

ca300-the-coastal-branch.q: What is the Coastal Branch for?
alts: Why do they need that pipe, Mom?
ca300-the-coastal-branch.a: It delivers water to San Luis Obispo, Santa Maria and Santa Barbara. It splits off the California Aqueduct and heads for the coast.
ca300-the-coastal-branch.quote: The Coastal Branch runs 116 miles, climbing through five pumping plants to deliver water to San Luis Obispo, Santa Maria and Santa Barbara.

ca300-the-coastal-branch.q: When was the Coastal Branch built?
alts: Is that water pipe really old?
ca300-the-coastal-branch.a: The first 15 miles, an open canal, were finished in 1968. The buried pipeline started in 1994, and the extension was finished in 1997.
ca300-the-coastal-branch.quote: The first 15 miles, an open canal, were finished in 1968. Most of the rest is a buried pipeline 42 to 57 inches across, built starting in 1994

ca300-the-coastal-branch.q: How does the Coastal Branch get water up the hills?
alts: How does the water climb, Dad?
ca300-the-coastal-branch.a: It climbs through five pumping plants. They have names like Las Perillas, Badger Hill, Devil's Den, Bluestone and Polonio Pass.
ca300-the-coastal-branch.quote: The pumping plants have names such as Las Perillas, Badger Hill, Devil's Den, Bluestone and Polonio Pass.

ca300-the-coastal-branch.q: How big is the pipe in the Coastal Branch?
alts: Could I fit inside that pipe?
ca300-the-coastal-branch.a: Most of it is a buried pipeline 42 to 57 inches across. The first 15 miles are an open canal instead.
ca300-the-coastal-branch.quote: Most of the rest is a buried pipeline 42 to 57 inches across, built starting in 1994, which runs to a tank on Vandenberg Space Force Base.

ca300-the-coastal-branch.q: Where does the Coastal Branch end?
alts: Where does that water go in the end?
ca300-the-coastal-branch.a: A 42-mile extension, finished in 1997, carries water through Lompoc, Buellton and Solvang to Lake Cachuma in the Los Padres National Forest.
ca300-the-coastal-branch.quote: an extension 42 miles long, finished in 1997, carries water through Lompoc, Buellton and Solvang to Lake Cachuma in the Los Padres National Forest.

alts: Who is that town named after?
ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.a: The town is named for John Alpaugh, an officer of the land colony that developed it.
ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.quote: The town is named for John Alpaugh, an officer of the land colony that developed it

alts: What was it before it was a town?
ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.a: It was the largest island in Tulare Lake, and the town of Alpaugh sits on what was once that island.
ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.quote: a town on what was once Atwell's Island, the largest island in Tulare Lake

ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.q: Who lived on Atwell's Island before the settlers?
alts: Did Native people live on it?
ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.a: The Wowol Yokuts village of Chawlowin stood on the island. After 1852, Yokuts families forced from their homes also hid there among the tules.
ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.quote: the Wowol Yokuts village of Chawlowin stood on the island, and after 1852 Yokuts families who had been forced from their homes hid there among the tules

ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.q: What happened to Alpaugh when the lake came back?
alts: Did it flood when the lake returned?
Did the lake come back to it?
ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.a: When the lake came back in 2023, parts of Alpaugh were ordered to evacuate.
ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.quote: When the lake came back in 2023, parts of Alpaugh were ordered to evacuate.

ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.q: What's the water situation in Alpaugh today?
alts: Can people drink the tap water there?
Why do they drink bottled water?
ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.a: The town's tap water carries too much arsenic, so residents rely on bottled water.
ca305-alpaugh-and-atwell-s-island.quote: The town's tap water carries too much arsenic, so residents rely on bottled water.

alts: What was that town, like, a real town?
ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.a: It's the first California town founded, financed and governed by African Americans. Today it's preserved as Colonel Allensworth State Historic Park.
ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.quote: Colonel Allensworth State Historic Park preserves the first California town founded, financed and governed by African Americans.

ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.q: Who started Colonel Allensworth's town and when?
alts: Who made that town, kid-style, who built it?
ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.a: Army veteran Allen Allensworth and four partners started it in 1908. They hoped to build a Tuskegee of the West, where Black families could own land, farm and run their own affairs.
ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.quote: Army veteran Allen Allensworth and four partners started it in 1908, hoping to build a Tuskegee of the West

ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.q: What did people do in Colonel Allensworth's town?
alts: What did they do there for a living?
What was in that town, did it have stores?
ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.a: Farmers grew alfalfa, wheat, sugar beets and cotton. The town had a bakery, drugstore, hotel, library and a school that became California's first African American school district.
ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.quote: Farmers grew alfalfa, wheat, sugar beets and cotton, and the town had a bakery, drugstore, hotel, library and a school

ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.q: Why did people leave Colonel Allensworth's town?
alts: Why did everybody leave that town?
ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.a: Troubles piled up. The water table dropped, alkali salts spread, and the railroad moved its stop to Alpaugh in 1914. Many residents left after World War I.
ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.quote: The water table dropped and alkali salts spread, the Santa Fe railroad moved its stop to Alpaugh in 1914

ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.q: What can we see at Colonel Allensworth State Historic Park?
alts: Is there stuff to see at that park, like old buildings?
ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.a: The park's restored buildings include the schoolhouse, hotel and general store. Every year it hosts a Juneteenth celebration and a rededication event in October.
ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.quote: its restored buildings include the schoolhouse, hotel and general store. Every year it hosts a Juneteenth celebration and a rededication event in October.

ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.q: How did Colonel Allensworth's town get saved as a park?
alts: How did that old town become a park, kid asking, who fixed it up?
When did it become a park?
ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.a: A former resident, Ed Pope, led the push to save the site. The park was established in 1976.
ca305-colonel-allensworth-s-town.quote: A former resident, Ed Pope, led the push to save the site. The park was established in 1976.

alts: What is that canal under the freeway?
Why is there a big concrete river here?
ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.a: It's a concrete river that carries water from the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta toward Southern California.
ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.quote: the concrete river that carries water from the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta toward Southern California

ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.q: How big is the California Aqueduct?
alts: How wide and deep is that water?
ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.a: A typical stretch is 40 feet wide at the bottom and holds water about 30 feet deep. The whole aqueduct runs more than 400 miles.
ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.quote: A typical stretch is 40 feet wide at the bottom and holds water about 30 feet deep, and the whole aqueduct runs more than 400 miles.

ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.q: Who is the California Aqueduct named after?
ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.a: It is named for Governor Edmund G. Pat Brown, and it's the main feature of the State Water Project.
ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.quote: It is named for Governor Edmund G. Pat Brown and is the main feature of the State Water Project.

ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.q: Where does the California Aqueduct begin?
alts: Where does all that water come from?
ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.a: It begins at Clifton Court Forebay in the Delta, where the first pumps lift the water 240 feet.
ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.quote: It begins at Clifton Court Forebay in the Delta, where the first pumps lift the water 240 feet.

ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.q: How many times does I-5 cross the California Aqueduct?
alts: Are we going over it more than once?
ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.a: I-5 crosses the aqueduct five times. Counting from the south, this is the second crossing.
ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.quote: Counting from the south, this is the second of I-5's five crossings of the aqueduct.

ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.q: Could solar panels cover the California Aqueduct?
alts: What could they do with it?
Why would anyone put solar panels on a canal?
ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.a: A 2021 study estimated that covering canals like this with solar panels could save 11 to 22 million gallons of water per mile each year from evaporation.
ca309-crossing-the-california-aqueduct.quote: A 2021 study estimated that covering canals like this with solar panels could save 11 to 22 million gallons of water per mile each year from evaporation.

alts: Was there really a giant lake here, Dad?
ca309-ghost-of-tulare-lake.a: Tulare Lake was once the largest freshwater lake west of the Mississippi River. It lay to the east of here, but the rivers that fed it were diverted for farming, and by 1899 it was dry except for marshes.
ca309-ghost-of-tulare-lake.quote: East of here lies the bed of Tulare Lake, once the largest freshwater lake west of the Mississippi River.

alts: What did the Native people call the lake?
ca309-ghost-of-tulare-lake.a: Pa'ashi means big water. It is what the Tachi Yokut Tribe calls Tulare Lake.
ca309-ghost-of-tulare-lake.quote: The Tachi Yokut Tribe calls it Pa'ashi, big water.

alts: Were there Native kids living by the lake?
ca309-ghost-of-tulare-lake.a: For thousands of years the lake supported perhaps the largest Native population north of Mexico. The Tachi, Wowol and Chunut Yokuts lived around its shores.
ca309-ghost-of-tulare-lake.quote: the lake supported perhaps the largest Native population north of Mexico, with the Tachi, Wowol and Chunut Yokuts living around its shores.

ca309-ghost-of-tulare-lake.q: Did Tulare Lake ever come back?
alts: Does the water ever return, Mom?
ca309-ghost-of-tulare-lake.a: Yes. In 1983 it took two years to dry out, and in 2023 storms brought back more than 114,000 acres of it. Yoimut, a woman who spent much of her life on the lake, had warned that it would return.
ca309-ghost-of-tulare-lake.quote: Yoimut, a woman who spent much of her life on the lake, had warned that it would return.

ca309-ghost-of-tulare-lake.q: What happened here during World War II?
alts: What did the Navy do with it?
Did planes land on the lake?
ca309-ghost-of-tulare-lake.a: During World War II, Navy flying boats used the lake as a backup landing place.
ca309-ghost-of-tulare-lake.quote: During World War II, Navy flying boats used it as a backup landing place.

ca309-a-landfill-and-a-town-s-fight.q: What is the Kettleman Hills landfill?
alts: What's that big dump out there?
ca309-a-landfill-and-a-town-s-fight.a: It's a landfill of about 1,500 acres for hazardous and household waste, run by a subsidiary of Waste Management. It sits off Highway 41, southwest of Kettleman City.
ca309-a-landfill-and-a-town-s-fight.quote: the Kettleman Hills facility is a landfill of about 1,500 acres for hazardous and household waste, run by a subsidiary of Waste Management

ca309-a-landfill-and-a-town-s-fight.q: Why did Kettleman City fight the landfill?
alts: Why did the town fight it?
Why were people mad at the dump?
ca309-a-landfill-and-a-town-s-fight.a: When the company asked to expand, many of the town's roughly 1,500 residents fought it, fearing more PCB waste.
ca309-a-landfill-and-a-town-s-fight.quote: When the company asked to expand, many of the town's roughly 1,500 residents fought it, fearing more PCB waste.

ca309-a-landfill-and-a-town-s-fight.q: What did Greenaction report about Kettleman City?
alts: What did the group say happened there?
What happened to the babies there?
What was the birth defects thing?
ca309-a-landfill-and-a-town-s-fight.a: In 2007 and 2008, Greenaction reported a cluster of birth defects and infant deaths in town and linked them to pollution sources, including the landfill.
ca309-a-landfill-and-a-town-s-fight.quote: In 2007 and 2008, the environmental justice group Greenaction reported a cluster of birth defects and infant deaths in town

ca309-a-landfill-and-a-town-s-fight.q: Did the landfill expansion get approved?
alts: Did they get to expand it?
ca309-a-landfill-and-a-town-s-fight.a: In 2014 state regulators approved the expansion and then denied two appeals. Opponents vowed to keep challenging it. The company says no link to the birth defects has been established.
ca309-a-landfill-and-a-town-s-fight.quote: In 2014 state regulators approved the expansion and then denied two appeals, and opponents vowed to keep challenging it.

ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.q: Why is Kettleman City such a popular stop?
alts: Why does everybody stop at it?
Why do we always stop here, mom?
ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.a: It sits near the halfway point between Los Angeles and San Francisco or Sacramento, which makes this exit a major stop for food and lodging.
ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.quote: Kettleman City is near the halfway point between Los Angeles and San Francisco or Sacramento, which makes this exit a major stop for food and lodging.

ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.q: Who founded Kettleman City and when?
ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.a: A real estate developer named A. Manford Brown founded the town in 1929, right after oil was found in the hills.
ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.quote: A real estate developer, A. Manford Brown, founded the town in 1929, right after oil was found in the hills

ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.q: How many people live in Kettleman City?
alts: Do lots of kids live in that town?
ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.a: About 1,200 people live in the town, which sits about a mile north of the travel stops, past the aqueduct.
ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.quote: the town itself, about 1,200 people, sits about a mile north, past the aqueduct.

ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.q: What did people do before Highway 41 existed near Kettleman City?
alts: How did people get across before the road?
Did they really use a boat here, dad?
ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.a: In the early 1900s, before Tulare Lake shrank, people traveled between Lemoore and Kettleman by ferry. As the lake receded in the late 1920s, that route became Highway 41.
ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.quote: In the early 1900s, before Tulare Lake shrank, people traveled between Lemoore and Kettleman by ferry

ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.q: What kind of work do people do in Kettleman City?
alts: What do people there do for a job?
What do the grown-ups there do, mom?
ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.a: Many residents work in agriculture, and most speak Spanish at home.
ca309-kettleman-city-halfway.quote: Most residents speak Spanish at home, and many work in agriculture.

ca314-kettleman-hills.q: How big are the Kettleman Hills?
alts: How big is that range of hills?
Are those hills really long, or tall?
ca314-kettleman-hills.a: The Kettleman Hills are about 30 miles long and rise up to about 1,200 feet high.
ca314-kettleman-hills.quote: The long, low hills along the west side are the Kettleman Hills, about 30 miles long and up to about 1,200 feet high.

ca314-kettleman-hills.q: Why are they called the Kettleman Hills?
alts: Who is Kettleman, and why are the hills named after him?
ca314-kettleman-hills.a: They're named, with a spelling change, for Dave Kettelman, who grazed sheep and cattle here in the 1860s.
ca314-kettleman-hills.quote: They are named, with a spelling change, for Dave Kettelman, who grazed sheep and cattle here in the 1860s.

ca314-kettleman-hills.q: How were the Kettleman Hills formed?
alts: How did those hills get here, anyway?
What are the hills made of?
ca314-kettleman-hills.a: They're a long fold in the rock, squeezed up by tectonic forces, and they run parallel to the San Andreas Fault, farther west.
ca314-kettleman-hills.quote: They are a long fold in the rock, squeezed up by tectonic forces, and they run parallel to the San Andreas Fault, farther west.

ca314-kettleman-hills.q: Is there oil in the Kettleman Hills?
alts: Do they still pump oil out of it?
Is there oil under those hills?
ca314-kettleman-hills.a: Yes. The range is two long domes, the North Dome and the Middle Dome, and each sits on an oil field. The North Dome's field alone is about 14 miles long.
ca314-kettleman-hills.quote: The range is really two long domes, the North Dome and the Middle Dome, and each sits on an oil field; the North Dome's field alone is about 14 miles long.

ca314-kettleman-hills.q: Did an earthquake ever happen at the Kettleman Hills?
alts: Was there an earthquake near it?
Did pumping oil cause a quake?
ca314-kettleman-hills.a: On August 4, 1985, an earthquake of about magnitude 6 caused slight damage in nearby towns. Some scientists suggest decades of oil pumping helped set it off.
ca314-kettleman-hills.quote: some scientists have suggested that decades of pumping oil out of these hills helped set it off.

ca319-the-1928-kettleman-gusher.q: What was so strange about the oil at Kettleman?
alts: What was weird about that oil?
ca319-the-1928-kettleman-gusher.a: It was so light that it was white. It reportedly could even run a car without being refined.
ca319-the-1928-kettleman-gusher.quote: spraying oil so light that it was white, and it reportedly could run a car without refining.

ca319-the-1928-kettleman-gusher.q: How long did it take to stop the Kettleman gusher?
alts: How long did it take to stop it?
Could they not turn it off?
ca319-the-1928-kettleman-gusher.a: The blowout took three years to bring under control. Thousands of spectators reportedly came to watch it.
ca319-the-1928-kettleman-gusher.quote: The blowout took three years to bring under control, and thousands of spectators reportedly came to watch it.

ca319-the-1928-kettleman-gusher.q: Why was Kettleman oil such a big deal for California?
alts: Why did that oil matter so much?
ca319-the-1928-kettleman-gusher.a: The Kettleman North Dome became one of the most productive oil fields in the country. Its flood of oil pushed prices down and caused bitter feelings in the oil industry.
ca319-the-1928-kettleman-gusher.quote: The Kettleman North Dome became one of the most productive oil fields in the country.

ca319-the-1928-kettleman-gusher.q: Is there still oil at Kettleman today?
ca319-the-1928-kettleman-gusher.a: Very little. Today less than half of one percent of the field's original oil is left.
ca319-the-1928-kettleman-gusher.quote: Today less than half of one percent of the field's original oil is left.

ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.q: Why is the town called Avenal?
alts: Why's it named oat field, mom?
ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.a: Avenal is Spanish for oat field. Spanish soldiers and explorers named it for the wild oats, waist high, that covered the plain like golden silk.
ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.quote: Spanish soldiers and explorers named it for the wild oats, waist high, that covered the plain like golden silk.

ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.q: Who built the town of Avenal?
ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.a: Standard Oil laid out the town in 1929, after oil was found in the hills.
ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.quote: Standard Oil laid out the town in 1929, after oil was found in the hills

ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.q: What was Avenal's first post office?
alts: What was it like at the start?
Was the first post office a real building?
What was in the old general store?
ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.a: Its first post office was a cigar box on the counter of the general store.
ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.quote: its first post office was a cigar box on the counter of the general store.

ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.q: Why does Avenal have a prison?
alts: Why is there a prison there?
Did the town want a prison?
ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.a: After Avenal became a city, it asked the state for a prison, the first California prison a community actively sought. Avenal State Prison opened in 1987.
ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.quote: After Avenal became a city, it asked the state for a prison, the first California prison a community actively sought.

ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.q: What is special about the gliderport in Avenal?
ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.a: Avenal has a gliderport, one of the few airports in the western U.S. just for gliders.
ca319-avenal-the-oat-field.quote: Avenal also has a gliderport, one of the few airports in the western U.S. just for gliders.

ca322-garlic-country.q: Where does most of America's garlic come from?
alts: Where does it all get grown?
Where's the garlic come from, Mom?
ca322-garlic-country.a: Most of the garlic in the United States is grown in Fresno County. West side towns such as Huron picked up the slack as Gilroy ran out of room.
ca322-garlic-country.quote: Fresno County grows most of the garlic in the United States, and west side towns such as Huron picked up the slack as Gilroy

ca322-garlic-country.q: How much garlic does Fresno County grow?
alts: How much of it do they harvest?
Is that a lot of garlic?
ca322-garlic-country.a: In 2022 the county harvested about 23,000 acres and 185,000 tons of garlic. That was nearly two-thirds of California's crop, worth about 350 million dollars.
ca322-garlic-country.quote: In 2022 the county harvested about 23,000 acres and 185,000 tons of garlic, nearly two-thirds of California's crop, worth about 350 million dollars.

alts: Why did it move away from there?
Why did the garlic go away from Gilroy?
ca322-garlic-country.a: Gilroy ran out of room. Urban growth spreading from San Jose pushed most of the garlic out, and Santa Clara County was down to about 300 acres in one count.
ca322-garlic-country.quote: Urban growth spreading from San Jose pushed most of the garlic out of Gilroy, and Santa Clara County, its home, was down to about 300 acres

ca322-garlic-country.q: How is garlic dried after it's harvested?
alts: What do they do with it after cutting?
Why does the field look like straw?
ca322-garlic-country.a: After the garlic is cut, it's left in the field to dry under its own tops. Those tops come to look like straw.
ca322-garlic-country.quote: After the garlic is cut, it is left in the field to dry under its own tops, which come to look like straw.

ca322-garlic-country.q: Does the whole world get its garlic from here?
alts: Is that where all garlic comes from?
Does everybody's garlic come from here?
What about the rest of the world?
ca322-garlic-country.a: Not even close. Worldwide, China grows nearly three-quarters of all garlic.
ca322-garlic-country.quote: Worldwide, though, China grows nearly three-quarters of all garlic.

ca322-garlic-country.q: Is the garlic harvest in Fresno County still big?
alts: Is it still that big now?
Did the harvest shrink over the years?
ca322-garlic-country.a: Yes, it's stayed huge for years. The harvest was about 178,000 tons in 2020 and 187,000 tons in 2021.
ca322-garlic-country.quote: Fresno County's harvest has stayed huge for years: about 178,000 tons in 2020 and 187,000 tons in 2021.

alts: What is that huge yard of electrical stuff?
What are all those towers for?
ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.a: It's a key junction on the power lines that link Northern and Southern California. You can spot it as a sprawling electrical yard east of the freeway.
ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.quote: The sprawling electrical yard east of the freeway is Gates Substation, a key junction on the power lines linking Northern and Southern California.

ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.q: What was the Gates Substation bottleneck?
alts: Why did the power lines have a problem here, mister?
ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.a: Between here and Los Banos, the corridor once had only two of its biggest lines. That limited how much power could flow.
ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.quote: Between here and Los Banos, the corridor once had only two of its biggest lines. That bottleneck limited how much power could flow

ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.q: How did the Gates bottleneck relate to the 2000 electricity crisis?
alts: Did that cause the electricity crisis?
Was that why the lights went out back then?
ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.a: It was one of the leading causes of the California electricity crisis of 2000 and 2001.
ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.quote: it was one of the leading causes of the California electricity crisis of 2000 and 2001.

ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.q: How much power could the lines carry at Gates?
alts: How much less could it carry than elsewhere?
How many megawatts could it hold?
ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.a: Between Los Banos and Gates only 3,900 megawatts could flow. Elsewhere the lines could carry about 5,400 megawatts from south to north.
ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.quote: Elsewhere the lines could carry about 5,400 megawatts from south to north, but between Los Banos and Gates only 3,900.

ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.q: Did anyone ever fix the Gates bottleneck?
alts: Did they ever build more power lines, mister?
ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.a: Yes. A third 500,000-volt line was finished on time and under budget on December 21, 2004. Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger attended the commissioning ceremony.
ca325-gates-substation-bottleneck.quote: built a third 500,000-volt line, finished on time and under budget on December 21, 2004, and Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger attended the commissioning ceremony.

alts: Why is there even a town out here?
ca325-huron-harvest-town.a: Huron began in 1888 as a water stop on the Southern Pacific Railroad. Joseph Mouren and his family later did much to grow the town in the late 1800s.
ca325-huron-harvest-town.quote: It began in 1888 as a water stop on the Southern Pacific Railroad.

ca325-huron-harvest-town.q: How many people live in Huron?
alts: How many folks are in Huron?
ca325-huron-harvest-town.a: About 6,200 people live in Huron. At harvest time, when migrant farmworkers arrive, the town swells to more than 15,000.
ca325-huron-harvest-town.quote: a farm town of about 6,200 people that swells to more than 15,000 at harvest time, when migrant farmworkers arrive

ca325-huron-harvest-town.a: Huron is a farm town. In the 2000 census it had the highest share of Hispanic or Latino residents of any city in the United States.
ca325-huron-harvest-town.quote: In the 2000 census, Huron had the highest share of Hispanic or Latino residents of any city in the United States.

ca325-huron-harvest-town.q: What happened in Huron during World War II?
alts: What happened there in the war?
Was Huron in World War II?
ca325-huron-harvest-town.a: Three training airstrips around town served Lemoore Army Air Field. They were called Huron Field, West Field and Indian Field.
ca325-huron-harvest-town.quote: three training airstrips around town, Huron Field, West Field and Indian Field, served Lemoore Army Air Field

ca325-huron-harvest-town.q: Why is there a Mouren Drive in Huron?
alts: Who is that street named after?
ca325-huron-harvest-town.a: Mouren Drive is named for Joseph Mouren. He and his family did much to grow the town in the late 1800s.
ca325-huron-harvest-town.quote: Joseph Mouren and his family did much to grow the town in the late 1800s, and Mouren Drive is named for him.

ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.q: What happened at the Arroyo Pasajero bridges?
alts: What happened here at that creek bridge?
Why did the bridges fall down?
What's the story with these bridges?
ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.a: On March 10, 1995, extreme rain sent fast floodwater down the creek. Both I-5 bridges failed, and four cars and a truck went into the creek. Seven people died.
ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.quote: On March 10, 1995, extreme rain sent fast floodwater down the creek.

ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.q: Why did the Arroyo Pasajero bridges fail in 1995?
alts: How did the flood break it?
How does water knock down a bridge?
ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.a: The flood scoured the creek bed down around the bridge supports. Water and debris then struck the columns at an angle and broke them.
ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.quote: the flood had scoured the creek bed down around the bridge supports, and that the force of water and debris, striking the columns at an angle, broke them

ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.q: Are the Arroyo Pasajero bridges the original ones?
alts: Is it the same bridge that failed?
Did they build new bridges after the flood?
ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.a: No. Both of the bridges standing here today were built in 1995, the same year the old bridges failed in the flood.
ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.quote: Both of the bridges standing here today were built that same year.

ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.q: Where does the creek at Arroyo Pasajero come from?
alts: Where does the water come from?
ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.a: The creek starts in the Diablo Range near Benito Pass. It flows past Coalinga into the valley.
ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.quote: The creek starts in the Diablo Range near Benito Pass and flows past Coalinga into the valley.

ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.q: What was Poso de Chane near Arroyo Pasajero?
alts: Was there a village near that creek?
Did people live here long ago?
ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.a: Poso de Chane was an old waterhole and the site of a Native village the Spanish called the Chane. It was later a stop on El Camino Viejo, until the Great Flood of 1862 destroyed it.
ca327-arroyo-pasajero-bridges.quote: was the site of a Native village the Spanish called the Chane, and later a stop on El Camino Viejo, until the Great Flood of 1862 destroyed it.

ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.q: When did the Harris Ranch restaurant open?
alts: When did this place start, mom?
How long has it been here?
ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.a: The Harris Ranch restaurant opened beside the freeway in 1977. It was aimed at local farmers, then became a popular stop for travelers.
ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.quote: The Harris Ranch restaurant opened beside the freeway in 1977, aimed at local farmers, and soon became a popular stop for travelers

ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.q: How big is the Harris Ranch Inn?
alts: How many rooms does it have?
ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.a: The hacienda-style inn has 153 rooms. It was added in 1987, ten years after the restaurant opened.
ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.quote: A 153-room hacienda-style inn was added in 1987

ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.q: What does the Harris Ranch restaurant serve?
alts: What kind of food is it known for?
What do they cook there, Dad?
ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.a: It serves the ranch's own beef, plus wine and other products the ranch makes. In the late 2000s it turned to a farm to fork menu.
ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.quote: the restaurant turned to a farm to fork menu, serving the ranch's own beef along with wine and other products the ranch makes

ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.q: Is Harris Ranch a popular stop?
alts: Do lots of people go there?
ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.a: Yes, it soon became a popular stop for travelers between Los Angeles and San Francisco. By 2008 the restaurant ranked sixth in California by sales.
ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.quote: by 2008 the restaurant ranked sixth in California by sales

ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.q: Is there an airport at Harris Ranch?
alts: Why are there airplanes next to the inn?
ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.a: Yes, Harris Ranch Airport sits next to the inn. It has a single runway 2,820 feet long and has been open since 1981.
ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.quote: Next to the inn is Harris Ranch Airport, a single runway 2,820 feet long, open since 1981.

ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.q: What exit is Harris Ranch Inn?
alts: Which exit do we take for it?
How do I find it from the freeway?
ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.a: Take exit 334. Look for the big hacienda-style inn right beside the freeway.
ca334-harris-ranch-inn-and-restaurant.quote: Look for the big hacienda-style inn right beside the freeway.

ca334-coalinga-oil-field.q: What is the Coalinga Oil Field famous for?
alts: Why is this oil field a big deal, mom?
ca334-coalinga-oil-field.a: It's one of only six California fields to have produced more than a billion barrels of oil. By 1910 it was the most productive oil field in the state.
ca334-coalinga-oil-field.quote: one of only six California fields to have produced more than a billion barrels of oil. By 1910 it was the most productive oil field in the state

ca334-coalinga-oil-field.q: What was the Silver Tip gusher at Coalinga?
alts: Was there a huge oil explosion here?
ca334-coalinga-oil-field.a: In September 1909 the Silver Tip well blew in at 20,000 barrels a day, then the biggest gusher California had seen.
ca334-coalinga-oil-field.quote: In September 1909 a well called Silver Tip blew in at 20,000 barrels a day, then the biggest gusher California had seen

ca334-coalinga-oil-field.q: What did Native people use the oil seeps for here?
alts: What did they do with the tar before drillers came?
Did people use the oil long ago, like cavemen?
ca334-coalinga-oil-field.a: Long before drillers came, Native people here used tar from natural seeps to line baskets and to trade.
ca334-coalinga-oil-field.quote: Long before drillers came, Native people here used tar from natural seeps to line baskets and to trade.

ca334-coalinga-oil-field.q: How did the local drillers fight back against Standard Oil?
alts: What did they do about that?
Did the little guys beat the big oil company?
ca334-coalinga-oil-field.a: They built their own pipeline to San Francisco Bay, working on a dummy pipeline in plain sight while the real one went in quietly.
ca334-coalinga-oil-field.quote: The independents answered by building their own pipeline to San Francisco Bay, working on a dummy pipeline in plain sight while the real one went in quietly.

ca334-coalinga-oil-field.q: What is the long ridge near the Coalinga Oil Field?
alts: What's that long low hill, dad?
ca334-coalinga-oil-field.a: It's Anticline Ridge, a long, low ridge between the freeway and Coalinga that's part of the Coalinga Oil Field.
ca334-coalinga-oil-field.quote: The long, low ridge between the freeway and Coalinga is Anticline Ridge, part of the Coalinga Oil Field

ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.q: How did Coalinga get its name?
alts: How did it get that name?
Why's this town called Coalinga, Mom?
ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.a: It began as a railroad coaling stop called Coaling Station A. Tradition says an official added an a to make it more musical, or a station sign may have squeezed Coaling A into Coalinga.
ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.quote: Local tradition says a railroad official made the name more musical by adding an a. It is just as likely that a small station sign squeezed Coaling A into Coalinga.

ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.q: When was Coalinga founded and why?
alts: When did it start and why?
How old is this town, Dad?
ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.a: Coalinga began in 1888 as a Southern Pacific coaling stop for steam locomotives.
ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.quote: Coalinga began in 1888 as a Southern Pacific coaling stop for steam locomotives.

ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.q: What is the Iron Zoo in Coalinga?
alts: What is that Iron Zoo thing?
Are there real animals at the Iron Zoo?
ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.a: It's a collection of oil pumps painted as animals and characters. It grew to include a zebra, a giraffe, a bald eagle and a bobbing goat.
ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.quote: The Iron Zoo grew to include a zebra, a giraffe, a bald eagle and a bobbing goat

ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.q: Who painted the Iron Zoo oil pumps?
alts: Who made the pumps look like animals?
ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.a: Jean Dakessian Jones began it in the early 1970s. By mid-1973 she had painted all 23 of Shell's pumps, then held a contest for local artists to paint 34 more.
ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.quote: by mid-1973 she had painted all 23 of Shell's pumps. She then held a contest for local artists to paint 34 more.

ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.q: Can we still see the painted pumps in Coalinga?
alts: Do the animal pumps still work?
ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.a: Not all of them. Many of the painted pumps have since been shut down and taken apart.
ca337-coalinga-and-the-iron-zoo.quote: Many of the painted pumps have since been shut down and taken apart.

ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.q: How strong was the 1983 Coalinga earthquake?
alts: How big was that earthquake, Dad?
ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.a: It was a magnitude 6.2 earthquake. It struck Coalinga at 4:42 on the afternoon of May 2, 1983.
ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.quote: At 4:42 on the afternoon of May 2, 1983, a magnitude 6.2 earthquake struck Coalinga.

ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.q: What damage did the Coalinga earthquake cause to the town?
alts: Did the earthquake wreck the whole town?
ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.a: The eight-block downtown was almost destroyed, and 94 people were injured. The worst damage hit buildings with unreinforced brick walls.
ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.quote: The town's eight-block downtown was almost destroyed, with the worst damage to buildings with unreinforced brick walls, and 94 people were injured.

ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.q: How far away was the Coalinga earthquake felt?
alts: Did people far away feel it?
ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.a: The shaking was felt from the Los Angeles area all the way to Susanville, in Lassen County.
ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.quote: The shaking was felt from the Los Angeles area to Susanville, in Lassen County.

ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.q: Did the Coalinga earthquake break open the ground?
alts: Did the ground split open, Mom?
ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.a: Not at the surface. The main shock broke no fault there; instead a ridge northeast of town rose about half a meter, roughly a foot and a half.
ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.quote: The main shock broke no fault at the surface. Instead, an anticline ridge northeast of town rose about half a meter, roughly a foot and a half.

ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.q: Were there aftershocks after the Coalinga earthquake?
alts: Did it keep shaking after that?
Were there more quakes after it?
ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.a: Yes, a lot. More than 5,000 aftershocks were recorded by the end of July.
ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.quote: More than 5,000 aftershocks were recorded by the end of July.

ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.q: Did the 1983 Coalinga earthquake hurt the oil fields?
alts: What happened to the oil wells in it?
Did the oil pumps get broken?
ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.a: Yes. Pumping units, tanks and pipelines were damaged, and 14 of 1,725 active wells had collapsed or broken casings underground.
ca337-the-1983-coalinga-earthquake.quote: In the oil fields, pumping units, tanks and pipelines were damaged, and 14 of 1,725 active wells had collapsed or broken casings underground.

ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.q: What is the Harris Ranch feedlot famous for?
alts: Why do people know that place, Mom?
ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.a: It's California's largest beef producer, and the feedlot sits right beside the freeway. Many travelers notice it by smell first.
ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.quote: Harris Ranch is California's largest beef producer, and its feedlot sits right beside the freeway.

ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.q: How many cows are at the Harris Ranch feedlot?
alts: How many animals does it hold?
Whoa, how many cows are in there?
ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.a: It holds more than 100,000 cattle on more than 800 acres.
ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.quote: It holds more than 100,000 cattle on more than 800 acres

ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.q: Who started Harris Ranch and when?
alts: Who started that place, and how long ago?
ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.a: Jack Harris and his wife, Teresa, started the ranch in 1937 on 320 acres of desert land that had never been farmed.
ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.quote: Jack Harris and his wife, Teresa, started the ranch in 1937 on 320 acres of desert land that had never been farmed.

ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.q: What else does Harris Ranch grow besides cattle?
alts: What do they grow there too?
Do they grow anything else, like fruit?
ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.a: Its fields grow onions, garlic, almonds, pistachios, lettuce, tomatoes, citrus and melons. A thoroughbred division started in 1966 also raises racehorses.
ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.quote: today its fields grow onions, garlic, almonds, pistachios, lettuce, tomatoes, citrus and melons.

ca337-harris-ranch-feedlot.q: What exit is the Harris Ranch feedlot?
alts: What exit do we take for that?
Mom, what's that big water district thing?
ca341-westlands-water-district.a: It's the water district serving much of the west side of Fresno and Kings counties along this part of the freeway. It was formed in 1952.
ca341-westlands-water-district.quote: Much of the west side of Fresno and Kings counties, along this part of the freeway, is served by Westlands Water District, formed in 1952.

ca341-westlands-water-district.q: How big is Westlands Water District?
alts: Is that a really huge farm area?
ca341-westlands-water-district.a: By irrigable acres it's the largest farm water district in the country, about 614,000 acres. Roughly 700 farmers own land there.
ca341-westlands-water-district.quote: By irrigable acres it is the largest farm water district in the country, about 614,000 acres, where roughly 700 farmers own land.

ca341-westlands-water-district.q: Where did the farms here get their water before the canal?
alts: How did they water the crops before that?
How did the farmers get water back then?
ca341-westlands-water-district.a: Farms here first irrigated from deep wells, starting around 1915. All that heavy pumping lowered the water table and made the land sink.
ca341-westlands-water-district.quote: Farms here first irrigated from deep wells, starting around 1915, and the heavy pumping lowered the water table and made the land sink.

ca341-westlands-water-district.q: When did federal water finally reach Westlands?
alts: When did it get canal water?
How did the water get here for the farms?
ca341-westlands-water-district.a: Federal water arrived through the San Luis Canal, which was finished in 1968.
ca341-westlands-water-district.quote: Federal water finally arrived through the San Luis Canal, finished in 1968.

alts: What went wrong with that drain?
Why did the birds get hurt?
ca341-westlands-water-district.a: Salty drainage water ended up in the ponds of Kesterson Reservoir. It was shut off in the mid-1980s after selenium in it harmed water birds there.
ca341-westlands-water-district.quote: Its water ended up in the ponds of Kesterson Reservoir, and the drainage was shut off in the mid-1980s after selenium in it harmed water birds there.

ca341-westlands-water-district.q: Why is Westlands in so many California water fights?
alts: Why is it always in the news about water?
Why do people argue about that place?
ca341-westlands-water-district.a: Because of its size, it sits at the center of many of California's water fights. It also still has no outlet for its salty drainage water.
ca341-westlands-water-district.quote: Westlands still has no outlet for that drainage water, and because of its size it sits at the center of many of California's water fights.

ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.q: What happened in the Plane wreck at Los Gatos?
alts: What was the plane crash about, mom?
ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.a: A chartered DC-3 crashed in the Diablo Range near Los Gatos Creek on January 28, 1948. All 32 people aboard died, most of them Mexican farmworkers being sent back to Mexico.
ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.quote: On January 28, 1948, a chartered DC-3 crashed in the Diablo Range about 20 miles west of Coalinga, near Los Gatos Creek. All 32 people aboard died.

ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.q: Why is there a famous song about the Los Gatos plane wreck?
alts: Why is it in a song?
Who wrote the song about that crash?
ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.a: Woody Guthrie wrote a poem about the nameless victims, and a decade later Martin Hoffman set it to music. It's called Deportee, and Johnny Cash, Joan Baez and Bruce Springsteen have sung it.
ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.quote: Woody Guthrie wrote a poem about the nameless victims, and a decade later a college student, Martin Hoffman, set it to music.

ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.q: Why were the victims of the Los Gatos crash nameless?
alts: Why didn't anyone know their names?
Why were they just called deportees, mom?
ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.a: The first news reports named only the pilot, copilot, flight attendant and immigration guard. They listed the rest simply as deportees.
ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.quote: First news reports named only the pilot, copilot, flight attendant and immigration guard, and listed the rest simply as deportees.

ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.q: Where were the Los Gatos plane crash victims buried?
ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.a: The Mexican victims were buried in a mass grave in Fresno marked only Mexican Nationals. On Labor Day 2013, a headstone listing all 28 names was unveiled.
ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.quote: The Mexican victims were buried in a mass grave in Fresno marked only Mexican Nationals.

ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.q: How did the Los Gatos plane wreck affect Cesar Chavez?
alts: Did it matter to Cesar Chavez?
Why does that crash matter, mom?
ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.a: News of the crash helped convince a young Cesar Chavez that farmworkers should be treated as important human beings, not as farm tools.
ca344-plane-wreck-at-los-gatos.quote: News of the crash helped convince a young Cesar Chavez that farmworkers should be treated as important human beings, not as farm tools.

ca345-joaquin-rocks.q: Why are they called the Joaquin Rocks?
alts: How did the rocks get their name, mom?
ca345-joaquin-rocks.a: They're named for the Gold Rush bandit Joaquin Murrieta, whose gang is said to have used them as a lookout.
ca345-joaquin-rocks.quote: They are named for the Gold Rush bandit Joaquin Murrieta, whose gang is said to have used them as a lookout.

ca345-joaquin-rocks.q: What did people used to call the Joaquin Rocks?
alts: Did the rocks have another name, Dad?
ca345-joaquin-rocks.a: They were once called Las Tres Piedras, which means the Three Rocks.
ca345-joaquin-rocks.quote: These are the Joaquin Rocks, once called Las Tres Piedras, the Three Rocks, and they can be seen for miles across the valley.

ca345-joaquin-rocks.q: How high up are the Joaquin Rocks?
alts: How tall is it up there?
Are the rocks really high up, Dad?
ca345-joaquin-rocks.a: The three stone pillars stand on a high ridge, about 4,100 feet up, and they can be seen for miles across the valley.
ca345-joaquin-rocks.quote: On the high ridge west of the freeway stand three stone pillars, about 4,100 feet up.

ca345-joaquin-rocks.q: What can you see from the top of the Joaquin Rocks?
alts: What does it look out over?
Can you see far from the rocks, Mom?
ca345-joaquin-rocks.a: From their tops you look out over much of the San Joaquin Valley, including the approaches to Arroyo de Cantua, where the gang kept its rancho.
ca345-joaquin-rocks.quote: From their tops the rocks look out over much of the San Joaquin Valley, including the approaches to Arroyo de Cantua, where the gang kept its rancho.

ca345-joaquin-rocks.q: Is there a town named after the Joaquin Rocks?
alts: Is there a town by the rocks, Dad?
ca345-joaquin-rocks.a: Yes, a man named Raymond Minnite noticed the three rocks in 1954 and named the little town he founded there Three Rocks. About 250 people lived there in 2020.
ca345-joaquin-rocks.quote: He noticed the three rocks on the skyline and named the little town he founded there Three Rocks. About 250 people lived there in 2020.

ca345-joaquin-rocks.q: How do we spot the Joaquin Rocks?
alts: What do the rocks look like, Mom?
ca345-joaquin-rocks.a: Look for three rock pillars standing on top of the high ridge to the west.
ca345-joaquin-rocks.quote: Look for three rock pillars standing on top of the high ridge to the west.

ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.q: Who was Joaquin Murrieta, the bandit at Arroyo de Cantua?
alts: Was there a real outlaw here, like in the movies?
ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.a: Joaquin Murrieta was a Gold Rush bandit said to have hidden out at Arroyo de Cantua. Evidence that he was a real person is thin, but the legend grew anyway.
ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.quote: is Arroyo de Cantua, said to be the hideout of the Gold Rush bandit Joaquin Murrieta.

ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.q: What happened at Arroyo de Cantua in 1853?
alts: Was there a real shootout here?
What went down at that place?
ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.a: On July 25, 1853, California Rangers led by Captain Harry Love attacked a band of armed Mexican men near here. They killed three and claimed one of them was Murrieta.
ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.quote: On July 25, 1853, California Rangers led by Captain Harry Love attacked a band of armed Mexican men near here, killed three, and claimed one of them was Murrieta.

ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.q: Was the Murrieta story at Arroyo de Cantua actually true?
alts: Was it true, or is it just a legend?
Did they get the right guy, or was it fake?
ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.a: Nobody knows for sure. A letter to a San Francisco newspaper claimed the rangers had killed innocent mustang catchers, and evidence for a real Murrieta is thin.
ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.quote: a letter to a San Francisco newspaper claimed the rangers had killed innocent mustang catchers. Evidence for a real Murrieta is thin

ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.q: Where is the head of Joaquin Murrieta now?
alts: What happened to it in the end?
Is the jar still around somewhere?
ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.a: It's gone. The head was destroyed in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire.
ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.quote: The head was destroyed in the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and fire.

ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.q: Who made the legend of Murrieta so famous?
alts: How did it get so famous?
Did somebody write a book about him?
ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.a: An 1854 novel by John Rollin Ridge, a Cherokee writer, helped the legend grow, even though the evidence for a real Murrieta is thin.
ca349-arroyo-de-cantua.quote: the legend grew, helped along by an 1854 novel by John Rollin Ridge, a Cherokee writer.

alts: Why do they call it the cantaloupe place?
ca349-mendota-cantaloupe-town.a: Mendota is known as the Cantaloupe Center of the World. It's reached by Highway 33 from the freeway.
ca349-mendota-cantaloupe-town.quote: Highway 33 leads from here to Mendota, known as the Cantaloupe Center of the World.

alts: Where does the canal water come from, and where does it go?
ca349-mendota-cantaloupe-town.a: It brings Delta water through 117 miles of canal from near Tracy. Since 1951 it has ended at the pool behind Mendota Dam.
ca349-mendota-cantaloupe-town.quote: Since 1951 the Delta-Mendota Canal has ended at the pool behind it, bringing Delta water through 117 miles of canal from near Tracy.

ca349-mendota-cantaloupe-town.q: Why does Mendota need canal water for its river?
alts: Why does it need that water?
Is the river dry here, or what?
ca349-mendota-cantaloupe-town.a: The San Joaquin River bed is often dry here. The Delta-Mendota Canal pours in water to refill it.
ca349-mendota-cantaloupe-town.quote: near where the Delta-Mendota Canal pours in water to refill a riverbed that is often dry.

ca349-mendota-cantaloupe-town.q: Did outlaws really hang out near Mendota?
alts: Were there bandits at that place?
Were there robbers here, like cowboys?
ca349-mendota-cantaloupe-town.a: Yes. After the Gold Rush, a nearby settlement called Las Juntas was a haven for fugitives, visited by bandits Joaquin Murrieta and Tiburcio Vasquez.
ca349-mendota-cantaloupe-town.quote: a nearby settlement called Las Juntas was a haven for fugitives, visited by the bandits Joaquin Murrieta and Tiburcio Vasquez.

ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.q: Why is Fresno County called the nation's top farm county?
alts: Why is it the top farm county?
Why is this the best farming place, Mom?
ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.a: Fresno County was the number one farm county in the nation in 2017. Its crops and livestock were worth almost 8 billion dollars that year.
ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.quote: Fresno County, which the freeway crosses here, was the number one farm county in the nation in 2017, when its crops and livestock were worth almost 8 billion dollars.

ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.q: How much of Fresno County is farmland?
alts: How much of it is farmed?
Is the whole county just farms, Dad?
ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.a: About 1.9 million acres are farmed here. That is nearly half of the whole county.
ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.quote: About 1.9 million acres, nearly half the county, are farmed.

ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.q: What crops grow in Fresno County?
alts: What are all those plants out the window?
ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.a: More than 300 crops grow here. The leaders range from grapes, pistachios and almonds to tomatoes, cotton and milk.
ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.quote: More than 300 crops grow here, and the leaders range from grapes, pistachios and almonds to tomatoes, cotton and milk.

ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.q: Why are there so many pistachio orchards in the Central Valley?
alts: Why do pistachios grow so well here?
Why do they grow so many nuts, Dad?
ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.a: The hardy trees can thrive with the somewhat salty water and soil found in parts of the Central Valley. California's pistachio orchards grew from about 106,000 acres in 2002 to 554,000 in 2022.
ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.quote: because the hardy trees can thrive with the somewhat salty water and soil found in parts of the Central Valley.

ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.q: How many of the country's pistachios come from Fresno County?
alts: How many pistachios does it grow?
Do we get a lot of our pistachios from here?
ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.a: Fresno County alone grew about 40 percent of the country's pistachios in 2021.
ca353-the-nation-s-top-farm-county.quote: Fresno County alone grew about 40 percent of the country's pistachios in 2021

ca355-the-farm-water-signs.q: Why are there big signs in the fields along I-5?
alts: Why do they put those signs up?
Why are there so many signs in the farms, Mom?
ca355-the-farm-water-signs.a: Farmers say federal rules meant to protect smelt and salmon have cut their water, and the signs are their protest. They carry slogans like No Water Equals No Jobs.
ca355-the-farm-water-signs.quote: Farmers say federal rules meant to protect smelt and salmon have cut their water.

ca355-the-farm-water-signs.q: When did the farm water signs start going up?
alts: Have those signs been there a long time, Dad?
ca355-the-farm-water-signs.a: Starting around 2008, big signs went up in fields along I-5. By June 2011 the Associated Press reported several hundred new signs along I-5 and Highway 99.
ca355-the-farm-water-signs.quote: Starting around 2008, big signs went up in fields along I-5, with slogans like Congress Created Dust Bowl and No Water Equals No Jobs.

ca355-the-farm-water-signs.q: Who put up the farm water signs?
alts: Who's the person that put the signs up, Mom?
ca355-the-farm-water-signs.a: Many came from Families Protecting the Valley, a loosely organized group of San Joaquin Valley farmers and other locals. Russ Waymire, a Hanford real estate broker and former farmer, put up the first sign with a friend.
ca355-the-farm-water-signs.quote: Many came from Families Protecting the Valley, a loosely organized group of San Joaquin Valley farmers and other locals.

ca355-the-farm-water-signs.q: What do the farm water signs say?
alts: What are the slogans on that?
What do the signs say, Dad?
ca355-the-farm-water-signs.a: Slogans include Congress Created Dust Bowl, No Water Equals No Jobs, Man-made drought, and Food grows where water flows.
ca355-the-farm-water-signs.quote: with lines like Man-made drought and Food grows where water flows.

ca355-the-farm-water-signs.q: Are the farm water signs telling the whole story?
alts: Is that really true, what the signs say?
Do the signs tell the truth, Mom?
ca355-the-farm-water-signs.a: Not everyone agrees. Environmentalists said the signs gave a false picture of the drought and its causes, and a congressional report found most of the supply cuts came from the drought itself.
ca355-the-farm-water-signs.quote: Environmentalists said the signs gave a false picture of the drought and its causes.

ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.q: What happened in the 1991 dust storm?
alts: What happened here with that dust storm?
Why did all those cars crash, Buddy?
ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.a: A sudden dust storm hit this stretch of I-5 and dropped visibility to near zero. In a series of chain-reaction crashes, 104 vehicles collided, 17 people died and 150 were hurt.
ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.quote: In a series of chain-reaction crashes, 104 vehicles collided, 17 people died and 150 were hurt.

alts: Was that dust storm a long time ago?
What day was the dust storm?
ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.a: It happened on November 29, 1991, the Friday after Thanksgiving. A sudden dust storm swept this stretch of I-5 north of Coalinga.
ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.quote: On November 29, 1991, the Friday after Thanksgiving, a sudden dust storm swept this stretch of I-5 north of Coalinga

ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.q: Why was the 1991 dust storm so bad?
alts: Why did it get so dusty?
Why was there so much dust, Buddy?
ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.a: The valley was in its sixth year of drought and the rainy season had not begun. Fields near the road had been plowed and left bare, with no crops to hold the dust.
ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.quote: fields near the road had been plowed and left bare, with no crops to hold the dust.

ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.q: How strong was the wind in the 1991 dust storm?
alts: How fast was the wind in it?
Was the wind really strong, Buddy?
ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.a: The nearest weather station tracking wind, at Naval Air Station Lemoore, recorded gusts of 48 miles an hour.
ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.quote: The nearest weather station tracking wind, at Naval Air Station Lemoore, recorded gusts of 48 miles an hour.

ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.q: How did rescuers respond to the 1991 dust storm crashes?
alts: Did help get there fast after it happened?
Did anyone come to help, Buddy?
ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.a: Rescuers reached the site within half an hour, even though a fire truck and an ambulance crashed on the way in. Several vehicles had caught fire.
ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.quote: A fire truck and an ambulance crashed on the way in, yet rescuers reached the site within half an hour.

ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.q: How much of I-5 was closed after the 1991 dust storm?
alts: Did they shut the road because of it?
Was the freeway closed for long, Buddy?
How long was the road closed?
ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.a: About 150 miles of I-5 were closed for a day. Most of the crashes happened in five groups along a mile and a half of freeway.
ca357-the-1991-dust-storm.quote: About 150 miles of I-5 were closed for a day.

ca362-the-diablo-range.q: How big is the Diablo Range?
alts: How far do these mountains go, Dad?
ca362-the-diablo-range.a: It stretches from the Carquinez Strait, near the Bay Area, south to Polonio Pass, near Cholame. Its highest point is San Benito Mountain at 5,241 feet.
ca362-the-diablo-range.quote: It stretches from the Carquinez Strait, near the Bay Area, south to Polonio Pass, near Cholame.

ca362-the-diablo-range.q: What is the highest point in the Diablo Range?
alts: What's the tallest part of it?
What's the biggest mountain there, Mom?
ca362-the-diablo-range.a: San Benito Mountain is the highest point, rising to 5,241 feet in remote country to the southwest.
ca362-the-diablo-range.quote: Its highest point, San Benito Mountain, rises to 5,241 feet in remote country to the southwest.

ca362-the-diablo-range.q: Why are the Diablo Range mountains so dry?
alts: Why is it so dry there?
How come those mountains look brown and grassy?
ca362-the-diablo-range.a: Other coastal ranges to the west catch most of the ocean's rain, so these mountains stay dry. They are mostly rolling grassland, chaparral and oak woodland.
ca362-the-diablo-range.quote: Other coastal ranges to the west catch most of the ocean's rain, so these mountains stay dry, mostly rolling grassland, chaparral and oak woodland

ca362-the-diablo-range.q: What Native peoples lived in the Diablo Range?
alts: Who lived in those mountains first?
Did Native Americans live there, Mom?
ca362-the-diablo-range.a: The range is part of the homelands of many Native peoples, including the Ohlone, Yokuts, Miwok, Amah Mutsun and Salinan.
ca362-the-diablo-range.quote: The range is part of the homelands of many Native peoples, including the Ohlone, Yokuts, Miwok, Amah Mutsun and Salinan.

ca362-the-diablo-range.q: What strange animal lives in the Diablo Range?
alts: What lives in it that's special?
Is there a bug with lots of legs there?
ca362-the-diablo-range.a: A millipede found only in the southern part of the range, Illacme plenipes, can have as many as 750 legs. Until 2021, no animal known to science had more.
ca362-the-diablo-range.quote: a millipede found only in the southern part of the range, Illacme plenipes, which can have as many as 750 legs. Until 2021, no animal known to science had more.

ca365-el-camino-viejo.q: Why is it called El Camino Viejo?
alts: What does El Camino Viejo mean, Mom?
ca365-el-camino-viejo.a: It means the Old Road to Los Angeles. It was an older road that ran along this side of the valley long before the freeway was built.
ca365-el-camino-viejo.quote: an older road ran along this side of the valley: El Camino Viejo, the Old Road to Los Angeles

ca365-el-camino-viejo.q: Where did El Camino Viejo actually go?
alts: How far did the old road go, Dad?
ca365-el-camino-viejo.a: It ran between San Pedro Bay and the shore of San Francisco Bay at Oakland, crossing Tejon Pass from Los Angeles and coming down through the San Emigdio Mountains into the valley.
ca365-el-camino-viejo.quote: between San Pedro Bay and the shore of San Francisco Bay at Oakland.

alts: Who traveled on that old road, like cowboys?
ca365-el-camino-viejo.a: Spanish ox carts used it, and later Californio vaqueros drove cattle along it. Mustang catchers herded wild horses on it, and it was also favored by people avoiding Spanish officials on the coast.
ca365-el-camino-viejo.quote: Later, Californio vaqueros drove cattle along it, while mustang catchers herded wild horses to the Bay Area, Southern California and Sonora.

ca365-el-camino-viejo.q: What were the creeks along El Camino Viejo called?
alts: Were there any funny names on that road?
ca365-el-camino-viejo.a: The names described what travelers found, like Creek of the Herons, Waterhole of the Pronghorns, and Creek of the Dust Storms.
ca365-el-camino-viejo.quote: Arroyo de las Garzas, Creek of the Herons, and Aguaje de las Berendas, Waterhole of the Pronghorns

ca365-el-camino-viejo.q: Is El Camino Viejo still used today?
alts: Can we drive on the old road now?
ca365-el-camino-viejo.a: Not as the old trail. Through Santa Nella, its route has been replaced by Interstate 5 and Highway 33.
ca365-el-camino-viejo.quote: Through Santa Nella, its route has been replaced by Interstate 5 and Highway 33.

ca368-the-sinking-ground.q: Why is the ground sinking near Mendota?
alts: How come the ground goes down, like, for real?
ca368-the-sinking-ground.a: Too much groundwater was pumped from under the fields. When that happens, loose layers underground compact, and past a certain point the ground cannot spring back.
ca368-the-sinking-ground.quote: When too much groundwater is pumped out, loose layers underground compact, and past a certain point the ground cannot spring back.

ca368-the-sinking-ground.q: How far did the ground sink at the sinking ground?
alts: How far down did the ground really go?
ca368-the-sinking-ground.a: About 28 feet, between 1925 and 1977. That's from all the groundwater pumped out from under the fields.
ca368-the-sinking-ground.quote: the ground sank about 28 feet between 1925 and 1977 because so much groundwater was pumped from under the fields

ca368-the-sinking-ground.q: What is the famous photo at the sinking ground?
alts: Is there a picture of the pole with the signs?
ca368-the-sinking-ground.a: It shows scientist Joseph Poland beside a utility pole. Signs high on the pole mark where the ground surface was in 1925 and 1955.
ca368-the-sinking-ground.quote: A famous photo shows U.S. Geological Survey scientist Joseph Poland beside a utility pole there, with signs high on the pole marking where the ground surface was in 1925 and 1955.

ca368-the-sinking-ground.q: Who was Joseph Poland, the man in the sinking ground photo?
alts: Who was the guy by the pole?
ca368-the-sinking-ground.a: He was a U.S. Geological Survey scientist who spent 50 years studying sinking land. He became known as Mr. Land Subsidence.
ca368-the-sinking-ground.quote: Poland spent 50 years studying sinking land and became known as Mr. Land Subsidence.

ca368-the-sinking-ground.q: How much of the valley has been affected by the sinking ground?
alts: Did it spread across the valley?
How big is the sinking area, like, huge?
ca368-the-sinking-ground.a: By 1970, more than a foot of sinking had spread across about 5,200 square miles, about half the valley.
ca368-the-sinking-ground.quote: by 1970 more than a foot of it had spread across about 5,200 square miles, about half the valley

ca368-the-sinking-ground.q: Does the sinking ground cause problems for canals?
ca368-the-sinking-ground.a: Yes. The sinking has cut how much water the Delta-Mendota Canal can carry and has meant expensive repairs to canals, including the California Aqueduct.
ca368-the-sinking-ground.quote: The sinking has cut how much water the Delta-Mendota Canal can carry and has meant expensive repairs to canals, including the California Aqueduct.

ca370-panoche-hills.q: How did the Panoche Hills get their name?
alts: How did it get that name?
ca370-panoche-hills.a: The name is thought to come from a local Native word for a cane that once grew in the valley beyond the hills. People made panoche, a kind of sugar, from that cane.
ca370-panoche-hills.quote: Their name is thought to come from a local Native word for a cane that once grew in the valley beyond them, from which people made panoche, a kind of sugar.

ca370-panoche-hills.q: What animals live around the Panoche Hills?
alts: What kind of animals live there?
Are there any cool animals out there?
ca370-panoche-hills.a: Panoche Valley, just west of the hills, is home to endangered animals like the San Joaquin kit fox, the giant kangaroo rat and the blunt-nosed leopard lizard.
ca370-panoche-hills.quote: West of the hills lies Panoche Valley, home to endangered animals such as the San Joaquin kit fox, the giant kangaroo rat and the blunt-nosed leopard lizard.

ca370-panoche-hills.q: What birds can you see near the Panoche Hills?
ca370-panoche-hills.a: The valley's grasslands are critical habitat, especially in winter, for birds such as golden eagles, ferruginous hawks, prairie falcons, mountain plovers and long-billed curlews.
ca370-panoche-hills.quote: Its grasslands are critical habitat, especially in winter, for birds such as golden eagles, ferruginous hawks, prairie falcons, mountain plovers and long-billed curlews.

ca370-panoche-hills.q: Are there dinosaur-age fossils in the Panoche Hills?
ca370-panoche-hills.a: Yes, the hills hold fossils of ancient cold seeps from the Mesozoic era, the age of dinosaurs.
ca370-panoche-hills.quote: The hills themselves hold fossils of ancient cold seeps from the Mesozoic era, the age of dinosaurs.

ca370-panoche-hills.q: Can you drive vehicles in the Panoche Hills recreation area?
alts: Can we take our car out there?
ca370-panoche-hills.a: Not all year. The Bureau of Land Management keeps motor vehicles out of its Panoche Hills recreation area from mid-April to mid-October, the fire season.
ca370-panoche-hills.quote: The Bureau of Land Management keeps motor vehicles out of its Panoche Hills recreation area from mid-April to mid-October, the fire season.

ca370-panoche-hills.q: Which exit is for the Panoche Hills?
alts: What exit do we take, Dad?
ca370-panoche-hills.a: The Panoche Hills exit is exit 370.

alts: Is that creek a big deal?
ca372-panoche-creek-and-the-mercury-mine.a: It drains a larger area than any other stream on the eastern slope of the Diablo Range.
ca372-panoche-creek-and-the-mercury-mine.quote: drains a larger area than any other stream on the Diablo Range's eastern slope.

ca372-panoche-creek-and-the-mercury-mine.q: How did people use Panoche Creek long ago?
alts: How did people use it long ago?
Did anybody live by that creek?
ca372-panoche-creek-and-the-mercury-mine.a: It was part of a route between Native settlements on the central coast and the valley, and a watering place on El Camino Viejo.
ca372-panoche-creek-and-the-mercury-mine.quote: It was part of a route between Native settlements on the central coast and the valley, and a watering place on El Camino Viejo.

ca372-panoche-creek-and-the-mercury-mine.q: What were the New Idria mercury mines?
alts: Why did they dig up mercury, Mom?
ca372-panoche-creek-and-the-mercury-mine.a: They dug mercury from 1854 until 1972 and were once the second most productive mercury mines in the country. Gold Rush miners needed mercury to pull gold out of ore.
ca372-panoche-creek-and-the-mercury-mine.quote: which dug mercury from 1854 until 1972 and were at one time the second most productive mercury mines in the country.

ca372-panoche-creek-and-the-mercury-mine.q: What is left of the New Idria mines today?
alts: What is left of it now?
Is there a ghost town up there?
ca372-panoche-creek-and-the-mercury-mine.a: The mines left behind a ghost town with more than 100 standing buildings. Mercury from the old workings has also polluted the creeks that feed Panoche Creek.
ca372-panoche-creek-and-the-mercury-mine.quote: The mines left behind a ghost town with more than 100 standing buildings

ca379-mercey-hot-springs.q: How old is Mercey Hot Springs?
alts: Has that place been around a long time?
How long has it been open?
ca379-mercey-hot-springs.a: It has been a resort since the early 1900s. Native people knew the springs long before settlers ever came.
ca379-mercey-hot-springs.quote: Mercey Hot Springs has been a resort since the early 1900s.

ca379-mercey-hot-springs.q: How hot is the water at Mercey Hot Springs?
ca379-mercey-hot-springs.a: Water flows from one spring at 119 degrees Fahrenheit. A hot artesian well feeds the swimming pool.
ca379-mercey-hot-springs.quote: Water flows from one spring at 119 degrees Fahrenheit, and the resort has cabins, campsites, bathtub soaking pools and a swimming pool fed by a hot artesian well.

ca379-mercey-hot-springs.q: What can you do at Mercey Hot Springs?
alts: What is there to do there?
ca379-mercey-hot-springs.a: There are cabins, campsites, bathtub soaking pools and a swimming pool fed by a hot artesian well.
ca379-mercey-hot-springs.quote: the resort has cabins, campsites, bathtub soaking pools and a swimming pool fed by a hot artesian well.

ca379-mercey-hot-springs.q: What happened at Mercey Hot Springs during the Gold Rush?
alts: What was it like back then?
Were there outlaws at that place?
ca379-mercey-hot-springs.a: It was a watering place called Aguaje Panochita, where mustang catchers held captured horses. The gang known as the Five Joaquins also stopped there while driving horses south.
ca379-mercey-hot-springs.quote: During the Gold Rush the spot was a watering place called Aguaje Panochita, where mustang catchers held captured horses

ca379-mercey-hot-springs.q: Who built the hotel at Mercey Hot Springs?
alts: Was there ever a hotel there?
What happened to the old hotel?
ca379-mercey-hot-springs.a: San Francisco developer Frederick Bourn bought the springs in 1912 and built cabins and a hotel. The hotel burned in the mid-1930s and a bathhouse and restaurant replaced it.
ca379-mercey-hot-springs.quote: In 1912 San Francisco developer Frederick Bourn bought the springs and built cabins and a hotel. The hotel burned in the mid-1930s

ca382-the-san-luis-canal.q: What is the San Luis Canal?
alts: What is that big canal we're driving next to?
Is that a river or a ditch, what is it?
ca382-the-san-luis-canal.a: It's the federally built section of the California Aqueduct. It carries water for both the state and federal water projects.
ca382-the-san-luis-canal.quote: the San Luis Canal, the federally built section of the California Aqueduct. It carries water for both the state and federal water projects

ca382-the-san-luis-canal.q: How big is the San Luis Canal?
alts: How much water does it hold?
Is it a really big canal, how big is it?
How much water is in it?
ca382-the-san-luis-canal.a: It has room for 13,100 cubic feet of water a second, which makes it one of the largest irrigation canals in the country.
ca382-the-san-luis-canal.quote: with room for 13,100 cubic feet of water a second, it is one of the largest irrigation canals in the country

ca382-the-san-luis-canal.q: Where does the San Luis Canal start and end?
alts: Where does all that water come from and go to?
ca382-the-san-luis-canal.a: It carries water from O'Neill Forebay to Kettleman City.
ca382-the-san-luis-canal.quote: It carries water for both the state and federal water projects from O'Neill Forebay to Kettleman City

ca382-the-san-luis-canal.q: How did the San Luis Canal change the land around here?
alts: Did it change anything out here?
Did the creeks here used to run somewhere else, kid-style: where did the water go?
