ca382-the-san-luis-canal.a: Little Panoche Creek shows it. Before irrigation its water may have reached a slough of the San Joaquin River in very wet years. Today it simply ends in the aqueduct.
ca382-the-san-luis-canal.quote: Before irrigation, its water may have reached a slough of the San Joaquin River in very wet years. Today it flows through Little Panoche Reservoir and simply ends in the aqueduct.

ca382-the-san-luis-canal.q: What does Little Panoche Creek's old name mean?
alts: Why was it called Arroyita de Panoche?
What did the Spanish call that creek?
ca382-the-san-luis-canal.a: Its old Spanish name, Arroyita de Panoche, meant Little Sugarloaf Creek. It was also a watering place on El Camino Viejo.
ca382-the-san-luis-canal.quote: Its old Spanish name, Arroyita de Panoche, meant Little Sugarloaf Creek, and it was a watering place on El Camino Viejo.

alts: Who was that guy the town is named after?
ca385-firebaugh-s-ferry.a: Andrew Firebaugh was a Virginian who ran a ferry across the San Joaquin River during the Gold Rush. The town is named after him.
ca385-firebaugh-s-ferry.quote: named for Andrew Firebaugh, a Virginian who ran a ferry across the river during the Gold Rush

ca385-firebaugh-s-ferry.q: What did Andrew Firebaugh build over Pacheco Pass?
alts: Did he build a road or something?
ca385-firebaugh-s-ferry.a: In 1857 he built a wagon road with a gentler grade over Pacheco Pass. It replaced a steep, rough horse and mule trail near today's Highway 152.
ca385-firebaugh-s-ferry.quote: In 1857 Firebaugh built a wagon road with a gentler grade over Pacheco Pass

ca385-firebaugh-s-ferry.q: What was the Butterfield Overland stage line connection?
alts: What did it have to do with stagecoaches?
ca385-firebaugh-s-ferry.a: The settlement of Firebaugh's Ferry became a station on the Butterfield Overland stage line.
ca385-firebaugh-s-ferry.quote: The settlement, then called Firebaugh's Ferry, became a station on the Butterfield Overland stage line.

ca385-firebaugh-s-ferry.q: What is there to see in Firebaugh?
alts: Is there anything to see in it?
What can we look at there?
ca385-firebaugh-s-ferry.a: A water tank in its small downtown is painted with the city's name. The town sits on the San Joaquin River, where the old ferry crossed.
ca385-firebaugh-s-ferry.quote: A water tank in its small downtown is painted with the city's name.

ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.q: What happened at the John Chuck Erreca Rest Area recently?
alts: Why does this rest area look so new?
ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.a: Caltrans rebuilt both sides of the rest area in a 30 million dollar project. One side reopened in August 2025 and the other in May 2026.
ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.quote: Caltrans rebuilt both sides of the John Chuck Erreca Rest Area in a 30 million dollar project, reopening one side in August 2025 and the other in May 2026.

ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.q: What makes the John Chuck Erreca Rest Area special?
alts: Why is this rest area such a big deal?
ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.a: Caltrans calls it one of the most sustainable rest areas it has ever built, with utilities designed to use little water and power.
ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.quote: Caltrans calls it one of the most sustainable rest areas it has ever built, with utilities designed to use little water and power.

ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.q: How does the John Chuck Erreca Rest Area save water?
alts: Do they really reuse toilet water here?
How do the toilets work here?
ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.a: A small treatment system cleans gray water so it can be used again to flush the toilets. That cuts its need for water from the state system during droughts.
ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.quote: A small treatment system cleans gray water so it can be used again to flush the toilets

ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.q: Why does the John Chuck Erreca Rest Area have Basque graphics?
alts: Why does it have Basque stuff on it?
What's the design supposed to look like?
ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.a: The plaza's design was inspired by aerial views of farmland, and graphics honor the region's Basque history.
ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.quote: the plaza's design was inspired by aerial views of farmland, and graphics honor the region's Basque history.

ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.q: Why is the parking at the John Chuck Erreca Rest Area light-colored?
alts: Why is the concrete so light?
ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.a: The parking areas used more than 180,000 cubic feet of light-colored concrete. It reflects sunlight, which helps keep the air cooler.
ca386-john-chuck-erreca-rest-area.quote: That light-colored concrete reflects sunlight, which helps keep the air cooler.

ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.q: Why is it called the San Joaquin River?
alts: Who named the river, and why?
ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.a: The Spanish name comes from explorer Gabriel Moraga, who named one of its branches for Saint Joachim between 1805 and 1808. The name was in common use by 1810.
ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.quote: Its Spanish name dates to explorer Gabriel Moraga, who named one of its branches for Saint Joachim between 1805 and 1808, and the name was in common use by 1810.

ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.q: Were there really salmon in the San Joaquin River?
alts: Did it used to have a lot of salmon?
Were there lots of fish in the river?
ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.a: Yes, a lot. Before irrigation, the San Joaquin and its branches had the third largest salmon run in California, likely 200,000 to 500,000 spawning fish a year.
ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.quote: Before irrigation, the San Joaquin and its branches had the third largest salmon run in California, likely 200,000 to 500,000 spawning fish a year.

ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.q: Why does the San Joaquin River run dry in places?
alts: Where did all the river's water go?
ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.a: Most of its water is held behind Friant Dam and sent into canals, so long stretches of the river often run dry.
ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.quote: With most of its water now held behind Friant Dam and sent into canals, long stretches often run dry.

ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.q: Are they trying to restore the San Joaquin River?
alts: Are they bringing the salmon back?
ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.a: Yes. In 2009 the federal government began releasing water from Friant again to restore two dry stretches, about 64 miles in all, with salmon to be brought back.
ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.quote: In 2009 the federal government began releasing water from Friant again to restore two dry stretches, about 64 miles in all

ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.q: Did everyone agree with the San Joaquin River restoration?
ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.a: Not everyone. Irrigators lost some water, and a lawsuit claimed the new flows were seeping through old levees onto farmland near Los Banos.
ca388-the-san-joaquin-river.quote: Not everyone welcomed it: irrigators lost some water, and a lawsuit claimed the new flows were seeping through old levees onto farmland near Los Banos.

ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.q: What does the Dos Amigos Pumping Plant do?
alts: What's that big building by the canal for?
ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.a: It lifts California Aqueduct water 118 feet. That single boost lets the water flow by gravity for about 95 miles, down to where the Coastal Branch splits off south of Kettleman City.
ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.quote: the Dos Amigos Pumping Plant lifts California Aqueduct water 118 feet.

ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.q: How old is the Dos Amigos Pumping Plant?
alts: When did they build that thing, like how long ago?
ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.a: It was built between 1963 and 1966 as part of the State Water Project.
ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.quote: The plant was built between 1963 and 1966 as part of the State Water Project.

ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.q: Why is it called Dos Amigos Pumping Plant?
alts: Why does it have a funny name?
ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.a: Dos Amigos means two friends in Spanish. That is what the plant's name means.
ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.quote: Its name means two friends in Spanish.

ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.q: How much water can the Dos Amigos Pumping Plant move?
alts: How much water can it move?
How many pumps does it have, like a lot?
ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.a: It has six pumps that can move 15,450 cubic feet of water a second.
ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.quote: Its six pumps can move 15,450 cubic feet of water a second

ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.q: Where does the Dos Amigos Pumping Plant get its water?
alts: Where does the water come from?
Where's the water come from that goes in there?
ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.a: Its water arrives through about 16 miles of canal from O'Neill Forebay.
ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.quote: Its water arrives through about 16 miles of canal from O'Neill Forebay.

ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.q: Is there a place to stop near Dos Amigos Pumping Plant?
alts: Can we get out and look at it?
ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.a: Yes. A vista point called Dos Amigos sits beside the freeway nearby.
ca391-dos-amigos-pumping-plant.quote: A vista point called Dos Amigos sits beside the freeway nearby.

alts: What is it out there east of the freeway?
ca393-the-grasslands.a: They're about 250 square miles of wetlands and grasslands along the San Joaquin River, named a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar treaty.
ca393-the-grasslands.quote: about 250 square miles of wetlands and grasslands along the San Joaquin River, named a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar treaty

ca393-the-grasslands.q: What birds can we see at the Grasslands?
alts: What kind of birds are in it?
Are there lots of birds there?
ca393-the-grasslands.a: Water birds, both resident and migrating. Each autumn more than 20,000 cranes and 60,000 Arctic-nesting geese fly in from Alaska and Canada.
ca393-the-grasslands.quote: Each autumn more than 20,000 cranes and 60,000 Arctic-nesting geese fly in from Alaska and Canada to spend about six months

ca393-the-grasslands.q: Why do so many birds come to the Grasslands?
alts: Why do they all stop there?
Why do the birds fly all the way here?
ca393-the-grasslands.a: The Grasslands sit on the Pacific Flyway, the great bird migration route, and are important habitat for resident and migrating water birds.
ca393-the-grasslands.quote: They sit on the Pacific Flyway, the great bird migration route, and are important habitat for resident and migrating water birds.

ca393-the-grasslands.q: Why was Merced National Wildlife Refuge created?
alts: Why did they set it up?
Why did they make a bird refuge?
ca393-the-grasslands.a: It was set up in 1951 to draw wintering ducks and geese away from nearby farm fields, where they were damaging crops.
ca393-the-grasslands.quote: The refuge was set up in 1951 to draw wintering ducks and geese away from nearby farm fields, where they were damaging crops.

ca393-the-grasslands.q: Are there wildflowers at the Grasslands?
alts: Does it have flowers in spring?
ca393-the-grasslands.a: Yes. In spring, wildflowers bloom in rings around drying vernal pools, the kind of color that led John Muir to call the valley floor the floweriest part of the world he had seen.
ca393-the-grasslands.quote: In spring, wildflowers bloom in rings around drying vernal pools

alts: What is that line of giant power towers?
Why are there so many big electric lines out here?
ca397-path-15-power-lines.a: Path 15 is part of California's main north-south power corridor. Its 500,000-volt lines run from the Los Banos substation to Midway, near Buttonwillow.
ca397-path-15-power-lines.quote: Path 15, part of California's main north-south power corridor, runs along this side of the valley, generally 3 to 7 miles west of the freeway.

ca397-path-15-power-lines.q: How powerful are the Path 15 power lines?
alts: How much electricity do those lines carry?
ca397-path-15-power-lines.a: They are 500,000-volt lines. They run from the Los Banos substation, west of Los Banos, down to Midway, near Buttonwillow.
ca397-path-15-power-lines.quote: Its 500,000-volt lines run from the Los Banos substation, west of Los Banos, to Midway, near Buttonwillow

alts: Where does all that power go?
ca397-path-15-power-lines.a: It links hydroelectric plants in the north with fossil fuel power plants in the south.
ca397-path-15-power-lines.quote: linking hydroelectric plants in the north with fossil fuel power plants in the south.

ca397-path-15-power-lines.q: Do the Path 15 lines ever cross the freeway?
alts: Do those lines go over us?
Do the wires cross the road, Dad?
ca397-path-15-power-lines.a: Yes. In places the lines run beside the freeway, and the two eastern lines cross it twice.
ca397-path-15-power-lines.quote: In places the lines run beside the freeway, and the two eastern lines cross it twice.

ca397-path-15-power-lines.q: Which Path 15 line is the newest?
alts: Which wires are the new ones?
ca397-path-15-power-lines.a: The newest line was finished in 2004 between Los Banos and the Gates substation near Coalinga. It runs apart from the older two, often out of sight.
ca397-path-15-power-lines.quote: The newest line, finished in 2004 between Los Banos and the Gates substation near Coalinga, runs apart from the older two, often out of sight.

ca397-path-15-power-lines.q: What is special about the Path 15 wires?
alts: Is it different from other power lines?
Why do some wires look funny, bundled together?
ca397-path-15-power-lines.a: The newest line is the only one in Path 15 that strings its wires in bundles of three.
ca397-path-15-power-lines.quote: It is the only line in Path 15 that strings its wires in bundles of three.

ca399-los-banos-the-baths.q: Why is it called Los Banos?
alts: Why's the town called the baths, Mom?
ca399-los-banos-the-baths.a: Los Banos is Spanish for the baths. The town is named for pools known as the baths of Padre Arroyo, and later the creek, post office and town all took the name.
ca399-los-banos-the-baths.quote: It is named for pools known as the baths of Padre Arroyo, a regular stop for priests from Mission San Juan Bautista

alts: Who was he, the baths guy?
Was there a real priest there?
ca399-los-banos-the-baths.a: The source doesn't say much about him. It says the pools were known as the baths of Padre Arroyo and were a regular stop for priests from Mission San Juan Bautista traveling into the valley.
ca399-los-banos-the-baths.quote: a regular stop for priests from Mission San Juan Bautista on trips into the valley, visited by Spanish explorers as early as 1805

ca399-los-banos-the-baths.q: Who was Henry Miller in Los Banos?
alts: Who was that rich cattle guy?
Who was the cowboy boss, Dad?
ca399-los-banos-the-baths.a: Henry Miller was a cattle baron who ran his valley empire from Canal Farm in Los Banos, set up in 1873. In the late 1800s he was one of the largest landowners in the United States.
ca399-los-banos-the-baths.quote: Cattle baron Henry Miller ran his valley empire from Canal Farm here, set up in 1873

ca399-los-banos-the-baths.q: What's the story with Uriah Wood and the ferryman?
alts: What did he do with the boat?
How'd he beat the cattle guy, Dad?
ca399-los-banos-the-baths.a: Wood raced Miller to the land office in Stockton. After crossing the San Joaquin River, he paid the ferryman five dollars to hold the boat on the east side, and won his land for 45 cents an acre.
ca399-los-banos-the-baths.quote: After crossing the San Joaquin River, Wood paid the ferryman five dollars to hold the boat on the east side, and won his land for 45 cents an acre.

ca399-los-banos-the-baths.q: When did Los Banos move to where it is now?
ca399-los-banos-the-baths.a: The town moved to its present site in 1889, when the railroad arrived.
ca399-los-banos-the-baths.quote: The town moved to its present site in 1889, when the railroad arrived.

ca399-los-banos-the-baths.q: Is there anything to see in Los Banos?
alts: What's there to see in it?
Is there a statue or anything, Dad?
ca399-los-banos-the-baths.a: Downtown there's a 10-acre plaza honoring Henry Miller, with a big bronze of him and his cattle.
ca399-los-banos-the-baths.quote: A 10-acre plaza downtown honors Miller with a big bronze of him and his cattle.

ca400-tomato-country.q: Who runs the big tomato factories around Tomato country?
alts: Who runs it all out here?
Whose tomato factories are those, Dad?
ca400-tomato-country.a: That would be the Morning Star Company, which was the world's leading tomato processor as of 2023. It opened its first tomato factory in Los Banos in 1990 and another at Santa Nella in 2002.
ca400-tomato-country.quote: The Morning Star Company, which opened its first tomato factory in Los Banos in 1990 and another at Santa Nella in 2002, was the world's leading tomato processor as of 2023.

ca400-tomato-country.q: What are all these tomatoes turned into?
alts: What do they make with them?
What happens to the tomatoes, Mom?
ca400-tomato-country.a: They become products like tomato paste and diced tomatoes. Morning Star supplied about a tenth of the world's ingredient tomato products as of 2023.
ca400-tomato-country.quote: for products like tomato paste and diced tomatoes.

ca400-tomato-country.q: How did the Morning Star tomato company get started?
alts: Did some kid start that company?
ca400-tomato-country.a: Chris Rufer started Morning Star in 1970 as an owner-operator trucker, hauling tomatoes from fields to canneries.
ca400-tomato-country.quote: Chris Rufer started Morning Star in 1970 as an owner-operator trucker, hauling tomatoes from fields to canneries.

ca400-tomato-country.q: What's special about how Morning Star's tomato company is run?
alts: Do they really not have bosses?
ca400-tomato-country.a: It's known for having no bosses. Workers define their own job duties, and pay is based on reviews from coworkers.
ca400-tomato-country.quote: The company is known for having no bosses: workers define their own job duties, and pay is based on reviews from coworkers.

ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.q: How old is San Luis National Wildlife Refuge?
alts: When did this place start, Mom?
ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.a: The refuge was established in 1967. It keeps a herd of reintroduced tule elk.
ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.quote: San Luis National Wildlife Refuge, established in 1967, keeps a herd of reintroduced tule elk, the smallest kind of elk.

alts: Why are the elk so small, Dad?
ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.a: Tule elk are the smallest kind of elk. They were nearly wiped out in the 1800s, and this refuge has played a vital role in their recovery.
ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.quote: The refuge has played a vital role in the recovery of tule elk, which were nearly wiped out in the 1800s.

ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.q: What else lives at San Luis refuge besides elk?
alts: What else is there besides the elk?
Are there other animals there, Dad?
ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.a: It's a major wintering ground and stopover for waterfowl and shorebirds on the Pacific Flyway. The land has wetlands, riverside woods, native grasslands and vernal pools.
ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.quote: are also a major wintering ground and stopover for waterfowl and shorebirds on the Pacific Flyway.

ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.q: How big is San Luis National Wildlife Refuge?
alts: Is it a huge place, Mom?
ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.a: It covers more than 26,800 acres of wetlands, riverside woods, native grasslands and vernal pools.
ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.quote: Its more than 26,800 acres of wetlands, riverside woods, native grasslands and vernal pools

ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.q: How can we see the tule elk at San Luis refuge?
alts: Where do we look for the elk, Dad?
ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.a: Start at the visitor center, which has an exhibit hall and a place to view tule elk. A Tule Elk auto tour route winds through the refuge, and in hot months mornings or early evenings are best.
ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.quote: in hot months the elk are easiest to see in the morning or early evening.

ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.q: What is there to do at the San Luis refuge visitor center?
alts: Is there stuff to look at inside, Mom?
ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.a: The visitor center has an exhibit hall with displays and a place to view tule elk. From there, a Tule Elk auto tour route and a Waterfowl route wind through the refuge.
ca403-tule-elk-at-san-luis-refuge.quote: The refuge visitor center has an exhibit hall with displays and a place to view tule elk.

alts: How high is it up there?
Are we going up a really tall mountain?
ca403-pacheco-pass.a: Pacheco Pass sits at 1,368 feet. It's the main route through the hills between the Central Valley and the Santa Clara Valley.
ca403-pacheco-pass.quote: Highway 152 heads west over Pacheco Pass, at 1,368 feet the main route through the hills between the Central Valley and the Santa Clara Valley.

ca403-pacheco-pass.q: Who is Pacheco Pass named after?
ca403-pacheco-pass.a: It's named for Francisco Perez Pacheco, a Californio rancher.
ca403-pacheco-pass.quote: The pass is named for Francisco Perez Pacheco, a Californio rancher.

ca403-pacheco-pass.q: Why was Pacheco Pass called Robber's Pass?
alts: Why did they call it that back then?
ca403-pacheco-pass.a: In the 1850s travelers called it Robber's Pass because of frequent holdups.
ca403-pacheco-pass.quote: In the 1850s travelers called it Robber's Pass because of frequent holdups.

alts: What was that old station for?
ca403-pacheco-pass.a: It was a stop on the Butterfield Overland Mail stagecoach route, which linked St. Louis with San Francisco from 1858 to 1861.
ca403-pacheco-pass.quote: Pacheco Pass Station was a stop on the Butterfield Overland Mail stagecoach route, which linked St. Louis with San Francisco from 1858 to 1861.

ca403-pacheco-pass.q: Is there a train tunnel planned under Pacheco Pass?
alts: What's the high-speed rail tunnel there?
ca403-pacheco-pass.a: Yes, the planned high-speed rail line would run beneath the pass in the Pacheco Pass Tunnels, about 13 miles long and expected to be the longest rail tunnels in North America.
ca403-pacheco-pass.quote: California's high-speed rail line is planned to run beneath the pass in the Pacheco Pass Tunnels, about 13 miles long

alts: Is that a lake or a dam?
ca405-san-luis-reservoir.a: It's the largest offstream reservoir in the nation. Most of its water isn't from a river at all. It's pumped in from canals fed by the Delta and stored for the dry months.
ca405-san-luis-reservoir.quote: holds back San Luis Reservoir, the largest offstream reservoir in the nation. Most of its water does not flow in from a river at all

ca405-san-luis-reservoir.q: How big is the dam at San Luis Reservoir?
alts: How tall is that dam, anyway?
ca405-san-luis-reservoir.a: B.F. Sisk Dam is 382 feet high and more than three and a half miles long. It holds back San Luis Reservoir.
ca405-san-luis-reservoir.quote: B.F. Sisk Dam, 382 feet high and more than three and a half miles long, holds back San Luis Reservoir

ca405-san-luis-reservoir.q: What was here before San Luis Reservoir?
alts: What was under the water before it?
Did people live where the reservoir is?
What was there before the lake?
ca405-san-luis-reservoir.a: The valley it flooded is Yokuts homeland. Later it was part of Rancho San Luis Gonzaga.
ca405-san-luis-reservoir.quote: The valley it flooded is Yokuts homeland, later part of Rancho San Luis Gonzaga

ca405-san-luis-reservoir.q: How does San Luis Reservoir work like a water battery?
ca405-san-luis-reservoir.a: When electricity demand is low, eight reversible units pump water up into the reservoir. When demand is high, the water runs back down through the same machines, making up to 424 megawatts.
ca405-san-luis-reservoir.quote: When demand for electricity is low, its eight reversible units pump water up into the reservoir, and when demand is high

ca405-san-luis-reservoir.q: Is San Luis Reservoir going to change?
alts: Are they building more on it?
ca405-san-luis-reservoir.a: A plan approved in 2023 would raise the dam 10 feet by 2032.
ca405-san-luis-reservoir.quote: A plan approved in 2023 would raise the dam 10 feet by 2032.

ca407-santa-nella-s-name.q: Who was Saint Nella, and why is the town called Santa Nella?
alts: Who was she, that Santa Nella lady?
Is there really a saint named Nella?
ca407-santa-nella-s-name.a: There is no Saint Nella. The name is an English mangling of the Spanish word centinela, which means sentinel.
ca407-santa-nella-s-name.quote: Santa Nella sounds like a saint's name, but there is no Saint Nella. The name is an English mangling of the Spanish word centinela, sentinel

ca407-santa-nella-s-name.q: Who started the ranch that gave Santa Nella its name?
alts: Who had the horse ranch, like, way back?
ca407-santa-nella-s-name.a: Stockmen from San Juan Bautista and Monterey started the horse ranch here in 1810.
ca407-santa-nella-s-name.quote: a horse ranch started here in 1810 by stockmen from San Juan Bautista and Monterey.

ca407-santa-nella-s-name.q: What happened to the horse ranch at Santa Nella?
alts: What happened to the ranch, did it fail?
ca407-santa-nella-s-name.a: It failed. Many of the horses escaped into the valley, and there was fighting with Native people.
ca407-santa-nella-s-name.quote: The ranch failed after many of its horses escaped into the valley, followed by fighting with Native people.

ca407-santa-nella-s-name.q: Why was Santa Nella an important stopping place in the old days?
alts: Why did people stop here back then?
Was it on some old road, like for stagecoaches?
What was here before the freeway?
ca407-santa-nella-s-name.a: It sat on El Camino Viejo. In the Gold Rush, the stage road from Hill's Ferry crossed San Luis Creek here on its way to Pacheco Pass.
ca407-santa-nella-s-name.quote: it sat on El Camino Viejo, and in the Gold Rush the stage road from Hill's Ferry crossed San Luis Creek here on its way to Pacheco Pass.

ca407-santa-nella-s-name.q: Is Santa Nella still a place for travelers to stop today?
alts: Is it still a stopping place?
Do people still stop at it today?
Is it just a rest stop town?
ca407-santa-nella-s-name.a: Yes. Santa Nella is still mostly a place for travelers to stop.
ca407-santa-nella-s-name.quote: Santa Nella is still mostly a place for travelers to stop.

ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.q: How old is Pea Soup Andersen's?
ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.a: This Santa Nella location opened in 1976. It was the second location of a roadside restaurant whose original opened in 1924.
ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.quote: Pea Soup Andersen's opened here in 1976 as the second location of a roadside restaurant famous for its pea soup.

ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.q: Is this the only Pea Soup Andersen's left?
alts: Are there more of them or just this one?
ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.a: Yes. The 1924 original in Buellton closed in January 2024, just before its 100th anniversary, so this one became the only Pea Soup Andersen's left.
ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.quote: When the 1924 original in Buellton closed in January 2024, just before its 100th anniversary, this became the only Pea Soup Andersen's left.

alts: Where did the pea soup recipe come from?
ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.a: Danish-born Anton Andersen and his French-born wife, Juliette, opened the first cafe in 1924. The pea soup recipe was handed down in Juliette's family.
ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.quote: Pea soup, made from a recipe handed down in Juliette's family, went on the menu three months later.

alts: Who are those two cartoon chefs?
Who are the little chef guys?
ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.a: They're the restaurant's mascots, two cartoon chefs splitting peas with a hammer and chisel. They came from a cartoon by Charles Forbell.
ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.quote: the mascots Hap-pea and Pea-wee, two cartoon chefs splitting peas with a hammer and chisel, came from a cartoon by Charles Forbell.

ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.q: What's the windmill at Pea Soup Andersen's?
ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.a: It's a 77-foot working windmill that you can see from the freeway. It still turns whenever the restaurant is open.
ca407-pea-soup-andersen-s.quote: the 77-foot windmill still turns whenever the restaurant is open.

ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.q: Who gave the land for San Joaquin Valley National Cemetery?
alts: Who donated the land for it?
Whose land was this cemetery built on?
ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.a: The Romero Ranch Company donated the land in 1989. It sits on McCabe Road near Santa Nella, west of the freeway.
ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.quote: on land the Romero Ranch Company donated in 1989

ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.q: How big is San Joaquin Valley National Cemetery?
ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.a: It covers 322 acres. By 2008, more than 30,000 burials had taken place there.
ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.quote: It covers 322 acres, its first section was finished in 1992, and more than 30,000 burials had taken place there by 2008.

ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.q: What is the Korean War memorial at San Joaquin Valley National Cemetery?
alts: What is that memorial made of?
What are those tall stone pillars for?
ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.a: It's a circle of 16 granite pillars, each five feet tall, engraved with the names of 2,495 Californians who died in the Korean War. It was set up in 1998.
ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.quote: is a circle of 16 granite pillars, each five feet tall, engraved with the names of the 2,495 Californians who died in the Korean War.

ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.q: What can we see at San Joaquin Valley National Cemetery?
alts: What's there to see at that cemetery?
Is there anything to look at there?
ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.a: There's the Korean War memorial of granite pillars, an 11th Airborne memorial, and a small museum displaying uniforms and medals.
ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.quote: An 11th Airborne memorial, dedicated in 2002, honors all airborne forces, and a small museum on the grounds displays uniforms and medals.

ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.q: Who is buried at San Joaquin Valley National Cemetery?
ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.a: Seaman William Troy, a Medal of Honor recipient for action against Korean forts in 1871, is buried here. So is boxer Mac Foster, a Marine sergeant.
ca409-san-joaquin-valley-national-cemete.quote: Among those buried here is Seaman William Troy, who received the Medal of Honor for action against Korean forts in 1871

ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.q: What are the two canals side by side?
alts: What are those canals out there?
Why are there two big ditches next to each other?
ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.a: They are the state's California Aqueduct and the federal Delta-Mendota Canal. Both run side by side along the western edge of the valley between here and Tracy.
ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.quote: Two big canals run side by side along the western edge of the valley between here and Tracy: the state's California Aqueduct and the federal Delta-Mendota Canal.

ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.q: When was the Delta-Mendota Canal built?
alts: How long ago did they finish that canal?
ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.a: The Delta-Mendota Canal was finished in 1951. Its builders worked three shifts a day, 21 hours a day, six days a week.
ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.quote: Its builders worked three shifts a day, 21 hours a day, six days a week.

ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.q: How long is the Delta-Mendota Canal?
ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.a: It runs 117 miles, from a pumping plant near Tracy to the San Joaquin River near Mendota.
ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.quote: it runs 117 miles to the San Joaquin River near Mendota.

ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.q: Why was the Delta-Mendota Canal built?
alts: Why did they dig that big ditch?
ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.a: It came from a water swap. Friant Dam sends San Joaquin River water to the east side of the valley, so the canal brings Sacramento River water from the Delta to farms downstream.
ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.quote: the Delta-Mendota brings Sacramento River water from the Delta to replace it for farms downstream.

ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.q: How does the Delta-Mendota Canal get its water?
alts: How does the water get into it?
ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.a: It starts at a pumping plant near Tracy that lifts water 197 feet out of the Delta.
ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.quote: starts at a pumping plant near Tracy that lifts water 197 feet out of the Delta

ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.q: What went wrong with the Delta-Mendota Canal over the years?
alts: Why did the ground sink by the canal?
ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.a: The ground beneath it sank more than 6 feet along its southern 30 to 40 miles. In places bridges, pipes and even cattle guards ended up underwater.
ca411-two-canals-side-by-side.quote: the ground beneath it sank, more than 6 feet along its southern 30 to 40 miles

alts: Why were the birds dying, Mom?
ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.a: In 1983 scientists found that 64 percent of the water bird embryos and hatchlings there were deformed or dead. Selenium in farm drainage water had poisoned them.
ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.quote: In 1983 scientists found that 64 percent of the water bird embryos and hatchlings there were deformed or dead, poisoned by selenium in farm drainage water.

ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.q: Where did the selenium at Kesterson come from?
alts: Why were the poisons in the water, Dad?
ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.a: It washed out of black shale in the Coast Ranges. It ended up in farm drainage water, which collected at Kesterson and evaporated, concentrating the selenium.
ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.quote: the drainage collected at Kesterson and evaporated, concentrating selenium that had washed out of black shale in the Coast Ranges.

ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.q: What was the San Luis Drain supposed to be?
alts: What was it supposed to do?
Why did they build a drain, Dad?
ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.a: It was planned to run 290 miles and carry away salty water from under west side fields. Only 82 miles were built before work stopped in 1975.
ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.quote: the San Luis Drain, planned to run 290 miles and carry away salty water from under west side fields. Only 82 miles were built before work stopped in 1975

ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.q: What did the poisoned birds look like at Kesterson?
alts: What happened to the birds in it?
What was wrong with the baby birds?
ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.a: Birds hatched with missing or deformed eyes, beaks, wings and legs.
ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.quote: Birds hatched with missing or deformed eyes, beaks, wings and legs.

alts: Why is it called the Kesterson effect, Mom?
ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.a: It's what scientists call selenium's path from rock to duck.
ca416-kesterson-and-the-selenium-birds.quote: scientists now call selenium's path from rock to duck the Kesterson effect.

ca418-gustine.q: How did Gustine get its name?
alts: Why is this town called Gustine, Mom?
ca418-gustine.a: Gustine is named for Sara Miller, the daughter of cattle king Henry Miller. Her middle name was Augustine and her nickname was Gussie.
ca418-gustine.quote: named for Sara Miller, the daughter of cattle king Henry Miller. Her middle name was Augustine and her nickname was Gussie

alts: What's special about this town, Dad?
ca418-gustine.a: In March 1970 Gustine became the first place in California with a 9-1-1 emergency phone system. It also has a Portuguese festa described as the largest in the nation.
ca418-gustine.quote: In March 1970 Gustine became the first place in California with a 9-1-1 emergency phone system.

ca418-gustine.q: How old is the town of Gustine?
alts: When did it become a town?
How long has this place been here?
ca418-gustine.a: Gustine grew up in the early 1900s as a Southern Pacific station. Its post office opened in 1907 and it became a city in 1915.
ca418-gustine.quote: Gustine grew up in the early 1900s as a Southern Pacific station, opened its post office in 1907 and became a city in 1915.

ca418-gustine.q: What is the festa in Gustine?
alts: Is there a big party in this town?
ca418-gustine.a: It's a festa steeped in Portuguese tradition, and it is described as the largest in the nation.
ca418-gustine.quote: The town is home to a festa steeped in Portuguese tradition that is described as the largest in the nation.

ca418-gustine.q: What is the Gustine High School basketball tournament?
alts: How long has that tournament been going?
Is there a basketball thing here?
ca418-gustine.a: Gustine High School hosts what is called the longest-running basketball tournament in California. The local Rotary Club puts it on, and it celebrated its 75th year in 2017.
ca418-gustine.quote: Gustine High School hosts what is called the longest-running basketball tournament in California. The local Rotary Club puts it on

alts: Mom, what was that place Hills Ferry?
ca421-hills-ferry.a: Hills Ferry was a river crossing where the Merced River meets the San Joaquin. It began in 1850 and grew into a busy grain shipping town.
ca421-hills-ferry.quote: where the Merced River meets the San Joaquin, stood Hills Ferry, a river crossing started in 1850

ca421-hills-ferry.a: When the railroad came through Newman in 1888, Hills Ferry quickly faded away. By 1976, not even the shadows of a ghost town were left.
ca421-hills-ferry.quote: When the railroad came through Newman in 1888, Hills Ferry quickly faded away.

ca421-hills-ferry.q: Did anyone famous cross at Hills Ferry?
alts: Did somebody important come through there?
ca421-hills-ferry.a: Yes, the naturalist John Muir crossed the river here in May 1868 on his long walk from Oakland to Yosemite.
ca421-hills-ferry.quote: In May 1868 the naturalist John Muir crossed the river here on his long walk from Oakland to Yosemite.

ca421-hills-ferry.q: How big was the town of Hills Ferry?
alts: Were lots of people living there?
ca421-hills-ferry.a: By the late 1870s it was a busy grain shipping town of several hundred people.
ca421-hills-ferry.quote: By the late 1870s it was a busy grain shipping town of several hundred people.

ca423-newman-and-orestimba-creek.q: Who founded the town of Newman?
ca423-newman-and-orestimba-creek.a: Newman was founded in 1888 by Simon Newman, a businessman who came to California from Bavaria as a teenager in 1862.
ca423-newman-and-orestimba-creek.quote: The town of Newman, east of the freeway, was founded in 1888 by Simon Newman, a businessman who came to California from Bavaria as a teenager in 1862.

alts: Is the creek a big deal?
ca423-newman-and-orestimba-creek.a: Orestimba Creek comes down from the Diablo Range and has the largest watershed of the 13 streams that feed the San Joaquin from its west side.
ca423-newman-and-orestimba-creek.quote: has the largest watershed of the 13 streams that feed the San Joaquin from its west side.

alts: When do the almond trees bloom?
When do the trees get all the flowers?
ca426-almond-bloom.a: February is the best month to see it. That's when the almond orchards are pollinated, the largest managed pollination event in the world.
ca426-almond-bloom.quote: Each February, the pollination of California's almonds is the largest managed pollination event in the world

ca426-almond-bloom.q: Why are there so many beehives in the almond orchards?
alts: Why do they bring bees to it?
ca426-almond-bloom.a: Most almond varieties can't pollinate themselves, so growers count on bees to carry pollen between the different varieties they plant.
ca426-almond-bloom.quote: Most almond varieties cannot pollinate themselves, so growers plant a mix of varieties and count on bees to carry pollen between them.

ca426-almond-bloom.q: How many beehives come for the almond bloom?
alts: How many hives do they bring for it?
ca426-almond-bloom.a: More than a million beehives are trucked in, nearly half of all the hives in the country.
ca426-almond-bloom.quote: more than a million beehives, nearly half of all the hives in the country, are trucked in to the orchards.

ca426-almond-bloom.q: Where do the bees for the almond orchards come from?
alts: Who brings the bees for that?
ca426-almond-bloom.a: Pollination brokers hire migratory beekeepers from at least 49 states to bring their hives to the orchards.
ca426-almond-bloom.quote: Pollination brokers hire migratory beekeepers from at least 49 states for the job.

ca426-almond-bloom.q: How big is California's almond industry?
alts: How many almonds does it grow?
ca426-almond-bloom.a: In 2017 California had about a million acres of almonds, producing 2.25 billion pounds of shelled nuts.
ca426-almond-bloom.quote: In 2017 California had about a million acres of almonds, which produced 2.25 billion pounds of shelled nuts.

ca426-almond-bloom.q: Do almond trees really need bees?
alts: Do they still need bees for it?
Can the trees make almonds without bees?
ca426-almond-bloom.a: Mostly yes, but after honey bees ran short around the turn of this century, government scientists developed almond trees that can pollinate themselves.
ca426-almond-bloom.quote: government scientists developed almond trees that can pollinate themselves.

ca428-crows-landing-airfield.q: When was Crows Landing airfield built?
alts: How old is this old airfield?
ca428-crows-landing-airfield.a: The Navy broke ground on it on December 1, 1942, during World War Two.
ca428-crows-landing-airfield.quote: The Navy broke ground on December 1, 1942, and trained pilots here in Wildcat and Avenger warplanes during World War Two

ca428-crows-landing-airfield.q: What happened at Crows Landing airfield during World War Two?
alts: What did they do there in the war?
What did the Navy do at that place?
Who used it in the war?
ca428-crows-landing-airfield.a: The Navy trained pilots there in Wildcat and Avenger warplanes, and later added big patrol bombers.
ca428-crows-landing-airfield.quote: trained pilots here in Wildcat and Avenger warplanes during World War Two, later adding big patrol bombers

ca428-crows-landing-airfield.q: How did the town of Crows Landing get its name?
alts: Why is it called Crows Landing?
Why's it called that, are there crows?
ca428-crows-landing-airfield.a: It began as a landing on the San Joaquin River, started by John Crow, who came west from Missouri by covered wagon.
ca428-crows-landing-airfield.quote: Crows Landing itself began as a landing on the San Joaquin River, started by John Crow, who came west from Missouri by covered wagon.

ca428-crows-landing-airfield.q: What exit do we take for Crows Landing airfield?
ca428-crows-landing-airfield.a: Take exit 428. The old airfield is about 1.7 miles off the freeway, east of the road.
ca428-crows-landing-airfield.quote: East of the freeway is the old Crows Landing airfield.

ca428-crows-landing-airfield.q: Do the Crow family still live around Crows Landing?
alts: Is the Crow family still there?
Are there still Crows around there?
ca428-crows-landing-airfield.a: Yes, members of the Crow family still farm walnuts there. The town moved four miles west in 1887 to be on the Southern Pacific railroad.
ca428-crows-landing-airfield.quote: In 1887 the town moved four miles west to be on the Southern Pacific railroad, and members of the Crow family still farm walnuts there.

ca434-patterson-the-paris-plan.q: Why does Patterson look different from other farm towns?
alts: Why does it look so different from other towns?
Why is the town laid out in circles, Mom?
ca434-patterson-the-paris-plan.a: Thomas Patterson wanted his town to stand out, so he laid it out like Washington, D.C., and Paris, with circles and streets spreading out like spokes.
ca434-patterson-the-paris-plan.quote: Thomas Patterson wanted his town to look different from other farm towns, so he laid it out like Washington, D.C., and Paris, with circles and streets spreading out like spokes

ca434-patterson-the-paris-plan.q: What trees were planted along Patterson's main streets?
alts: What trees are on the streets there?
What kind of trees does the town have, Mom?
Are there palm trees in Patterson?
ca434-patterson-the-paris-plan.a: The main streets were planted with palms, eucalyptus and sycamores.
ca434-patterson-the-paris-plan.quote: its main streets were planted with palms, eucalyptus and sycamores

ca434-patterson-the-paris-plan.q: When did Patterson become a city?
alts: When did it become a city?
How old is this town, Dad?
ca434-patterson-the-paris-plan.a: Sales of farms and town lots began in 1909, and Patterson became a city in 1919.
ca434-patterson-the-paris-plan.quote: Sales of farms and town lots began in 1909, and Patterson became a city in 1919.

ca434-patterson-the-paris-plan.q: What is the Apricot Fiesta in Patterson?
alts: Is there a party for apricots, Dad?
ca434-patterson-the-paris-plan.a: It's held on the first weekend of June and has run since 1971. It started when California grew 95 percent of the nation's apricots.
ca434-patterson-the-paris-plan.quote: Its Apricot Fiesta, held on the first weekend of June since 1971, started when California grew 95 percent of the nation's apricots.

alts: What is that place up in the hills?
Is Diablo Grande a real town?
What kind of place is it?
ca434-diablo-grande.a: Diablo Grande is a gated hillside community in the Diablo Range, about 9 miles southwest of Patterson, at 1,535 feet.
ca434-diablo-grande.quote: Diablo Grande, a gated hillside community about 9 miles southwest of Patterson, at 1,535 feet.

ca434-diablo-grande.q: Who planned Diablo Grande and what was the dream?
alts: Who started it and what were they building?
What was it supposed to be?
ca434-diablo-grande.a: Developer Donald Panoz dreamed of a resort town with up to 10,000 homes, six golf courses, a resort hotel and spa, vineyards and a winery.
ca434-diablo-grande.quote: Developer Donald Panoz dreamed of a resort town with up to 10,000 homes, six golf courses, a resort hotel and spa, vineyards and a winery.

ca434-diablo-grande.q: How many homes were actually built at Diablo Grande?
alts: Did they build all those houses there?
ca434-diablo-grande.a: Only about 350 homes were built, far short of the 10,000 that were planned. The owners filed for bankruptcy in March 2008.
ca434-diablo-grande.quote: the owners filed for bankruptcy in March 2008, with about 350 homes built.

ca434-diablo-grande.q: What went wrong with the Diablo Grande plan?
alts: What was the trouble with that project?
ca434-diablo-grande.a: A court rejected the environmental report by 1999, partly because it hadn't shown where the water would come from. After about 120 million dollars invested, the owners filed for bankruptcy in 2008.
ca434-diablo-grande.quote: By 1999 a court had rejected the project's environmental report, in part because it had not shown where its water would come from

ca434-diablo-grande.q: Are the golf courses at Diablo Grande still open?
alts: Is it still a golf resort?
ca434-diablo-grande.a: No. A course designed by Jack Nicklaus and Gene Sarazen closed in 2014 during the drought, and the last course closed in 2019.
ca434-diablo-grande.quote: A golf course designed by Jack Nicklaus and Gene Sarazen closed in 2014 during the drought, and the last course closed in 2019.

ca434-diablo-grande.q: Did a fire ever threaten Diablo Grande?
alts: Was there a wildfire up there?
ca434-diablo-grande.a: Yes. In August 2020 the community was ordered to evacuate for about a day as the SCU Lightning Complex fires burned in the hills.
ca434-diablo-grande.quote: In August 2020 the community was ordered to evacuate for about a day as the SCU Lightning Complex fires burned in the hills.

ca436-del-puerto-canyon.q: Why is it called Del Puerto Canyon?
ca436-del-puerto-canyon.a: Spanish travelers called its creek Arroyo de La Puerta, the Creek of the Door, for the narrow gap where it squeezes out of the canyon into the valley.
ca436-del-puerto-canyon.quote: Spanish travelers called its creek Arroyo de La Puerta, the Creek of the Door, for the narrow gap where it squeezes out of the canyon into the valley.

ca436-del-puerto-canyon.q: Who lived in Del Puerto Canyon long ago?
alts: Were there Native Americans there, Dad?
ca436-del-puerto-canyon.a: It is the homeland of the Hoyumne and Miumne, Northern Valley Yokuts peoples. They left grinding rocks and a path carved into the Gateway rocks at the canyon's mouth.
ca436-del-puerto-canyon.quote: This is the homeland of the Hoyumne and Miumne, Northern Valley Yokuts peoples, who left grinding rocks and a path carved into the Gateway rocks at the canyon's mouth.

ca436-del-puerto-canyon.q: Did outlaws really hide in Del Puerto Canyon?
ca436-del-puerto-canyon.a: Many place names there, like Hideout Canyon and Murderers Gulch, recall Gold Rush bandits. Joaquin Murrieta is said to have hidden wild mustangs up Adobe Creek before driving them to Sonora.
ca436-del-puerto-canyon.quote: Many of the canyon's place names, like Hideout Canyon and Murderers Gulch, recall Gold Rush bandits

ca436-del-puerto-canyon.q: What wildlife did people see in Del Puerto Canyon?
alts: Were there cool animals there, Mom?
ca436-del-puerto-canyon.a: In June 1862, William Brewer camped there and wrote of meeting a herd of thirty or forty antelope, as fleet as the wind.
ca436-del-puerto-canyon.quote: In June 1862, William Brewer camped in the canyon and wrote in his book Up and Down California of meeting a herd of thirty or forty antelope, as fleet as the wind.

ca436-del-puerto-canyon.q: What is special about the water in Del Puerto Canyon?
alts: What's up with the spring there?
ca436-del-puerto-canyon.a: A spring up the canyon, Adobe Springs, gives magnesium-rich water that is sold to the 7 Up bottling plant in Modesto.
ca436-del-puerto-canyon.quote: A spring up the canyon, Adobe Springs, gives magnesium-rich water that is sold to the 7 Up bottling plant in Modesto.

ca436-del-puerto-canyon.q: What exit is Del Puerto Canyon on I-5?
alts: Which exit do we take, Mom?
ca436-del-puerto-canyon.a: Del Puerto Canyon is at exit 436. From there, Del Puerto Canyon Road follows the creek west into the mountains.
ca436-del-puerto-canyon.quote: Del Puerto Canyon Road follows the creek west into the mountains.

ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.q: How big were the 2020 lightning fires?
ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.a: The SCU Lightning Complex burned nearly 400,000 acres, more than 600 square miles, across six counties. It was one of the largest wildfires in modern California history.
ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.quote: The SCU Lightning Complex burned nearly 400,000 acres, more than 600 square miles, across six counties between August 16 and October 1

ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.q: When did the 2020 lightning fires happen?
alts: When did the fire start, and when did it stop?
ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.a: They burned in August 2020. The SCU Lightning Complex ran from August 16 to October 1, burning through the Diablo Range west of the freeway.
ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.quote: In August 2020 a cluster of wildfires burned through the Diablo Range west of the freeway.

ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.q: Did the 2020 lightning fires burn Lick Observatory?
ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.a: The fires reached Lick Observatory on Mount Hamilton on August 20, but the telescope domes did not burn.
ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.quote: The fires reached Lick Observatory on Mount Hamilton on August 20, but the telescope domes did not burn.

ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.q: Did anyone die in the 2020 lightning fires?
alts: Were people hurt in the fire?
ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.a: No one died, though six people were hurt and 222 buildings were destroyed.
ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.quote: In all, 222 buildings were destroyed and six people were hurt, but no one died.

ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.q: Was the burn from the 2020 lightning fires bad for nature?
alts: Was it bad for the land?
ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.a: A year later, a study of 6,000 acres of East Bay parkland found the burn was mostly good for the land. It spared most trees, renewed plants and set off sprouting of rare fire poppies.
ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.quote: a study of 6,000 acres of East Bay parkland found that the burn had been mostly good for the land

ca438-the-2020-lightning-fires.q: What exit is the 2020 lightning fires stop?
alts: Which exit do we take for that?

ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.q: What caused the Westley tire fire?
alts: How did a pile of tires even catch fire?
ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.a: Lightning. It struck a huge pile of about six million old tires near Westley on September 22, 1999.
ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.quote: On September 22, 1999, lightning struck a huge pile of about six million old tires near Westley.

ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.q: How long did the Westley tire fire burn?
alts: How many days was the fire going?
How long was it on fire?
ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.a: It burned for 34 days. The melting rubber turned into at least 250,000 gallons of oil.
ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.quote: The fire burned for 34 days, and the melting rubber turned into at least 250,000 gallons of oil.

ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.q: How many tires were in the Westley tire fire?
alts: How many tires were in it?
ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.a: About six million old tires were in the pile that lightning struck near Westley.
ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.quote: lightning struck a huge pile of about six million old tires near Westley.

ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.q: Why were so many tires piled up at Westley?
alts: Why was that pile of tires there?
Why did they have a mountain of tires?
ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.a: Waste tires had been stockpiled at the site since the 1960s. They were used to fuel a waste-to-energy operation.
ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.quote: Waste tires had been stockpiled at the Westley site since the 1960s and were used to fuel a waste-to-energy operation.

ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.q: How much did the Westley tire fire cleanup cost?
alts: How much did the cleanup cost?
How expensive was it to clean up?
ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.a: Cleanup was estimated to cost more than 20 million dollars. In April 2000 the state sued the landowners, tire haulers and operators to make them pay.
ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.quote: Cleanup was estimated to cost more than 20 million dollars.

ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.q: What damage did the Westley tire fire do?
alts: Was it bad for the environment?
ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.a: It poured tons of smoke and pollutants into the air and threatened surface water and groundwater. It also left contaminated soil behind.
ca441-the-westley-tire-fire.quote: The fire poured tons of smoke and pollutants into the air and threatened surface water and groundwater.

alts: How big is that mountain, Dad?
ca444-mount-diablo.a: Mount Diablo is 3,849 feet tall. It stands alone on the skyline, with two peaks, and you can spot it on clear days.
ca444-mount-diablo.quote: On clear days a lone, double-peaked mountain stands on the northwest skyline: Mount Diablo, 3,849 feet tall and about 40 miles away.

ca444-mount-diablo.q: What is Mount Diablo famous for?
alts: Why is that mountain a big deal?
ca444-mount-diablo.a: Surveyors use it as a starting point. In 1851 its south peak became the base for land surveys, and land in most of Northern California and all of Nevada is still described from it.
ca444-mount-diablo.quote: In 1851 Colonel Leander Ransom chose its south peak as the starting point for land surveys, and land in most of Northern California and all of Nevada is still described from it.

ca444-mount-diablo.q: What does Tuyshtak mean for Mount Diablo?
alts: What did people call it before?
What did the Ohlone call that mountain?
ca444-mount-diablo.a: The Chochenyo-speaking Ohlone call it Tuyshtak, meaning at the dawn of time. In Miwok and Ohlone tradition it was the place of creation.
ca444-mount-diablo.quote: The Chochenyo-speaking Ohlone call the mountain Tuyshtak, meaning at the dawn of time, and in Miwok and Ohlone tradition it was the place of creation.

ca444-mount-diablo.q: Who lived on Mount Diablo long ago?
alts: Did people live on that mountain, Mom?
ca444-mount-diablo.a: Most of the mountain, including its peak, was the homeland of the Volvon, a Bay Miwok-speaking people.
ca444-mount-diablo.quote: Most of the mountain, including its peak, was the homeland of the Volvon, a Bay Miwok-speaking people.

ca444-mount-diablo.a: Yes, it is still growing. A hidden thrust fault beneath the mountain keeps pushing it up.
ca444-mount-diablo.quote: The mountain is still growing, pushed up by a hidden thrust fault beneath it.

ca444-mount-diablo.q: What was the Eye of Diablo on Mount Diablo?
alts: What was that light on top?
Was there a giant flashlight on the mountain?
ca444-mount-diablo.a: It was a 10-million-candlepower aviation beacon Standard Oil put on top in 1928. It could be seen for a hundred miles, and Pearl Harbor survivors have relit it every Pearl Harbor Day since 1964.
ca444-mount-diablo.quote: In 1928 Standard Oil put a 10-million-candlepower aviation beacon on top, the Eye of Diablo, which could be seen for a hundred miles.

ca446-the-i-580-junction.q: Where does I-580 go from the I-580 junction?
alts: Where does it go from here?
Where does that road take us, Buddy?
ca446-the-i-580-junction.a: I-580 heads for the Bay Area over Altamont Pass, a major crossing of the Diablo Range. It runs about 76 miles in all, from San Rafael through Oakland to this meeting with I-5.
ca446-the-i-580-junction.quote: At this junction, I-580 heads for the Bay Area over Altamont Pass, a major crossing of the Diablo Range.

alts: How long is it in total?
How far does that whole road go?
ca446-the-i-580-junction.a: I-580 runs about 76 miles, from San Rafael through Oakland to this meeting with I-5 south of Tracy.
ca446-the-i-580-junction.quote: In all, I-580 runs about 76 miles, from San Rafael through Oakland to this meeting with I-5 south of Tracy.

ca446-the-i-580-junction.q: Why is the I-580 junction important?
alts: Why do so many people use that road?
ca446-the-i-580-junction.a: Together with I-5, I-580 is a main route between the Bay Area and Southern California.
ca446-the-i-580-junction.quote: Together with I-5, it is a main route between the Bay Area and Southern California.

ca446-the-i-580-junction.q: Who is the William Elton Brownie Brown Freeway named for?
ca446-the-i-580-junction.a: A stretch of I-580 is named for a Tracy man who helped decide the route of I-5 through the San Joaquin Valley.
ca446-the-i-580-junction.quote: One stretch of I-580 is named the William Elton Brownie Brown Freeway, for a Tracy man who helped decide the route of I-5 through the San Joaquin Valley.

ca446-the-i-580-junction.q: When was this part of I-580 built?
alts: Was that road built a long time ago?
ca446-the-i-580-junction.a: The piece between the I-205 split and this junction was built in the late 1960s and early 1970s on new right-of-way through low hills near Patterson.
ca446-the-i-580-junction.quote: The piece between the I-205 split and this junction was built in the late 1960s and early 1970s on new right-of-way through low hills near Patterson.

ca446-the-i-580-junction.q: Is the I-580 junction on a scenic highway?
ca446-the-i-580-junction.a: Yes. That piece of I-580 is an official state scenic highway, and so is I-5 from Highway 152 near Santa Nella to this junction, the only stretch of I-5 the state has named one.
ca446-the-i-580-junction.quote: That piece is an official state scenic highway, and so is I-5 from Highway 152 near Santa Nella to this junction, the only stretch of I-5 the state has named a scenic highway.

alts: Why does this town have such a weird name?
ca449-vernalis.a: Vernalis is Latin for springlike. But a local historian, Earle Williams, said it was named after two ranchers' daughters, Verna Carpenter and Alice Hamilton.
ca449-vernalis.quote: whose name is Latin for springlike. Local historian Earle Williams said it was named after two ranchers' daughters, Verna Carpenter and Alice Hamilton.

ca449-vernalis.q: What happened in Vernalis during World War Two?
alts: What was it used for in the war?
Was there a war thing here, like soldiers or planes?
ca449-vernalis.a: Vernalis had a Navy airfield, Naval Auxiliary Air Station Vernalis. It also had a reconditioning center and a camp for prisoners of war.
ca449-vernalis.quote: During World War Two, Vernalis had a Navy airfield, Naval Auxiliary Air Station Vernalis, along with a reconditioning center and a camp for prisoners of war.

ca449-vernalis.q: When did the Vernalis post office start?
alts: Is this an old town, like how long ago?
ca449-vernalis.a: Its post office began in 1851 at nearby San Joaquin City. It moved to Vernalis in 1888.
ca449-vernalis.quote: Its post office began in 1851 at nearby San Joaquin City and moved here in 1888.

ca449-vernalis.q: What was San Joaquin City, near Vernalis?
alts: What happened to that old town nearby?
Was there a boomtown near here, kids?
ca449-vernalis.a: It was probably the largest of the boomtowns that sprang up after the Gold Rush. Founded in 1851, it kept its size until 1880, when competition from Stockton drew its trade away.
ca449-vernalis.quote: San Joaquin City, near where the Stanislaus River joins the San Joaquin, was probably the largest of the boomtowns that sprang up after the Gold Rush.

ca449-vernalis.q: Which exit do we take for Vernalis?
alts: How do we get to that town, which road?
ca449-vernalis.a: Take exit 449 and follow Highway 33. Vernalis is east of the freeway.
ca449-vernalis.quote: Highway 33 leads to Vernalis, east of the freeway, whose name is Latin for springlike.

ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.q: What is the San Joaquin River refuge for?
alts: Why do they have this place, Mom?
ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.a: It protects more than 7,000 acres of river woodland, wetlands and grassland where the Tuolumne and Stanislaus rivers join the San Joaquin.
ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.quote: San Joaquin River National Wildlife Refuge protects more than 7,000 acres of river woodland, wetlands and grassland.

ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.q: When was the San Joaquin River refuge set up?
ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.a: It was set up in 1987 to protect the winter home of the Aleutian cackling goose, which was endangered at the time.
ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.quote: It was set up in 1987 to protect the winter home of the Aleutian cackling goose, then endangered

ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.q: What animals can we see at the San Joaquin River refuge?
ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.a: Swainson's hawks nest in tall cottonwoods, and herons and cormorants nest together in big oaks. From autumn through spring, big flocks of geese and sandhill cranes gather.
ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.quote: Swainson's hawks nest in the tall cottonwoods, and herons and cormorants nest together in big oaks on Christman Island.

ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.q: When is the best time to visit the San Joaquin River refuge?
alts: Is there a good season for it?
ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.a: The best months are November through February. That fits the season when big flocks of geese and sandhill cranes gather there, from autumn through spring.
ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.quote: Best months: November, December, January, February

ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.q: What is special about the trees at the San Joaquin River refuge?
alts: Are the trees real or did people put them there?
ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.a: A nonprofit called River Partners led the planting of about 400,000 native trees across 1,700 acres of floodplain, one of California's largest projects to bring back streamside forest.
ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.quote: A nonprofit, River Partners, led the planting of about 400,000 native trees across 1,700 acres of the river's floodplain

ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.q: What happened to the rabbits at the San Joaquin River refuge?
ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.a: Endangered riparian brush rabbits, raised in captivity, have been returned to their old habitat there.
ca449-san-joaquin-river-refuge.quote: Endangered riparian brush rabbits, raised in captivity, have been returned to their old habitat here.

ca451-estanislao-s-river.q: Who was Estanislao, the man this river is named for?
alts: Who's the guy the river is named after?
ca451-estanislao-s-river.a: Estanislao was the baptized name of Cucunuchi, a leader of the Lakisamni, a Yokuts people. He was also a Native official at Mission San Jose.
ca451-estanislao-s-river.quote: Estanislao, the baptized name of Cucunuchi, a leader of the Lakisamni, a Yokuts people, and a Native official at Mission San Jose

ca451-estanislao-s-river.q: What did Estanislao do that made him so famous?
alts: What did that guy do, did he fight someone?
ca451-estanislao-s-river.a: In the late 1820s he left the mission with about 400 followers and led raids on missions and settlers, until a Mexican army under Mariano Vallejo drove his people from the river in 1829.
ca451-estanislao-s-river.quote: In the late 1820s he left the mission with about 400 followers and led raids on missions and settlers

alts: Is it true he inspired Zorro?
Was he like the real Zorro?
ca451-estanislao-s-river.a: He is thought to be one of the inspirations for Zorro. Legend says he carved an S to mark his raids.
ca451-estanislao-s-river.quote: Legend says he carved an S to mark his raids, and he is thought to be one of the inspirations for Zorro.

ca451-estanislao-s-river.q: How did Estanislao train his fighters?
alts: How did it work, did he have an army?
How big was his army, like soldiers and forts?
ca451-estanislao-s-river.a: He used tactics learned from Spanish and Mexican soldiers, digging trenches and building palisades. At one point he led as many as 4,000 men.
ca451-estanislao-s-river.quote: Estanislao trained his fighters in tactics learned from Spanish and Mexican soldiers, digging trenches and building palisades

ca451-estanislao-s-river.q: What happened to Estanislao in the end?
alts: What happened to him after that?
Did he get in trouble, or get away?
ca451-estanislao-s-river.a: He was pardoned in 1829. He spent his last years at Mission San Jose teaching others the Yokuts language and culture until his death in 1838.
ca451-estanislao-s-river.quote: Estanislao was pardoned in 1829, and he spent his last years at Mission San Jose teaching others the Yokuts language and culture until his death in 1838.

alts: Is that town really old, like ancient?
ca457-banta.a: Banta is a settlement dating to the 1840s, so it goes back to stagecoach days.
ca457-banta.quote: West of the freeway is Banta, a settlement dating to the 1840s.

ca457-banta.q: Why is the town called Banta?
ca457-banta.a: Henry Banta bought its inn in 1863 and changed the sign to Banta's White House. Travelers soon called the whole place Bantas.
ca457-banta.quote: Henry Banta bought its inn in 1863 and changed the sign to read Banta's White House, and travelers soon called the whole place Bantas.

ca457-banta.q: What was Banta used for in stagecoach days?
alts: What did it do back then?
What was it for in the old days?
ca457-banta.a: In stagecoach days it was the last stop before Altamont Pass on the road between Stockton and the Bay Area.
ca457-banta.quote: In stagecoach days it was the last stop before Altamont Pass on the road between Stockton and the Bay Area.

ca457-banta.q: Did a railroad ever come through Banta?
alts: Were there choo-choo trains in Banta?
ca457-banta.a: Yes, in 1869 it became a stop on the new Western Pacific Railroad. In 1878 the railroad built its junction at Tracy instead, and Banta went quiet.
ca457-banta.quote: In 1878 the railroad built its new junction at Tracy instead, and Banta became a quiet village at the far edge of the rail yards.

alts: Are there ghosts in that old inn?
ca457-banta.a: Some locals say so. The Banta Inn, established in 1879, is said by some locals to be haunted.
ca457-banta.quote: The Banta Inn, established in 1879, is said by some locals to be haunted.

ca457-banta.q: Did anyone famous live in Banta?
alts: Did a famous person come from there?
ca457-banta.a: Yes, Steve Perry, later the lead singer of Journey, once called Banta home. His band Alien Project formed there in the mid-1970s.
ca457-banta.quote: Steve Perry, later the lead singer of Journey, once called Banta home, and his band Alien Project formed there in the mid-1970s.

ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.a: Tracy was born on September 8, 1878, when a Southern Pacific line from Oakland was joined to the Central Pacific line there.
ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.quote: Tracy, west of the freeway, was born on September 8, 1878, when a Southern Pacific line from Oakland was joined to the Central Pacific line there

ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.a: The junction was named for Lathrop J. Tracy, a railroad executive from back east, according to the Tracy Historical Museum.
ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.quote: The Tracy Historical Museum says the junction was named for Lathrop J. Tracy, a railroad executive from back east.

ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.q: What happened to the old railroad town of Ellis near Tracy?
alts: Where did the people from Ellis go?
ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.a: Once the railroad moved its facilities to the new Tracy station, railroad families and businesses followed, and Ellis faded.
ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.quote: Once the railroad moved its facilities to the new Tracy station, railroad families and businesses followed, and Ellis faded.

ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.q: What was Tracy's main business over the years?
alts: What did Tracy used to be about?
ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.a: It began as a railroad town, with a roundhouse added in 1896. By the 1950s farming had become Tracy's main business.
ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.quote: a roundhouse followed in 1896. By the 1950s farming had become Tracy's main business

alts: Is it a big place now?
ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.a: Growth from the Bay Area spilling over the Altamont since the 1970s has turned the railroad town into a city of more than 90,000.
ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.quote: since the 1970s Bay Area growth spilling over the Altamont has made the railroad town a city of more than 90,000

ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.q: Whose land was Tracy built on?
alts: Were there people there before the railroad?
Do native people still live there?
ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.a: This is Yokuts homeland, and Yokuts people still live in the region.
ca458-tracy-the-railroad-town.quote: This is Yokuts homeland, and Yokuts people still live in the region.

ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.q: What do San Joaquin County farms grow the most?
alts: What do they grow on that land?
What's all this farm stuff growing, mom?
ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.a: In the 2024 crop report, milk was the top commodity and almonds came second. Walnuts ranked fifth and cherries sixth.
ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.quote: In its 2024 crop report, milk was the top commodity and almonds came second, with walnuts fifth and cherries sixth.

ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.q: What are San Joaquin County farms famous for?
alts: Is there anything special about these farms?
ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.a: It has more acres of wine grapes than any other county in California. It also grows about half of California's cherries.
ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.quote: The county also has more acres of wine grapes than any other county in California.

ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.q: How big is farming in San Joaquin County?
alts: Is that a lot of money?
How much stuff do these farms make?
ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.a: In 2024 its farms produced about 3.1 billion dollars' worth of crops and livestock. The source calls the county a major national center of farming.
ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.quote: In 2024 its farms produced about 3.1 billion dollars' worth of crops and livestock.

ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.q: What happens to the cherries grown in San Joaquin County?
alts: Where do the cherries go, mom?
ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.a: The county's more than a dozen cherry packing houses handle nearly all the cherries grown in the state.
ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.quote: its more than a dozen cherry packing houses handle nearly all the cherries grown in the state.

ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.q: What is special about walnuts in San Joaquin County?
alts: Do they make walnut stuff here?
ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.a: The county is home to one of the largest walnut processing plants in the world. It handles a lot of Livermore red walnuts, a variety developed in the San Joaquin Valley.
ca459-san-joaquin-county-farms.quote: It is also home to one of the largest walnut processing plants in the world, a major handler of Livermore red walnuts

ca460-mossdale-crossing.q: What happened at Mossdale Crossing in 1869?
alts: Why was that railroad bridge such a big deal?
What was the first train thing here?
ca460-mossdale-crossing.a: The first railroad bridge opened here on September 6, 1869. That afternoon the first through train from Sacramento crossed it, and it was the last link of the first transcontinental railroad to the Pacific.
ca460-mossdale-crossing.quote: The first railroad bridge at this spot opened on September 6, 1869, and that afternoon the first through train from Sacramento crossed it

ca460-mossdale-crossing.q: Why is it called Mossdale Crossing?
alts: Who was Moss, and why is his name on it?
Where does the name come from?
ca460-mossdale-crossing.a: William Moss, a former Ohio riverboat captain, bought the ferry here in 1856. The valley beside it became Moss' Dale.
ca460-mossdale-crossing.quote: William Moss, a former Ohio riverboat captain, bought the ferry in 1856, and the valley beside it became Moss' Dale.

ca460-mossdale-crossing.q: What was Mossdale Crossing before the railroad?
alts: What was it before the trains came?
Did people live here a long time ago?
What did the Spanish call it?
ca460-mossdale-crossing.a: A sharp bend slowed the river and made a shallow ford, a favorite fishing ground of the Yokuts. The Spanish called it El Pescadero, the fishing place.
ca460-mossdale-crossing.quote: a sharp bend slowed the river here and made a shallow ford, a favorite fishing ground of the Yokuts, whose homeland this is.

ca460-mossdale-crossing.q: Who built the railroad bridge at Mossdale Crossing?
alts: How many people built the bridge?
Who worked on the train bridge?
ca460-mossdale-crossing.a: By August 1869 about 600 men were building the railroad bridge, and 500 of them were Chinese.
ca460-mossdale-crossing.quote: By August 1869 about 600 men were building the railroad bridge, 500 of them Chinese.

ca460-mossdale-crossing.q: Is the Mossdale Crossing bridge the original one?
alts: Is that the same bridge from 1869?
Is the old bridge still there?
ca460-mossdale-crossing.a: No. The first bridge was a wooden swing bridge, rebuilt in steel in 1895 and replaced with today's lift bridge in 1942.
ca460-mossdale-crossing.quote: The wooden swing bridge was rebuilt in steel in 1895 and replaced with today's lift bridge in 1942.

alts: Why's this town named after lard, Dad?
ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.a: Nobody agrees. One story says locals wanted a word for butter and the railroad got it wrong. Another says the Southern Pacific simply liked giving its stops appealing Spanish names.
ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.quote: One story says locals wanted a word for butter and the railroad got it wrong.

alts: What's Manteca mean, is it food?
ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.a: Manteca is Spanish for lard. That's an odd name for a town whose railroad stop was there to ship dairy products.
ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.quote: Highway 120 leads east to Manteca, whose name is Spanish for lard.

alts: Who built this town, who was the first guy?
ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.a: Joshua Cowell founded the town and brought dairy farming to the area. When Manteca incorporated in 1918, Cowell was elected its first mayor.
ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.quote: Joshua Cowell, the town's founder, brought dairy farming to the area.

ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.q: What was Manteca called before it was Manteca?
alts: Was it named something else before?
ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.a: The railroad stop was first called Cowell Station. The line already had a second Cowell Station, named for his brother Henry, so a new name was needed.
ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.quote: The railroad stop was first called Cowell Station, but the line had a second Cowell Station, named for his brother Henry

alts: Is it still a farming town?
Do people still farm there, or is it a big city now?
ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.a: Manteca lived mostly on farming into the 1970s. Rising Bay Area home prices then turned it into a commuter town, and its population has more than tripled since 1980.
ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.quote: Rising Bay Area home prices then turned it into a commuter town, and its population has more than tripled since 1980.

ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.q: Did the railroad really misprint the name Monteca?
alts: Did the railroad mess up the name, was it a typo?
ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.a: That's a local legend, but a local columnist points out that the word monteca is nowhere to be found in Spanish dictionaries.
ca461-manteca-a-dairy-town-named-lard.quote: but a local columnist points out that the word monteca is nowhere to be found in Spanish dictionaries.

alts: Why was it built in the first place?
Why does this town even exist?
ca462-lathrop-born-of-a-quarrel.a: It began with a quarrel. Stockton dragged its feet on where the railroad should run, so Leland Stanford built the line around the city and started a new town here.
ca462-lathrop-born-of-a-quarrel.quote: When Stockton dragged its feet on where the railroad should run, Central Pacific president Leland Stanford built the line around the city and started a new town here

alts: Where did that name come from?
How did this town get its name?
ca462-lathrop-born-of-a-quarrel.a: It was first a depot called Wilson's Station. In 1869 it was renamed for the family of Jane Lathrop Stanford, Leland Stanford's wife, and her brother Charles, an engineer for the railroad.
ca462-lathrop-born-of-a-quarrel.quote: In 1869 it was renamed for the family of his wife, Jane Lathrop Stanford, and her brother Charles, an engineer for the railroad.

ca462-lathrop-born-of-a-quarrel.q: What did Lathrop do in World War Two?
alts: What was it used for in the war?
ca462-lathrop-born-of-a-quarrel.a: Permanente Metals made aircraft parts and magnesium bombs here. Sharpe Army Depot was also here, one of the Army's major supply depots in the West.
ca462-lathrop-born-of-a-quarrel.quote: World War Two brought Permanente Metals, which made aircraft parts and magnesium bombs, and the Sharpe Army Depot, one of the Army's major supply depots in the West.

alts: Is it still a small town?
Is it a real city now?
What's out west of the freeway there?
