Why are there bees in the sunflowers?
How do they make the seeds?
ca548-sunflower-seed-fields.a: Bees carry pollen between interplanted rows of male and female plants. That's how the hybrid seed gets made.
ca548-sunflower-seed-fields.quote: Bees carry pollen between interplanted rows of male and female plants to make the hybrid seed.

alts: Why do farmers want that kind of seed?
ca548-sunflower-seed-fields.a: Hybrid seed grows into plants with more vigor and other traits farmers want.
ca548-sunflower-seed-fields.quote: Hybrid seed grows into plants with more vigor and other traits farmers want.

ca548-sunflower-seed-fields.q: Are the sunflower seed fields still as big as they used to be?
alts: Is it still a big business?
Why are there fewer sunflower fields now?
ca548-sunflower-seed-fields.a: No, the business has been shrinking here. Certified fields topped 53,600 acres in 2018 and fell to about 27,000 acres by 2023, as seed companies moved production overseas.
ca548-sunflower-seed-fields.quote: Certified hybrid sunflower seed fields in California topped 53,600 acres in 2018 and fell to about 27,000 acres by 2023

ca548-sunflower-seed-fields.q: Why did sunflower seed production move overseas?
alts: Why is it going to Europe?
What happened to the seed business?
ca548-sunflower-seed-fields.a: Pioneer said it had enough capacity in Europe for the European market, so it no longer needed extra capacity at Woodland. One grower blamed the exchange rate.
ca548-sunflower-seed-fields.quote: Pioneer said it no longer needed the extra production capacity at its Woodland location, because it had enough capacity in Europe for the European market

ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.q: Why was Zamora first called Black's?
alts: Why did it used to be called that?
Why was the town named after some guy?
ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.a: It was named after J. J. Black, who settled here in 1865. Zamora was once called Black's in his honor.
ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.quote: The farm community of Zamora was once called Black's, after J. J. Black, who settled here in 1865.

ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.q: How did the town of Zamora get started?
alts: How did it start growing up?
How did a town get built here, anyway?
ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.a: When the Northern Railway built a line north from Woodland in the 1870s, Black donated land for a depot. A little town grew up around the station.
ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.quote: When the Northern Railway built its line north from Woodland in the 1870s, Black donated a strip of land for a depot

ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.q: What was in Zamora when the railway town was growing?
alts: What was in it back then?
Did it have stores and stuff, like a real town?
ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.a: The little railroad town had a hotel, stores, a jail, blacksmith shops and six warehouses.
ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.quote: a little town grew up around the station, with a hotel, stores, a jail, blacksmith shops and six warehouses.

ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.q: What happened to Zamora when the highways came?
alts: What did the highways do to it?
Why is the town so tiny now?
ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.a: Modern highways rolled through in 1949 and 1969, and a local history says they cut the heart from the town. It was left with no services.
ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.quote: modern highways rolled through in 1949 and 1969, cutting the heart from the town. What remained was a town with no services

ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.q: Who lived in the Zamora area before the town?
alts: What did people hunt there long ago?
ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.a: This is Patwin homeland. Patwin hunters stalked deer, tule elk and antelope, and hunted ducks, geese and swans with bows and nets in the tule marshes.
ca548-zamora-cut-by-the-highways.quote: This is Patwin homeland. Patwin hunters stalked deer, tule elk and antelope here

ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.q: Why was I-505 once called I-5W?
alts: Why did it have a W in its name, Mom?
ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.a: It was first planned as I-5W, a western loop of Interstate 5 through the Bay Area. The route through Sacramento was to be I-5E.
ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.quote: It was first planned as part of I-5W, a western loop of Interstate 5 through the Bay Area, while the route through Sacramento was to be I-5E.

ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.q: What happened to the I-5W name?
ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.a: The split numbering was dropped. The western loop became parts of I-580, I-80 and I-505.
ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.quote: The split numbering was dropped, and the western loop became parts of I-580, I-80 and I-505.

ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.q: When did the top end of I-505 open?
alts: How old is this road, Dad?
ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.a: The northernmost piece, from Highway 16 at Madison to this junction, opened in August 1977.
ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.quote: The northernmost piece of I-505, from Highway 16 at Madison to this junction, opened in August 1977.

ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.q: What is I-505 used for today?
alts: What is it used for now?
Why do people drive on it, Mom?
ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.a: It's the main route between the Bay Area and the northern Sacramento Valley. Drivers can skip Sacramento and its traffic.
ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.quote: Today it is the main route between the Bay Area and the northern Sacramento Valley, letting drivers skip Sacramento and its traffic.

ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.q: Where does I-505 go from here?
alts: Where does that road end, Dad?
ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.a: It runs south to I-80 at Vacaville. It's a four-lane freeway the whole way and skirts the eastern edge of Winters.
ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.quote: Interstate 505 meets I-5 here and runs south to I-80 at Vacaville.

ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.q: Are there other split Interstates like I-5W?
alts: Do other roads have a W or E, Mom?
ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.a: Most were renumbered too, but I-35E and I-35W survive in Texas and Minnesota.
ca553-i-505-once-i-5w.quote: Most other split Interstates around the country were renumbered too, but I-35E and I-35W survive in Texas and Minnesota.

alts: Why did people settle here in the first place?
ca556-dunnigan-once-antelope.a: In the winter of 1853 a flood washed two settlers, Copp and Wilson, off their claims near the Sacramento River. They moved up to higher ground here.
ca556-dunnigan-once-antelope.quote: a flood washed two settlers, Copp and Wilson, off their claims near the Sacramento River, and they moved up to higher ground here.

alts: How long has it been around?
ca556-dunnigan-once-antelope.a: Its story goes back to 1853, when settlers moved here after a flood. A post office opened in 1856, the first store in 1866, and the railroad arrived in 1876.
ca556-dunnigan-once-antelope.quote: A post office opened here in 1856, and the first store in 1866. The railroad arrived in 1876

ca556-dunnigan-once-antelope.q: Who lived in the Dunnigan area before the settlers?
alts: Who were the first people here?
Did Native Americans live around it?
Do many people live in it?
ca556-dunnigan-once-antelope.a: Dunnigan is a small freeway community of about 1,400 people. It sits nearly 40 miles from both Vacaville and Sacramento.
ca556-dunnigan-once-antelope.quote: Today Dunnigan is a small freeway community of about 1,400 people, nearly 40 miles from both Vacaville and Sacramento.

ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.q: How do we spot a yellow-billed magpie?
alts: How can we tell that bird is one?
What does a yellow-billed magpie look like, mister?
ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.a: Look for a black-and-white bird with a bright yellow bill and a small patch of yellow skin around each eye. In good light its black feathers shine green, blue or purple.
ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.quote: a black-and-white bird with a bright yellow bill and a small patch of yellow skin around each eye

alts: Are those birds only here, Buddy?
ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.a: They live only in California, in the Central Valley and the foothills and mountains beside it. Watch the fields and tall trees along here.
ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.quote: It lives only in California, in the Central Valley and the foothills and mountains beside it.

alts: What do those birds munch on?
ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.a: They eat mostly insects, especially grasshoppers, plus acorns, fruit and carrion.
ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.quote: They eat mostly insects, especially grasshoppers, plus acorns, fruit and carrion.

ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.q: Do yellow-billed magpies really hold funerals?
alts: Is it true that they have a funeral?
Do the birds have funerals for dead ones?
ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.a: Sort of. When one dies, others gather around it and call loudly for 10 to 15 minutes, a kind of funeral. They're social birds that roost together.
ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.quote: When one dies, others gather around it and call loudly for 10 to 15 minutes, a kind of funeral.

ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.q: Where do yellow-billed magpies build their nests?
alts: Where does it make its nest?
What do the bird houses look like?
ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.a: Pairs build dome-shaped nests of sticks and mud high in tall trees. Sometimes they build far out on long branches to keep predators away.
ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.quote: Pairs build dome-shaped nests of sticks and mud high in tall trees, sometimes far out on long branches to keep predators away.

ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.a: The IUCN lists them as vulnerable, though they're still common in many places. West Nile virus hit them hard, and about half are thought to have died of it between 2004 and 2006.
ca559-yellow-billed-magpie.quote: The IUCN now lists the species as vulnerable, though it is still common in many places.

ca566-college-city-no-college.q: Why is it called College City if there's no college?
alts: Why is it named that if it has no college?
Why does it say college when there's no college, Mom?
ca566-college-city-no-college.a: The town began with a school, Pierce Christian College, paid for with money from the estate of Andrew Pierce. The college opened in 1875 and left town in 1896.
ca566-college-city-no-college.quote: The town began with a school, Pierce Christian College, paid for with money from the estate of Andrew Pierce.

ca566-college-city-no-college.q: Who paid for the college in College City?
alts: Who was the guy who gave money for the school?
ca566-college-city-no-college.a: The school was paid for with money from the estate of Andrew Pierce. Pierce died around 1871, and the sale of his property paid for the school.
ca566-college-city-no-college.quote: Pierce died around 1871, and the sale of his property paid for the school.

ca566-college-city-no-college.q: When did the college in College City open and close?
alts: When did it open and when did it leave?
How long was there a real college there, Dad?
ca566-college-city-no-college.a: The college opened in 1875 and left town in 1896. The College City post office had opened two years before classes began, in 1873.
ca566-college-city-no-college.quote: The college opened in 1875 and left town in 1896.

ca566-college-city-no-college.q: What was College City like back in 1875?
alts: What was in it back then?
What did the town have long ago, Dad?
ca566-college-city-no-college.a: A January 1875 newspaper story listed two general stores, a hotel, a livery stable, a saddle shop, two blacksmith shops, a bakery, a drug store, a milliner and Chinese wash houses.
ca566-college-city-no-college.quote: A newspaper story in January 1875 listed two general stores, a hotel, a livery stable, a saddle shop, two blacksmith shops, a bakery, a drug store, a milliner and Chinese wash houses.

ca566-college-city-no-college.q: How big was the college building in College City?
alts: Was the college building huge, Mom?
ca566-college-city-no-college.a: Pretty small. The college building measured just 30 by 40 feet.
ca566-college-city-no-college.quote: The college building measured just 30 by 40 feet.

ca566-college-city-no-college.q: What happened to the college buildings in College City?
alts: What happened to them after it left?
Who got the school buildings when the college left, Dad?
ca566-college-city-no-college.a: When the college left, the local high school district took over its buildings. Today College City is served by the Pierce Joint Unified School District.
ca566-college-city-no-college.quote: When the college left, the local high school district took over its buildings, and today College City is served by the Pierce Joint Unified School District.

ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.q: How did Arbuckle get its name?
ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.a: The town was named for Tacitus Arbuckle, on whose ranch it grew. It was laid out in 1875.
ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.quote: Arbuckle was laid out in 1875 and named for Tacitus Arbuckle, on whose ranch it grew.

ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.q: How did Tacitus Arbuckle get people to move to his town?
alts: How did he get it started?
Did he just give people land?
ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.a: He gave lots to anyone who would build on them. He also became the town's first postmaster.
ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.quote: To get a town going, he gave lots to anyone who would build on them, and he became its first postmaster.

ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.q: When did the first train come to Arbuckle?
alts: When did the train get to it?
When did the first choo-choo come?
ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.a: The first train pulled in on July 4, 1876, just two months after the depot was finished.
ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.quote: The first train pulled in on July 4, 1876, just two months after the depot was finished.

ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.q: Is the Arbuckle train depot still there?
alts: Can we see the old train station?
ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.a: Yes. According to the county, Arbuckle's depot is now the only train depot left in Colusa County.
ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.quote: According to the county, the town's depot is now the only train depot left in Colusa County.

ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.q: What do they grow around Arbuckle?
alts: What are those trees in the fields?
ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.a: The farmland mixes field crops with orchards, mostly almonds. Several almond hullers work nearby.
ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.quote: Today the farmland around Arbuckle mixes field crops with orchards, mostly almonds, and several almond hullers work nearby.

ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.q: Is it true that Arbuckle is sinking?
alts: Is it sinking into the ground?
ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.a: Yes. The town dropped 2.14 feet between 2008 and 2017, more than any other area in a state study. Pumping water out of the aquifers made the soil collapse upon itself.
ca566-tacitus-arbuckle-s-town.quote: the town dropping 2.14 feet between 2008 and 2017. As water was pumped out of the aquifers below, the soil collapsed upon itself.

ca567-almond-orchards.q: How much are the almond orchards worth?
alts: How much money do they make from it?
How much money do almonds make?
ca567-almond-orchards.a: In 2024 almonds were Colusa County's most valuable crop, worth about 279 million dollars, from roughly 63,000 acres.
ca567-almond-orchards.quote: In 2024 almonds were Colusa County's most valuable crop, worth about 279 million dollars, from roughly 63,000 acres.

ca567-almond-orchards.q: When do the almond orchards bloom?
alts: When do the trees get flowers?
ca567-almond-orchards.a: Pollination season usually runs from about mid-February to mid-March. The trees bloom with fragrant white to pale pink flowers before their leaves come out.
ca567-almond-orchards.quote: Almond pollination season usually runs from about mid-February to mid-March, when the trees bloom with fragrant white to pale pink flowers before their leaves come out.

ca567-almond-orchards.q: Is an almond really a nut?
ca567-almond-orchards.a: Not quite. An almond is the seed of a fruit related to the peach, sealed in a hard shell inside a leathery hull.
ca567-almond-orchards.quote: An almond is not a true nut but the seed of a fruit related to the peach, sealed in a hard shell inside a leathery hull

alts: When are almonds ready to pick?
ca567-almond-orchards.a: Almonds ripen in autumn, seven to eight months after the bloom.
ca567-almond-orchards.quote: it ripens in autumn, seven to eight months after the bloom.

ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.q: How old are the Sutter Buttes?
alts: How long ago did that mountain thing form, like a million years?
ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.a: They are the worn remains of a volcano that was active roughly a million and a half years ago.
ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.quote: They are the worn remains of a volcano that was active roughly a million and a half years ago

alts: Are those real mountains or what?
ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.a: They are the worn remains of an old volcano, and they are often called the world's smallest mountain range.
ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.quote: they are often called the world's smallest mountain range

ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.q: What do the Native names for the Sutter Buttes mean?
alts: What did Native people call it?
What's the Native name for those mountains?
ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.a: The Maidu, Nisenan and Wintun names for them all roughly mean the Middle Mountains.
ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.quote: The Maidu, Nisenan and Wintun names for them all roughly mean the Middle Mountains.

ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.q: Who was the first European to see the Sutter Buttes?
ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.a: The Spanish explorer Gabriel Moraga was the first European to see them, in 1806.
ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.quote: The Spanish explorer Gabriel Moraga was the first European to see them, in 1806.

ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.q: Can we visit the Sutter Buttes?
ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.a: Not yet. The state bought land there for a park in 2003, but it is still not open to the public, and almost all the land around the Buttes is privately owned.
ca572-sutter-buttes-closest-view.quote: In 2003 the state bought 1,785 acres there for a park, but it is still not open to the public

alts: Who are they, the people whose homeland this is?
ca575-patwin-homeland.a: The Patwin are the southern branch of the Wintun peoples. The western Sacramento Valley is their homeland.
ca575-patwin-homeland.quote: The western Sacramento Valley is the homeland of the Patwin, the southern branch of the Wintun peoples.

ca575-patwin-homeland.q: What language do the Patwin speak?
alts: What language is it that they speak?
Do the Patwin have their own language, like a secret one?
ca575-patwin-homeland.a: Patwin has two main dialects: River Patwin, spoken along the Sacramento River, and Hill Patwin, in the hills and plains to the west.
ca575-patwin-homeland.quote: Their language has two main dialects: River Patwin, spoken along the Sacramento River, and Hill Patwin, in the hills and plains to the west.

ca575-patwin-homeland.q: Are there Patwin people living here today?
alts: Do real Patwin people still live here now?
ca575-patwin-homeland.a: Yes. Today Patwin people are citizens of three federally recognized tribes, including the Kletsel Dehe Wintun Nation, headquartered in Williams.
ca575-patwin-homeland.quote: Today Patwin people are citizens of three federally recognized tribes, including the Kletsel Dehe Wintun Nation, headquartered in Williams.

ca575-patwin-homeland.q: What happened to the Patwin during the Gold Rush?
alts: What happened to them back then?
What went wrong for the Patwin in the Gold Rush?
ca575-patwin-homeland.a: The Gold Rush brought disaster. Settlers took over acorn groves and water sources, disease swept through the villages, and many Patwin were forced into unpaid labor.
ca575-patwin-homeland.quote: Settlers took over acorn groves and water sources, smallpox and measles swept through the villages, and many Patwin were forced into unpaid labor.

ca575-patwin-homeland.q: How big is the Kletsel Dehe Wintun Nation's land?
alts: How much land do they have, is it big?
ca575-patwin-homeland.a: The nation holds the Cortina Rancheria, a 640-acre reservation in the hills, and has about 270 citizens.
ca575-patwin-homeland.quote: The Kletsel Dehe Wintun Nation has about 270 citizens and holds the Cortina Rancheria, a 640-acre reservation in the hills

ca575-patwin-homeland.q: Is the Patwin language still spoken?
alts: Is it still spoken by anyone?
Can anybody still talk Patwin, or is it gone?
ca575-patwin-homeland.a: Very few speak it. As of 2021, one person was documented as a first-language speaker, and tribal members are working to bring the language back.
ca575-patwin-homeland.quote: As of 2021, one person was documented as a first-language Patwin speaker, and tribal members are working to bring the language back.

ca577-granzella-s-in-williams.q: How old is Granzella's in Williams?
alts: How long has it been around?
How old is this place, mom?
ca577-granzella-s-in-williams.a: Granzella's has served the public since 1976. It's a family business in Williams.
ca577-granzella-s-in-williams.quote: In Williams, Granzella's has served the public since 1976. The family business includes a restaurant, deli, bakery and sports lounge

ca577-granzella-s-in-williams.q: What can we get at Granzella's?
alts: What do they have at that place?
Do they have anything besides a restaurant?
ca577-granzella-s-in-williams.a: It's a family business with a restaurant, deli, bakery and sports lounge. They also sell hand-packed jars of olives.
ca577-granzella-s-in-williams.quote: The family business includes a restaurant, deli, bakery and sports lounge, and it sells hand-packed jars of olives.

ca577-granzella-s-in-williams.q: Can we stay overnight at Granzella's?
alts: Can we sleep near that place?
ca577-granzella-s-in-williams.a: Yes. Across the parking lot, the family runs Granzella's Inn, a 42-room motel.
ca577-granzella-s-in-williams.quote: Across the parking lot, the family runs Granzella's Inn, a 42-room motel.

ca577-granzella-s-in-williams.q: What exit is Granzella's in Williams?
alts: Which exit do we take for it?
What exit do we get off at, dad?
ca577-granzella-s-in-williams.a: Take exit 577 for Granzella's in Williams.
ca577-granzella-s-in-williams.quote:
Name: Granzella's in Williams
Kind: good stop
Exit: 577

ca578-colusa-and-korusi.q: How did Colusa get its name?
alts: Where did that name come from?
ca578-colusa-and-korusi.a: The name comes from Korusi, a Patwin village that stood on the west bank of the Sacramento River, right where the city is today.
ca578-colusa-and-korusi.quote: Its name comes from Korusi, a Patwin village that stood on the west bank of the river, where the city is today.

alts: Who started it and when was that?
ca578-colusa-and-korusi.a: Charles Semple bought Rancho Colus in 1850 and founded the town. The land had first been given to John Bidwell as a Mexican land grant.
ca578-colusa-and-korusi.quote: In 1850 Charles Semple bought Rancho Colus, a Mexican land grant first given to John Bidwell, and founded the town

alts: Did it have a different name before?
Did Colusa have another name, Mom?
ca578-colusa-and-korusi.a: No. Charles Semple first called the spot Salmon Bend, and the legislature settled on the spelling Colusa in 1854. The 1850 county law even spelled it Colusi.
ca578-colusa-and-korusi.quote: first calling the spot Salmon Bend. The legislature settled on the spelling Colusa in 1854.

ca578-colusa-and-korusi.q: What is there to see in Colusa?
alts: What can we see in that town?
Is there anything cool to look at there?
ca578-colusa-and-korusi.a: There's a historic Chinatown, a Carnegie library from 1905, and a courthouse built in 1861 that is a California Historical Landmark.
ca578-colusa-and-korusi.quote: Colusa still has a historic Chinatown, a Carnegie library from 1905, and a courthouse built in 1861 that is a California Historical Landmark.

ca578-colusa-and-korusi.q: What are the Mile Houses near Colusa?
alts: What were those rest stops about?
What's a Seventeen Mile House, Mom?
ca578-colusa-and-korusi.a: They were rest stops for travelers that grew up at set road distances from town, running from Five Mile House out to Seventeen Mile House.
ca578-colusa-and-korusi.quote: Rest stops for travelers grew up at set road distances from town, from Five Mile House to Seventeen Mile House.

ca582-rice-country.q: Why are these fields covered in water in Rice country?
alts: Why is it all flooded out here?
Why are the fields full of water, are they broken?
ca582-rice-country.a: Many of the flat fields around here are rice paddies. Many growers also flood their fields in winter and let the leftover straw break down.
ca582-rice-country.quote: Many now flood their fields in winter instead and let the straw break down.

ca582-rice-country.q: What are all those birds doing in Rice country?
alts: What are those birds doing in the fields?
Why are there so many birds in the water?
ca582-rice-country.a: The flooded rice fields feed and shelter about 7 million ducks and geese, according to the California Rice Commission. More than 200 kinds of wildlife use them, including sandhill cranes.
ca582-rice-country.quote: the California Rice Commission says they feed and shelter about 7 million ducks and geese. More than 200 kinds of wildlife use them, including sandhill cranes.

ca582-rice-country.q: How much rice does Colusa County grow around Rice country?
alts: How much rice do they grow here?
How big are all these rice fields?
Is that a lot of rice?
ca582-rice-country.a: In 2024, Colusa County harvested rice from about 118,000 acres, roughly 185 square miles. That made a crop of more than half a million tons.
ca582-rice-country.quote: In 2024, Colusa County harvested rice from about 118,000 acres, roughly 185 square miles, for a crop of more than half a million tons.

ca582-rice-country.q: Is rice a big crop in Rice country?
alts: Do they make a lot of money from rice?
Is rice the main thing they grow?
ca582-rice-country.a: Yes. Rice was Colusa County's most valuable crop in 2023, and in 2024 it was second only to almonds.
ca582-rice-country.quote: Rice was the county's most valuable crop in 2023, and second only to almonds in 2024.

ca582-rice-country.q: What do farmers do with the leftover rice straw in Rice country?
alts: What happens to the straw after harvest?
What do they do with the leftovers?
ca582-rice-country.a: Growers once burned the straw, but a state law since 1992 has limited burning. Many now flood their fields in winter and let the straw break down.
ca582-rice-country.quote: Growers once burned the leftover straw after harvest, but since 1992 a state law has limited burning.

alts: What is it going to be?
Is it a real lake yet, or what?
ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.a: It's a planned new lake in a valley in the hills west of Maxwell. Instead of damming a river, it would be filled with water taken from the Sacramento River during high flows.
ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.quote: In a valley in the hills west of Maxwell, a new lake is planned: Sites Reservoir.

ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.q: How does Sites Reservoir get its water?
alts: Where would it get its water from?
How do they fill a lake without a river?
ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.a: Water would be taken from the Sacramento River during high flows, carried by canals and pumped up into the valley. It would arrive through the Tehama-Colusa Canal and another canal from Hamilton City.
ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.quote: Instead of damming a river, it would be filled with water taken from the Sacramento River during high flows, carried by canals and pumped up into the valley.

ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.q: How big would Sites Reservoir be?
alts: Is it gonna be a huge lake?
ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.a: It would stretch 13 miles north to south and 4 miles across, about 260 feet deep at its lowest point. That would make it the eighth largest reservoir in California.
ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.quote: It would stretch 13 miles north to south and 4 miles across, about 260 feet deep at its lowest point, making it the eighth largest reservoir in California.

ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.q: How much water would Sites Reservoir hold?
alts: How much water can it hold?
How many people could it give water to?
Is it a lot of water?
ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.a: Full, it would hold up to 1.5 million acre-feet. That's enough to serve 7.5 million people for a year.
ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.quote: Full, it would hold up to 1.5 million acre-feet, enough to serve 7.5 million people for a year.

ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.q: When was Sites Reservoir first proposed, and when will it be built?
alts: How long have they wanted to build it?
ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.a: It was first proposed in the 1950s. Construction is planned to begin in 2027, with operations by 2034.
ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.quote: The reservoir was first proposed in the 1950s

ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.q: What are the concerns about Sites Reservoir?
alts: Is there a downside to it?
ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.a: Diversions could at times take 60 percent of the river's flow, which could harm salmon and other fish.
ca586-sites-reservoir-a-lake-to-come.quote: Diversions could at times take 60 percent of the river's flow, which could harm salmon and other fish.

ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.q: Why did they build Swift's Stone Corral out of stone?
alts: Why did they build it out of stone?
Why isn't the corral made of wood, mom?
ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.a: There was no timber anywhere around, so Swift and his partner Frank Sears built the corral from the flat stones scattered over the land.
ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.quote: there was no timber anywhere around, so they built one out of the flat stones scattered over the land

ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.q: How old is Swift's Stone Corral?
alts: Is that corral really, really old?
ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.a: It was built in 1850 by rancher Granville Swift and his partner Frank Sears, who needed a corral for their ranch.
ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.quote: In 1850, rancher Granville Swift and his partner Frank Sears needed a corral

alts: Who was he, the guy who built it?
Who was that Swift guy, dad?
ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.a: He was a Kentuckian whose great-uncle was Daniel Boone. He came to California at 19, and in 1846 he helped capture Sonoma in the Bear Flag Revolt.
ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.quote: Swift, a Kentuckian whose great-uncle was Daniel Boone, came to California at 19.

ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.q: Is Swift's Stone Corral a historic landmark?
alts: Is the old corral a big deal, dad?
ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.a: Yes. It has been a state historical landmark since 1936.
ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.quote: Swift's Stone Corral, a state historical landmark since 1936

ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.q: What exit is Swift's Stone Corral?
alts: What exit do we take for it?
Which exit is that one, dad?
ca588-swift-s-stone-corral.a: Swift's Stone Corral is at exit 588.

ca588-delevan-refuge.a: It's nearly 5,800 acres of managed marsh and upland, and more than 4,500 of those acres are intensively managed wetlands.
ca588-delevan-refuge.quote: nearly 5,800 acres of managed marsh and upland

ca588-delevan-refuge.q: What can we see at Delevan refuge?
alts: What is there to see at it?
ca588-delevan-refuge.a: You can watch wildlife from a simple roadside overlook on the Maxwell-Colusa Highway.
ca588-delevan-refuge.quote: Visitors can watch wildlife from a simple roadside overlook on the Maxwell-Colusa Highway.

ca588-delevan-refuge.q: What animals live at Delevan refuge?
alts: Are there any cool animals there?
ca588-delevan-refuge.a: Beavers, muskrats and black-tailed deer live there year round, and peregrine falcons and bald eagles spend the winter. It also shelters the rare giant garter snake.
ca588-delevan-refuge.quote: Peregrine falcons and bald eagles spend the winter, and beavers, muskrats and black-tailed deer live there year round.

ca588-delevan-refuge.q: Why are refuges like Delevan important?
alts: Why do the birds need that place?
ca588-delevan-refuge.a: About 95 percent of the Central Valley's wetlands have been lost over the last 100 years, so waterfowl depend more and more on refuges like this one.
ca588-delevan-refuge.quote: Over the last 100 years about 95 percent of the Central Valley's wetlands have been lost, so waterfowl depend more and more on refuges like this one.

alts: Which exit do we take for it?

ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.q: Why was Rancho Larkin's Children named that?
alts: Why did kids get a ranch?
ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.a: The land grant was made out to children. Thomas Larkin couldn't get land himself, so in 1844 he had three of his children naturalized, and they received the grant.
ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.quote: In 1844 he had three of his children naturalized, and two days later the children received a grant of about 44,000 acres.

ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.q: Why couldn't Thomas Larkin get the land himself?
alts: Why couldn't he just own it?
Why did the kids need to get it?
ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.a: Larkin was the United States consul in Monterey and wouldn't become a Mexican citizen, so he couldn't receive land himself. His naturalized children could.
ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.quote: Thomas Larkin, the United States consul in Monterey, would not become a Mexican citizen, so he could not get land himself.

ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.q: How big was Rancho Larkin's Children?
alts: How much land did the kids get?
Was it a lot of land?
ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.a: The grant covered about 44,000 acres, and it was given to the children two days after they were naturalized in 1844.
ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.quote: two days later the children received a grant of about 44,000 acres.

ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.q: Who ran Rancho Larkin's Children for Larkin?
alts: Who ran the ranch for the kids?
ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.a: Larkin sent a Missourian named John S. Williams to run the rancho. In 1847 Williams built an adobe near an abandoned Patwin village called Chah'de'-he.
ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.quote: Larkin sent a Missourian named John S. Williams to run the rancho, and in 1847 Williams built an adobe

ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.q: How did the town of Princeton get started?
alts: Where did that town come from?
ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.a: Princeton began in 1851 as a roadhouse called the Sixteen-Mile House. Later it shipped grain down the river by boat.
ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.quote: The town itself began in 1851 as a roadhouse, the Sixteen-Mile House, and later shipped grain down the river by boat.

ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.q: Was there a ferry at Princeton?
ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.a: Yes. For nearly 130 years a ferry carried people across the river at Princeton, until it shut down for good in the late 1990s.
ca595-rancho-larkin-s-children.quote: For nearly 130 years a ferry carried people across the river at Princeton, until it shut down for good in the late 1990s.

ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.q: Who built the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge wetlands?
alts: Did people make this marsh, Mom?
ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.a: The Civilian Conservation Corps built the first wetlands here between 1937 and 1942, on dry, alkaline land.
ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.quote: The Civilian Conservation Corps built the first wetlands here between 1937 and 1942, on dry, alkaline land between Willows and Maxwell.

ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.q: Why was the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge created?
alts: Why did they make this place for birds?
ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.a: Migrating birds kept eating rice in farm fields, so the refuges were created partly to settle that conflict between the birds of the Pacific Flyway and farmers.
ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.quote: Migrating birds kept coming anyway and ate rice in the fields, so the refuges were created partly to settle that conflict

ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.q: What birds can you see at the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge?
ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.a: More than 250 kinds of birds use the refuge, from snow geese and white pelicans to bald eagles.
ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.quote: More than 250 kinds of birds use the refuge, from snow geese and white pelicans to bald eagles.

ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.q: When is the best time to visit the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge?
alts: When should we come to see it?
When are the most geese here, Dad?
ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.a: Fall is the big show. Waterfowl counts average about 1.5 million in October and 1.8 million in November, when geese arrive by the thousands.
ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.quote: Fall is the big show. On the refuge's own calendar, waterfowl counts average about 1.5 million in October and 1.8 million in November

ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.q: What is there to do at the Sacramento National Wildlife Refuge?
alts: Is there anything to do there, Mom?
ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.a: The refuge has a visitor center and a 6-mile auto tour. At dusk in November, flocks still fly off to feed in the rice.
ca595-sacramento-national-wildlife-refug.quote: The refuge has a visitor center and a 6-mile auto tour.

ca601-mendocino-national-forest.q: How big is Mendocino National Forest?
alts: Is that forest really huge, like how many acres?
ca601-mendocino-national-forest.a: It covers about 913,000 acres across six counties. It's also the only national forest in California without a major paved road entering it.
ca601-mendocino-national-forest.quote: The forest covers about 913,000 acres in six counties, and it is the only national forest in California without a major paved road entering it.

ca601-mendocino-national-forest.q: When did Mendocino National Forest become a forest?
alts: Who made that forest, and when?
ca601-mendocino-national-forest.a: President Theodore Roosevelt set the land aside in 1907 as the Stony Creek Forest Reserve.
ca601-mendocino-national-forest.quote: President Theodore Roosevelt set the land aside in 1907 as the Stony Creek Forest Reserve.

ca601-mendocino-national-forest.q: Why is it called Mendocino National Forest?
alts: Why did it get that name?
Why'd they change the name of that forest?
ca601-mendocino-national-forest.a: President Hoover renamed it Mendocino in 1932 to avoid confusion with the name of the state. It had been called the California National Forest since 1908.
ca601-mendocino-national-forest.quote: It was renamed the California National Forest in 1908, and in 1932 President Herbert Hoover renamed it again, to Mendocino, to avoid confusion with the name of the state.

ca601-mendocino-national-forest.q: What animals live in Mendocino National Forest?
alts: Are there any big animals in that forest?
ca601-mendocino-national-forest.a: Tule elk live there. They were once hunted nearly to extinction, and were brought back to the Lake Pillsbury basin in the late 1970s.
ca601-mendocino-national-forest.quote: Tule elk, once hunted nearly to extinction, were brought back to the Lake Pillsbury basin in the late 1970s.

ca601-mendocino-national-forest.q: What happened in Mendocino National Forest in 2020?
alts: Was there a big fire in it?
What was the huge fire there?
ca601-mendocino-national-forest.a: The August Complex burned mostly through this forest. It began as 38 separate lightning fires and grew to more than a million acres, the largest wildfire in California history.
ca601-mendocino-national-forest.quote: In 2020 the August Complex, which began as 38 separate lightning fires, burned mostly through this forest and grew to more than a million acres

alts: Why's the town named after trees, Dad?
ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.a: It's named for a shady watering place ringed by willow trees, where cattle drivers traveling through the valley stopped to rest.
ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.quote: Willows takes its name from a shady watering place ringed by willow trees, where cattle drivers traveling through the valley stopped to rest.

ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.q: When did Willows become a town?
alts: When did it become a town?
ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.a: Willows incorporated in 1886. Its post office had opened earlier, in 1862, under the singular name Willow.

ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.q: Did Willows ever have big fires?
alts: Did the town catch on fire, Dad?
ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.a: Yes. Fires swept through downtown twice in the 1880s, and each time the town rebuilt. In 1887 it replaced its volunteer bucket brigade with a formal fire department.
ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.quote: Fires swept through downtown twice in the 1880s, and each time the town rebuilt, finally replacing its volunteer bucket brigade with a formal fire department in 1887.

ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.q: What's the Glenn County Courthouse in Willows like?
alts: Is there a cool old building there, Mom?
ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.a: It was finished in 1894. Its central dome was taken off for safety reasons in 1951. Willows has been the Glenn County seat since 1891.
ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.quote: The Glenn County Courthouse was finished in 1894, and its central dome came off for safety reasons in 1951.

ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.q: What's the history of the Willows airport?
alts: What did it do in the war?
Did planes fly there a long time ago, Dad?
ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.a: It opened in 1928 as a training ground for early pilots. In World War II it hosted practice missions linked to the Doolittle Raiders.
ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.quote: The airport opened in 1928 as a training ground for early pilots, and in World War II it hosted practice missions linked to the Doolittle Raiders.

ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.q: Is Willows a good place to stop on I-5?
alts: Is it a good rest stop, Mom?
ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.a: It's a handy stopover between Sacramento and Redding. That's been true since the state finished building Interstate 5 in 1979.
ca603-willows-the-cattle-stop.quote: In 1979 the state finished building Interstate 5, making Willows a handy stopover between Sacramento and Redding.

ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.q: Who was Hugh Glenn, the Wheat King?
alts: Who was that Wheat King guy?
ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.a: Hugh Glenn was a doctor who came west in the Gold Rush and became California's Wheat King. Glenn County is named for him.
ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.quote: Glenn County is named for Hugh Glenn, a doctor who came west in the Gold Rush and became California's Wheat King.

ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.q: How big was Hugh Glenn's wheat ranch?
alts: How much land did the Wheat King have?
ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.a: His land along the Sacramento River grew to 55,000 acres. At harvest he hired 150 men to bring in the crop.
ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.quote: His land along the Sacramento River grew to 55,000 acres. At harvest he hired 150 men

ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.q: How much wheat did Hugh Glenn harvest in one day?
alts: How much did it produce in a day?
How much wheat is that, in one day?
What was his big harvest record?
ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.a: On August 8, 1879, his crews brought in 5,779 bushels of wheat in a single day.
ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.quote: on August 8, 1879, his crews brought in 5,779 bushels of wheat in a single day.

ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.q: How did Hugh Glenn get started in California?
alts: How did he travel out west?
What did he do before wheat?
ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.a: He trained as a doctor in St. Louis and left Missouri in 1849 with an ox team and a wagon. He became a cattle rancher, then bought Rancho Jacinto land and kept adding to it.
ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.quote: Glenn trained as a physician in St. Louis and left Missouri for California in 1849 with an ox team and a wagon.

ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.q: What happened to Hugh Glenn in the end?
alts: What happened to the Wheat King?
ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.a: On February 17, 1883, Glenn was shot from ambush on his ranch by his bookkeeper, Huram Miller. It came several days after Glenn had struck him for his drunken insults.
ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.quote: On February 17, 1883, Glenn was shot from ambush on his ranch by his bookkeeper, Huram Miller

ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.q: Did Hugh Glenn ever run for governor?
alts: Did the Wheat King win an election?
ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.a: Yes, he ran for governor in 1879, but he lost.
ca607-hugh-glenn-the-wheat-king.quote: In 1879 he ran for governor and lost.

alts: Why did it get that name?
Why's this town got a weird French name, mom?
ca610-artois-once-germantown.a: It was named after the battles fought in the Artois region of France during World War One. Before 1918 the town was called Germantown.
ca610-artois-once-germantown.quote: on May 21, 1918, Germantown became Artois, after the battles fought in that region of France.

alts: What was it called before that?
What was this town's old name, dad?
ca610-artois-once-germantown.a: It was called Germantown until 1918. The Germantown post office had opened back in 1877.

ca610-artois-once-germantown.q: Why did Germantown change its name to Artois?
alts: How come they got rid of the old name?
ca610-artois-once-germantown.a: Local belief says a World War One troop train stopped here for water, and the soldiers took offense at the German name. Petitions to change the post office name then succeeded.
ca610-artois-once-germantown.quote: a troop train stopped here for water and the soldiers took offense at the German name.

ca610-artois-once-germantown.q: Did anything dramatic ever happen in Artois?
alts: Was there ever a tornado there?
ca610-artois-once-germantown.a: Yes. On June 1, 2011, a tornado touched down east of Artois, uprooting hundreds of almond trees and damaging farm equipment.
ca610-artois-once-germantown.quote: On June 1, 2011, a tornado touched down east of Artois, uprooting hundreds of almond trees and damaging farm equipment.

ca610-artois-once-germantown.q: How many people live in Artois today?
alts: Do lots of people live there?
ca610-artois-once-germantown.a: About 300 people live there today, so it's a very small town.

ca614-prune-orchards.q: How much of the world's prunes come from California?
alts: Is that a lot of the country's prunes?
Does everybody get their prunes from here?
ca614-prune-orchards.a: California grows more than 90 percent of the nation's prunes and about 40 percent of the world's.
ca614-prune-orchards.quote: California grows more than 90 percent of the nation's prunes and about 40 percent of the world's.

ca614-prune-orchards.q: How do they harvest the prune plums?
alts: How do they get the fruit off the trees?
How do they pick all those plums, Mom?
ca614-prune-orchards.a: Machines grab each trunk and shake the plums onto catching frames. Harvest runs from mid-August into early September and usually takes about 30 days.
ca614-prune-orchards.quote: At harvest, machines grab each trunk and shake the plums onto catching frames

ca614-prune-orchards.q: How does a plum turn into a prune?
alts: How do they dry the fruit?
How do plums become prunes, Dad?
ca614-prune-orchards.a: The fruit's high sugar lets it dry without fermenting around the pit. In the dryers, three pounds of fresh fruit become one pound of prunes.
ca614-prune-orchards.quote: The fruit's high sugar lets it dry without fermenting around the pit.

ca614-prune-orchards.q: Did anyone really try using monkeys to pick prunes?
alts: Is it true they used monkeys on it?
ca614-prune-orchards.a: Yes. In 1905, during a labor shortage, one grower tried 500 monkeys to pick the fruit. They picked well, but they ate the crop.
ca614-prune-orchards.quote: During a labor shortage in 1905, one grower even tried using 500 monkeys to pick the fruit. They picked well, but they ate the crop.

ca619-orland-queen-bee-capital.q: Why is Orland called the Queen Bee Capital?
alts: Why does it call itself that?
Why is this town about bees, Dad?
ca619-orland-queen-bee-capital.a: Orland's city council adopted the title in 2017 because the town's locally owned commercial apiaries produce so many queen bees.
ca619-orland-queen-bee-capital.quote: In 2017 the city council adopted the title because of how many queen bees the town's locally owned commercial apiaries produce.

ca619-orland-queen-bee-capital.q: Is there a bee museum in Orland?
alts: Is there anything to see about bees there?
Can we go see real bees there?
ca619-orland-queen-bee-capital.a: Yes, Orland has the Honeybee Discovery Center, a museum all about bees.
ca619-orland-queen-bee-capital.quote: Orland even has a museum about bees, the Honeybee Discovery Center, and it holds a Queen Bee Festival every June.

ca619-orland-queen-bee-capital.q: How many US queen bees are raised near Orland?
alts: How many of the country's queens come from there?
Do most queen bees come from here?
Where do queen bees come from?
ca619-orland-queen-bee-capital.a: The Honeybee Discovery Center says about 80 percent of the queen bees used in the United States are raised in Butte, Glenn, Shasta and Tehama counties.
ca619-orland-queen-bee-capital.quote: about 80 percent of the queen bees used in the United States are raised in Butte, Glenn, Shasta and Tehama counties

ca619-orland-queen-bee-capital.q: How many bees live in a hive with a queen?
alts: How big is one of those hives?
How many bees are in a hive, Mom?
ca619-orland-queen-bee-capital.a: A hive can hold 60,000 to 80,000 bees, and the queen is usually the mother of most of them.
ca619-orland-queen-bee-capital.quote: a queen is usually the mother of most of the bees in her hive, which can hold 60,000 to 80,000 of them

ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.q: What was Will Green's water notice?
alts: What was that notice he posted?
What did that guy put on the tree?
ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.a: On December 18, 1883, Will S. Green posted a notice on an oak tree on the river's west bank. He claimed 500,000 miner's inches of river water to irrigate the west side of the valley.
ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.quote: on December 18, 1883, Will S. Green posted a notice on an oak tree on the river's west bank, claiming 500,000 miner's inches of river water

ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.q: Why did Will Green claim the river water?
alts: Why did he want that water?
Why did he want all the river water, anyway?
ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.a: He wanted it to irrigate the west side of the valley. His notice claimed 500,000 miner's inches of river water for that purpose.
ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.quote: claiming 500,000 miner's inches of river water to irrigate the west side of the valley

alts: Who was the man who posted it, anyway?
ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.a: He packed a lot into one life. He was a ferryboat captain, mail carrier, surveyor, newspaper editor, writer and legislator, and later U.S. Surveyor General and California's State Treasurer.
ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.quote: He was a ferryboat captain, mail carrier, surveyor, newspaper editor, writer and legislator, and later served as U.S. Surveyor General and as California's State Treasurer.

ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.q: Is Will Green's water notice a historical landmark?
alts: Is that spot officially a big deal?
ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.a: Yes. The spot is now a state historical landmark.
ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.quote: The spot is now a state historical landmark.

ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.q: What is Hamilton City known for?
alts: What's the town near it about?
What did the town start with?
ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.a: Hamilton City began in 1905 with a big sugar beet plant. The plant closed in 2006, but its tall silos can still be seen from all over town.
ca619-will-green-s-water-notice.quote: Hamilton City itself began in 1905 with a big sugar beet plant

ca621-stony-creek.q: Why is it called Stony Creek?
alts: Why is that creek called that?
How did the creek get its name, Mom?
ca621-stony-creek.a: It was named for the loads of rock and sediment it once washed down from the mountains in floods.
ca621-stony-creek.quote: The creek was named for the loads of rock and sediment it once washed down from the mountains in floods

ca621-stony-creek.q: Did Stony Creek ever have another name?
alts: Was it called something else before?
Did the creek used to have a different name?
ca621-stony-creek.a: Yes, it was once called the Capay River.
ca621-stony-creek.quote: and it was once called the Capay River

alts: Is that a big creek, or a little one?
ca621-stony-creek.a: It runs 73.5 miles, and it's the second largest stream feeding the Sacramento from the west, after Cottonwood Creek.
ca621-stony-creek.quote: Stony Creek runs 73.5 miles and is the second largest stream feeding the Sacramento from the west, after Cottonwood Creek.

ca621-stony-creek.q: What did Peter Lassen do at Stony Creek?
alts: Did somebody take rocks from the creek?
ca621-stony-creek.a: In 1845 his party quarried grindstones on one of its tributaries, now called Grindstone Creek. They took them down the river to sell at Sutter's Fort and San Francisco.
ca621-stony-creek.quote: In 1845 a party led by Peter Lassen quarried grindstones on one of its tributaries, now called Grindstone Creek

ca621-stony-creek.q: What is hungry water at Stony Creek?
alts: Why is the creek eating its own banks?
Why does the creek eat the ground, Dad?
ca621-stony-creek.a: Black Butte Dam, built in 1963, traps most of the sediment. Without fresh gravel from upstream, the creek below the dam eats away at its own banks, an effect called hungry water.
ca621-stony-creek.quote: Without fresh gravel from upstream, the creek below the dam now eats away at its own banks, an effect called hungry water.

ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.a: Rolling Hills Casino belongs to the Paskenta Band of Nomlaki Indians, the Hill Nomlaki people of this part of the valley.
ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.quote: Rolling Hills Casino, beside the freeway, belongs to the Paskenta Band of Nomlaki Indians, the Hill Nomlaki people of this part of the valley.

ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.q: What happened to the Paskenta Band in 1959?
alts: Why did the tribe lose its land?
ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.a: In 1959 the federal government terminated the tribe's rancheria, and its land was sold. The Paskenta Band kept its identity and culture, though.
ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.quote: In 1959 the federal government terminated the tribe's rancheria and its land was sold. The Paskenta Band kept its identity and culture

ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.q: When did the Paskenta Band get its tribal status back?
alts: When did they get it back?
Did the tribe ever win back its status?
ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.a: The Paskenta Band won back full tribal status in 1994, after losing its rancheria in 1959.
ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.quote: The Paskenta Band kept its identity and culture and won back full tribal status in 1994.

ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.q: What was the Nomi Lackee Indian Reservation?
alts: What was that old military place?
ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.a: Set up in 1854 in the foothills west of here, it was a military post that controlled 300 to 2,500 Native people. In 1866 they were moved to Round Valley.
ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.quote: In 1854 the government set up the Nomi Lackee Indian Reservation in the foothills west of here, a military post that controlled 300 to 2,500 Native people.

ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.q: When did Rolling Hills Casino open?
alts: How long has the casino been here?
When did they build the casino?
ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.a: The tribe signed a gaming compact with the state in 1999 and opened the casino in 2002.
ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.quote: the tribe signed a gaming compact with the state in 1999 and opened the casino in 2002.

ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.q: How big is the Paskenta Band today?
alts: How many people are in the tribe?
How much land do they have?
ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.a: The tribe has about 240 members and is headquartered in Corning. Its rancheria covers about 2,000 acres.
ca628-paskenta-band-of-nomlaki.quote: Today the tribe has about 240 members, is headquartered in Corning, and has a rancheria of about 2,000 acres.

ca628-walnut-orchards.q: What kind of walnuts grow in the Walnut orchards?
alts: What kind of walnuts are those?
ca628-walnut-orchards.a: Many of the orchards in Tehama County are English walnuts.
ca628-walnut-orchards.quote: Many of the orchards in Tehama County are English walnuts.

ca628-walnut-orchards.q: How big is the walnut business in Tehama County?
alts: How much are those orchards worth?
How many walnut trees are there?
Is walnut a big crop here?
ca628-walnut-orchards.a: In 2024 the county had about 31,000 acres of bearing walnut trees, worth about 95 million dollars. That makes walnuts its second most valuable crop after almonds.
ca628-walnut-orchards.quote: In 2024 the county had about 31,000 acres of bearing walnut trees, worth about 95 million dollars, its second most valuable crop after almonds.

ca628-walnut-orchards.q: Why did walnut orchards move north to central California?
alts: Why aren't walnuts grown in Los Angeles anymore?
ca628-walnut-orchards.a: Walnuts were first grown mainly in Southern California. By 1910 oranges and lemons were crowding them out of Los Angeles and Orange counties, so orchards spread into central California.
ca628-walnut-orchards.quote: Walnuts were first grown mainly in Southern California, but by 1910 oranges and lemons were crowding them out of Los Angeles and Orange counties

alts: Who's that guy the mountain is named after?
ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.a: Peter Lassen was a Danish blacksmith whose name is on Lassen Peak. He owned Rancho Bosquejo, a land grant near Vina.
ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.quote: Rancho Bosquejo, the land grant of Peter Lassen, the Danish blacksmith whose name is on Lassen Peak.

alts: Why is there no town now?
ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.a: Lassen laid out Benton City on Deer Creek in 1845. Its settlers soon left for the gold fields.
ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.quote: in 1845 he laid out a town on Deer Creek called Benton City, but its settlers soon left for the gold fields.

ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.q: What did Leland Stanford build at Vina?
alts: Why did Stanford have vines here?
ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.a: In 1881 Stanford built the Vina Ranch, with what was then the largest vineyard and winery in the world.
ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.quote: In 1881 Leland Stanford bought the land and built the Vina Ranch, with what was then the largest vineyard and winery in the world.

ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.q: Why did Stanford's ranch make brandy instead of wine?
alts: Why did it switch to that?
ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.a: The vines made poor wine, so brandy became the ranch's main product.
ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.quote: The vines made poor wine, so brandy became the main product.

ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.q: What is on the old Vina Ranch land today?
alts: Can we see anything from back then?
ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.a: A Trappist monastery, the Abbey of New Clairvaux, occupies part of the old homestead. The rest was sold off piece by piece by Stanford University.
ca630-lassen-s-rancho-and-stanford-s-vin.quote: Today a Trappist monastery, the Abbey of New Clairvaux, occupies part of the old homestead.

alts: When did this town start, mom?
ca631-corning-olive-town.a: Corning began in 1882, when the railroad was extended to this point.
ca631-corning-olive-town.quote: Corning began in 1882, when the railroad was extended to this point, and it was named for John Corning, a railroad official.

alts: Why do they call it the olive town?
ca631-corning-olive-town.a: Olives. Growing and preparing table olives is its biggest local industry, and it's home to Bell-Carter Foods, maker of Lindsay Olives and the largest table olive processor in the United States.
ca631-corning-olive-town.quote: Corning is home to Bell-Carter Foods, maker of Lindsay Olives and the largest table olive processor in the United States.

ca631-corning-olive-town.q: What is the Corning Olive Festival?
alts: Is there a party for olives?
ca631-corning-olive-town.a: It's held the second Saturday in October. It began in 1946 as a fundraiser for the local Catholic church and is called the longest-running olive festival in the country.
ca631-corning-olive-town.quote: The Corning Olive Festival, held on the second Saturday in October, began in 1946 as a fundraiser for the local Catholic church

ca631-corning-olive-town.q: How big is the olive business around Corning?
alts: How many olive trees are there?
ca631-corning-olive-town.a: In 2024, Tehama County's table olives were worth about 25.6 million dollars, from about 3,900 acres of bearing trees. Oil olives covered about 3,800 acres more.
ca631-corning-olive-town.quote: In 2024, Tehama County's table olives were worth about 25.6 million dollars, from about 3,900 acres of bearing trees

ca633-helmick-rest-area.q: Who is the Helmick rest area named after?
ca633-helmick-rest-area.a: It's named for Lieutenant John C. Helmick, the California Highway Patrol's Red Bluff Area commander.
ca633-helmick-rest-area.quote: These rest areas are named for Lieutenant John C. Helmick, the California Highway Patrol's Red Bluff Area commander.

alts: How did the guy it's named after die?
ca633-helmick-rest-area.a: On February 27, 1989, he was driving to speak at a Rotary Club luncheon in Oroville when his car crashed into a Caltrans truck parked on the shoulder of Highway 99. He was 43.
ca633-helmick-rest-area.quote: On February 27, 1989, while driving to speak at a Rotary Club luncheon in Oroville, he was killed when his car crashed into a Caltrans truck parked on the shoulder of Highway 99.

ca633-helmick-rest-area.q: How long was Helmick with the Highway Patrol?
alts: How long did he do that job?
How long was he a cop?
ca633-helmick-rest-area.a: Helmick was a 20-year veteran of the Highway Patrol and had led the Red Bluff Area for three years.
ca633-helmick-rest-area.quote: Helmick was a 20-year veteran of the Highway Patrol and had led the Red Bluff Area for three years.

ca633-helmick-rest-area.q: How old is the Helmick rest area?
alts: How long has it been here?
ca633-helmick-rest-area.a: The rest areas were first built in 1965. Caltrans completely rebuilt them starting in 2015, and they reopened on May 8, 2017.
ca633-helmick-rest-area.quote: The rest areas here were first built in 1965. Caltrans completely rebuilt them starting in 2015, and they reopened on May 8, 2017

ca633-helmick-rest-area.q: What's new at the rebuilt Helmick rest area?
alts: What did they change about it?
ca633-helmick-rest-area.a: The rebuild added LED lights, low-flow plumbing, shade structures and drought-tolerant plants. The builders also added sundials around each flagpole as a finishing touch.
ca633-helmick-rest-area.quote: with LED lights, low-flow plumbing, shade structures and drought-tolerant plants. As a finishing touch, the builders added sundials around each flagpole.

ca633-helmick-rest-area.q: What exit is the Helmick rest area?
alts: Which exit do we take for it?
ca633-helmick-rest-area.a: It's at exit 633, right at the freeway.

ca633-thomes-creek.q: Who was Thomes Creek named after?
ca633-thomes-creek.a: It's named for Robert Thomes, a pioneer who arrived in the 1840s.
ca633-thomes-creek.quote: named for Robert Thomes, a pioneer who arrived in the 1840s

ca633-thomes-creek.q: Why is Thomes Creek spelled so many different ways?
alts: Why do they spell it wrong?
Why does the name have so many spellings, Dad?
ca633-thomes-creek.a: Robert Thomes's name was misspelled so often that official records list the creek as Thomas Creek, Thoms Creek and Toms Creek.
ca633-thomes-creek.quote: His name has been misspelled so often that official records list the creek as Thomas Creek, Thoms Creek and Toms Creek.

ca633-thomes-creek.q: Why is Thomes Creek just rocks and no water?
alts: Why is it dry in summer?
Where did the water go, Mom?
ca633-thomes-creek.a: It's a highly seasonal stream. In summer its wide bed of gravel and boulders is often dry.
ca633-thomes-creek.quote: It is a highly seasonal stream. In summer its wide bed of gravel and boulders is often dry

ca633-thomes-creek.q: How big does Thomes Creek get in a flood?
alts: How much water can it carry?
Does it ever get really huge, Dad?
ca633-thomes-creek.a: On December 22, 1964, during that year's Christmas flood, it carried 37,800 cubic feet of water per second.
ca633-thomes-creek.quote: on December 22, 1964, during that year's Christmas flood, it carried 37,800 cubic feet of water per second

ca633-thomes-creek.q: Where does Thomes Creek start and where does it go?
alts: Where does the creek begin, Mom?
ca633-thomes-creek.a: It runs about 62 miles from the Coast Range to the Sacramento River. It begins at a small pond called Kingsley Lake in the Mendocino National Forest.
ca633-thomes-creek.quote: The creek runs about 62 miles from the Coast Range to the Sacramento River, with no permanent dams.

ca633-thomes-creek.q: What fish live in Thomes Creek?
alts: Are there salmon in the creek, Dad?
ca633-thomes-creek.a: Steelhead trout and spring-run Chinook salmon still use the creek.
ca633-thomes-creek.quote: Steelhead trout and spring-run Chinook salmon still use it.

alts: Where did it get that name?
ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.a: Tehama is most often said to come from a Wintun word for high water, though other meanings have been suggested.
ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.quote: The name Tehama is most often said to come from a Wintun word for high water, though other meanings have been suggested.

ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.q: Why do the houses in Tehama have such tall stairs?
alts: Why does it have those tall stairways?
Why are the houses up so high, Dad?
ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.a: Because the town floods easily, its houses must sit above flood level, so most have tall stairways to the front door.
ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.quote: Because the town floods easily, its houses must sit above flood level, so most have tall stairways to the front door.

ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.q: Was Tehama really the county seat?
alts: How long was it the county seat?
Why isn't it the county seat anymore?
ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.a: Yes, when Tehama County formed in 1856. But a county-wide election moved the seat to Red Bluff just the next year.
ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.quote: When Tehama County was formed in 1856, Tehama was its county seat, but a county-wide election moved the seat to Red Bluff the very next year.

ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.a: Robert Thomes laid out the town in 1850. He had received the Mexican land grant Rancho Saucos in 1844.
ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.quote: Robert Thomes, who received the Mexican land grant Rancho Saucos in 1844, laid out the town in 1850.

ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.q: Who lived where Tehama is before the town?
alts: Did anyone live there before it was a town?
ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.a: A Nomlaki village of the Wintun people once stood where the town is.
ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.quote: A Nomlaki village of the Wintun people once stood where the town is.

ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.q: How many people live in Tehama?
ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.a: Tehama is a little city, home to 435 people in 2020. Its population peaked around 2,000 in the 1890s.
ca636-tehama-the-first-county-seat.quote: the little city of Tehama, home to 435 people in 2020.

ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.q: How old is Gerber, the railroad stop?
alts: Was this place around a long time ago, or is it new?
ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.a: Gerber was platted in 1910, so the town goes back over a century. The railroad made it a division point starting in 1916.
ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.quote: Gerber was platted in 1910 and named for the Gerber family, who owned the town site.

ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.q: Why is the town called Gerber?
alts: Who's Gerber? Is it a person?
ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.a: It was named for the Gerber family, who owned the town site when it was platted in 1910.
ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.quote: Gerber was platted in 1910 and named for the Gerber family, who owned the town site.

ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.q: What did the railroad do in Gerber?
alts: What happened there on the railroad?
Did trains do stuff there, like stop for fuel?
Why was it a train town?
ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.a: From 1916 to 1965 it was a Southern Pacific division point. Steam locomotives took on fuel, got repairs and changed crews there.
ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.quote: From 1916 to 1965 it was a division point on the Southern Pacific Railroad, where steam locomotives took on fuel, got repairs and changed crews.

ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.q: What else was in Gerber besides the railroad?
ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.a: The town had livestock yards and an icing plant for refrigerator cars. In its early years it also served ranchers and alfalfa growers.
ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.quote: The town also had livestock yards and an icing plant for refrigerator cars.

ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.q: Do people still live in Gerber today?
ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.a: Yes, about 1,000 people live there today. The railroad work wound down after diesel locomotives replaced steam.
ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.quote: In its early years the town served ranchers and alfalfa growers, and about 1,000 people live there today.

ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.q: When did the passenger trains stop at Gerber?
alts: Did it stop being a train station?
Why don't trains stop there anymore?
ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.a: Passenger trains kept stopping until 1972, when Amtrak's Coast Starlight dropped the station.
ca642-gerber-the-railroad-stop.quote: Passenger trains kept stopping until 1972, when Amtrak's Coast Starlight dropped the station.

ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.q: What does the name Ishi mean?
ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.a: Ishi means man in the Yana language. Anthropologist Alfred Kroeber gave him the name, because Yahi custom kept a person from speaking his own name until another Yahi introduced him.
ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.quote: Ishi means man in the Yana language. Anthropologist Alfred Kroeber gave him the name

ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.a: The Yahi were the southernmost group of the Yana people. Their ancestral homeland was the foothill canyons east of here, along Mill and Deer creeks.
ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.quote: are the ancestral homeland of the Yahi, the southernmost group of the Yana people.

ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.q: What happened to the Yahi after the Gold Rush?
ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.a: Settlers killed nearly all of the Yahi. In 1865, about 40 were killed in the Three Knolls Massacre on Mill Creek, and a few survivors hid in the canyons for decades.
ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.quote: After the Gold Rush, settlers killed nearly all of the Yahi; in 1865, about 40 were killed in the Three Knolls Massacre on Mill Creek.

ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.q: What did Ishi do at the museum in San Francisco?
alts: What happened to him after he came out?
What did he do in the city?
Did he live in a museum?
ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.a: University of California anthropologists took him to their museum, where he worked as a janitor and showed how he made bows and stone arrowheads. He was also recorded singing and telling stories on 148 wax cylinders.
ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.quote: where he worked as a janitor, showed how he made bows and stone arrowheads, and was recorded singing and telling stories on 148 wax cylinders.

alts: Is there a park for Ishi?
ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.a: The 41,339-acre Ishi Wilderness protects canyons believed to be his people's ancestral grounds. The 2024 Park Fire burned nearly all of it.
ca642-ishi-and-the-yahi.quote: The 41,339-acre Ishi Wilderness, about 20 miles east of Red Bluff, protects canyons believed to be his people's ancestral grounds

ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.q: How big is the Red Bluff Diversion Dam?
alts: Is that dam really long, Mom?
ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.a: It's a concrete dam nearly 6,000 feet long, stretching all the way across the Sacramento River.
ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.quote: a concrete structure nearly 6,000 feet long, crosses the Sacramento River

ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.q: When was the Red Bluff Diversion Dam built?
alts: What year was the dam done?
ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.a: It was finished in 1964. It raised the river so water could flow into the Tehama-Colusa and Corning canals.
ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.quote: Finished in 1964, it raised the river to feed the Tehama-Colusa and Corning canals

ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.q: What is the Red Bluff Diversion Dam used for?
alts: Why did they build that dam?
ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.a: It raised the river to feed two canals that water about 150,000 acres of farms.
ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.quote: it raised the river to feed the Tehama-Colusa and Corning canals, which water about 150,000 acres of farms

ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.q: What happened to the salmon at the Red Bluff Diversion Dam?
alts: What happened to the fish there?
Did the dam hurt the fish?
ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.a: Winter-run Chinook counts fell from 118,000 in 1969 to a record low of 191 in 1991. Fish ladders and a fish screen did not solve the problem.
ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.quote: the count of winter-run Chinook salmon fell from 118,000 in 1969 to a record low of 191 in 1991

ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.q: How does water reach the canals now at Red Bluff Diversion Dam?
alts: How do the farms get water now?
Where does the canal water come from?
ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.a: A new pumping plant with a fish screen, just upstream, now lifts water into the canals.
ca647-red-bluff-diversion-dam.quote: A new pumping plant with a fish screen, just upstream, now lifts water into the canals.

ca649-john-brown-s-widow.a: Mary Brown was the widow of the abolitionist John Brown. She arrived in Red Bluff in the fall of 1864 with her children, poor and homeless.
ca649-john-brown-s-widow.quote: In the fall of 1864, Mary Brown, widow of the abolitionist John Brown, arrived in Red Bluff with her children, poor and homeless.

ca649-john-brown-s-widow.q: What happened to John Brown, her husband?
alts: What did her husband do, dad?
ca649-john-brown-s-widow.a: He was executed in 1859 after leading a raid on Harpers Ferry, Virginia. The raid was meant to start a campaign to free enslaved people.
ca649-john-brown-s-widow.quote: John Brown had been executed in 1859 after leading a raid on Harpers Ferry, Virginia, meant to start a campaign to free enslaved people.

ca649-john-brown-s-widow.q: What was her trip west like?
ca649-john-brown-s-widow.a: It was risky. Confederate sympathizers chased the family, who reached a Union army post in Idaho just three hours ahead of them. Soldiers then escorted them 200 miles.
ca649-john-brown-s-widow.quote: the family was chased by Confederate sympathizers and reached a Union army post in Idaho just three hours before them, and soldiers escorted them 200 miles.

ca649-john-brown-s-widow.q: What did she do in Red Bluff, and did she stay?
alts: Did she like it here, mom?
ca649-john-brown-s-widow.a: She worked as a nurse and midwife. But pro-slavery people harassed her, and in 1870 the family sold the house and moved to Humboldt County.
ca649-john-brown-s-widow.quote: In Red Bluff, Mary worked as a nurse and midwife. But she was harassed by pro-slavery people, and in 1870 the family sold the house and moved to Humboldt County.

ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.q: Why is it called Red Bluff?
alts: Why Red Bluff? Is there a red hill?
ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.a: It's named for red bluffs that once stood out along the banks of the Sacramento River. It was first called Leodocia, then Covertsburg, before it became Red Bluff.
ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.quote: Red Bluff is named for red bluffs that once stood out along the banks of the Sacramento River

ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.q: What does head of navigation mean in Red Bluff?
alts: What's head of navigation, like a boat thing?
ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.a: It's the farthest point riverboats could reach on the river. The town grew up there, and miners landed here on their way to the gold fields of Trinity County.
ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.quote: The town grew up at the head of navigation, the farthest point riverboats could reach, and miners landed here bound for the gold fields of Trinity County.

ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.q: What is the Red Bluff Round-Up?
alts: What is it, the rodeo thing?
Is there a real rodeo in Red Bluff?
ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.a: It's a rodeo the town hosts every April, billed as the largest three-day rodeo in the country. In 2024 it drew 675 competitors and about 35,000 fans.
ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.quote: Every April the town hosts the Red Bluff Round-Up, billed as the largest three-day rodeo in the country

ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.q: What happened in Red Bluff's Chinatown in 1886?
alts: What happened to the people there?
Did the Chinese people have to leave?
ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.a: In February 1886, thousands of white people in an Anti-Coolie League marched on Chinatown and ordered the Chinese residents to leave. The Chinese community refused and stayed.
ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.quote: The Chinese community refused, called on white merchants who supported them, and stayed.

ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.q: When did the railroad come to Red Bluff?
alts: When did it get a train?
Did trains come here way back?
Was it the end of the line?
ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.a: The railroad arrived in 1872. For a few years the town was the end of the line.
ca649-red-bluff-head-of-navigation.quote: The railroad arrived in 1872, and for a few years the town was the end of the line.

alts: Who was he and why is this place named after him?
Who's the guy this park is named for?
ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.a: William Ide was the only president of the California Republic. That short-lived republic was born in the Bear Flag Revolt in 1846.
ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.quote: a state historic park honors William Ide, the only president of the California Republic. That republic, born in the Bear Flag Revolt

ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.q: How long did the California Republic last?
alts: Was the California Republic a real country for long?
ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.a: Not long at all. The California Republic lasted from June 14 to July 9, 1846, less than a month.
ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.quote: That republic, born in the Bear Flag Revolt, lasted from June 14 to July 9, 1846, less than a month.
