ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.q: Did William Ide actually live in the Ide Adobe?
alts: Did he really live in it?
Did the president live here, for real?
ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.a: Surprisingly, no. Research later showed that Ide never owned or lived in the adobe that bears his name.
ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.quote: research later showed that Ide never owned or lived in the adobe that bears his name.

ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.q: Who built the Ide Adobe and when?
alts: Who made this old house, kid-style?
ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.a: An early Red Bluff settler named A. M. Dibble built the adobe in 1852. About 20 different owners held the property before 1942.
ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.quote: An early Red Bluff settler named A. M. Dibble built the adobe in 1852. About 20 different owners held the property before 1942

ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.q: What can we see and do at the William B. Ide Adobe?
alts: What is there to see at it?
What's fun to do there for kids?
ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.a: You can see the restored adobe, a recreated 1850s homestead with a blacksmith shop, and a picnic area above the river. On special days you can try Gold Rush card games like faro and monte.
ca650-william-b-ide-adobe.quote: the park has the restored adobe, a recreated 1850s homestead with a blacksmith shop, and a picnic area above the river.

alts: Who's the guy at Alvin Coffey's freedom?
ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.a: Alvin Coffey was born enslaved in Kentucky in 1822. He was taken to California to mine gold, later bought freedom for himself and his family, and settled in Red Bluff.
ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.quote: Red Bluff was home to Alvin Coffey, born enslaved in Kentucky in 1822.

ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.q: How did Alvin Coffey get his freedom?
alts: How did the slave guy get out?
ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.a: He worked mines around Shasta and Sutter until he could pay 1,000 dollars. His new owners had agreed to let him buy his own freedom for that price.
ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.quote: His new owners agreed to let him buy his freedom for 1,000 dollars, and he worked mines around Shasta and Sutter until he could pay.

ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.q: Why was Alvin Coffey brought to California?
alts: Why did he come to California?
Why did the owner bring him out west?
ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.a: In 1849 his enslaver forced him to come to California to mine gold. Later the enslaver took him back east and sold him.
ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.quote: In 1849 his enslaver forced him to California to mine gold, then took him back east and sold him.

ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.q: Did Alvin Coffey get to keep the money he earned?
alts: Did the bad guy take his money?
ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.a: Not at first. His enslaver hired out his labor as a cobbler, laundryman and miner and kept the money. Later he mined enough gold to buy freedom for himself and his family.
ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.quote: his enslaver hired out Coffey's labor as a cobbler, laundryman and miner and kept the money.

ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.q: What did the Coffey family do in Red Bluff?
alts: What did they do after settling there?
What jobs did his family have?
What did they do for work?
ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.a: In Red Bluff the Coffeys farmed, raised turkeys and ran a laundry. In 1887 Alvin joined the Society of California Pioneers, and he is buried at Oak Hill Cemetery.
ca651-alvin-coffey-s-freedom.quote: In Red Bluff the Coffeys farmed, raised turkeys and ran a laundry.

alts: Why is that place named Bend?
How did Bend get its name, Mom?
ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.a: It's named for a loop in the Sacramento River nearby. It was first called Horsethief Bend, then Sander's Bend, and finally just Bend.
ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.quote: It was first called Horsethief Bend, then Sander's Bend, and finally just Bend, after a loop in the Sacramento River nearby.

alts: What was it called in the old days?
Did Bend have a funny old name?
ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.a: It started out as Horsethief Bend, then became Sander's Bend, and eventually just Bend.
ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.quote: It was first called Horsethief Bend, then Sander's Bend, and finally just Bend

ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.q: How many people live in Bend?
alts: How big is it, how many people live there?
Is Bend a big town or a tiny one?
ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.a: Bend is a little river community. About 600 people live there today.
ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.quote: East of the freeway lies the little river community of Bend.

ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.q: What wildlife can you see near Bend?
alts: Are there eagles or fish near Bend?
ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.a: The Sacramento River Bend Area protects habitat for bald eagles, osprey, songbirds, deer and salmon.
ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.quote: protects public land along the river, with habitat for bald eagles, osprey, songbirds, deer and salmon.

ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.q: Is there anything to do near Bend?
alts: Can we stop and do something there?
Can kids go on the river or hike there?
ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.a: Boaters launch at Bend Bridge Park, and the Jellys Ferry day-use site is a trailhead for the Yana Trail. The trail can be impassable in wet weather.
ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.quote: The Jellys Ferry day-use site is a trailhead for the Yana Trail, which fords Inks Creek and can be impassable in wet weather.

ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.q: Did Bend ever have its own post office?
alts: Did it have a post office once?
Did that little town used to get mail?
ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.a: Yes, Bend had its own post office from 1897 to 1935.
ca653-bend-once-horsethief-bend.quote: Bend had its own post office from 1897 to 1935.

alts: Who was he, the guy this rest area is named after?
ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.a: He was a highway engineer who spent 42 years working on California's state highways. As a district engineer, he helped lead the creation of the state's Safety Roadside Rest program.
ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.quote: a highway engineer who spent 42 years working on California's state highways. As a district engineer, he helped lead the creation of the state's Safety Roadside Rest program.

ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.q: Is there anything honoring Herbert S. Miles at the rest area?
alts: Is there anything there about him?
Is there a statue of that guy or something?
ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.a: Yes, a plaque honoring him stands at the rest area on the east side of the freeway.
ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.quote: A plaque honoring him stands at the rest area on the east side of the freeway.

ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.q: How long have California rest areas been around?
alts: How old is that whole rest stop system?
Were there rest stops way back in the day, like in the olden days?
ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.a: California's modern rest stop system dates to 1963, when a state law directed the state to plan, build and maintain safety roadside rests along its highways.
ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.quote: California's modern rest stop system dates to 1963, when a state law directed the state to plan, build and maintain safety roadside rests along its highways.

ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.q: How many rest areas does California have today?
alts: How many rest stops are there in the whole state, do you know?
ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.a: Today California has 87 rest areas. The original 1963 plan called for 257 of them, and later plans cut that number down over the years.
ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.quote: The plan behind that law called for 257 of them.

ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.q: What was along California's roads before modern rest areas?
alts: What did they have before rest stops, like in the old days?
ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.a: In the 1930s, highway crews built roadside fountains and picnic areas. They were wiped out by highway work after World War II.
ca653-herbert-s-miles-rest-area.quote: in the 1930s, highway crews built roadside fountains and picnic areas, but they were wiped out by highway work after World War II.

alts: How big is that mountain, Mom?
ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.a: It towers nearly 9,800 feet above the land around it, and it rises abruptly from the surrounding landscape.
ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.quote: It rises abruptly, towering nearly 9,800 feet above the land around it.

ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.q: How far away can you see Mount Shasta from?
alts: How far can you see it from?
Can we really see that mountain from way far away?
How far can you see it?
ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.a: On a clear winter day, it can be seen from the floor of the Central Valley as far as 140 miles to the south.
ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.quote: On a clear winter day, it can be seen from the floor of the Central Valley as far as 140 miles to the south.

ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.q: How high is Mount Shasta compared to other mountains?
alts: Is it the tallest one in California?
Is that the biggest mountain ever?
ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.a: It's the second-highest peak in the Cascade Range and the fifth-highest in California.
ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.quote: Shasta is the second-highest peak in the Cascade Range and the fifth-highest in California.

ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.q: How long has Mount Shasta been a landmark for travelers?
alts: Did people use it to find their way?
Did old-time travelers see that mountain too?
ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.a: From the 1820s on, it was a landmark for travelers on the Siskiyou Trail.
ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.quote: From the 1820s on, it was a landmark for travelers on the Siskiyou Trail.

alts: Does anybody think that mountain is special?
ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.a: The mountain holds religious significance for the Wintu people.
ca657-mount-shasta-from-afar.quote: The mountain holds religious significance for the Wintu people.

ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.q: What are the Cottonwood truck scales for?
alts: Why do the trucks pull in there?
ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.a: It's the Cottonwood Commercial Vehicle Enforcement Facility, run by the California Highway Patrol. Officers and inspectors check trucks and their drivers against safety standards and state law.
ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.quote: Officers and inspectors check trucks and their drivers against North American safety standards and state law.

ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.q: How old are the Cottonwood truck scales?
alts: How long has it been there?
ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.a: The first station opened in 2000. A second one, for trucks going the other way, opened in 2025.
ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.quote: The first station, on one side of the freeway, opened in 2000, and a second, for trucks going the other way, opened in 2025.

ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.q: Who runs the Cottonwood truck scales?
ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.a: The California Highway Patrol runs it. Officers and inspectors check the trucks and their drivers there.
ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.quote: The truck scales here are the Cottonwood Commercial Vehicle Enforcement Facility, run by the California Highway Patrol.

ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.q: What else do the officers at the Cottonwood truck scales look for?
alts: Do they check for more than weight at that place?
What are they hunting for there, kids ask?
ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.a: Staff there are trained to spot impaired drivers, stolen vehicles and human trafficking.
ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.quote: Staff here are also trained to spot impaired drivers, stolen vehicles and human trafficking.

ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.q: Why are the big rigs going slower than us?
alts: Why can't trucks go as fast as cars?
Why are the trucks so slow, kids say?
ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.a: By law, California limits trucks with three or more axles, and every vehicle towing a trailer, to 55 miles an hour, even where cars may go 70.
ca662-cottonwood-truck-scales.quote: California limits trucks with three or more axles, and every vehicle towing a trailer, to 55 miles an hour, even where cars may go 70

ca662-cottonwood-creek.q: Why is it called Cottonwood Creek?
alts: Why is it named after cotton, kid?
ca662-cottonwood-creek.a: John C. Frémont named it in 1846. He described cottonwoods growing along its sandy, gravelly bed.
ca662-cottonwood-creek.quote: John C. Frémont named it in 1846, describing cottonwoods along its sandy, gravelly bed.

ca662-cottonwood-creek.q: What is Cottonwood Creek famous for?
ca662-cottonwood-creek.a: It is the largest undammed tributary of the Sacramento River. That is why it still has runs of Chinook salmon and steelhead.
ca662-cottonwood-creek.quote: It is the largest undammed tributary of the Sacramento River, which is why it still has runs of Chinook salmon and steelhead.

ca662-cottonwood-creek.q: What county line is Cottonwood Creek on?
alts: What's the creek got to do with the counties?
ca662-cottonwood-creek.a: The creek forms the line between Tehama and Shasta counties along its whole length. When Tehama County was created in 1856, the line was drawn along the creek.
ca662-cottonwood-creek.quote: The freeway crosses Cottonwood Creek here, which forms the line between Tehama and Shasta counties along its whole length.

ca662-cottonwood-creek.q: Does Cottonwood Creek always have lots of water?
alts: Is it a river or what?
ca662-cottonwood-creek.a: No, it changes with the seasons. It often runs like a large river in winter and spring and shrinks to a trickle by summer.
ca662-cottonwood-creek.quote: The creek often runs like a large river in winter and spring and shrinks to a trickle by summer.

ca662-cottonwood-creek.q: Why is Cottonwood Creek still undammed?
alts: Did anyone try to dam it?
ca662-cottonwood-creek.a: Since the 1940s, the government has proposed big dams, including one 247 feet tall. Local opposition and concern for salmon stopped them.
ca662-cottonwood-creek.quote: Since the 1940s, the government has proposed big dams on the creek, including one 247 feet tall, but local opposition and concern for salmon stopped them.

alts: When did people start living here, Mom?
How long's this town been around?
ca664-cottonwood-the-halfway-town.a: Cottonwood was settled in 1849 as a stagecoach town. It got its first post office in 1852.
ca664-cottonwood-the-halfway-town.quote: Cottonwood was a stagecoach town, settled in 1849, and it got its first post office in 1852.

alts: Is there a cotton tree here, Dad?
ca664-cottonwood-the-halfway-town.a: It's named after Cottonwood Creek, which the town sits beside, on both banks of the creek.
ca664-cottonwood-the-halfway-town.quote: on both banks of Cottonwood Creek, which gave it its name.

ca664-cottonwood-the-halfway-town.q: How many people live in Cottonwood?
alts: Is it a big town, Mom?
ca664-cottonwood-the-halfway-town.a: About 6,300 people live there now, nearly twice as many as in 2010.
ca664-cottonwood-the-halfway-town.quote: About 6,300 people live here now, nearly twice as many as in 2010.

ca664-cottonwood-the-halfway-town.q: What was Rancho Buena Ventura near Cottonwood?
alts: What was that old land grant?
Who owned all this land, Mom?
ca664-cottonwood-the-halfway-town.a: It was a 26,632-acre Mexican land grant given in 1844 to pioneer Pierson B. Reading. It was the northernmost land grant in California.
ca664-cottonwood-the-halfway-town.quote: a 26,632-acre Mexican land grant given in 1844 to Pierson B. Reading, a pioneer of 1843. It was the northernmost land grant in California

ca665-coleman-fish-hatchery.q: How big is Coleman fish hatchery?
alts: Is that hatchery a big one, Mom?
ca665-coleman-fish-hatchery.a: It's the largest salmon hatchery in the continental United States. Its goal is to raise about 12 million fall-run Chinook salmon each year.
ca665-coleman-fish-hatchery.quote: Coleman National Fish Hatchery, the largest salmon hatchery in the continental United States.

ca665-coleman-fish-hatchery.q: Why was Coleman fish hatchery built?
alts: Why did they make a fish place, Dad?
ca665-coleman-fish-hatchery.a: It was built in 1942 to make up for spawning grounds lost when Shasta Dam blocked the river.
ca665-coleman-fish-hatchery.quote: It was built in 1942 to make up for spawning grounds lost when Shasta Dam blocked the river.

ca665-coleman-fish-hatchery.q: How does Coleman fish hatchery make baby salmon?
alts: Where do the baby fish come from, Mom?
ca665-coleman-fish-hatchery.a: Salmon swim up Battle Creek and are drawn in by the flow of water. Workers collect and fertilize their eggs, and the young fish grow in ponds until they're big enough to head to sea.
ca665-coleman-fish-hatchery.quote: Workers collect and fertilize their eggs, and the young fish grow in ponds until they are big enough to head to sea.

ca665-coleman-fish-hatchery.q: What kinds of fish are raised at Coleman fish hatchery?
alts: What fish do they raise there?
Is it just salmon at that hatchery?
ca665-coleman-fish-hatchery.a: Besides fall-run Chinook, Coleman raises late-fall Chinook and steelhead. A sister hatchery at the base of Shasta Dam raises winter-run salmon.
ca665-coleman-fish-hatchery.quote: Besides fall-run fish, Coleman raises late-fall Chinook and steelhead, and a sister hatchery at the base of Shasta Dam raises winter-run salmon.

ca668-lassen-peak.q: What happened at Lassen Peak in 1915?
alts: What happened on that mountain back in 1915?
Did the volcano explode, for real?
ca668-lassen-peak.a: On May 22, 1915, it blasted a column of ash more than 30,000 feet into the sky. A hot avalanche of ash, pumice and rock also rushed down the mountain.
ca668-lassen-peak.quote: On May 22, 1915, it blasted a column of ash more than 30,000 feet into the sky.

ca668-lassen-peak.q: How long was Lassen Peak quiet before it erupted?
alts: How long was it asleep before it woke up?
How long was that volcano sleeping?
ca668-lassen-peak.a: It had been quiet for about 27,000 years. Then steam explosions began on May 30, 1914, and about 400 eruptions followed through 1921.
ca668-lassen-peak.quote: Lassen had been quiet for about 27,000 years when steam explosions began on May 30, 1914, and about 400 eruptions followed through 1921.

ca668-lassen-peak.q: What is the Devastated Area at Lassen Peak?
alts: What is that scar on the mountain called?
ca668-lassen-peak.a: It's a 3-square-mile scar left by the 1915 blast, when a hot avalanche of ash, pumice and rock came down the mountain. It's now called the Devastated Area.
ca668-lassen-peak.quote: leaving a 3-square-mile scar now called the Devastated Area

ca668-lassen-peak.q: Does Lassen Peak have another name?
alts: What do the native people call that mountain?
Does it have a different name?
ca668-lassen-peak.a: Yes. The Mountain Maidu call the peak Kom Yamani, which means Snow Mountain.
ca668-lassen-peak.quote: The Mountain Maidu call the peak Kom Yamani, Snow Mountain

ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.q: Why is the town called Anderson?
alts: Who is Anderson named after, Mom?
ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.a: It's named for Elias Anderson, a rancher and hotel keeper. He deeded the Central Pacific Railroad a right of way through his land, and the railroad named its depot after him.
ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.quote: a rancher and hotel keeper named Elias Anderson deeded the Central Pacific Railroad a right of way through his land, and in return the railroad named its depot after him

ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.q: When did Anderson get started as a railroad town?
alts: How long ago did the railroad come, Dad?
ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.a: It goes back to 1872. That's when Elias Anderson gave the Central Pacific Railroad a right of way through his land, and the railroad named its depot after him.
ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.quote: In 1872, a rancher and hotel keeper named Elias Anderson deeded the Central Pacific Railroad a right of way through his land

alts: Who was the guy the town is named after?
ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.a: He was a rancher and hotel keeper. He bought the American Ranch in 1856 and built the American Ranch Hotel in what became downtown, with the post office inside.
ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.quote: Elias Anderson bought the American Ranch in 1856 and built the American Ranch Hotel in what became downtown, with the post office inside.

ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.q: How big is Anderson, and what is it known for today?
alts: Do lots of people live there, Dad?
ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.a: Anderson is a city of about 11,000 people. It's the headquarters of Sierra Pacific Industries, the second-largest lumber producer in the United States.
ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.quote: Today Anderson is a city of about 11,000, and it is the headquarters of Sierra Pacific Industries.

ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.q: How much land does Sierra Pacific own?
ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.a: About 1.7 million acres, which makes it the largest private landowner in California. That's twice the area of Yosemite National Park.
ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.quote: is the largest private landowner in California, with about 1.7 million acres, twice the area of Yosemite National Park.

ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.q: Is there anything to do in Anderson?
alts: Is there a park there, Mom?
ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.a: There's Anderson River Park, which sits on part of Elias Anderson's old land. The town is also the headquarters of Sierra Pacific Industries.
ca668-anderson-a-railroad-town.quote: The city's Anderson River Park sits on part of his old land.

ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.q: Who found gold on Clear Creek?
ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.a: Pierson B. Reading and his Native workers found gold at a spot called Reading's Bar, five miles up the creek, in 1848.
ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.quote: Five miles up the creek, at a spot called Reading's Bar, Pierson B. Reading and his Native workers found gold in 1848.

ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.q: When did Reading find gold on Clear Creek?
alts: When did they find the gold, like how long ago?
ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.a: Reading's strike came in March 1848, shortly after James Marshall's discovery at Sutter's Mill.
ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.quote: Reading's strike came in March 1848, shortly after James Marshall's discovery at Sutter's Mill.

ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.q: Is Reading's gold site a historical landmark?
alts: Is it a real famous place?
ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.a: Yes. Both Clear Creek and Reading's Bar are now state historical landmarks, and the gold discovery site was declared a California Historical Landmark in 1932.
ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.quote: The gold discovery site was declared a California Historical Landmark in 1932.

ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.q: Where does Clear Creek start and end?
alts: Where does the creek go, kids?
ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.a: It begins in the Trinity Mountains, between Shasta Lake and Trinity Lake, flows through Whiskeytown Lake, and joins the Sacramento River.
ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.quote: It begins in the Trinity Mountains, between Shasta Lake and Trinity Lake, and flows through Whiskeytown Lake before reaching the river.

ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.q: What is the Spring Creek Tunnel on Clear Creek?
alts: Is there a tunnel for the water?
ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.a: Below Whiskeytown Dam, it bypasses the lower creek, carrying water from Whiskeytown Lake straight to Keswick Reservoir as part of the Central Valley Project.
ca673-reading-s-gold-on-clear-creek.quote: Below Whiskeytown Dam, the Spring Creek Tunnel bypasses the lower creek, carrying water from Whiskeytown Lake straight to Keswick Reservoir

ca673-redding-rancheria.q: Who are the people of the Redding Rancheria?
alts: Who are they, the people there?
Who lives at that rancheria, anyway?
ca673-redding-rancheria.a: It's a federally recognized tribe made up of Wintu, Pit River and Yana people.
ca673-redding-rancheria.quote: the Redding Rancheria, a federally recognized tribe of Wintu, Pit River and Yana people

ca673-redding-rancheria.q: How did the Redding Rancheria get started?
alts: Why did they get that land, Mom?
ca673-redding-rancheria.a: The Bureau of Indian Affairs bought the 31-acre site in 1922 as a place to camp and live for Native people who had been made landless by settlers.
ca673-redding-rancheria.quote: Its 31-acre site was bought by the Bureau of Indian Affairs in 1922, as a place to camp and live for Native people who had been made landless by settlers.

ca673-redding-rancheria.q: When did the Redding Rancheria become one official tribe?
alts: When did they become a real tribe, Dad?
ca673-redding-rancheria.a: The three groups organized as one tribe and were recognized in 1979. They adopted a constitution in 1989.
ca673-redding-rancheria.quote: The three groups organized as one tribe and were recognized in 1979, and they adopted a constitution in 1989.

ca673-redding-rancheria.q: How is the Redding Rancheria governed?
alts: Who's the boss of the tribe?
ca673-redding-rancheria.a: The tribe is governed by seven councilors elected by its members.
ca673-redding-rancheria.quote: The tribe is governed by seven councilors elected by its members.

ca673-redding-rancheria.q: What did the Redding Rancheria build near the freeway?
ca673-redding-rancheria.a: The tribe built the Win-River Resort and Casino along Highway 273, near the freeway.
ca673-redding-rancheria.quote: It built the Win-River Resort and Casino along Highway 273, near the freeway.

ca673-redding-rancheria.q: What does the casino money do for the Redding Rancheria?
alts: What's the casino money used for?
Where does the casino money go, Mom?
Does the tribe make money from it?
ca673-redding-rancheria.a: The casino's revenue has funded payments to each tribal member.
ca673-redding-rancheria.quote: The casino's revenue has funded payments to each tribal member.

ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.q: What happened at the 1846 river massacre?
alts: Mom, what was the massacre about?
ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.a: On April 5, 1846, an armed expedition led by Captain John C. Frémont attacked a large Wintu camp on the Sacramento River near what is now Redding. Most of the people there were women and children.
ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.quote: On April 5, 1846, an armed expedition led by Captain John C. Frémont attacked a large Wintu camp on the banks of the Sacramento River near what is now Redding.

ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.q: Who was killed in the 1846 river massacre?
alts: Who got hurt in the massacre?
ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.a: The victims were Wintu people, most of them women and children, trapped against the river. Estimates of the dead range from 125 to 900.
ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.quote: The Wintu, most of them women and children, were trapped against the river. Estimates of the dead range from 125 to 900

ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.q: Why did Frémont attack the Wintu camp in 1846?
alts: Why did those soldiers attack the camp?
ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.a: Frémont's party had come up from Peter Lassen's ranch after settlers claimed that Native people were preparing to attack.
ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.quote: Frémont's party had come up the valley from Peter Lassen's ranch after settlers claimed that Native people were preparing to attack.

ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.q: Was anyone punished for the 1846 river massacre?
alts: Did anyone get in trouble for it?
Did the bad guys get caught?
ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.a: No. No one was ever punished. Frémont went on to become one of California's first United States senators and, in 1856, a candidate for president.

ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.q: Could the Wintu men defend the camp in the 1846 river massacre?
alts: Did they fight back at that massacre?
ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.a: They tried. The camp's men formed a line to shield the women and children, but their arrows could not reach the riflemen.
ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.quote: The camp's men formed a line to shield the women and children, but their arrows could not reach the riflemen.

ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.q: Do Wintu people still live near the 1846 river massacre site?
alts: Are there Wintu people around there today?
Do Native people still live here?
ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.a: Yes. Wintu people live in this region today, including as members of the Redding Rancheria.
ca675-the-1846-river-massacre.quote: Wintu people live in this region today, including as members of the Redding Rancheria.

alts: How did the fire start, Buddy?
ca677-the-carr-fire.a: It started when a trailer's tire blew out and its steel rim scraped the pavement. That threw sparks into dry brush near Whiskeytown, west of Redding.
ca677-the-carr-fire.quote: a trailer's tire blew out and its steel rim scraped the pavement, throwing sparks into dry brush

ca677-the-carr-fire.q: How big was the Carr Fire?
ca677-the-carr-fire.a: It burned 229,651 acres and destroyed 1,604 buildings, including more than a thousand homes.
ca677-the-carr-fire.quote: It burned 229,651 acres and destroyed 1,604 buildings, including more than a thousand homes.

ca677-the-carr-fire.q: How many people had to evacuate because of the Carr Fire?
alts: How many people left their homes for it?
Did people have to run away from the fire?
ca677-the-carr-fire.a: About 38,000 people had to evacuate. The fire jumped the Sacramento River into the west side of Redding on July 26, 2018.
ca677-the-carr-fire.quote: the Carr Fire jumped the Sacramento River into the west side of Redding, and 38,000 people had to evacuate

ca677-the-carr-fire.q: Did anyone die in the Carr Fire?
alts: Did people get hurt in that fire?
ca677-the-carr-fire.a: Yes, eight people died. One was Redding fire inspector Jeremy Stoke, who was killed by the fire whirl.
ca677-the-carr-fire.quote: Eight people died, among them Redding fire inspector Jeremy Stoke, who was killed by the fire whirl.

ca677-the-carr-fire.q: What did the Carr Fire whirl do to the land?
alts: What did that fire tornado do?
ca677-the-carr-fire.a: The whirl stayed on the ground for about half an hour, toppling transmission towers and stripping bark from trees.
ca677-the-carr-fire.quote: The whirl stayed on the ground for about half an hour, toppling transmission towers and stripping bark from trees.

alts: Who was Redding, did he live here?
ca678-redding-once-poverty-flats.a: It's named for Benjamin Redding, the Central Pacific Railroad's land agent. He bought land here in 1868 for a northern terminus, and the railroad built a town and named it for him.
ca678-redding-once-poverty-flats.quote: In 1868 the Central Pacific Railroad's land agent, Benjamin Redding, bought land here for a northern terminus, and the railroad built a town and named it for him.

ca678-redding-once-poverty-flats.q: Was Redding ever called a different name?
ca678-redding-once-poverty-flats.a: Yes. In 1874, local legislators renamed it Reading to honor the pioneer Pierson B. Reading, whose land grant it sits on. By 1880 it was officially Redding again.
ca678-redding-once-poverty-flats.quote: In 1874, local legislators renamed the town Reading, to honor the pioneer Pierson B. Reading, whose Mexican land grant it sits on.

alts: Is it really that hot there?
ca678-redding-once-poverty-flats.a: Very hot. The average July high is near 100 degrees, and on July 6, 2024, Redding hit 119, its all-time record.
ca678-redding-once-poverty-flats.quote: Redding is known for very hot summers: the average July high is near 100 degrees, and on July 6, 2024, Redding hit 119, its all-time record.

ca678-redding-once-poverty-flats.q: Has it ever snowed in Redding?
alts: Does it snow there, even though it's hot?
ca678-redding-once-poverty-flats.a: Yes, it can. On December 23, 1968, 16 inches of snow fell in a single day.
ca678-redding-once-poverty-flats.quote: Yet it can snow too. On December 23, 1968, 16 inches fell in a single day.

alts: Who came up with that crazy bridge, Mom?
ca678-sundial-bridge.a: It was designed by Santiago Calatrava. It's a 700-foot footbridge that crosses the Sacramento River.
ca678-sundial-bridge.quote: the Sundial Bridge, a 700-foot footbridge designed by Santiago Calatrava, crosses the Sacramento River

ca678-sundial-bridge.q: How does the Sundial Bridge work as a sundial?
alts: Wait, is the bridge really a clock?
ca678-sundial-bridge.a: Its 217-foot mast points due north and casts a shadow on a giant dial. The shadow tip moves about a foot a minute, so you can watch the Earth turn.
ca678-sundial-bridge.quote: The tip of that shadow moves about a foot a minute, so you can watch the Earth turn.

ca678-sundial-bridge.q: Why doesn't the Sundial Bridge touch the water?
alts: Why does it skip the river?
Why isn't the bridge in the water, Dad?
ca678-sundial-bridge.a: The bridge crosses the river without touching the water. That helps protect the salmon spawning grounds beneath it.
ca678-sundial-bridge.quote: The bridge crosses the river without touching the water, which helps protect the salmon spawning grounds beneath it

ca678-sundial-bridge.q: When did the Sundial Bridge open and what did it cost?
alts: Is that bridge new or old?
ca678-sundial-bridge.a: Calatrava's design opened in 2004, three years late, at a cost of 23.5 million dollars. The McConnell Foundation paid for it.
ca678-sundial-bridge.quote: Calatrava's design opened in 2004, three years late, at a cost of 23.5 million dollars, paid for by the McConnell Foundation.

ca678-sundial-bridge.q: What can we see and do near the Sundial Bridge?
alts: Is there more to do there than the bridge?
Is there stuff for kids there?
ca678-sundial-bridge.a: The bridge links the two halves of Turtle Bay Exploration Park, with a museum, animal exhibits, gardens and playgrounds. It also joins the Sacramento River Trail.
ca678-sundial-bridge.quote: 300 acres along the river with a museum, animal exhibits, gardens and playgrounds.

ca678-sundial-bridge.q: What does the Sundial Bridge look like at night?
alts: Does it glow in the dark?
ca678-sundial-bridge.a: Its glass walkway glows aquamarine at night.
ca678-sundial-bridge.quote: its glass walkway glows aquamarine at night.

alts: Why is nobody living there, Dad?
ca680-old-shasta.a: In the 1850s it was the biggest town in the area, with about 3,500 people. Then in 1873 the railroad bypassed it for Redding, and Shasta faded into a near ghost town.
ca680-old-shasta.quote: Then in 1873 the railroad bypassed it for Redding, and Shasta faded into a near ghost town.

ca680-old-shasta.q: What can we see in Old Shasta?
alts: Are there real old buildings, Mom?
ca680-old-shasta.a: There's a row of Gold Rush brick buildings, now a state historic park. The courthouse is restored to its 1861 look and holds exhibits and historic California art.
ca680-old-shasta.quote: Its row of Gold Rush brick buildings is now a state historic park.

ca680-old-shasta.q: What is special about the Old Shasta courthouse?
alts: Is the courthouse like it used to be?
ca680-old-shasta.a: It has been restored to the way it looked in 1861. Today it holds exhibits and a collection of historic California art.
ca680-old-shasta.quote: Its courthouse has been restored to the way it looked in 1861 and now holds exhibits and a collection of historic California art.

ca680-old-shasta.q: Who got jailed in Old Shasta?
alts: Did anyone famous get jailed there?
Did a bad guy escape from jail there?
ca680-old-shasta.a: Poet Joaquin Miller wrote about being jailed here for horse stealing. He said he escaped with help from his Native American wife.
ca680-old-shasta.quote: Poet Joaquin Miller wrote about being jailed here for horse stealing and escaping with help from his Native American wife.

ca680-old-shasta.q: Did a wildfire hit Old Shasta?
alts: Did a fire wreck that place?
ca680-old-shasta.a: Yes, the 2018 Carr Fire destroyed the old elementary school and damaged the cemetery.
ca680-old-shasta.quote: The 2018 Carr Fire destroyed the old elementary school and damaged the cemetery.

ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.q: Why did they build the 9.5-mile conveyor belt?
alts: Why did they build that belt?
Why was there a giant belt, anyway?
ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.a: Builders needed mountains of sand and gravel to make concrete for Shasta Dam. So they built a huge belt to carry the material from Redding to the dam site.
ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.quote: To make concrete for Shasta Dam, builders needed mountains of sand and gravel.

ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.q: How big was the 9.5-mile conveyor belt?
alts: Was that belt really the biggest one ever?
ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.a: It ran 9.5 miles from Redding to the dam site, and it was then the largest conveyor belt system in the world.
ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.quote: they built what was then the largest conveyor belt system in the world, 9.5 miles long, running from Redding to the dam site.

ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.q: How much could the conveyor belt carry?
alts: How much stuff could it carry?
How many rocks did that belt move?
ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.a: It could carry 1,100 tons of material an hour. Over the whole job, it hauled more than 12 million tons of rock.
ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.quote: It could carry 1,100 tons of material an hour.

ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.q: How did the 9.5-mile conveyor belt work?
alts: How did that belt move without stopping?
ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.a: Twenty-three of its 26 sections had their own 200-horsepower motors. The other three ran downhill and needed no power. Builders rigged those to make electricity for other sections.
ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.quote: Twenty-three sections had their own 200-horsepower motors. The other three ran downhill, so they needed no power at all

ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.q: What happened at the end of the conveyor belt?
alts: Where did the rock go after that?
What did they do with all the gravel?
What was at the end of the line?
ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.a: A mixing plant at the end of the line made concrete. Steel buckets holding 8 cubic yards then rode cables out from a main tower 465 feet tall.
ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.quote: At the end of the line, a mixing plant made concrete, and steel buckets holding 8 cubic yards rode cables out from a main tower 465 feet tall.

ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.q: Is anything from the conveyor belt project still there?
alts: Is any of it still standing?
Can you still see part of it?
Is there a tower under the lake?
ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.a: Yes. The 465-foot main tower was never fully torn down. It still stands underwater behind the dam and shows up when the lake drops low enough.
ca682-the-9-5-mile-conveyor-belt.quote: That tower was never fully torn down. It still stands underwater behind the dam and appears when the lake drops low enough.

ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.q: Why did the Shasta Lake dam towns spring up?
alts: Why did it start up in the first place?
Why are there towns here, Dad?
ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.a: The city of Shasta Lake grew out of five small communities that sprang up in 1938, when work began on Shasta Dam.
ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.quote: The city of Shasta Lake grew out of five small communities that sprang up in 1938, when work began on Shasta Dam

ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.q: What were the five communities that became Shasta Lake?
alts: What were they called before it became one city?
What were the little towns named?
ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.a: They were Central Valley, Project City, Summit City, Pine Grove and Toyon.
ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.quote: Central Valley, Project City, Summit City, Pine Grove and Toyon.

ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.q: When did the Shasta Lake dam towns become one city?
alts: When did it become one city?
When did they all join up?
What year did it become a city?
ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.a: The five communities did not join into one city until 1993.
ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.quote: The communities did not join into one city until 1993.

ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.q: Who lived in Toyon, the old government camp?
alts: Who got to live in that camp?
ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.a: Toyon was first called Government Camp. The Bureau of Reclamation built it, and everyone who lived there worked for the Bureau.
ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.quote: Toyon, first called Government Camp, was built by the Bureau of Reclamation on what had been the Seaman Ranch. Everyone who lived there worked for the Bureau.

ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.q: What happened to Toyon after the Bureau left?
alts: What happened to it after they left?
Why is the camp gone now?
ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.a: It became a Job Corps site until 1972. Then local Native Americans occupied it, hoping to have it recognized as tribal land, but that never happened.
ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.quote: Bureau employees had to leave by the end of 1964, and the camp became a Job Corps site until 1972.

ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.q: Is anything left of Toyon today?
alts: Can we still see the old camp?
Is there anything to see there?
ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.a: Not much. A metal storage building and a flagpole are all that remain, on a fenced-off site along Shasta Dam Boulevard.
ca684-shasta-lake-the-dam-towns.quote: Today a metal storage building and a flagpole are all that remain, on a fenced-off site along Shasta Dam Boulevard.

ca685-shasta-dam.a: Shasta Dam is 602 feet tall. When it was finished in 1945, only Hoover Dam was taller.
ca685-shasta-dam.quote: Shasta Dam stands about four miles west, 602 feet tall. When it was finished in 1945, 26 months earlier than planned, only Hoover Dam was taller.

alts: When did they finish the dam?
ca685-shasta-dam.a: It was finished in 1945, which was 26 months earlier than planned.
ca685-shasta-dam.quote: When it was finished in 1945, 26 months earlier than planned, only Hoover Dam was taller.

ca685-shasta-dam.q: Who built Shasta Dam during World War II?
ca685-shasta-dam.a: With so many men gone to fight, many of the workers were women and high school students.
ca685-shasta-dam.quote: During World War II, with so many men gone to fight, many of the workers were women and high school students.

ca685-shasta-dam.q: What was Shasta Dam called before?
alts: Did the dam have another name?
ca685-shasta-dam.a: It was called Kennett Dam, and it was planned to stand more than 800 feet tall.
ca685-shasta-dam.quote: Before it was built, it was called Kennett Dam, and it was planned to stand more than 800 feet tall.

ca685-shasta-dam.q: Why isn't Shasta Dam taller than 602 feet?
alts: Why did they make it shorter?
Why is the dam not as tall as planned?
ca685-shasta-dam.a: Wartime shortages of supplies and labor cut it down from the planned height of more than 800 feet to 602 feet.
ca685-shasta-dam.quote: Wartime shortages of supplies and labor cut it to 602 feet.

alts: Why is there a whole town under the lake?
ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.a: Kennett was flooded. By 1944 the whole town was underwater, and it now sits under roughly 400 feet of water, depending on the lake level.
ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.quote: By 1944 the whole town was underwater, and it now sits under roughly 400 feet of water, depending on the lake level.

alts: What did people do in that town?
ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.a: Mining. Kennett was once the largest mining town in the area outside Redding and Shasta, and its two biggest mines held unusually pure copper ore.
ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.quote: Kennett, once the largest mining town in the area outside Redding and Shasta. Its two biggest mines held unusually pure copper ore.

alts: Why does it have two t's?
ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.a: It was named for a railroad man known as Squire Kennet. The second t may have come from a mapmaker's mistake.
ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.quote: The town was named for a railroad man known as Squire Kennet, and the second t may have come from a mapmaker's mistake.

ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.q: Who lived at the Kennett site before the town?
alts: Did anyone live there before the miners?
ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.a: The site lies in the homeland of the Wintu people, who called the place Munuktsiraw.
ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.quote: The town site lies in the homeland of the Wintu people, who called the place Munuktsiraw.

ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.q: When did Kennett's mining boom happen?
alts: When did that town get rich?
ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.a: Kennett boomed during World War I, when metal prices were high. Its biggest mine, the Mammoth, closed for good in 1923.
ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.quote: Kennett boomed during World War I, when metal prices were high. Its biggest mine, the Mammoth, closed for good in 1923

ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.q: What Kennett event happened for Shasta Dam?
alts: What happened here for the dam?
Was it part of building the dam?
ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.a: The groundbreaking ceremony for Shasta Dam was held in Kennett in 1937.
ca687-kennett-the-drowned-town.quote: The groundbreaking ceremony for Shasta Dam was held in Kennett in 1937.

alts: What is that, the old road under the lake?
Is there really a road under the water?
ca688-the-drowned-highway.a: It's old Highway 99, which ran through Mountain Gate and then plunged into the valley that Shasta Lake now fills.
ca688-the-drowned-highway.quote: Before the lake, old Highway 99 ran through Mountain Gate and then plunged into the valley that Shasta Lake now fills.

ca688-the-drowned-highway.q: Can you ever see the drowned highway?
alts: Can we see it when the water goes down?
Does the old road ever come back out of the lake?
ca688-the-drowned-highway.a: Yes, in drought years. When the water falls, old bridges, road cuts and guardrails come back into view.
ca688-the-drowned-highway.quote: In drought years, when the water falls, old bridges, road cuts and guardrails come back into view.

ca688-the-drowned-highway.q: What happened to the highway and railroad when the dam went in?
alts: Where did the road and train go after the dam?
Did the trains have to move too?
ca688-the-drowned-highway.a: Both the highway and the Southern Pacific railroad had to move east onto a brand-new, much higher bridge over the Pit River.
ca688-the-drowned-highway.quote: both the highway and the Southern Pacific railroad had to move east onto a brand-new, much higher bridge over the Pit River.

ca688-the-drowned-highway.q: When did the lake start filling over the old highway?
alts: When did it fill up with water?
When did they start filling the lake?
What year did the water come?
ca688-the-drowned-highway.a: The lake began filling in February 1944, when the diversion tunnel was sealed.
ca688-the-drowned-highway.quote: The lake began filling in February 1944, when that diversion tunnel was sealed.

ca688-the-drowned-highway.q: What exit is the drowned highway?
alts: Which exit do we take for it?

ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.q: What was the Bass Hill stage road?
alts: What was that old road about?
Was this a road for horses and wagons?
ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.a: It was part of the California and Oregon stage road. The route crossed the top of Bass Hill and then dropped down to the Pit River.
ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.quote: The California and Oregon stage road crossed the top of Bass Hill here and dropped down to the Pit River

ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.q: What does the Bass Hill marker honor?
alts: Who is the sign about, kids want to know?
ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.a: The marker honors the stage drivers. It is titled Pioneers Who Held the Ribbons.
ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.quote: The marker honors the stage drivers under the title Pioneers Who Held the Ribbons.

ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.q: How far did the California and Oregon stage line run?
alts: How far did the stagecoach go?
How far did the old stagecoaches travel, kids ask?
ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.a: By 1860 the line ran all the way from Sacramento to Portland. It carried mail and passengers every day.
ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.quote: The California and Oregon stage line ran all the way from Sacramento to Portland by 1860, carrying mail and passengers every day.

ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.q: What happened to the stagecoaches in winter?
alts: How did they cross the mountains in snow?
Did the stage use sleds, kids ask?
ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.a: In winter the line switched to sleighs to get over the Scott Mountains.
ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.quote: In winter it switched to sleighs to get over the Scott Mountains.

ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.q: When did the Bass Hill marker go up?
alts: How long ago was the sign put there, kids ask?
ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.a: The marker went up in 1920, and the site is California Historical Landmark No. 148. The stages ran until the railroad replaced them in 1887.
ca690-bass-hill-stage-road.quote: The marker went up in 1920, and the site is California Historical Landmark No. 148.

ca689-shasta-lake.a: Shasta Lake is California's largest reservoir, with 365 miles of steep, wooded shoreline. At its deepest, it's 517 feet.
ca689-shasta-lake.quote: Shasta Lake is California's largest reservoir, with 365 miles of steep, wooded shoreline.

ca689-shasta-lake.a: At its deepest, Shasta Lake is 517 feet deep.

ca689-shasta-lake.q: What rivers flow into Shasta Lake?
alts: Where does the lake's water come from?
ca689-shasta-lake.a: Shasta Lake has four big arms, made by the Sacramento River, the McCloud River, the Pit River and Sulanharas Creek.
ca689-shasta-lake.quote: It has four big arms, made by the Sacramento River, the McCloud River, the Pit River and Sulanharas Creek.

ca689-shasta-lake.q: Which is the biggest river flowing into Shasta Lake?
alts: Which river is biggest for it?
Is the Sacramento the biggest river there?
ca689-shasta-lake.a: It's the Pit River, not the Sacramento. Before the dam, the Pit carried about four times as much water as the Sacramento where the two met.
ca689-shasta-lake.quote: The biggest river flowing into the lake is not the Sacramento but the Pit.

ca689-shasta-lake.q: Why is it called the Pit River?
alts: Why is that river called the Pit?
Why does the river have such a weird name?
ca689-shasta-lake.a: It's named for the pits its people dug, both for winter homes and as traps for game that came to drink.
ca689-shasta-lake.quote: The river is named for the pits its people dug, both for winter homes and as traps for game that came to drink.

ca689-shasta-lake.q: Can we rent a houseboat on Shasta Lake?
alts: Can we stay on a boat on the lake?
ca689-shasta-lake.a: Yes. Bridge Bay, the lake's largest marina, has more than 700 slips and about 100 houseboats for rent.
ca689-shasta-lake.quote: Bridge Bay is the lake's largest marina, with more than 700 slips and about 100 houseboats for rent.

ca691-pit-river-bridge.q: How old is the Pit River Bridge?
alts: When did they build this bridge, mom?
ca691-pit-river-bridge.a: The Pit River Bridge was built in 1942.
ca691-pit-river-bridge.quote: Built in 1942, it stands about 500 feet above the old bed of the Pit River

ca691-pit-river-bridge.q: What makes the Pit River Bridge special?
alts: Why is this bridge a big deal, dad?
ca691-pit-river-bridge.a: It's a double-decker, and it's the highest double-deck bridge in the United States. I-5 rides the top deck while the railroad runs underneath.
ca691-pit-river-bridge.quote: making it the highest double-deck bridge in the United States

ca691-pit-river-bridge.q: How high is the Pit River Bridge?
alts: Are we really high up on this bridge?
ca691-pit-river-bridge.a: It stands about 500 feet above the old bed of the Pit River. When the lake is full, the water comes within about 40 feet of the bridge.
ca691-pit-river-bridge.quote: it stands about 500 feet above the old bed of the Pit River

ca691-pit-river-bridge.q: Is there a train under the Pit River Bridge?
alts: Is there really a train down there?
Can a train go under us, dad?
ca691-pit-river-bridge.a: Yes, it's a double-decker. I-5 rides the top deck and the railroad runs underneath.
ca691-pit-river-bridge.quote: I-5 rides the top deck and the railroad runs underneath.

ca691-pit-river-bridge.q: What happened on the Pit River Bridge in 1953?
alts: What happened here in the old days?
Did something crazy happen on this bridge?
ca691-pit-river-bridge.a: On May 3, 1953, a produce truck's steering failed and the cab crashed through the railing, dangling over the water with two men inside. Walter Schau and other drivers rescued both men.
ca691-pit-river-bridge.quote: On May 3, 1953, back when this was a two-lane highway, a produce truck's steering failed on the bridge.

ca691-pit-river-bridge.q: What famous photo was taken at the Pit River Bridge?
alts: Did someone win a prize for a photo here?
ca691-pit-river-bridge.a: Virginia Schau took a photo of the rescue with her Kodak Brownie. It won the 1954 Pulitzer Prize for Photography, the first ever won by a woman.
ca691-pit-river-bridge.quote: Her photo won the 1954 Pulitzer Prize for Photography, the first ever won by a woman.

ca693-the-giant-median.q: What is the giant median on I-5?
alts: Why is the road split in two like that?
What's that big gap in the middle?
ca693-the-giant-median.a: Just north of the Pit River Bridge, the two directions of I-5 split apart, leaving a huge median between them.
ca693-the-giant-median.quote: Just north of the Pit River Bridge, the two directions of I-5 split apart, leaving what is said to be the second-largest median in California.

ca693-the-giant-median.q: Is the giant median the biggest median in California?
alts: Is it the biggest one in the state?
Is there a bigger median than this one?
Is this the biggest gap ever?
ca693-the-giant-median.a: Not quite. It's said to be the second-largest in California. Only Interstate 8's In-Ko-Pah grade has a bigger one.
ca693-the-giant-median.quote: Only Interstate 8's In-Ko-Pah grade has a bigger one.

ca693-the-giant-median.q: Where does the giant median start?
alts: Where does the road split apart?
ca693-the-giant-median.a: It starts just north of the Pit River Bridge, where the two directions of I-5 split apart.
ca693-the-giant-median.quote: Just north of the Pit River Bridge, the two directions of I-5 split apart

ca693-the-giant-median.q: What exit is the giant median near?
alts: Which exit do we look for?
What's the exit number for that?
ca693-the-giant-median.a: The giant median is listed at exit 693.

ca693-the-giant-median.q: Does this part of I-5 have a nickname?
alts: Does the highway here have a nickname?
Does this road have a special name?
ca693-the-giant-median.a: Yes. From Red Bluff all the way to the Oregon line, the road carries the nickname Cascade Wonderland Highway.
ca693-the-giant-median.quote: From Red Bluff all the way to the Oregon line, this road carries a nickname: the Cascade Wonderland Highway.

ca693-the-giant-median.q: Does it snow on I-5 north of Redding?
alts: Will there be snow up ahead?
Do we need chains up here?
Do trucks need chains in winter?
ca693-the-giant-median.a: North of Redding it regularly gets snow at higher elevations from fall to spring. In winter, trucks must carry chains whether or not chain controls are in force.
ca693-the-giant-median.quote: North of Redding it regularly gets snow at higher elevations from fall to spring.

alts: Are those little lizards or something?
ca694-shasta-salamanders.a: They're salamanders found nowhere else on Earth, hiding in the limestone hills around this lake. Scientists once thought there was just one kind.
ca694-shasta-salamanders.quote: The limestone hills around this lake hide salamanders found nowhere else on Earth. Scientists once thought there was just one kind.

ca694-shasta-salamanders.q: How many kinds of Shasta salamanders are there?
ca694-shasta-salamanders.a: Three. Scientists once thought there was only one kind, but in 2018 they found three, including the Wintu Shasta salamander.
ca694-shasta-salamanders.quote: Scientists once thought there was just one kind. In 2018 they found three, including the Wintu Shasta salamander

ca694-shasta-salamanders.q: How can you tell the Shasta salamanders apart?
alts: How can you tell them apart?
Do they look different from each other?
ca694-shasta-salamanders.a: You mostly can't just by looking. The three species look so alike that only their ranges and their genes tell them apart.
ca694-shasta-salamanders.quote: The three species look so alike that only their ranges and their genes tell them apart.

ca694-shasta-salamanders.q: Where do the Shasta salamanders live?
ca694-shasta-salamanders.a: They favor damp limestone cracks and caves, where females lay their eggs. The Samwel kind lives on the north-central and northwest sides of the lake.
ca694-shasta-salamanders.quote: They favor damp limestone cracks and caves, where females lay their eggs.

ca694-shasta-salamanders.q: Why are the Shasta salamanders in trouble?
ca694-shasta-salamanders.a: Building the dam and filling the lake probably broke their small range into pieces. Raising the lake higher would flood more of their homes, and limestone quarrying is another threat.
ca694-shasta-salamanders.quote: Building the dam and filling the lake probably broke their small range into pieces.

ca694-shasta-salamanders.a: Not under the Endangered Species Act. In 2021, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service found that they did not warrant that protection.
ca694-shasta-salamanders.quote: In 2021, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service found that they did not warrant Endangered Species Act protection.

ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.q: How do you get to Lake Shasta Caverns?
alts: How do we get up to it?
Do we have to hike to the caves, Mom?
ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.a: You take a catamaran ride across the lake's McCloud arm, then a bus up a steep mountain road. The caves sit about 900 feet above the lake.
ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.quote: Getting to these limestone caves takes a catamaran ride across the lake's McCloud arm and then a bus ride up a steep mountain road.

ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.q: Why were the caves once called Baird Cave?
ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.a: They were named for U.S. Fisheries Commissioner Spencer Fullerton Baird. Richardson worked for the federal fish hatchery on the McCloud River.
ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.quote: the caves were once called Baird Cave, after U.S. Fisheries Commissioner Spencer Fullerton Baird.

ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.q: What is the Discovery Room at Lake Shasta Caverns?
alts: Was there a secret room, Dad?
ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.a: Workers blasted a tunnel into the mountain and broke into a room nobody knew about. It contains every type of limestone formation found there.
ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.quote: workers blasted a tunnel into the mountain and broke into a room nobody knew about, now called the Discovery Room.

ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.q: How did people get into Lake Shasta Caverns before 1964?
alts: How did they get in back then?
Could anyone go in it before?
ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.a: Only a few hardy cavers squeezed in, through a hole in the ceiling barely big enough for one person. Then workers blasted a tunnel to open the caves to visitors.
ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.quote: Until 1964, only a few hardy cavers squeezed in, through a hole in the ceiling barely big enough for one person.

ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.q: What exit is Lake Shasta Caverns and where does the name come from?
alts: What exit is it, and why that name?
Which exit do we take, Dad?
ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.a: It's exit 695, at O'Brien, named for Con O'Brien, who ran a resort here.
ca695-lake-shasta-caverns.quote: The exit is at O'Brien, named for Con O'Brien, who ran a resort here.

ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.a: Winnemem Wintu means middle water people or middle river people.
ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.quote: whose name means middle water people or middle river people

ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.q: What happened to the Winnemem Wintu villages when the lake filled?
alts: What happened to their villages when it filled up?
Did the water cover their homes?
ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.a: Scores of their village sites, burial grounds and sacred places went underwater when the lake filled.
ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.quote: When the lake filled, scores of their village sites, burial grounds and sacred places went underwater.

ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.q: Are the Winnemem Wintu still here today?
ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.a: Yes. The Winnemem are still here. They have long sought federal recognition, and they oppose plans to raise the dam.
ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.quote: The Winnemem are still here. They have long sought federal recognition, and they oppose plans to raise the dam.

ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.q: What happened to the Winnemem Wintu at Kabyai Creek in 1854?
alts: What happened to them at that creek in 1854?
What did the settlers do to them?
ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.a: In 1854, settlers killed 42 Winnemem men, women and children at Kabyai Creek on the McCloud River.
ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.quote: In 1854, settlers killed 42 Winnemem men, women and children at Kabyai Creek on the McCloud River.

ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.q: What was the Winnemem Wintu war dance in 2004?
alts: Why did they hold a war dance in 2004?
What was that war dance about?
ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.a: In 2004 the Winnemem held a war dance against raising the dam, which they said was the first since 1887.
ca696-winnemem-wintu-homeland.quote: In 2004 the Winnemem held a war dance against raising the dam, which they said was the first since 1887.

alts: How'd the fire start, did somebody do it?
ca698-the-salt-fire.a: Forest officials believe it was likely sparked by hot material that fell from a vehicle on the interstate. It started beside I-5 near the Salt Creek exit.
ca698-the-salt-fire.quote: Forest officials believe it was likely sparked by hot material that fell from a vehicle on the interstate.

ca698-the-salt-fire.q: When did the Salt Fire happen?
alts: What year was it, how long ago?
ca698-the-salt-fire.a: It started on June 30, 2021, beside I-5 near the Salt Creek exit, and it shut down the freeway.
ca698-the-salt-fire.quote: On June 30, 2021, a fire started beside I-5 near the Salt Creek exit and shut down the freeway.

ca698-the-salt-fire.q: How much damage did the Salt Fire do?
alts: How many houses did it burn?
ca698-the-salt-fire.a: It destroyed 27 homes and 14 other buildings around Lakehead. By evening it covered about 1,000 acres.
ca698-the-salt-fire.quote: It destroyed 27 homes and 14 other buildings around Lakehead.

ca698-the-salt-fire.q: Did the Salt Fire close the freeway?
alts: Was I-5 shut down because of it?
Could cars not drive on the highway?
How long was the road closed?
ca698-the-salt-fire.a: Yes, it shut down I-5. The freeway reopened the next morning, and firefighters built their lines near the interstate to keep it open.
ca698-the-salt-fire.quote: The freeway reopened the next morning, and firefighters built their lines near the interstate to keep it open.

ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.q: When did the first federal fish hatchery open?
alts: How old is that hatchery, like, really old?
ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.a: It opened in 1872 on the McCloud River, and it was the nation's first federal fish hatchery.
ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.quote: In 1872, the nation's first federal fish hatchery opened on the McCloud River, which now flows into this lake.

ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.q: Who built the first federal fish hatchery?
alts: Who made the fish place, mom?
ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.a: Livingston Stone built it, at a spot where he found Wintu people catching Chinook salmon.
ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.quote: Livingston Stone built it at a spot where he found Wintu people catching Chinook salmon.

ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.q: What happened to the salmon eggs from the first federal fish hatchery?
alts: Where did the eggs from it go?
Did the fish eggs go far away?
ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.a: Its eggs were shipped across the country and as far as Japan and New Zealand.
ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.quote: Its eggs were shipped across the country and as far as Japan and New Zealand.

ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.q: How did the Wintu people react when the hatchery crew arrived?
alts: How did the Wintu feel about it?
Were the Native people mad at them?
ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.a: Wintu people gathered with bows and arrows on the far bank and spent a whole day trying to drive the crew off. Stone later hired Wintu workers until 1883.
ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.quote: Wintu people gathered with bows and arrows on the far bank and spent a whole day trying to drive them off.

ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.q: What fish came from the second station Stone started upriver?
alts: What did he raise at the other station?
Do we still have those fish today?
ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.a: It raised rainbow trout, and its eggs went all over the country. Many rainbow trout in the world's waters today descend from McCloud River fish.
ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.quote: Many rainbow trout in the world's waters today descend from McCloud River fish.

ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.q: What happened to the McCloud River salmon run?
alts: Did the salmon go away from there?
Why are there fewer fish, dad?
ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.a: The salmon run declined after a railroad was built nearby in the 1880s.
ca700-the-first-federal-fish-hatchery.quote: The McCloud's salmon run declined after a railroad was built nearby in the 1880s.

ca702-lakehead-top-of-the-lake.q: How many people live in Lakehead?
alts: Is it a big town, or just a few people?
ca702-lakehead-top-of-the-lake.a: About 470 people lived in Lakehead in 2020. In summer, more than 1,500 seasonal residents can join them.
ca702-lakehead-top-of-the-lake.quote: About 470 people lived here in 2020, and in summer more than 1,500 seasonal residents can join them.

alts: Which exit do we take for that?

ca707-delta-end-of-the-line.q: Why was Delta called the end of the line?
alts: Why was it the end of the line?
Why did the train stop at Delta, Mom?
What does end of the line mean?
ca707-delta-end-of-the-line.a: When the railroad pushed up this canyon in the 1880s, Delta was where the tracks stopped, and it stayed the end of the line for about two years.
ca707-delta-end-of-the-line.quote: When the railroad pushed up this canyon in the 1880s, the town of Delta was the end of the line for about two years.

ca707-delta-end-of-the-line.q: What happened to the town of Delta?
ca707-delta-end-of-the-line.a: In 1887 the tracks moved on up the canyon and Delta slowly emptied out. Its post office closed in 1954.
ca707-delta-end-of-the-line.quote: In 1887 the tracks moved on up the canyon, and Delta slowly emptied out; its post office closed in 1954.

ca707-delta-end-of-the-line.q: What was Dog Creek, and why do people mention it with Delta?
alts: Why did people call it Dog Creek?
Dog Creek? Like a dog, Mom?
ca707-delta-end-of-the-line.a: Dog Creek was a mining town founded in 1855 a few miles west. Many people kept calling the place Dog Creek even after it became Delta.
ca707-delta-end-of-the-line.quote: Many people kept calling the place Dog Creek, after a mining town founded in 1855 a few miles west.

ca707-delta-end-of-the-line.q: Is anything from old Delta still standing?
alts: Is any of it still there?
Can we see an old building, Mom?
ca707-delta-end-of-the-line.a: A few buildings remain. The old one-room Delta school, since enlarged, is one of the few still standing.
ca707-delta-end-of-the-line.quote: The old one-room Delta school, since enlarged, is one of the few buildings still standing.

ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.q: Where does the upper Sacramento River begin?
alts: Where does the river come from, mom?
ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.a: It begins near Mount Shasta, where its North, Middle and South forks meet. From there it passes through Lake Siskiyou and runs down this canyon.
ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.quote: It begins near Mount Shasta, where its North, Middle and South forks meet, passes through Lake Siskiyou

ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.q: How long is this stretch of the upper Sacramento River?
alts: How far does it run through this canyon?
Is the river really long, Dad?
ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.a: It runs about 60 miles through this canyon, past Dunsmuir and Castella, before reaching Shasta Lake near Lakehead.
ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.quote: then runs about 60 miles through this canyon, past Dunsmuir and Castella, to Shasta Lake near Lakehead.

ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.q: Why is the upper Sacramento River famous for fishing?
alts: What makes it so good for fishing?
Are there fish in the river, Dad?
ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.a: It's a blue ribbon trout stream where wild rainbow trout abound. Anglers come from all over the world to fish it.
ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.quote: Up here it is a blue ribbon trout stream, where wild rainbow trout abound.

ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.q: Where does the water from the upper Sacramento River go?
alts: What happens to the water from it?
Where does the river end up, Dad?
ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.a: It flows into Shasta Lake, supplying about 15 percent of that lake's inflow. That water later becomes part of the Central Valley Project and is sent on through the valley.
ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.quote: This stretch supplies about 15 percent of the water flowing into Shasta Lake, water that later becomes part of the Central Valley Project

ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.q: Are there salmon in the upper Sacramento River?
alts: Did salmon ever live in it?
Why don't the salmon come up here, mom?
ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.a: Salmon once spawned up here, but dams built in the 20th century cut them off from the whole upper river.
ca711-the-upper-sacramento-river.quote: Salmon once spawned up here too, until dams built in the 20th century cut them off from the whole upper river.

alts: What was Portuguese Flat, like, back then?
ca712-portuguese-flat.a: Portuguese Flat was a Gold Rush camp of the early 1850s, made up largely of Portuguese miners. It had rich diggings and a reputation as one of the roughest camps in northern Shasta County.
ca712-portuguese-flat.quote: Portuguese Flat, a Gold Rush camp of the early 1850s made up largely of Portuguese miners. It had rich diggings and a reputation as one of the roughest camps in northern Shasta County.

ca712-portuguese-flat.q: Who ran the inn at Portuguese Flat?
alts: Who ran the old hotel at Portuguese Flat?
ca712-portuguese-flat.a: Ross and Mary Campbell McCloud ran an inn at Portuguese Flat from about 1853 to 1855. After that they moved on to Upper Soda Springs.
ca712-portuguese-flat.quote: Ross and Mary Campbell McCloud ran an inn at Portuguese Flat from about 1853 to 1855, before moving on to Upper Soda Springs.

ca712-portuguese-flat.q: What famous poet was connected to Portuguese Flat?
alts: Did anyone famous stay at that inn?
Did a famous person ever come to Portuguese Flat?
ca712-portuguese-flat.a: Joaquin Miller, who later became a well-known poet. In 1855, as a young man, he was brought to the McClouds' inn at Portuguese Flat after being hurt in the Battle of Castle Crags.
ca712-portuguese-flat.quote: In 1855, a young Joaquin Miller was brought to their inn after, by his own account, an arrow pierced his jaw and neck in the Battle of Castle Crags.

ca712-portuguese-flat.q: How did Joaquin Miller get better at Portuguese Flat?
alts: Who took care of him after he got hurt?
How did the kid with the arrow get saved?
ca712-portuguese-flat.a: Mary McCloud nursed him back to health at the inn. By his own account, an arrow had pierced his jaw and neck. Miller went on to become a well-known poet.
ca712-portuguese-flat.quote: Mary McCloud nursed him back to health, and Miller went on to become a well-known poet.

ca715-river-rails-and-road.q: What is the River, rails and road canyon?
alts: What is it about this canyon?
Why are there so many things squeezed in here?
ca715-river-rails-and-road.a: It's one canyon where the river, the railroad and the freeway all squeeze through together. The railroad follows the old Siskiyou Trail.
ca715-river-rails-and-road.quote: The river, the railroad and the freeway all squeeze through this one canyon. The railroad follows the old Siskiyou Trail.

ca715-river-rails-and-road.q: Do trains still run along the river here?
alts: Do real trains still come through, Dad?
ca715-river-rails-and-road.a: Yes. Amtrak's Coast Starlight still runs these tracks every day, traveling between Los Angeles and Seattle.
ca715-river-rails-and-road.quote: Amtrak's Coast Starlight still runs these tracks every day on its trips between Los Angeles and Seattle.

ca715-river-rails-and-road.q: What was the Shasta Daylight train?
alts: Was there a fancy old train here?
Tell me about the old train
ca715-river-rails-and-road.a: It was a Southern Pacific streamliner that ran this route from 1949, between Oakland and Portland, in about 15 and a half hours.
ca715-river-rails-and-road.quote: From 1949, the Southern Pacific's Shasta Daylight streamliner ran this route between Oakland and Portland in about 15 and a half hours.

ca715-river-rails-and-road.q: Where does the Coast Starlight stop near here?
alts: Does the train stop near here?
Is there a train station close by?
ca715-river-rails-and-road.a: Dunsmuir is a Coast Starlight stop. It's the train's only stop in Siskiyou County and the northernmost passenger station in California.
ca715-river-rails-and-road.quote: Dunsmuir became a stop on the Coast Starlight. It is the train's only stop in Siskiyou County and the northernmost passenger station in California.

alts: Who was that guy who ran it?
ca718-southern-s-stage-station.a: Simeon Southern, nicknamed Sims, opened a log stage station and hotel here in 1859. He was born on a Kentucky farm in 1822 and reached Shasta County in 1854.
ca718-southern-s-stage-station.quote: Sims Southern was born on a Kentucky farm in 1822 and reached Shasta County in 1854.

ca718-southern-s-stage-station.q: How old is Southern's stage station?
alts: How long ago did people start coming here, dad?
ca718-southern-s-stage-station.a: Sims Southern opened it as a log stage station and hotel in 1859. Travelers stopped there to rest and eat for 50 years.
ca718-southern-s-stage-station.quote: opened a log stage station and hotel here in 1859, where travelers stopped to rest and eat for 50 years

ca718-southern-s-stage-station.q: What happened at Southern's stage station?
alts: Did anything cool happen here, dad?
ca718-southern-s-stage-station.a: Travelers rested and ate there for 50 years. In September 1880, President Rutherford B. Hayes stayed there with Generals Sherman and Sheridan.
ca718-southern-s-stage-station.quote: In September 1880, President Rutherford B. Hayes stayed here with Generals Sherman and Sheridan.

ca718-southern-s-stage-station.q: Why is this exit called Sims?
ca718-southern-s-stage-station.a: The exit's name goes back to Sims Southern, whose station was the center of town. The settlement of Hazel Creek took the name Sims in 1871.
ca718-southern-s-stage-station.quote: The settlement of Hazel Creek took the name Sims in 1871, since his station was the center of town.

ca718-southern-s-stage-station.q: What happened to Southern's stage station?
ca718-southern-s-stage-station.a: Sarah Southern sold the station to a timber company in 1902, and a sawmill followed. The site is California Historical Landmark No. 33.
ca718-southern-s-stage-station.quote: Sarah sold the station to a timber company in 1902, and a sawmill followed.

ca718-southern-s-stage-station.q: Did Black Bart have anything to do with this place?
alts: Was that connected to Black Bart?
ca718-southern-s-stage-station.a: Not here directly. In September 1880, Black Bart robbed a stage in Oregon, and three days later Hayes and Sherman rode that same stage.
ca718-southern-s-stage-station.quote: the gentleman bandit Black Bart robbed the Yreka to Roseburg stage in Oregon, and three days later Hayes and Sherman rode that very stage.

alts: What was it before it was a freeway?
What's this old trail we're on, Mom?
ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.a: It started as a web of Native American footpaths between California and the Northwest. Fur trappers later followed them south, and the route became known as the Siskiyou Trail. I-5 follows the same path today.
ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.quote: Long before this was a freeway, it was a web of Native American footpaths between California and the Northwest.

ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.q: Who first used the Siskiyou Trail?
alts: Who made that trail in the first place?
Who walked here before cars, Dad?
ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.a: Native Americans did. The route began as a web of footpaths between California and the Northwest, and Hudson's Bay Company fur trappers followed those paths south from the Columbia River in the 1820s.
ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.quote: In the 1820s, Hudson's Bay Company fur trappers followed them south from the Columbia River, and the route became known as the Siskiyou Trail.

ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.q: What was the Siskiyou Trail called at first?
alts: Did it always have that name?
Did the trail have another name, Dad?
ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.a: At first it was called the California Brigade Trail. That was after trapper Alexander McLeod reached the Sacramento River in 1828.
ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.quote: Trapper Alexander McLeod reached the Sacramento River in 1828, and at first the route was called the California Brigade Trail.

ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.q: What happened on the Siskiyou Trail in 1837?
alts: What did Ewing Young do on it?
Did cowboys really drive cows up this trail?
ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.a: Ewing Young bought hundreds of cattle in Mexican California and drove them up the trail to Oregon, a trip of nearly three months.
ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.quote: In 1837, Ewing Young bought hundreds of cattle in Mexican California and drove them up this trail to Oregon, a trip of nearly three months.

ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.q: How far could travelers go in a day on the Siskiyou Trail?
alts: How far did people get on it each day?
Did it take them forever to get anywhere?
ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.a: Early travelers on mules and horses managed perhaps 20 miles a day.
ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.quote: Early travelers on mules and horses managed perhaps 20 miles a day.

ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.q: When did stagecoach roads and telegraph lines reach the Siskiyou Trail?
alts: When did it get real roads?
When did they get the telegraph, Dad?
ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.a: Toll roads for stagecoaches were not carved through these mountains until the 1860s, and the first telegraph line arrived in 1864.
ca720-the-siskiyou-trail.quote: Toll roads for stagecoaches were not carved through these mountains until the 1860s, and the first telegraph line arrived in 1864.

ca723-homeland-and-the-1855-battle.q: Whose homeland is the Castle Crags area?
alts: Who lived around it before the miners came?
Who are the original people here?
